en: Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and Nara, the best of men,
and also to the goddess Sarasvatī, one should then utter the word "Victory.
This immeasurable [work] has issued from the lips of Dvaipāyana.
For one who listens to the *Bhārata* as it is being recited— which is meritorious, purifying, a destroyer of sin, and auspicious—
what need is there for ablutions with the waters of Puṣkara?
That alone is the auspicious moment; that alone is the fortunate day; that alone is the strength of the stars; that alone is the strength of the moon;
and all the planets are likewise well-disposed.
When one remembers the pair of feet of the Lord of Lakṣmī,
there arises delight in all scriptures and affection for all living beings;
by that, O Bhārata, one is said to be a savior in all the worlds.
If these three— the sun, the moon, and fire— did not exist, O Bhārata,
what would be the condition of this world, which is blinded by the darkness of ignorance?

I bow to Vyāsa, the grandson of Vasiṣṭha, the great-grandson of Śakti, the sinless son of Parāśara, the father of Śuka, and a treasure-house of asceticism; to Vyāsa who is a form of Viṣṇu, and to Viṣṇu who is in the form of Vyāsa.
Salutations indeed to the treasure of Brahman, the descendant of Vasiṣṭha; salutations, salutations!
Janamejaya said:
"How did my ancestors [behave] in the city of Virāṭa?"
Having lived their period of concealment, tormented by the fear of Duryodhana—
[thus spoke] Vaiśampāyana—
the illustrious and devoted wife, who was constantly engaged in the recitation of sacred knowledge.

And how, O Brahmin, did Draupadī dwell unrecognized and in sorrow? And how did those foremost of Brahmins, along with the Sūtas and the cooks, as well as the attendants, live their life in concealment?
The Pāṇḍavas, whose valor is truth, have been granted permission by you in accordance with dharma;
they shall dwell in concealment for the thirteenth year, living incognito.
Having sat down together, those wise men, who are like *snātakas* firm in their vows, [prepared themselves].
Those ascetics who lived there devoted to him, dwelling in the forest,
were then addressed by those high-souled and disciplined ones with palms joined in reverence; firm in their vows, they sought his permission for their departure.
Everything is known to you all: how we were deprived of our kingdom by the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra through deceit, how we were rendered destitute in many ways,
and how we dwelt in forest exile for twelve years.
"Accompanied by you yourselves, O best of the twice-born, subsisting on forest fare,
we shall spend the remaining thirteenth year of our period of living incognito;
you ought to grant us permission for that."
The evil-minded Duryodhana, Karṇa, and the son of Subala (Śakuni),
being our extreme enemies, would act treacherously toward us even while knowing [our situation];
for they are disciplined in conduct and intent on the destruction of their own people.
For who among those evil-minded ones would be fit to place his trust in them?
Might it happen again that we, together with the brahmins,
might establish our own sovereignty over all the kingdoms?
Having spoken thus, King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, afflicted by pain and grief, pure and with a throat choked with tears, then fainted;
then all the brahmins, together with his brothers, consoled him.
Then Dhaumya spoke these words of great significance to the king:
"O King, you are learned, self-controlled, true to your promise, and a master of your senses; men such as you do not lose their composure in any calamity whatsoever."
Even the gods, those great-souled ones, have encountered calamities while remaining concealed in various places for the sake of subduing their enemies; at that time,
Indra reached the mountain plateau hermitage of Niṣadha.
Having performed deeds in secret for the suppression of his enemies,
and when his kingdom had been seized by the sons of Diti, the King of the Gods was deeply distressed;
desiring to propitiate a Brahmin, he assumed the form of a Brahmin.
O King, through the grace of Brahmā, having swiftly conquered the immensely powerful sons of Diti as his enemies, he protected the worlds once again; then,
Viṣṇu, who was about to dwell in Ādityā, reached the mountain of stone.
He dwelt for a long time in the womb of a demoness, unknown, for the purpose of slaying the Daityas;
and having lived there in the guise of a dwarf, disguised as a celibate student,
he seized the kingdom of Bali by his strides— this too has been heard by you.
O dear one, you have heard everything that was done in the worlds by the Brahman-sage Aurva while he lived in concealment within a thigh; and you have also heard,
O knower of dharma, how it was performed in secret by Hari during the slaying of Vṛtra.

You have heard what was done by you after entering the thunderbolt of Śakra; and you have also heard of the deed performed for the benefit of the gods when you entered the waters and remained hidden from the fire-god.

Likewise, O dear one, all the enemies were utterly consumed for many years by Vivasvat, who dwelt in disguise with supreme splendor upon the earth; and so too by Viṣṇu while dwelling in the house of Daśaratha.
The ten-necked Rāvaṇa was slain in battle by one of terrible deeds while remaining concealed; in this same way, these great-souled ones conquered their principal enemies while hidden here and there,
and so you too shall conquer.
Thus encouraged by Dhaumya with words, Yudhiṣṭhira, the knower of dharma, regained his composure through the wisdom of the scriptures; then the mighty-armed and immensely powerful Bhīmasena spoke.
Gladdening the king with his words, that best of the strong said:
"O Great King, observe how nothing at all rash has been done by you, the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, through an intellect following the path of dharma."

Sahadeva and Nakula have always been restrained by me; they are capable of destroying those enemies and possess terrible prowess as slayers of foes. We shall not abandon the path upon which you will set us.

"May you, sir, ordain all this; we shall quickly conquer our enemies. When Bhīmasena had spoken thus, the brahmins, having offered supreme blessings and taken leave of the Bharatas, departed for their respective homes.
Then all the preeminent knowers of the Vedas, ascetics, and sages,
having uttered blessings according to tradition, departed while longing for a future meeting. Likewise,
the servants, messengers, artisans, and attendants [departed].
Having taken leave according to custom,
O Bhārata, those five wise Pāṇḍavas— those heroes longing for a future reunion— together with Dhaumya, rose up and departed, taking Kṛṣṇā with them.
Having traveled a distance of one *krośa* from that dwelling for the sake of concealment,
on the following day, those tigers among men—
each an expert in the various sciences and all proficient in counsel— prepared themselves for their period of incognito residence.
Knowing the proper time for peace and war, they sat down for counsel.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Just as in the city of Virāṭa, so did your ancestors [behave]."
O lord of men, listen to how they lived their life in concealment. Having completed their forest exile, those illustrious Pāṇḍavas, true to their promise, held another council together with Dhaumya.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira,

the son of Kuntī and King of Dharma, having obtained those boons from Dharma— the best among the upholders of righteousness— looked toward his brothers, Kṛṣṇā, and Dhaumya, O joy of the Kurus, and spoke.
Having gone to the hermitage, he related all of that to the brahmins. After Yudhiṣṭhira had told all of this to the brahmins,
he presented the fire-drills together with them to that brahmin.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, the high-minded son of Dharma,
having turned back all his younger brothers, spoke thus, O Bhārata:
"For these twelve years we have been living in exile from our kingdom."
Having been robbed of our kingdom through deceit and reduced to poverty many times over,
and having lived in the forest in hardship for twelve years,
we shall now live in concealment for the thirteenth year, dwelling in disguise.
"This thirteenth year has arrived— a hardship most difficult to endure—
during which we shall spend this year free from harm. Therefore, O Arjuna, son of Kuntī, choose a dwelling from here that is suitable."
Unobserved by the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, together with Kṛṣṇā,
let us spend this year moving about as we please,
dwelling here in all these abodes unknown to our enemies.
Arjuna said:
"O lord of men, O bull of the Bharatas, by virtue of that very boon from Dharma, we shall wander unrecognized among men."
However, I shall mention certain kingdoms for your residence—delightful and well-guarded; please choose one among them. There are beautiful regions with abundant food surrounding the Kuru lands.
The Pañcālas, Cedis, Matsyas, Śūrasenas, Paṭaccaras,
Daśārṇas, Navarāṣṭra, Mallas, Śālvas, Yugandharas,
the vast Kuntirāṣṭra, as well as Surāṣṭra and Avantī;
O crusher of enemies, it is also heard that Virāṭa’s city is delightful, teeming with people, abundant in food, and truly prosperous; furthermore,
many other various kingdoms are also renowned.
"O King, which among these places for residence pleases you,
where we, O Indra among kings, shall dwell for this year? O King, wherever it pleases you, there we shall go."
"In which country, O Great King, will you dwell?
Do not set your mind on despair anywhere because of the loss of your kingdom.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O mighty-armed one, it is exactly as the Blessed Lord, the Master and Lord of all beings, has said; it is so and not otherwise.
However, for the sake of dwelling there, it must necessarily be delightful, auspicious, and pleasant."
Having consulted together, all of you must visit that place which is free from fear on any side;
it is designated as a sacred region, devoid of all afflictions.
Indeed, the words of whomever [spoke] this gladdened the Pāṇḍavas.
The powerful Matsya Virāṭa would protect the Pāṇḍavas; for he is virtuous, generous, aged, and possessed of great wealth—
endowed with excellent qualities, world-renowned, firm in devotion, and highly skilled.
"O Pārtha, O sinless one, it pleases me that we spend this year in the city of Virāṭa, in the presence of the King of Matsya; O dear son,
O Bhārata, we shall dwell there performing service for him."
"O descendants of Kuru, let him state whatever tasks we shall be able to perform for him, and what each of us is capable of doing. Arjuna said:

"O god among men, what work will you perform in the kingdom of that virtuous King Virāṭa? By what occupation will you find delight? For you are one who wears a blameless garb, righteous, and free from malice."
Such cruel and deceitful deeds are not worthy of you;
you are truthful in speech, a performer of sacrifices, and free from greed and anger. You are gentle, generous, modest, righteous, and one whose valor is rooted in truth.
"O King, O Pāṇḍava, afflicted as you are by calamity, what will you do? O King, no one knows suffering as well as you do;
having encountered this terrible misfortune, how will you cross over it?"
Thus addressed by Arjuna, Yudhiṣṭhira replied.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Listen, O descendants of Kuru, to the deed that I shall indeed perform."
Having reached King Virāṭa, that bull among men,
I shall become a courtier to that high-souled king; having become a brahmin named Kaṅka, skilled at dice and fond of gambling.
I shall produce beautiful dice made of beryl, gold, and ivory, together with *jyotīrasa* seeds; some with black dots and others with red dots,
auspicious, marked with the sign of the royal bull, lovely to behold, and radiant.
"O dear one, I possess riches such as rubies and emeralds;
there are beautiful, delightful pavilions,
skillfully constructed by artisans, at the mere touch of which men rejoice."
Having scattered them upon a level, delightful, and dustless spot, I shall sport there at my pleasure; that will be my place of recreation.
And as for Kaṅka by name, he is a wandering mendicant who sits in Virāṭa’s assembly.
I have studied the Veda of Bṛhaspati, as well as all the auxiliary sciences (*vedāṅgas*), including astrology, the science of omens from birds, the knowledge of portents, and skill in dice-play;
I have reached the further shore of the treatises on ethics regarding virtue, pleasure, wealth, and liberation.
"Being asked, I shall speak words that are pleasing and beneficial to the king. Thus engaged, I shall dwell forever in concealment in the city of Virāṭa,
delighting King Virāṭa along with his ministers and kinsmen."
"No one shall recognize me, yet I shall satisfy that king.
'In former times, I was Yudhiṣṭhira’s friend, as dear to him as his own life'—
this is what I shall say to the king if he questions me."
04,001.023a Thus have I declared this to you, and how I shall dwell;
04,001.023b Vaiśampāyana said:
Having thus identified himself, he sighed hotly from his distress.
Shedding tears from his eyes, Yudhiṣṭhira spoke to Bhīmasena:
"Bhīmasena, how will you carry out your duties in that kingdom?"
O dear one, having slain on Mount Gandhamādana the hosts of Krodhavaśas—
yakṣas whose eyes were copper-red with rage, and rākṣasas of exceeding prowess—
you gave many lotuses even to the princess of Pañcāla.
O Kaunteya, subduer of enemies, you slew the terrifying man-eating Rākṣasa king Baka for the sake of the Brāhmaṇas; by you,
the city of Ekacakrā was made secure and enveloped in fearlessness.

O mighty-armed one, having slain the highly powerful Hiḍimba and the exceedingly manly Kimmīra, you have cleared the forest of all thorns; yet even Draupadī of the lovely smile has fallen into distress.
Having slain Jaṭāsura, we were liberated;
and in the presence of the King of Matsya, O dear one, Vṛkodara was full of prowess and exceedingly indignant toward the weak Virāṭa.
O Vṛkodara, how will you find pleasure in the service of King Bhīma in Virāṭa’s city, residing in the midst of it— a difficult task for that monarch?
Having heard that speech concerning the deeds of a god among men, the wise deity honored it and spoke at the appropriate time words that were both beneficial and consistent with his own duty.
Having reflected and cast aside his anxiety,
the eloquent Bhīma said: "I am a chief cook, known by the name Ballava."
"It is my intention that I shall serve King Virāṭa. I will prepare various kinds of juices— both savory and sweet— as well as soups for him,
for I am skilled in the kitchen."
I shall surpass even those well-trained cooks who have previously prepared his side dishes,
generating delight for him;
first, I shall prepare those dishes endowed with excellent qualities that he has never tasted before.
Having tasted the savory condiment, I think he will be pleased;
for those who have been well-trained will have fulfilled their duty for him. I shall also bring great heaps of wood.
Seeing that vast feat, O Bhārata, the king will be delighted; and as I perform those superhuman deeds,
the king’s attendants will regard me as if I were the king himself.
I shall likewise be the lord of his foods, edibles, juices, and drinks.
O King, for his amusement I shall slay elephants and lions;
I shall slay other warriors as well, increasing his delight.
O King, whether it be powerful elephants or mighty bulls that must be restrained by me, I shall subdue them as well— be they bulls,
buffaloes, or even sixty-year-old elephants.
And when lions and tigers are to be seized by him—
those who are difficult for others to capture and are like the venom of poisonous serpents— I shall seize them all by force while the King of Fish looks on.
And whatever wrestlers there may be who will fight in the assemblies,
and those great champions of his who are undefeated in battles,
who have repeatedly displayed their prowess and are trusted by the king in matters of strength—
Those who subsist on the stage, who are clever and bring fear to others—
I shall slay them, increasing his joy;
but I will by no means kill these men while they are fighting.
In this manner, fighting them, I shall slay them all;
I shall strike them down so that they shall not go to their destruction.
Whether they be cooks or kitchen-stewards who are employed in his great kitchen—
I shall gratify those men with my own skill;
when asked, I will say, "I was the chief cook, the butcher, the sauce-maker, and the wrestler for Yudhiṣṭhira."
"O Lord of the People, protecting myself by my own self,
I shall live in disguise in the city of Virāṭa, in the presence of the King of Matsya;
this I promise you, and I shall conduct myself accordingly."
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"In the past, Agni, having become a brahmin, approached that best of men while he was with the descendant of Daśārha, desiring to burn the Khāṇḍava forest."
"Of great strength and mighty arms, unconquered, the joy of the Kurus—
what deed will this Dhananjaya, the son of Kuntī, perform? For he,
having approached that forest fire, satisfied the god of fire."
Having conquered Indra with a single chariot, having slain serpents and rākṣasas,
and having carried off the sister of Vāsuki, the king of snakes—
he who is known as the foremost among combatants, that Arjuna, what will he do?
Among mountains, Himavat is the foremost; among sacred sites, Kurukṣetra;
among planets, the Moon; and among birds, Garuḍa. Vāyu is the best among the powerful, and Bhṛgu is the best among ascetics.

The sun is the best among those that give heat; the Brahmin is the most excellent among bipeds; the venomous serpent is the chief among snakes; and fire is the foremost among radiant things. The thunderbolt is the best of weapons; and the humped bull is the preeminent among cattle.
The ocean is the best among lakes; Parjanya is the foremost among those who rain;
Dhṛtarāṣṭra is the chief among nāgas; Airāvata is the best among elephants; a son is the greatest of all that is dear; and a wife is the most excellent of friends.
O Vṛkodara, just as the mother is the foremost among elders and the rain-cloud is the best among those that pour water— these being distinguished in their respective classes—
so too is the youthful Guḍākeśa the most excellent among all archers.
O Bhārata, what will this Bībhatsu do— he who is not inferior to Indra or Vāsudeva, the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow with white horses—
who has lived for five years in the abode of the thousand-eyed god?
Engaged in the vow of celibacy, he became proficient in all weapons; having mastered the application of missiles through his own prowess— a marvel among men—
he acquired divine weapons by means of his radiant, celestial form.
I consider him the twelfth Rudra, the thirteenth Āditya;
I consider him the ninth Vasu and likewise the tenth of the planets—
he whose two arms are equal and long, their skin hardened by the striking of the bowstring.
A path was made for him on both the right and the left, like the flow of cattle;
he was like Himavat among mountains, like the ocean among rivers,
like Śakra among the thirty gods, and like Agni among the Vasus.
Like the sun among the planets, like the moon among the stars,
like Mount Meru among all mountains, and like Vāsuki among the serpents;
like the tiger among beasts, and like Garuḍa among those that fly.
What will Arjuna do, the best among those who don armor?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Fire, disguised in the form of a brahmin, begged for food."

"O Arjuna, release me, who am a great eater, at the Khāṇḍava forest. And that righteous-souled one heard it; he of great fame then fulfilled that purpose for him who was in the form of a brahmin, namely the Fire-god.
But he who, on a single chariot, conquered both gods and men— all of them—
what will that Pāṇḍava do, he of the terrible bow and white horses,
whose touch is like a venomous serpent, like Vāsuki among the Nāgas?
Like the venomous gaze of snakes, like fire among the radiant,
like the ocean among rivers, like the Himavat among mountains,
like Mahendra among the gods, and like Bali among the Dānavas.
He was like Supratīka among elephants, or a horse among draft animals;
like Kubera among the Yakṣas, or a lion among wild beasts;
like the Ten-necked one among the Rākṣasas, or Śambara among the Daityas.
Like Kapālin among the Rudras, like Viṣṇu among the powerful,
like Takṣaka among serpents, and like Garuḍa among winged creatures when roused by the force of the wind’s speed, he was filled with wrath and indignation.
Like the sun among those that give heat, like the Brahmin among living beings,
like the netherworld among lakes, like the rain-cloud among givers;
as the thunderbolt is the best of weapons, so the humped bull is the best of cattle.
Among the *nāgas*, Dhṛtarāṣṭra is the foremost; among elephants, Airāvata is the best.
A son is the greatest of dear things, and a wife is the most excellent of friends. Among mountains, Meru is the preeminent; among the gods, Madhusūdana is the supreme.
The moon is the foremost of the planets, and Lake Mānasa is the best of lakes;
just as these are preeminent within their own kind, O Vṛkodara,
so too is the youthful Guḍākeśa the most excellent among all archers.
O Bhārata, he who is not inferior to Indra or Vāsudeva—
having lived for five years in the abode of the thousand-eyed god,
practicing celibacy and intent on his vows— is the best among all wielders of weapons.
Though unversed in weaponry, he who was esteemed by the All-Knowing acquired all weapons—
the swift, the subtle, the variegated, and the steadfast— O best of speakers;
and having been permitted by the Lord of the Gods, he returned once more to the earth.
For the destruction of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons and for the victory of the Pāṇḍavas,
I consider him to be the twelfth Rudra and the thirteenth Āditya—
his two long, symmetrical arms are calloused from the striking of the bowstring.
Like the two forelegs of a bull, his right and left arms were well-rounded; with palms and fingers protected by leather guards, they resembled the trunks of the lords of serpents.
Dark-complexioned, youthful, with curly hair, the Pāṇḍava was handsome to behold.
The wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, he of white horses, the wearer of the diadem, whose banner bears the monkey—
what form does he assume, what is his task, what is his conduct, and what is his prowess?
What will Arjuna do— he who is Bībhatsu and the one with the formidable bow?
By what occupation will the son of Kuntī find delight in the service of Virāṭa?
He who was like Citraratha among the Gandharvas and Kapila among the Siddhas—
those two arms, resembling iron clubs, yet always so soft and auspicious.
O bull of the Bharatas, you who are equal to Vāsudeva in fame and prowess in this world— how will you, O Arjuna, perform your duties in the kingdom of King Virāṭa?
Arjuna said:
"O lord of the earth, I shall make the vow, 'I am a eunuch,' for the two great scars from the bowstring on my arms are difficult to conceal, O King."

"O King, descendant of Bharata, I was indeed cursed by Urvaśī in the past for a certain reason; impelling that curse, I shall sport [with you]. These two arms of mine have been calloused from being struck by the bowstring and pressed against its notch."

"O best of the Bharatas, my two arms are always covered by a bodice; otherwise, I would not venture to protect them. However, out of necessity, I shall perform this loathsome act. My arms, O best of the Bharatas, are marked with great auspicious signs."
I shall cover these two arms, scarred by calluses, with bracelets;
with conch-shell ornaments bound upon my wrists, I shall assume the appearance of a third gender. Thus, through this effeminate attire, I shall declare, "I am a eunuch."
"O King, having fastened these two earrings, which resemble blazing fire, upon my ears,
with my hair braided and my name Bṛhannaḍā,
I shall repeatedly recite stories in the guise of a woman."
I shall delight the protector of the earth and the other people in the inner apartments;
O King, I will teach singing, various dances, and diverse instrumental music to the women in Virāṭa’s palace.
With the conduct of a woman, resorting to dance, song, and storytelling,
and speaking of the various behaviors of people as being produced by many actions,
O son of Kuntī, I shall conceal myself by means of my own self through illusion.
"O Bhārata, when asked by the king, I shall say: 'I was a maidservant of Draupadī in Yudhiṣṭhira’s house; I have lived there.
And furthermore, O King, it was through the curse of Urvaśī that I attained this state of impotence."
"O King of Kings, through the grace of Śakra, I have been released after thirteen years;
thus disguised by this artifice like Nala,
I shall dwell happily in the palace of Virāṭa."
Having spoken thus, that hero among men,
Arjuna, the foremost of those who uphold dharma,
then ceased speaking further.
The king spoke further to his other brother;
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Nakula, my dear, what will you do while wandering there?"
"Tell me truly of the conduct of that lord of the earth in his kingdom;
for on this surface of the earth, I see no one endowed with such beauty as yours.
Having encountered such a calamity, how will you dwell there?"
Unworthy of suffering, yet a child who was always cherished; now he is both afflicted and at peace—what indeed would please him here?
You, however, are both gentle and brave; what indeed would please you here?
"Delicate yet brave, handsome and accustomed to comfort," Nakula said,
"I shall become the horse-keeper for King Virāṭa."
In every respect endowed with knowledge and skilled in protection, I am known by the name Granthika; this work is very dear to me. I am renowned as Dāmagranthin, skilled in the art of harnessing.
People will never at any time treat me with contempt,
for I am skilled in the training of horses as well as in the medical treatment of horses;
and horses are always dear to me, O King of the Kurus, just as they are to you.
The colts and even the mares will not be vicious;
they will not be ill-behaved on the backs or in the chariots,
nor will the colts and mares treat me with contempt.
They shall not be ill-behaved, whether behind me or at my head, being devoted to me.
To those people in the city of Virāṭa who address me, I shall speak thus: "In this manner I shall conduct myself."

O bull of the Bharatas, in former times I was the horse-keeper for Yudhiṣṭhira; I was the most excellent groom for those Pāṇḍava kings. O dear one, in the past, I was formerly appointed by the Pāṇḍava to oversee the horses.
The horse-keeper of Yudhiṣṭhira knows me;
wandering here and there, I have arrived at your city, O Lord of Matsya.
O King, I shall live incognito in the city of Virāṭa.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Equal to Bṛhaspati in intelligence and equal to Uśanas in statesmanship,
you have been guided by various kinds of mantras that are beneficial and well-established.
Established upon the excellent path, he protected the kingdom with most refined methods;
those who knew him saw not the slightest deviation in him. He was a leader of noble conduct, heroic, and proficient in all counsel.
"O Sahadeva, you who have always been more dear to our mother Kuntī than anyone else, how will you dwell in his presence? O son of Mādrī, by what work will you find delight in the service of Virāṭa?"
"Or what, dear brother, will you do while wandering in disguise for a year in the city of Virāṭa, which is filled with many predatory beasts? Sahadeva replied:

"I shall become the cow-counter for Virāṭa, the lord of the earth; I shall be the restrainer and the milker, skilled in the counting of cattle. Let it be known to you that I am renowned by the name Tantipāla."
But because of my pride, O King, the Pāṇḍavas will say of me:
"The cows are free from disease, numerous, well-nourished, yielding milk, prolific, full of vigor,
well-tended, and free from distress and blemish."

O King, protected by me, the cattle of Virāṭa will always be free from the fear of thieves, forever devoid of the tiger of disease, and will exist in great happiness, undisturbed and free from ailment, O Monarch.
"I shall conduct myself with skill; let the fever of your mind depart. No one shall recognize me, and I shall satisfy that king.
O King, son of Virāṭa, I shall dwell there in disguise."
"I shall serve Virāṭa, the best of kings"— this is my vow, and I shall live accordingly. When Nakula had spoken thus, Dharmarāja replied with these words.
"For in the past, I was constantly employed by you among the cattle; therefore, O lord of the people, my skill in that work is well known to you,
as are the characteristics, the behavior, and the auspicious rites of cows."
"O Lord of the Earth, all that is well known to me, as is much else besides;
O King, I also know bulls endowed with auspicious marks,
by smelling whose urine even a barren woman brings forth offspring."

Thus shall I conduct myself, for in this I always find joy; hidden in the city of Virāṭa, I shall take delight in that work and satisfy the king as well— let there be no anxiety on your part, O sinless one.
"And no one else shall know me; let that be pleasing to you, O King.
This is the promise I have made to you, and I shall act accordingly.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"But this beloved wife of ours is dearer to us than our very lives;
what will Pāñcālī do, even though she has been consecrated in the Rājasūya sacrifice? She is to be protected like a mother and honored like an elder sister."
"By what work will Kṛṣṇā Draupadī sustain herself? For she knows nothing at all of how to perform the tasks of women;
she is delicate, young, and a princess of great renown."
"How indeed will that illustrious woman, devoted to her husband, conduct herself?

Having spoken thus regarding Draupadī, the princess of Pañcāla, to his brothers— Vaiśampāyana said: ||| 04,003.014d*0092_001 ||| Vaiśampāyana said: ||| 04,003.014d*0092_001 ||| Vaiśampāyana said: ||| 04,003.014d*0092_001 ||| Vaiśampāyana said: ||| 04,003.014d*0092_001 ||| Vaiśampāyana said: ||| 04,003.014d*0092_001 ||| Vaiśampāyana said: ||| 04,003.014d*0092_001 ||| Vaiśampāyana said: ||| 04,003.014d*0092_001 ||| Vaiśampāyana said: ||| 04,003.014d*0092_001 ||| Vaiśampāyana said: ||| 04,003.014d*0092_001 ||| Vaiśampāyana said: ||| 04,003.014d*0092_001 ||| Vaiśampāyana said: ||| 04,003.014d*0092_001 ||| Vaiśampāyana said: ||| 04,003.014d*0092_001 ||| Vaiśampāyana said: ||| 04,003.014d*0092_001 ||| Vaiśampāyana said: ||| 04,003.014d*0092_001 ||| Vaiśampāyana said: ||| 04,003.014d*0092_001 ||| Vaiśampāyana said: ||| 04,003.014d*0092_001 ||| Vaiśampāyana said: ||| 04,003.014d*0092_001 ||| Vaiśampāyana said: ||| 04,003.014d*0092_001 ||| Vaiśampāyana said: ||| 04,003.014d*0092_001 ||| Vaiśampāyana said: ||| 04,003.014d*0092_001 ||| Vaiśampāyana said: ||| 04,003.014d*0092_001 ||| Vaiśampāyana said: ||| 04,003.014d*0092_001 ||| Vaiśampāyana said: ||| 04,003.014d*0092_001 ||| Vaiśampāyana said: ||| 04,003.014d*0092_001 ||| Vaiśampāyana said: ||| 04,003.014d*0092_001 ||| Vaiśampāyana said: ||| 04,003.014d*0092_001 ||| Vaiśampāyana said: ||| 04,003.014d*0092_001 ||| Vaiśampāyana said: ||| 04,003.014d*0092_001 ||| Vaiśampāyana said: ||| 04,003.014d*0092_001 ||| Vaiśampāyana said: ||| 04,003.014d*0092_0
Then Kṛṣṇā spoke these words to Yudhiṣṭhira:
"Garlands, perfumes, ornaments, and various garments—
since she was born, this spirited lady has known only these."
Draupadī said:
"O Bhārata, there are maidservants in the world who are unprotected;
it is the settled conviction of the world that other women do not behave in such a manner."
"I shall dwell [here], O Indra among kings; be at peace, O ruler of men.
Listen, O King, to how there may be no sorrow for you on my account. I shall act, O Lord, so that they do not recognize me."
"I shall dwell in concealment so that no one will recognize me;
I will tell you what has happened, O lord of the people—attain peace. I am a Sairandhrī, well-born by lineage, known by name as one who observes her vows."

"O Great King, it is my intention that I shall become [the wife] of Virāṭa; it is the world's conviction that these women are devoted to the vow of having only one husband. Therefore, declaring myself a *sairandhrī* skilled in the work of hair, I shall serve him."
O Bhārata, when questioned by the king, I shall say: "I am a maidservant of Draupadī in Yudhiṣṭhira’s house; I have lived there. I am a woman who brings food to men traveling abroad in this world.
"I shall not be difficult to support there in the royal palace, O lord of men;
for I shall always maintain my protection through my own vow. I will conduct myself with self-restraint, just as you have asked of me."
"I shall wait upon the illustrious Sudeṣṇā, the king’s wife;
she will protect me once I have arrived, so let there be no such sorrow for you. This is my vow, and I shall conduct myself accordingly."
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Kṛṣṇā, you speak auspiciously, as one born in a noble family would speak. You do not recognize evil; you are virtuous, established in the vow of a faithful wife."

"O virtuous lady, you should act in such a way that those who harbor ill-will and are wicked do not become happy again, and so that they may not even notice you. Having heard these words spoken, the son of Dharma [Yudhiṣṭhira]...
Adorned with a multitude of renowned virtues, the princess—though submerged in hundreds of calamities—is not corrupted; for virtuous women do not change.
With a joyful heart and disposition, he spoke these words.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"The duties that have been described by you, those you shall perform;
and as for my own, they are pleasing to me according to my understanding and firm resolve."
"Let this priest of ours protect our *agnihotra* sacrifices together with the cooks and the cowherds in the palace of Drupada;
and let these men, headed by Indrasena, take all the chariots."
"It is my firm resolve that they should go quickly to Dvāravatī;
and let these women, all the attendants of Draupadī,
go to the Pañcālas along with the cooks and the stewards."
Having gone to Dvāravatī and Kāmpilya, the best of cities,
it must be said by everyone: "The high-souled Pāṇḍavas are not known even to the Brahmins who receive alms at midnight."
"For they have all departed from the Dvaitavana forest, casting us aside.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Thus they addressed one another, each describing his own actions individually."
They addressed Dhaumya, and he spoke this counsel to them. Vaiśampāyana said:
That righteous-souled one, who knew the distinctions of all duties, gave them these instructions.
04,004.005d*0104_002 Dhaumya, the family priest, [addressed] the Pāṇḍavas, those bulls among men, O King.
04,004.006 Dhaumya said:
04,004.006*0105_001 "O Pāṇḍavas, everything has been provided for you among the Brāhmaṇas and your friends."

O Bhārata, you and Phālguna must provide protection for Kṛṣṇā against vehicles, weapons, and likewise against fires. O King, it is known to you all how this conduct of the world functions in its entirety.
Even when something is already known, it should be spoken by friends out of affection;
for this is eternal dharma, pleasure, and wealth.
Therefore, I too shall speak; listen to my brief reasoning.
"Come now, O princes, I shall tell you about this royal residence,
so that having reached the king's court, a servant may conduct himself without coming to harm. But it is indeed difficult to dwell, O Kauravyas, in a royal palace even for one who is experienced."
Though unworshipped, you who are worthy of great honor shall remain unrecognized for a full year;
then, in the fourteenth year, you shall live as you please.
This fire of the Pāṇḍavas in this world is a great one, composed of all weapons.

The king is the sustainer and protector of all beings, a personification of Puruṣa. Learn now the conduct of that king who lives by supporting his subjects, so that no fault may touch him as he conducts himself with his whole soul.
A wise person should never, under any circumstances, despise a Kṣatriya, a serpent, or a learned Brāhmaṇa, even if they are weak;
for these three, when treated with contempt, may utterly consume a man.

Therefore, a king should always be honored with great effort by the wise. A man who is esteemed by the king should not transgress the bounds of propriety; furthermore, the learned know that in this world, such conduct constitutes the standard of legal procedure.
Even while proceeding toward the highest state, if unasked and unappointed,
one should indeed consider the bounds of propriety like a man blind from birth;
for those who subdue their enemies [do not act thus] toward a son, a grandson, or a brother.
Kings honor one who has transcended all bounds;
one should obtain an entrance through a prescribed gate, yet never place trust in kings. One should seek only that seat where another would not feel resentment.

He should not mount a vehicle, a couch, a seat, an elephant, or a chariot, thinking "I am highly regarded"; thus he should dwell in the royal residence. Furthermore, he should avoid any place where evildoers might suspect him while he is seated there.
He should never sit there; he may dwell in the royal residence, but he should never instruct the king unless asked. He should attend upon him in silence, honoring him at the proper time.
For kings resent people who speak untruths,
and likewise they hold in contempt a counselor who speaks falsely; therefore,
a wise man should never form a friendship with their wives under any circumstances.

Those who move within the inner apartments and those who are hostile or unfriendly— once they have been identified, one should perform even very minor tasks through them. Furthermore, a wise person should never, at any time, shake his feet or his arms.
For a king who conducts himself in this manner, no harm arises anywhere.
One should serve him with diligence, as if he were fire or a god;
for if he is served with falsehood, he will undoubtedly cause injury.
Whatever her husband may command, she should follow that very instruction;
she should avoid negligence, disdain, and anger,
and in all matters of justification, she should speak only what is beneficial and pleasing.

One should praise that very [quality] and speak what is beneficial even more than what is pleasant; one should be agreeable to him in all matters and in all conversations. One should not describe to him anything that is unpleasant or harmful.

A wise person should serve another not with the thought, "I am dear to him," but rather by being vigilant and self-restrained, performing what is beneficial and what is pleasing. One should not indulge in things that are undesirable to him, nor should one dwell with those who are harmful to him.

He should not waver from his proper place; he may dwell in the royal residence. A wise man should sit either on the right or the left side, for the position behind is prescribed for guards who have taken up their weapons.
But sitting on a large seat in the presence [of the king] is always strictly forbidden. One should always remain vigilant in this manner, and thus become dear to the king;
nor should one utter even a word of praise when in his sight, however great it may be.
For this is the greatest source of offense for the poor:
that one should not disclose to people a false statement made by a king;
nor should one speak ill of a man whom kings hold in contempt.
In that same way, those who consider themselves wise treat other men with contempt;
yet one should not be arrogant, thinking "I am a hero" or "I am intelligent.
By acting only for the pleasure of the king, one becomes beloved and possesses enjoyments.
Having obtained sovereignty so difficult to attain and having gained the favor of the king, one should remain vigilant regarding both what is pleasing and what is beneficial to the king—
[for] his anger brings great affliction, while his grace yields great fruit.
Who that is esteemed by the wise would even in his mind desire harm for him?
He should never gnash his lips, nor should he ever interrupt another's speech;
he should always perform sneezing, passing wind, and spitting quietly.
Even when certain objects of laughter are present before him,
he should not exult excessively, nor should he laugh like a madman;
nor should he behave with excessive gravity, for in that way he would become overly solemn.
One should display a smile preceded by gentleness, born of serenity. He who does not exult at gain, nor is distressed when insulted,
and who remains ever undeluded— he may dwell in the royal residence.
That wise minister who always serves the king or the prince remains long in possession of royal fortune;
for he is both honored by the king and restrained by him through various means.
One who does not press the king too hard gains his favor once again;
being discerning and speaking of his virtues both in his presence and in his absence,
one should live as a dependent of the king, even if one merely dwells within his realm.

For that minister who seeks to enjoy the king by force shall not remain in his position for long, and he shall face a threat to his life. Seeing what is truly for his own ultimate welfare, he should not speak in opposition to the king.
He should never disparage the king, even on occasions where he is worthy of it; unwithered, strong, and brave, he should always remain like a shadow that never departs.
Speaking the truth, gentle, and self-controlled—he may dwell in the king’s residence.
But when another is being sent on an errand, he who springs forward first,
saying, "What shall I do?", may dwell in the royal residence;
whether in heat or in cold, by night or by day.
Whether in times of adversity or prosperity, he who is always commanded by the king and does not hesitate shall dwell in the royal residence;
indeed, he who departs from his home should not dwell on his beloved ones.

One who seeks happiness through suffering shall dwell in the king’s residence. One should use the same vehicle and eat the same food; one should not laugh excessively or in many ways. One should not dress identically [to the king], nor should one laugh loudly in his presence.
One should not disclose the king's counsel in many ways; thus one will remain dear to the king.
When appointed to a task, one should not touch even the slightest bit of wealth for oneself;
for by misappropriating property, one incurs either imprisonment or death.
Whatever vehicle, clothing, ornament, or anything else he bestows upon him, that very thing one should always wear; in this way, one will become most beloved.
Thus, O sons of Pāṇḍu, having restrained their minds with effort, [they should act].
A man living in a royal court should seek such a seat where, while seated, he would not be thwarted by more powerful persons; so that those of evil conduct might not suspect him as he sits there.
One who dwells in the royal residence should never sit there;
he may sit or stand at his own ease in the presence of the king,
but he should never seek out a seat for himself from another.
For if he is seated on another's seat, the attendants of that other person might drag him away from the assembly, and he would be mocked by his enemies; therefore,
sitting in front [of one's superior] is considered always forbidden.
For when a servant approaches the king for the sake of some purpose,
that wise man, O King, should stand humbly, leaning upon either the right or the left arm; he should not stand in front, nor behind.
A position behind the guards bearing weapons is prescribed for her;
she should always address [the king] by his mother’s lineage, her own lineage, or again by name or character, for the purpose of winning over people.
Even when honored by the king, the man who does not return the honor will not be propitiated by others,
just as indolent disciples do not please their teacher.
He shall have neither a draft animal, nor a couch, nor a seat, nor likewise a chariot.

He who would dwell in the king’s residence, thinking "I am being conciliated," should ascend [to that position]. Indeed, he who, departing from his home, should remember what was done [there], being ever intent on exertion, free from sloth, and self-controlled— [he may dwell there].
Overcome by hunger and thirst, having abandoned lamentation,
one who seeks happiness through suffering should dwell in the king’s residence;
when others are being sent forth, the wise man should spring forward ahead of them.
He who thinks, "I shall do this," succeeds among kings;
he who, whether in heat or in cold, by night or by day,
does not hesitate when commanded, succeeds among kings.
A wise mortal should never, even when in such a position, look down upon others;
he who is upright, gentle, and truthful succeeds among kings.
He should not give way to elation through gain, nor should he be distressed when treated with contempt.
He who dwells in the royal residence should be as even as a full scale-bowl;
possessing few desires, wise, and illustrious, he should always be like a shadow that never departs. Skillful, courteous, and steadfast—he is one who may dwell in the royal residence.
One who knows the *itihāsas* and *purāṇas*, who is skilled in excellent discourses, generous, and truthful in speech— such a person may dwell in the royal residence.
One must not disclose to other people what has been spoken in private by the king.
One should not speak ill of a man whom kings despise;
one should not touch even the slightest wealth connected to their affairs,
for by taking it, one will surely incur either imprisonment or death.
Seeing that my own [reputation] and that of another are equally established, the wise man does not become deluded by thinking, "He nourishes the other while I am inferior. For,
having abandoned a superior physician in every task, [one suffers].
One should not make their conduct such that it becomes worse; a wise man should never, under any circumstances, cultivate intimacy with their wives.
Furthermore, one who dwells in the king’s residence should not associate with the guards.
For when he sees that [the minister] has come together with the king's female servants,
the king may despise his intelligence or, moreover, become suspicious of him. Furthermore, toward what servant who is suspected by the king regarding women would the lord of the earth [behave]?
One who is established in their natural state and not coerced by force should consider life itself to be good;
even when certain causes for joy are present here,
one should not be excessively delighted, but should instead honor those very things [with equanimity].
For out of joy, a dull-witted man might easily commit some transgression;
therefore, the lord of the earth should keep watch over what occurs within his harem.
For when he has entered the harem, women and eunuchs may act toward him in every way.
They would undoubtedly disparage his present conduct as well;
therefore, keeping himself profound and restraining his joy,
he should never disclose his activities within the royal harem to those outside.
For just as a very great mantra, when broken, may carry away one's happiness,
so too what occurs within the inner apartments, when heard outside, may have that same effect.
Such conduct belongs only to those who are not outsiders, yet it is now being practiced even by outsiders.
Listen to what applies to all those who live off the king, both collectively and individually:
neither a woman nor anyone else, whether an outsider or an insider, should ever entertain such thoughts;
for if the lord of men were to harbor [such thoughts], he would surely create a very great danger for his dependents.
Considering himself dear to him, a wise man who is not a king should not, like a king, make use of royal jewels that are fit for a king;
for jewels beloved by kings do not belong to one who is not a king.

A king should not tolerate a dependent who eats in his presence; therefore, one who desires prosperity should eat with unobtrusive moderation. For a king might treat a servant with anger if their enjoyment of resources is equal.
One should not cause the king to take pleasure in offspring through anyone;
one should avoid that which is censured, harmful, and hateful. For by serving these four types of human boundaries, [one prospers].
The root of those who live off the king’s roots is severed in two ways;
however, by these lowest of men, the boundary of humanity is transgressed. One should associate with such a woman, but never oppose her in any way.

One should consider association with the kinsmen of a king and with powerful men to be beneficial, and never conflict with them in any way; for one who opposes those two foremost of men will possess little luster.

First, sleep is cut off; second, fear arises. One should clearly avoid all those who wear the dress of the uprooted, those who possess the guise of deceivers, and those with the distinct appearance of kings.
But by the other two modes of dress, she would be mocked by her kinsmen—
by those who are not men as well as by men, and by women as well as by men who look upon women.
Even when it is possible, she should never at any time engage in conversation with them.
For a man who converses with these three while lacking true discernment takes up his own prosperity like a hawk seizing a piece of meat;
and those who receive honor from a king as if it were due to some specific cause.
Honored by those envoys from neighboring realms, the sage should remain so; yet,
unless commanded by the lord of the earth, the wise man who dwells in the royal residence should not frequent any ground that has not been assigned to him.

One should not even whisper of a continuous connection with the king upon being seen by him; moreover, this is the ultimate source of offense for those who are poor. Furthermore, a woman who desires wealth and presents herself before the king [is likewise liable].
Likewise, a dependent who gazes upon a woman engaged in such [sexual] activity suffers from distress. Therefore, a wise man should not gaze upon a woman so engaged.
Furthermore, one should perform sneezing, passing wind, and spitting slowly.
One should never laugh at jests, for that is known to be the conduct of the foolish. Instead, one should display a smile born of serenity preceded by gentleness.
One should never brandish one's eyes, nor one's arms, nor ever interrupt another's speech.
One should not look askance, but should behave with proper decorum; one should not knit one's brows, nor scratch the earth with one's thumbs,
nor should one ever yawn excessively in the presence of a king.
One should neither praise nor find fault with things that are pleasant and beneficial,
whether they are being heard about there, or being criticized,
or even when those pleasant and beneficial things are being directly perceived.
When words are being heard, one should describe them as if they were nectar;
one who serves what is contrary to the king will not find happiness,
whether he be a son, a brother, or even one as dear as himself.
For one who is vigilant should please the king through the perfection of virtuous conduct;
moreover, the wise man [should please him] through diligence and various forms of purity. Indeed, bathing and the cleansing of clothes are called physical purity.
Non-attachment to worldly objects is said to be the second form of purity. One who is praised with such titles as King, Bhoja, Virāṭ, Samrāṭ, Kṣatriya, Bhūpati, and Nṛpa— who would not honor him?

Therefore, one who is devoted, disciplined, truthful, and has conquered his senses— being intelligent, steadfast, and wise— should seek refuge with a lord of the earth who is grateful, discerning, noble-minded, firm in devotion, and self-controlled.

One should seek refuge with a lord of the earth who is increasing in power and established in his station. O Pārtha, this proper conduct has been prescribed for you according to the rule, so that those who live off the king may obtain their rightful rewards.
O Kauravya, purposes are accomplished, and purposes do not fail;
for one who clearly adopts the guise of a king is not slain. O dear one, those who desire to thrive should maintain such conduct for this entire year.
"Then, having reached your own domain, you shall roam according to your desire.
Vaiśampāyana said:
The sons of Pṛthā replied "So be it" to that illustrious one, who was like a father to them.
Delighted, those subduers of enemies saluted him and stood before him; as they were departing,
the Brahmin recited mantras for their well-being,
for the acquisition of the kingdom, and for supreme victory.
Then that brahmin, having uttered words of blessing, spoke for the sake of obtaining his own wealth and for the crushing of his enemies:
"May it be well with you; may your path be auspicious; may I see you again when you have returned."
Having been addressed thus by that wise preceptor, all of them, headed by Yudhiṣṭhira, set out with joyful minds. Yudhiṣṭhira said:

We have been instructed— blessings be upon you— and there is no one else who could speak thus except for our mother Kuntī and the high-minded Vidura. You ought to perform whatever task must be done immediately thereafter.
"For the sake of crossing over this suffering, for setting forth, and for victory.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having been addressed thus by the king, Dhaumya, the best of the twice-born, then—
He performed everything according to the rules that is prescribed for a departure; having kindled those fires, he offered oblations with mantras for the sake of attaining prosperity,
growth, and the conquest of the earth.
As they were setting out, Dhaumya recited the mantras that pacify all obstacles and bring about the accomplishment of their goals;
then, having kindled the fire with the offering of mantras placed before it.
Having circumambulated the fire and saluted the Brahmins whose wealth was their asceticism, they all then fled together with Kṛṣṇā;
placing Yājñasenī at their head, the six of them set forth.
When those heroes had departed, Dhaumya, the best among those who recite prayers,
took the sacred *agnihotra* fires and went toward the Pañcālas;
and Indrasena and the others, as previously instructed, reached the Yādavas.
Guarding their chariots and horses, they dwelt happily and securely;
thus, being surrounded and filled with joy, their bellies grew full.
Such was the command of Yudhiṣṭhira.
Then, O son, the charioteers and riders, who were not overly weary,
approached very swiftly and every day performed auspicious rites in their hearts.
They fled from forest to forest together with Dhaumya, their weapons girded.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Those heroes, with swords girt and equipped with bows and quivers...
Having bound on their leather arm-guards and finger-protectors, they proceeded along both banks of the Kālindī;
then, traveling on foot, they followed the southern shore,
killing lions, tigers, and boars everywhere.
Having completed their forest exile and desiring to regain their own kingdom,
they then set out toward the west, moving from forest to forest;
armed with bows, they dwelt in mountain fastnesses and forest retreats.
In delightful ponds and at the confluences of rivers,
they saw trees of various forms, thick with diverse kinds of creepers—
abounding in flowers, pleasing to the mind, and enchanting with their auspicious fragrance.
The sons of Pṛthā beheld those trees, adorned with garlands of flowers— campakas, bakulas, punnāgas, and likewise ketakīs, pāribhadrakas, karañjas, and various other kinds of trees.
Inhaling the fragrant and delightful scents of flowers,
those great archers of immense strength pierced various species of deer;
they passed to the north of the Daśārṇas and to the south of the Pañcālas.
Having dwelt for twelve years in the forest, those conquerors of enemy cities,
the Pāṇḍavas, while passing between the Yakṛllomas and the Śūrasenas,
entered the territory of Matsya from the woods, calling themselves hunters.
Armed with bows and girt with swords, pale and bearded,
the sons of Pāṇḍu dispatched the high-souled Dhaumya to that place which was rich in cattle, abundant in wealth, and filled with joyful and well-fed people.
While performing the *agnihotra* sacrifice, he lived in the hermitage unaware [of their departure]. Then,
after those high-souled Pāṇḍavas had departed, Indrasena and the others, having received the instructions as told, were at ease.
Guarding their chariots and horses, they dwelt there happily and well-protected.
Then, having reached the countryside, Kṛṣṇā said to the king:
"Look! Footpaths are visible, as are various fields."
Seeing these trees belonging to the groves of both villages and the city, it is clear that King Virāṭa’s capital must be far away. Let us dwell here for the final night; my exhaustion is great.
Having heard those words of hers, King Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O son of Mādrī, [protect] this lotus-eyed Draupadī."
"O Nakula, take her in your arms and walk for a moment;
O bull of the Bharatas, Virāṭa’s city is not far from here.
We shall dwell in the capital as if we were well-released from the forest."
Nakula,
having gone hunting in the forest during the forenoon, pierced great beasts;
desiring to kill deer, I have traversed a vast distance through the wilderness.
"For it is uneven, exceedingly difficult to traverse, and rushes along with great speed.
Being scorched by the heat, O Yudhiṣṭhira, I truly do not venture to take it up."
"Sahadeva, take Draupadī and lead her away for a moment.
Sahadeva:
"We shall dwell in the capital as if it were our own well-prepared forest."
"I too am thirsty and oppressed by hunger;
exhausted and scorched by the heat, I truly do not have the strength to take her.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Dhanañjaya, O Bhārata, lift up the princess of Pañcāla and carry her!
Come, O hero, O large-eyed Arjuna, like a lion among men;
[carry] this lotus-petal-eyed Draupadī, the daughter of Drupada."
"Taking hold of you for a moment with both arms, go safely;
we shall dwell in the capital, released from this forest.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having received the command of his preceptor, Dhananjaya was filled with joy;
taking Draupadi with him like a lordly elephant, the mighty-armed and handsome Arjuna set forth in haste.
Wearing matted hair and garments of bark, carrying a quiver and bow, Arjuna placed the beautiful, long-eyed young woman upon his shoulder; having reached the vicinity of the city, he set her down.
Having reached the capital, the son of Kuntī spoke to Arjuna:
"Where shall we hang our weapons before entering the city, O tiger among men, O scorcher of foes? "These are the weapons," [he replied].
"Where should these items be deposited, and how can their protection be ensured? Father, if we enter the city armed,
there is no doubt that we will cause great alarm among the people."
The great and formidable Gāṇḍīva bow is well known among men in the world;
if we go to the city taking that weapon with us,
people will recognize us quickly— of this there is no doubt.

"How, O noble one, may we remain undiscovered by the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and how may we cause suspicion to arise in these people? Of this there is no doubt. Therefore, we must enter the forest again for twelve years."
For we maintain that when even one [of these] is known, it is as if all have been accepted;
therefore, all the treatises should be concealed, or rather, wherever they may be,
according to Vaiśampāyana.

"Then we shall enter the excellent city, and thus it will be properly accomplished. Having heard these words of Ajātaśatru, the highly illustrious Arjuna, slayer of enemy heroes, spoke to that son of Dharma.
Arjuna said:
"O lord of men, here on this peak is a vast and dense *śamī* tree with formidable branches; it is difficult to climb and stands near the cremation ground."
"Moreover, O King, there is no man here who would see us as we place these weapons—
bows and arrows— into a human figure made of leather, hair, and bone."
Having fashioned it like a noose for hanging, with its bowstring serving as a loop,
forest-dwelling humans will thus evade [us]; yet,
even here, some humans do not recognize this weapon.
For this *śamī* tree, born in a forest on a wrong path frequented by wild beasts and serpents,
with its wide-spreading branches inhabited by crows—
though it is difficult to climb, I look upon it with a heart bound by affection.
"O Bhārata, let us hang our weapons here, especially near this dense cemetery, and proceed toward the city; thus we shall dwell here according to our pleasure."
This *śamī* tree always removes evil;
it is the cause for the victory of processions and festivals. Here, the weapons have been arranged in their proper places.
Having fulfilled their desires and performed the auspicious rites for victory, those great heroes circumambulated the *śamī* creeper, bowed down, and then paid it homage.
Taking a lump of clay with his own garment,
the Diademed One first performed the purificatory rite;
the *śamī* tree pacifies sin, the *śamī* tree pacifies enemies.

The *śamī* tree pacifies diseases; the *śamī* accomplishes all purposes. By your grace, Rāma, having taken Sītā to the foot of a *śamī* tree, has achieved his goal and returned to the city; may it be so for me through your favor.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus to King Yudhiṣṭhira, the righteous-souled one,
O bull of the Bharatas, proceeded to lay down his weapons.
Having all equipped themselves with armor, those five, who were like immovable mountains,
took up their weapons, quivers, and swords of incomparable luster;
then King Yudhiṣṭhira spoke to Sahadeva.
"O hero, having climbed this *śamī* tree, deposit our weapons here.
Having thus instructed Dhananjaya, O bull of the Bharatas, Pārtha spoke again to him regarding the depositing of the weapons there.
By whom, as a single warrior on his chariot, the scorcher of foes conquered the gods, humans, and serpents,
as well as the *piśācas*, *uragas*, and *rākṣasas*,
and even the Nivātakavacas and Paulomas.
The joy of the Kurus conquered the invincible Kālakeyas and other prosperous regions;
that noble and loud-sounding [army] was the destroyer of hosts of enemies.
Pārtha unstrung the Gāṇḍīva, which brings fearlessness and with which that hero,
the scorcher of foes, protected Kurukṣetra; and when the bow had been stretched, that best of kings deposited his weapons for safekeeping.
The son of Dharma, possessed of great majesty, [is] the subjugator of all the worlds; resembling the coils of a serpent, adorned with jewels and gold,
he is a constant terror to the Dānavas and Rākṣasas.
Yudhiṣṭhira unstrung the inexhaustible bowstring of that [bow],
by which the lord Bhīmasena had conquered the Pañcālas in battle and alone had repelled many enemies during his conquest of the quarters.
Hearing the twang of his bow, the enemies fled in battle,
as if from the bursting of a mountain or the crash of a thunderbolt; by him,
O sinless one, the King of the Sindhus was seized.
By whom Krodhavaśa was slain on Mount Gandhamādana;
by whom that Pāṇḍava won the divine Saugandhika flower;
and by whom, having defeated the Trigartas in battle, he brought away the Traigarta maiden.
Bhīmasena removed the bowstring of that bow, which had a touch like Indra’s rainbow and was adorned with diamonds and gold. Then Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira called Nakula back once more.
He spoke [of that bow] by which you wish to slay all enemies in battle,
with which you conquered the Surāṣṭras, which resembles the Śārṅga and Gāṇḍīva bows,
is fashioned with gold, is of excellent substance, and is as beautiful as Indra’s rainbow.
"This bow is well-suited to you and very firm; it is adorned.
Therefore, loosen the string-noose and set aside the bow.
Having looked toward Sahadeva, the son of Dharma spoke again.
O crusher of enemies, having subdued the Kaliṅgas, the Southerners, and the Magadhas,
and by which very means you have consumed your foes in battle, O crusher of enemies—
having loosened that bowstring, take up your bow to lay it aside.
With that bow by which the Pāṇḍava conquered the southern quarter,
Nakula made his own bow stringless; with it,
that tamer of foes had defeated the Kaliṅgas and the Southerners.
With that bow by which the Pāṇḍava had conquered the western quarter,
the mighty-armed son of Mādrī— whose face was copper-hued and whose speech was measured— conquered the west.
The heroic Saṃkrandana drew back its bowstring in battle.

"Among his kin there was none equal to him in beauty; therefore, O Dhanañjaya, he was known by the name Nakula. By that lord, who followed the path of righteousness, the southern quarter was conquered.
Since there was nothing lighter than a shield for a warrior, the hero Sahadeva then rendered that weapon stringless. He also took up polished, long swords and costly quivers.
They placed together upon their bows arrows that were as sharp as razors and as swift as the Vipāśā river.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, gave instructions to Nakula.
"O hero, having climbed this *śamī* tree, cast down these bows,
as well as the weapons, the quivers, and the massive maces;
having bound them all together and wrapped them in cloths,"
Having climbed up so as to deposit these [weapons] upon that place surrounded by birds—
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Having climbed the great *śamī* tree, I shall set down our weapons."
Then, in that most terrible forest,
at the time of the Araṇī-parvan, that righteous-souled scorcher of foes,
Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, who had been granted boons, took up those weapons according to dharma.
That tiger among men,
Yudhiṣṭhira, having purified himself and bowed in his mind, spoke these words in sweet syllables.
Brahmā, Indra, Varada, Kubera, Varuṇa, Anila,
Rudra, Yama, Viṣṇu, Soma, Arka, and Dharma;
as well as the Earth, the intermediate space, the quarters, and the intermediate directions.
The Vasus, the Maruts, and the exceedingly radiant Agni;
those who roam by day and those who roam by night—
all the beings that have been enumerated here.
Having paid homage to those of excellent vows and having prostrated before them,
I have gone for refuge to them;
here [are] all weapons of great power.
I shall indeed perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) in the presence of Mahādeva, and I shall also perform it in the presence of Vāyu and of the lords of the forest together with the mountains.
"This pledge has been given by me in the presence of the Sun, the Moon, and the Wind:
it must be returned to me or to Pārtha at the completion of the thirteenth year.
This must not be given to Bhīma; this Vṛkodara is prone to anger."
Constantly agitated by indignation toward the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
and filled with envy born of anger, he might strike before his time has come;
otherwise, we would surely have to enter the forest once again.
"When the time is fully ripe, we shall slay the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
This is wealth, righteousness, pleasure, fame, lineage, and glory.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"All this and my very life are at your disposal; of this there is no doubt.
Having descended, that highly wise Pāṇḍava of true valor, the lord of men, embraced Bhīma around the neck and consoled him.
Having paid homage to the deities and circumambulated the *śamī* tree,
all those brothers together set out to go to the city.
Having climbed it, Nakula himself placed the bows upon it.
And there he set down the Gāṇḍīva bow along with four others in those places which he considered to be firm ground,
where he saw that rain would not fall for many years.
There, they bound those [bodies] very tightly with strong ropes;
and the Pāṇḍavas tied together the single corpse of the dead man.
Men will avoid this śamī tree from afar.
Smelling the putrid odor of a corpse tied up there, they said, "This mother of ours is one hundred and eighty years old," and they spoke thus: "By her we were born; she is indeed old."
"This is our family custom, practiced by our ancestors as well," they said, "for we are born upon this tree. Then,
departing from that tree, they spoke here and there.
Proclaiming their arrival even to the cowherds and shepherds, those subduers of enemies,
the sons of Pṛthā, destroyers of foes, approached the vicinity of the city.
There, those high-souled ones, placing devotion before them, [encountered] the difficult terrain.
Remembering her, they paid homage to the goddess who destroys all difficulties. Then, having been worshipped by all the Pāṇḍavas with concentrated minds,
she spoke these gracious words, smiling as she stood in the sky.

"O fortunate ones, you must not fear; you shall cross this difficult passage. Having sharpened your wits, you will obtain weapons; and having fulfilled your vow, O wise ones, you shall conquer even your enemies."
Having spoken thus, she vanished instantly, and the Pāṇḍavas were filled with wonder.
Vaiśampāyana said:
O lord of the earth, even as he was entering the beautiful city of Virāṭa...
O King, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī and your own great-grandfather, together with his brothers and Draupadī, praised the goddess with his mind,
being tormented by grief and sorrow, O Bhārata.
Having joined his palms in reverence and emerged from his forest dwelling,
he, endowed with supreme devotion, [worshipped] Durgā, the destroyer of misfortune,
the crusher of the pride of the demon Mahiṣāsura, who is honored by all the worlds.
To Gaurī, the daughter of the King of Mountains, the bestower of boons and the giver of fearlessness—[Yudhiṣṭhira gave her these names].
Yudhiṣṭhira bestowed these secret names upon them: Jaya, Jayanta, Vijaya, Jayatsena, and Jayadbala.
As Yudhiṣṭhira was proceeding toward the beautiful city of Virāṭa,
he mentally offered praise to the goddess Durgā, the sovereign of the three worlds,
who was born from the womb of Yaśodā and is the beloved sister of the Lord.
Born in the family of the cowherd Nanda, she is auspicious and the increaser of the lineage;
she is the one who caused Kaṃsa to flee and brought about the destruction of the Asuras;
she is the one who lifted up the surface of the stone and traveled through the midst of the sky.
And those who always remember the divine Śivā, the supreme master of illusion, who remembers Vāsudeva during the meritorious descent of the burden—
they indeed deliver them from sin, just as one rescues a weak cow from the mud.
Oṃ! Homage be to you, O goddess who grants boons, O maiden of lovely appearance; O daughter of the Lord of Asuras in your youthful state, Ghaṇṭālī, Vikaṭotkaṭā;
four-armed, four-faced, four-fanged, O great Asura-woman!
O Great Goddess, wielder of the great bow, victorious, bestower of victory; O Bhūtarātri, most fierce one, beloved of the eighth and ninth lunar days;
O tawny one, reddish-brown one, flame-like one, bestower of gold and precious metal!
O you of great fortune, like the moon and the sun; O you whose earrings blaze with lightning; O you who dwell between Mount Meru and Mount Vindhya; O you served by hosts of *apsarases*;
O Kālī, Kālī, Mahākālī, wielder of the sword and the *khaṭvāṅga* staff!

O Goddess who holds the excellent trident, O three-eyed Mistress of the World! O Goddess, the gods worship you on the full moon and the fourteenth day. As for me, I have been deprived of my kingdom and am especially powerless.
"I have come to you for refuge, O Goddess, Sovereign of the Gods.
The Goddess Śrī said:
"Protect me, O lotus-petal-eyed one; by truth, become my mistress."

"Listen, O child, O mighty-armed one: victory shall be yours in battle. Released by my grace and having slain the Kaurava host, you shall enjoy the kingdom made free of thorns together with your brothers."
Those people who shall recite this most secret hymn, which is purifying and destructive of evil, for them no fear exists—
whether in battle crowded with enemies, in a dispute, or in the peril of thieves.
"Whether on a journey or upon entering [the city], whoever shall remember me—
" Vaiśampāyana said:
"O Pāṇḍava, I shall accomplish all his tasks."
Having spoken thus to the Pāṇḍava, the goddess vanished on the spot.
Then, in accordance with their vows, they entered the great city,
intending to live in concealment within the kingdom for the thirteenth year.
Vaiśampāyana said:
As Yudhiṣṭhira was proceeding toward the delightful city of Virāṭa,
he mentally offered praise to the goddess Durgā, the sovereign of the three worlds.
Born from the womb of Yaśodā, the beloved recipient of Nārāyaṇa’s boon, she was born into the family of the cowherd Nanda; she is auspicious, the increaser of her lineage,
the one who puts Kaṃsa to flight, and the destroyer of the Asuras.
[He saw] Vāsudeva’s sister, cast down upon the surface of a rock, ascending toward the sky— divinely adorned with garlands,
wearing celestial garments, a goddess bearing a sword and a shield.
Having addressed the queen, the king, together with his younger brother and longing for a vision [of her], began once more to offer praise with various hymns:
"Homage be to you, O Kṛṣṇā, granter of boons, maiden, and observer of celibacy!"
O you whose form resembles the rising sun, whose face is like the full moon,
who possess four arms and four faces, with full hips and breasts,
wearing a peacock-feather bracelet and bearing armlets and bracelets.

O Goddess, you shine like Padmā, the consort of Nārāyaṇa; O sky-walker, your true form and your celibate life are radiant. You are dark-complexioned like Kṛṣṇa, and your face is like that of Saṃkarṣaṇa.
Bearing broad arms raised like the banner of Śakra,
she holds a vessel, a lotus, a bell, and that which on earth is the purity of woman;
she also holds a noose, a bow, a great discus, and various other weapons.
Adorned with ears graced by two perfectly formed earrings,
O Goddess, you shine with a face that rivals the moon,
further beautified by a variegated crown and a splendid arrangement of hair.
You shine with a girdle fashioned from the coils of a serpent, appearing like Mount Mandara here with its winding ridges;
you are resplendent with a raised banner made of peacock feathers.
By observing the vow of maidenhood (*kaumāra-vrata*), you have purified the triple heaven;
therefore, O Goddess, you are praised by the thirty gods and worshiped as well,
O destroyer of the demon Mahiṣāsura, for the sake of protecting the three worlds.

O best of goddesses, I am devoted to you; have mercy and be auspicious to me. You are Jaya and Vijayā, the bestower of victory in battle. Grant me victory as well, for you are the giver of boons even now.
Indeed, your eternal abode is upon the Vindhya, the best of mountains.
O Kālī, Kālī, Mahākālī, you who are fond of wine, meat, and animal sacrifice;
followed by all beings, you are the giver of boons, moving at will.
Those men on earth who shall remember you at the time of your descent as the burden-bearer,
and those who bow down to you at dawn—
for them, nothing whatsoever is difficult to obtain, whether in terms of progeny or wealth.

You rescue [beings] from distress; O Durgā, you are remembered as such by people. For men who have perished in wildernesses, those submerged in the great ocean, or those obstructed by bandits, you are the supreme refuge.
O Great Goddess, those men who remember you while crossing waters, or while in deserts and forests, do not come to grief;
for you are fame, fortune, fortitude, accomplishment, modesty, knowledge, progeny, and intelligence.
You are twilight, night, radiance, sleep, moonlight, beauty, patience, and compassion;
when worshipped, you shall destroy the bondage, delusion, loss of sons, depletion of wealth, disease, death, and fear of men.
Thus, fallen from my kingdom, I have come to you for refuge. O Goddess, Sovereign of the Gods, as I bow my head before you, protect me, O lotus-petal-eyed one; O Truth, be true to us!
"O refuge in times of distress, O you who are worthy of being sought for shelter, O you who are affectionate toward your devotees, be my refuge!
When the Goddess had been praised in this way, she revealed herself to the son of Pāṇḍu.
The Goddess said:
Having approached the king, he spoke these words:
"Listen, O King, O mighty-armed lord, to my words:
victory in battle shall be yours before long."
"By my grace, having conquered and slain the Kaurava host,
and having made the kingdom free of thorns, you shall once again enjoy the earth;
O King, together with your brothers, you will attain abundant joy."
And by my grace, there shall be happiness and health for you;
and to those in the world who shall proclaim [this], being free from stain,
I, being pleased, shall grant a kingdom, long life, a beautiful body, and sons.
Whether in exile or in the city, in battle or in the peril of enemies, in the forest, in a difficult wilderness, upon the ocean, or on a deep mountain—
O King, those who remember me shall be remembered by me just as I have been remembered by you.
Nothing whatsoever in this world shall be difficult for them to obtain. O Pāṇḍavas, whoever listens to or recites this supreme hymn with devotion, all their undertakings shall attain success.
"And by my grace, neither the Kurus nor the men dwelling there shall recognize any of you while you remain in the city of Virāṭa.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus to Yudhiṣṭhira, the subduer of enemies, the boon-granting goddess,
having provided protection for the Pāṇḍavas, vanished right there.
Vaiśampāyana said:
While proceeding toward the beautiful city of Virāṭa, Yudhiṣṭhira was then being praised as he [honored] the goddess Durgā, the sovereign of the three worlds,
who was born from the womb of Yaśodā and is dear to Nārāyaṇa’s offering.
Born in the family of Nanda the cowherd, auspicious and the increaser of the lineage; the one who caused Kaṃsa to flee and the destroyer of the Asuras;
she who was cast upon the surface of a rock and traveled through the midst of the sky.
And she remembers Vāsudeva, the divine, the supreme wielder of *māyā*.
Those who always remember that auspicious one during the meritorious descent of the burden—
she indeed delivers them from sin, just as one rescues a weak cow from the mud.
Desiring a vision of her, the king, together with his younger brother, addressed the goddess and once again began a hymn of praise composed of various eulogies:
"Homage be to you, O boon-granting goddess, O maiden of lovely appearance!"
O you who are more powerful than the lords of the gods, whose garland of bells resounds with fierce resonance;
O four-armed, four-faced, and four-tusked Great Goddess; O Great Devi, wielder of the great bow, bestower of victory, glory, and triumph!
O Bhūtarātri, most fierce one, you who delight in the eighth and ninth lunar days; O tawny one, ruddy one, flaming one, bestower of gold and refined gold;
you who possess a radiance equal to the moon and sun, with earrings blazing like lightning.
O Kālī, Kālī, Mahākālī, you who bear the sword and shield; O Goddess, giver of boons, three-eyed Mistress of the World, who dwells between Meru and Vindhya and is served by hosts of Apsaras!

O Goddess, you are worshipped on the fourteenth and the full-moon day; I am that very person, fallen from my kingdom and especially devoted to you. O Goddess, Sovereign of the Gods, I have come to you for refuge.
The Goddess said:
"Save me, O lotus-petal-eyed one; by truth, become my mistress.
"Listen, child of mighty arms, victory shall be yours in battle."
"Through my grace, having been liberated and having conquered the Kaurava host,
you shall enjoy the kingdom made free of thorns together with your brothers.
And this [knowledge] of mine is the most secret, purifying, and destroyer of sins."

Those who shall recite [this] with devotion, for them no fear exists. O Pāṇḍava, whoever shall perform my [rites] at the time of departure or at the time of entry, I shall accomplish all their undertakings.
