Having spoken thus to the Pāṇḍava, the goddess vanished on the spot.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Yudhiṣṭhira, proceeding toward the delightful city of Virāṭa—
Then he praised the goddess Durgā, the sovereign of the three worlds,
who had been cast upon the surface of a rock yet was moving through the expanse of the sky—
the sister of Vāsudeva, adorned with divine garlands.
Born from the womb of Yaśodā, the beloved sister of the Lord,
born in the family of the cowherd Nanda, Durgā, the sovereign of the three worlds,
who causes Kaṃsa to flee and brings about the destruction of the asuras.

Desiring a vision of the goddess, the king, together with his younger brother, addressed her— who was clad in divine garments and bearing a sword and a shield— and once again began to praise her with various hymns of praise.
Homage be to you, O Kṛṣṇā, the giver of boons, who observes the vow of maidenhood; whose radiance resembles the rising sun, whose face is like the full moon,
who possesses four arms, a slender waist, and full hips and breasts.
O Goddess, with the peacock-feather parasol and bearing the discus, sword, and mace, you shine like Padmā, the consort of Nārāyaṇa;
your beauty is that of one in the celibate life, and your conduct is irreproachable.
Those who always remember the auspicious one who removes the burden and brings merit—
you indeed deliver them from evil, just as one rescues a weak cow from the mud.
Her luster faded by her astonishment at Kṛṣṇa, her face bore a resemblance to Saṃkarṣaṇa’s.
Bearing two broad arms raised high like the banner of Śakra,
you cut down the Dānavas while brandishing a trident with three prongs;
your feet are adorned with anklets, armlets, and ornaments of bells.
His garment was smeared with fat and marrow; his chest was covered by a yellow cloth,
and from it hung a necklace as bright as moonbeams,
while he shone with two earrings the color of molten gold.
With a face like the orb of the moon, you shine here;
with your variegated crown and the arrangement of your hair, you are resplendent;
and with a hip-string resembling the coils of a serpent, you are radiant.
Indeed, you shine like Mount Mandara encircled by the serpent;
having undertaken the vow of lifelong celibacy, heaven was protected by you. For that reason, O Goddess, you are honored and always worshipped by the ṛṣis.

O Sovereign of the Gods, Great Goddess, Destroyer of the Asura Mahiṣa! I have sought refuge in you, O Best of Deities; show me mercy and be auspicious. You are Jaya and Vijaya, the bestower of victory in battle.
"You shall become well-pleased; remain with me now. For on the Vindhya, the best of mountains, there is indeed an eternal abode.
O Kālī, Kālī, Mahākālī, you who are fond of spirits, meat, and fat!"
O you who abide as the bestower of desires upon all beings and devotees,
may you grant boons to those men who, terrified by fear, shall remember you and who always bow down to you.
For them, nothing whatsoever is difficult to obtain, whether in terms of sons or wealth.
Because you constantly rescue them from misfortune, you are remembered as the excellent Durgā. [You save] those who are submerged even in wildernesses and those who have sunk into the great ocean.
For those who have fallen into the company of bandits, may you be their supreme refuge.
And those men who remember the Goddess when crossing waters, or while in wildernesses and forests, shall not come to grief.
You, who are like the twilight, night, radiance, sleep, moonlight, patience, forbearance, and compassion—
when honored, you shall destroy for them the suffering of bondage and slaughter, the loss of children, wives, and wealth, as well as the fear of disease and death.
Thus, fallen from my kingdom, I have come to you for refuge;
and bowing my head, O Goddess, Sovereign of the Gods,
protect me— you whose eyes are like lotus petals— and be true to us in your truth.
"O you who are compassionate toward those who have come for refuge, be my refuge in this difficult terrain of suffering.
Thus praised, that goddess revealed herself to the son of Pāṇḍu.
The Goddess Śrī said:
Having approached the king, he spoke these words:
"Listen, O King, mighty-armed one, and have faith in my words;
victory in battle shall be yours before long."
Having encountered and agitated the assembled host of the Kurus,
you shall once again enjoy the earth, having made the kingdom free of thorns;
O King, together with your brothers, you will attain abundant steadfastness.
And by my grace, you shall possess happiness and health;
and to those who, free from envy, shall praise me in the world,
I will grant contentment, sovereignty, long life, strength, and sons.
Whether in a village or a city, in battle or amidst the peril of enemies, in the forest, in an impassable wilderness, at sea, or in a mountain cave—
O King, those who remember me shall be remembered by me just as I have been remembered by you.
For them, nothing whatsoever in this world will be difficult to obtain. O Pāṇḍava, whoever should hear or recite this supreme and meritorious hymn, all their undertakings shall reach fulfillment.
"And by my grace, while they all dwell in the residence of Virāṭa,
neither the Kurus nor the men living there shall recognize them.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus to Yudhiṣṭhira, the subduer of enemies, that goddess,
having provided protection for the Pāṇḍavas, vanished right there.
Vaiśampāyana said:
As Yudhiṣṭhira was proceeding toward the beautiful city of Virāṭa,
he mentally offered praise to the goddess Durgā, the sovereign of the three worlds,
who was born from the womb of Yaśodā and is the beloved recipient of Nārāyaṇa’s boon.
Born in the family of Nanda the cowherd, she is auspicious and the increaser of the lineage;
she is the one who causes Kaṃsa to flee and strikes terror into the asuras;
she was cast against the surface of a rock and traveled through the midst of the sky.
He again began to praise Vāsudeva’s sister— who was adorned with divine garlands, clad in celestial garments, a goddess bearing a sword and a shield— with various hymns of praise.
Having addressed the queen, the king—desiring a vision of her and accompanied by his younger brothers—said:
"Homage be to you, O Kṛṣṇā, granter of boons, who observes the vow of perpetual maidenhood;
you whose radiance is like the rising sun and whose face resembles the full moon."
O you with four arms and four faces, with full hips and breasts, wearing a bracelet of peacock feathers, bearing a mace, a discus,
and a sword— salutations to you, O lotus-petal-eyed one; salutations to you, worshipped by the thirty gods.
O enemy of the gods, salutations to you; salutations to you, beloved of Paśupati.
O destroyer of the pride of the Daityas and Dānavas, worshipped by the Daityas and Dānavas; O Goddess, daughter of the King of Mountains, salutations to you who dwell in the Vindhya.
O you who are endowed with all weapons, O omniscient one, O omnipresent one, O eternal one; O unconquered one, O victorious one, O auspicious one, O Bhadrakālī, O lover of battle;
O Goddess Kṛṣṇā, salutations to you, salutations to the destroyer of Kaiṭabha!
Salutations, O Gāyatrī, O Sāvitrī; salutations to you, O Jātavedas. Salutations to you, O Mistress of Speech; salutations to you, daughter of Menakā.
Salutations to you who abide as half the body of Śaṅkara; salutations to you, who are worshipped by Viṣṇu.

The lord of the Matsyas, Virāṭa, replied joyfully:
Virāṭa said:
"Indeed, I grant you this boon for the kitchen."
And so you should act, for what you speak is indeed wholesome;
yet I do not consider that deed of yours to be equal [to its words],
for you deserve the earth girt by the ocean.
Just as the Guardian of the Three Worlds shines forth,
so do you shine upon me today like Viṣṇu. Whatever desire you have, that has been fulfilled.
"Be you my chief in the kitchen;
and those men who were previously appointed there by me— be you their lord, as appointed by me."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus appointed in the kitchen,
Bhīma became very dear to King Virāṭa.
He dwelt there, O King, and neither the common people nor any of his attendants there knew of him.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then that Kṛṣṇā, with her beautiful hair, lovely to behold and possessing a pure smile,
gathered up her faultless locks—
black, fine, soft, and long— with their tips curled, and having tied them together, she of the pure smile remained there.
The dark-eyed woman hid [the child] on her right side;
then, having put on a single large, very soiled black garment,
the men and women, beholding her, were struck with the utmost amazement.
Having assumed the guise of a *sairandhrī*, Kṛṣṇā wandered about as if in distress.
Having entered the city in the dress of a *sairandhrī*,
the timid woman was pursued by men and women as she ran along.
Upon seeing her, they asked, "Who are you, and what do you intend to do?
Then, O king of kings, she—clad in bark and deerskin with two torn pieces of cloth—said to them: "I have come here as a *sairandhrī*."
"I truly wish to perform the work of him who wishes to nourish me. Yet,
because of her appearance, her dress, and her gentle speech,
they did not believe that she was a maidservant who had arrived for the sake of food.
Now, Virāṭa’s wife, the highly esteemed Kaikeyī,
while looking out from her palace, beheld the daughter of Drupada.
Having observed her in such a state— helpless and clad in but a single garment— she [approached].
Surrounded on all sides by women and men,
the queen Virāṭa’s wife, overcome with compassion and agitation,
dispatched the elderly women standing nearby who were devoted to her service.
"Therefore, setting all others aside, bring her right here.
When I have seen that virtuous woman, my mind trembles;
therefore, if you wish [to please me], bring her here quickly and show her to me."
Having been thus addressed, they approached Draupadī as she sat gathered with her companions;
bringing her forward in every way, they spoke these sweet words:
"O blessed lady, Sudeṣṇā desires to see you upon the terrace of her palace."
"For it was for that purpose indeed that we have come here into your presence.
Then she, clad in bark and deerskin with her silken garments torn away,
approached the royal palace where the chief queen resided.

The illustrious Kṛṣṇā approached Sudeṣṇā, the king’s wife. Having tied up her long, soft, black hair— whose tips were curled, which was very fine, and which was beautiful to behold— the large-eyed lady [prepared herself].
The dark-eyed woman hid them on her right side;
having entered the inner apartments of Virāṭa, the beautiful Draupadī,
that young woman overcome by modesty, trembled like a creeper.
And having approached, that woman of beautiful hips, endowed with all auspicious marks,
beheld her seated upon a golden throne covered with jewels,
wearing fine red silk garments like lightning amidst a cloud.
Variegated with many colors and adorned with all kinds of ornaments,
she had beautiful brows, lovely hair, and shapely hips; she stood amidst hunchbacks and dwarfs upon the ground strewn with many flowers, like a sacrificial altar at a ritual.
Sudeṣṇā, the queen-consort, adorned with every ornament,
illustrious and surrounded by a hundred princesses—
all those supreme women were deeply distressed upon seeing Draupadī.
They rose suddenly from their seats and approached in haste;
they all gazed upon her as she had arrived like the goddess Śacī—
Kṛṣṇā, with concealed ankles, beautiful hips, and long, copper-hued eyes.

She possessed every limb beyond reproach, with a curved body and a slender waist; she was neither too short nor too tall, born in a forest thick with grass like an irreproachable female ruru deer, with beautiful hair and eyes like those of a doe.
Like a doe terrified and strayed from the herd, like the fortune of an elephant deprived of its troop;
like the large-eyed Lakṣmī, like illustrious Vidyā,
like Rohiṇī among the stars, or like a blazing crest of fire.
Like Rudrāṇī, the consort of Rudra; like the shore of the great ocean; like Sulabhā among the Nāga women; like a Kiṃnarī among the deer-women;
like the Gaṅgā with her pure limbs; like an autumnal night.
Sudeṣṇā, her eyes wide with wonder, questioned her who was most inconceivable in the world, illustrious like Ilā, as invincible as Sāvitrī, and endowed with the splendor of Brahman.
"Who are you, O lady of entirely faultless limbs? From where have you come here?
To whom do you belong, O large-eyed one, and what may I do for you?
Having thus addressed her, he said: "O blessed lady, who are you and what do you wish to accomplish?"
She said to her, "O Indra among kings, I have come here as a *sairandhrī*;
I wish to perform service for whoever will support me.
Sudeṣṇā said:
"O beautiful lady, they are not at all like what you describe;
indeed, they employ many such female and male servants.
Their ankles are hidden, their thighs are well-knit, they possess the three deep qualities and the six elevated features."
Reddish in complexion among those five who were red, speaking with a voice like a swan’s or a faltering whisper,
she possessed beautiful hair, fine breasts, and was dark-complexioned with full hips and bosom;
endowed with every such excellence, she was like a Kashmiri mare.
The queen of the universal monarch was a woman with red [complexion], possessing five auspicious marks;
her eyes had long, curved lashes, her lips were like the *bimba* fruit, and her waist was slender. Her neck was shaped like a conch shell, her veins were hidden, and her face resembled the full moon.
With eyes like the petals of an autumn lotus, with the fragrance of an autumn lotus,
and devoted to the autumn lotus, you are equal in beauty and splendor;
endowed with all the auspicious marks, you shall be the wife of the lord of the earth.

"Tell me, O blessed lady, who are you? For you do not appear to be a slave in any way. Are you a yakṣī, or perhaps a goddess, a gandharvī, or an apsaras? Are you a daughter of the gods, a daughter of the nāgas, or else a deity of the city?"
"Are you a Vidyādharī or a Kinnarī, or perhaps Rohiṇī herself?
Are you an Apsaras, or a Nāgī, or Tārā, O playful one? Are you Alambuṣā, Miśrakeśī, Puṇḍarīkā, or Mālinī?"
"Are you Menakā, or Ahalyā, or Rambhā, or Tilottamā?
Or are you Indrāṇī, or Vāruṇī, or the wife of Tvaṣṭṛ, Dhātṛ, or Prajāpati?
Among those goddesses renowned among the gods, O auspicious one, which of them are you?"
For your form is indeed incomparable, even when devoid of ornaments;
I believe that the Lord, the Creator of the world, ceased his work after fashioning you.
Women are never satiated by looking at it; what pleasure, then, could there be for men?
The forest deities, covered with clusters of coral-like flowers,
gaze upon you alone in wonder at the perfection of your form;
so too do the women within the inner apartments and the multitudes of beasts and birds.

"O auspicious one, everyone gazes at you alone in great wonder. O beautiful one, no woman like you has ever been seen or heard of by me before in the three worlds, nor does such a one exist in her physical form."
Having been addressed thus, Draupadī, the best of women, stood with her palms joined in reverence; filled with wonder, she spoke to Sudeṣṇā.
Draupadī said:
"I am neither a goddess, nor a Gandharva woman, nor an Asura, nor a Rākṣasī;
I am a Sairandhrī, a servant—this I tell you truly.
While my husbands were looking on, for a certain reason..."
Seized by the hair, I fled in terror to the forest;
there, for twelve years, subsisting on wild roots and fruits,
I wandered without shelter, O fair-browed one, and have now come into your presence.
"I know how to dress the hair and grind fine unguents; O auspicious lady, I fashion ear-ornaments from jasmine, blue lotuses, red lotuses, campakas,
sinduvāras, and jātis."
I shall grind lotus leaves, lotus stalks, aloe-wood, and yellow sandalwood;
I shall weave various garlands of supreme beauty,
thereby propitiating Satyabhāmā, the beloved queen of Kṛṣṇa.
And Kṛṣṇā, the wife of the Pāṇḍus, the peerless beauty of the Kurus—
by her I was well-supported and gratified with the attainment of my desires. Thus I wander here and there, obtaining what is most beautiful.
"As long as I obtain garments, so long shall I rejoice;
thus did that goddess herself give me the name Mālinī.
That dark-complexioned lady with eyes like lotus petals is my friend, dear to me as my own life."
"O fair-faced one, I do not wish to dwell anywhere for long;
this is indeed our vow, and such is the family custom of ours:
that whoever should take away our wealth, our land, or even our clothing [must be punished]."
"We must certainly not be angry, for our preceptor is free from wrath.
Thus, I have traversed difficult forests, sacred fords, lakes,
various delightful mountains, and rivers flowing to the ocean.
With my limbs overwhelmed by grief for my husband, I wander this difficult terrain as a fellow celibate student with my husband, making camp wherever evening falls,
since I am the wife of a hero whose husbands are now wandering abroad.

Desiring to dwell with you according to the prescribed rite, O sweet-spoken one, I have come from Mount Gandhamādana; for I have heard of your virtuous character and the greatness of your husband from the mouths of the brahmins.
I desire to attend upon you, and for that reason I have come here. My elders, as well as Dharma, Vāyu, Śakra, and the two Aśvins—
by their grace, no man can overcome me.
"O Queen Sudeṣṇā, I have come here to your residence. Sudeṣṇā said:
"I would indeed place you upon my head; of this I have no doubt."
"If the king here were to pursue you with his whole heart,
O fair-hipped one, I do not consider it right for me to have you living here in my house;
this would be a fault in this matter— what do you think, O timid one?"
"Behold the women in the royal palace, and those here in my own dwelling; they gaze at you with longing. What man would you not infatuate?
O woman of excellent complexion, they gaze only at you in wonder."
"Behold these trees standing here within my dwelling; they too seem to bow down before you. What man would you not infatuate?
You possess a supreme, superhuman, and wondrous form."
Even those born of the animal realm gaze upon you with wonder, O lady of faultless limbs; how much more so the humans on earth! O woman of beautiful hips, King Virāṭa beheld your superhuman form.
"O lady of beautiful hips, having abandoned me, he would follow you with his whole heart.
For that man whom you, O faultless-limbed one with long eyes,
might look upon with longing, would surely fall under the power of desire."
For whatever man you should look upon, well-bathed and adorned,
he shall experience neither exhaustion nor suffering, neither lethargy nor defeat;
he shall not grieve, nor be tormented, nor become angry, nor speak untruth.
O lady of entirely faultless limbs, whoever you should attend to while beautifully adorned—
for him there shall be no disease, no old age, no thirst, and no hunger;
for he with whom you, O fair-browed one, remain in his lap under his control.
Even if you have reached the state of death,
if you were to embrace him with your two well-proportioned arms, it is my conviction that he would return to life— for he whose wife you are, and whom you embrace with joy.
He would live longer than all the gods, like Purandara; yet,
O fair-browed one, just as a man might climb trees only for his own destruction,
so would it be for me if you were in the royal palace instead of in my house.
O lady of lovely smiles, any man who should constantly behold you,
O you of entirely faultless limbs, would likewise fall under the power of the bodiless god (Kāma),
just as a female crab conceives a fetus that brings about her own death.

"O lady of pure smiles, I consider such a dwelling as yours to be [unfit for me]. O Sairandhrī, I infer this of you; I do not despise you in any way. Yet, O blessed one, out of fear for my husband's character, I find no pleasure in staying with you."
Draupadī said:
"I am not to be obtained by Virāṭa, nor by anyone else in any way;
I cannot even be looked upon with an evil mind by gods, Gandharvas, or Yakṣas."
"O beautiful lady, I have five youthful Gandharva husbands,
the sons of a certain great-souled king of the Gandharvas;
they constantly protect me, for my conduct is such that it would lead to suffering."
And whatever mortal of immoral conduct should touch me with a wicked mind,
he shall quickly lie down that very night struck by pestles.
For even if one should have a full hundred of kinsmen here in this world—
O large-eyed one, whether it be a thousand or even ten million,
if one with a wicked mind should speak against me, he shall not live before you;
neither the gods of the thirty-three, nor the asuras, nor the pannagas can protect him.
They will undoubtedly provide protection from those Gandharva kings.
Sudeṣṇā, place your trust in me, whether toward your own kin or your relatives;
I cannot be touched by men, nor is my conduct such as that.
"He who would not give me his leftovers, nor would he wash my feet—
by dwelling with such a man, my Gandharva husbands would be pleased.
For whatever man should lust after me as he would any other common woman,"
Then, during that very night, he entered another body;
yet, O lady, I cannot be shaken by anyone,
for the Gandharvas are of a difficult disposition and they are more powerful than I.
"And even while remaining hidden, they protect me constantly, O lady of pure smiles.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"While I was living in this manner, let there be no fear for you."
Thus addressed by Sairandhrī, Sudeṣṇā spoke these words:
Sudeṣṇā said:
"I shall have you dwell here in such a manner as you desire, O Nandinī."

"You shall never touch my feet nor my leavings in any way. Stay here with me, O auspicious lady, if your conduct is such as this. And what man, O beautiful one, would deserve to give you his leavings?"

And what wise man, having seen Lakṣmī, would run away on his feet? Thus endowed with proper conduct and thus devoted to the divine, you are to be protected by all beings, just as Sāvitrī is by the twice-born.
"O auspicious one, O woman of excellent complexion, you are like a goddess, honored and worshipped.
Dwell with me, O blessed lady, being well-pleased, for my affection for you is great; remain here happily, endowed with all desires and with a mind free from anxiety."
Vaiśampāyana said: Thus consoled by the wife of Virāṭa, the virtuous Kṛṣṇā, devoted to her husbands,
dwelt in that city.
Then, free from apprehension, Yājñasenī entered the inner apartments of Virāṭa, O lord of the people, serving Sudeṣṇā; and no one else there knew her in her true identity, O Janamejaya.
Thus the Pāṇḍavas lived in Virāṭa’s kingdom;
likewise, the beautiful Kṛṣṇā, having entered the inner apartments,
remained there with her mind constrained by the life of concealment.
Just as fires have their brilliance concealed by ashes.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Sahadeva also, having assumed the unsurpassed dress of cowherds, [entered the city].
Then, adopting their speech, he approached Virāṭa. Having reached the cow-pen, he stood near the palace;
seeing him there, the king was filled with wonder and dispatched his men.
Beholding that bull among men approaching, resplendent as he was, the king rose to meet him and questioned that joy of the Kurus:
"Whose are you? From where do you come? And what, my dear, do you intend to do?"
"For you have never been seen by me before; tell me the truth, O bull among men.
Having approached the king, that scorcher of enemies then spoke with a voice like the roar of a massive cloud.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then another appeared, like the moon,
resembling a sacrificial fire fed with oblations at a ritual sacrifice.
Thus was he of beautiful appearance beheld,
like the radiant sun that has just risen;
Sahadeva, the leader, [beheld] him as he approached.
King Virāṭa soon beheld him;
there, all the members of the assembly gathered together gazed upon him,
whose splendor was captivating to all minds.
A youth approaching, the crusher of enemies,
like the orb of the moon released from the clouds,
handsome and endowed with a staff of proper proportions.
Having tied a leather strap and a noose behind him,
he also wore a large, well-woven girdle of muñja grass,
which was completely covered with many hair-straps.
And that powerful one spoke to the king:
"O King, station me among the cattle;
for let your livestock be protected by me."
O Ballava, I am one whose sleep has vanished; there is no fear for me from wild beasts nor from disease,
nor is there any fear for them from thieves.
O lord of men, when cows are well-tended, they become abundant in milk, prolific, and free from disease;
having heard these words spoken by Sahadeva, the king—
Having gazed upon the son of Mādrī, he greeted him;
pleased and with a joyful heart, he said:
"O hero, I do not perceive any deficiency in you."
By your fortitude, your body appears here as firm as that of a Kṣatriya, or like one born of the Kaurava lineage;
this form of yours does not appear unlearned.
"Abide here in my kingdom as a bearer of my counsel and dharma; rule these Matsyas along with their kings,
just as Bṛhaspati rules the immortals joined with Śakra."
O Suveṣa, protect my army in every way;
take up a sword worthy of yourself,
you who hold the tip of the spear-head at the head of my forces.
"May you be our lord; take up the bow.
Thus addressed by King Virāṭa, that best of the Kurus praised the king and bowed down to him.
The high-minded one spoke to the foremost of fish:
"Listen, O King, to my supreme words;
for I am but a child, defiled by the lowliness of my birth."
"O Lord of Men, where is my skill in policy and counsel today? We are content with our own duties;
O sinless one, command me to protect the cows."
"I am a Vaiśya named Ariṣṭanemi; I was formerly the cattle-counter for the bulls of the Kuru lineage.
O best of men, I wish to dwell with you."
I do not know those lion-like kings, the sons of Pṛthā;
it is not possible to live by any other occupation,
and no king other than you pleases me, O King.
Virāṭa said:
"Are you a Brāhmaṇa or perhaps a Kṣatriya? You possess the form of a lord whose domain is the ocean-girdled earth."
Tell me the truth, O crusher of enemies;
the work of a Vaiśya does not befit you at all.
From the territory of which king have you come here?
Moreover, what craft have you mastered? How will you live among us forever?
Tell us also what your wages here shall be.
Sahadeva said:
"Among the five sons of Pāṇḍu, King Yudhiṣṭhira is the eldest;
he possesses eight hundred thousand herds of cattle, each consisting of hundreds."
There were ten thousand others, and twice as many more besides;
among them was one who counted the cattle, whom they knew as Tantipāla.
Whatever has been, whatever is to be, and whatever will be—whatever can be numbered anywhere—he knew it all.
Within ten yojanas in every direction, there is nothing unknown to me; indeed,
the virtues of that great-souled one were well known to me,
and King Yudhiṣṭhira of the Kurus was highly pleased with me.
Cows multiplied many times over are difficult to comprehend and are exceedingly great;
cows that yield much milk are numerous, and they quickly produce offspring. Indeed, cows multiply rapidly.
No disease whatsoever occurs among them here;
this has been understood by me through various means,
for these arts reside within me.
"O King, I also know bulls endowed with auspicious marks,
by smelling whose urine even a barren woman gives birth," said Vaiśampāyana.
The lord of the Matsyas, with a heart full of joy,
addressed the Pāṇḍava, the son of Mādrī:
"I do not approve at all of this contemptible deed of yours."
You ought to protect the entire earth;
however, O Lord, if it now pleases you,
look upon my cattle as you wish.
"May my cattle indeed be dedicated to you.
King Virāṭa spoke thus to that most excellent man.
Virāṭa said:
I give you a hundred thousand well-composed cattle, each determined by its specific qualities and accompanied by their keepers.
"May my cattle here be under your protection.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O lord of people, thus he remained unknown to the king."
The lord of men dwelt there in comfort,
and no others knew of his presence in any way whatsoever; moreover,
he provided him with sustenance according to his desire.
Having thus met with Virāṭa and obtained the position of a cowherd at his pleasure, the high-souled Pāṇḍava lived there in concealment.
Just as the sun has set behind the western mountain,
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then another [being] was seen, endowed with perfect beauty.
A large man, wearing women’s ornaments— having fastened earrings upon the ramparts and walls, as well as long, beautiful conch-shell necklaces and golden bracelets— stood there.
Having put on two garments, one black and one long,
he whose body possessed the splendor of Śakra and Bṛhaspati scattered his hair, both thick and long.
Possessing mighty arms and the prowess of an elephant in rut,
he did not shine with his effeminate appearance; yet he still shone,
like the moon in the sky when seized by an eclipse.
Then, shaking the earth as he went,
he approached Virāṭa near the assembly hall;
seeing him arrived at the floor of the assembly, the king [observed him].
Clad in armor, crushing his enemies,
shining with supreme splendor,
the son of Mahendra possesses the prowess of a lordly elephant.
And he questioned all those who were moving about nearby:
"From where does this man come? I have never heard of him before.
But at that time, the men did not say they knew him.
King Virāṭa, who moved with the grace of a lordly elephant and the gait of the king of beasts, spoke these words in wonder:
Whose son is this man with the eyes of a bull, possessing fierce splendor,
with thick shoulders and arms, radiant as gold—
who is he that has entered my city?
Is he the son of the Lord of Gods? Is he the son of Brahmā? Or is he the Self-Existent One? Or perhaps the son of Umā, or the son of Vaiśravaṇa?
"Having beheld him, he sat down; such is my conjecture," said Vaiśampāyana.
And having passed through the assembly hall, he who resembled Vāsava—
Being gazed upon by many who had gathered there,
that slayer of enemies spoke to the king:
"O god among men, I am Bṛhannalā, a dancer."
I shall arrange my braid and put on beautiful earrings; I shall string garlands and gather my upper garments;
I shall prepare for my bath and polish the mirror.
My skill lies precisely in these specialized arts:
in [acting as] eunuchs, children, and water-deities;
and I possess the fitness for providing instruction in dance.
"I place flower-filled ornaments upon their braided hair;
no women possess greater skill than I in this craft.
Looking up at that tall man, he spoke to him in wonder:
The highly illustrious one approached King Virāṭa— a man endowed with every excellence, pleasing to the mind,
dark-complexioned, youthful, and resembling the leader of a herd of elephants.
"Know who this is standing before me;
let him obtain without delay whatever he desires. While the Slayer of the Enemy was thus reflecting,
Having approached the king, the slayer of enemies said:
"O god among men, O subduer of foes, I am Bṛhannaḍā, a dancer; I have come to serve you."
"O King, enjoy me today as I have come to you;
for I am indeed your dancer. Having cast off my beautiful conch-shell and golden bracelets,"
Having loosened your braid and put on your earrings,
O fair-haired one, let your hair be tied in a topknot and your garments changed; likewise, become equipped with a bow, armor, and arrows.
"Ascend the vehicle and drive about;
be equal to my sons, or be equal to me.
For I am indeed old and desire to be exempt from such duties."
Protect all the fish with your might! It does not seem possible to my mind that those of such a nature could ever be of a weak or effeminate form.
This feeble attire does not befit you;
O lion among god-kings, such lack of manliness is unworthy of you.
This dress of yours is [unfitting] for one adorned with beautiful ornaments.
Adorned like the Lord of Beings (Śiva),
he shines like the sun garlanded with rays,
like the sun when its path in the sky is obstructed by clouds.
Indeed, I believe that a bow would adorn your arms,
for they are so exceedingly full and long;
having taken up a bow worthy of yourself, [you would shine].
Protect the country and the city today, remaining well-established; O Bṛhannalā, be like a son to me. I am old; I entrust this wealth to you.
"O Lord, protect all this city for me;
I do not perceive any impotence in you.
Rule over the Matsyas, causing them to flourish through your prowess."
Vaiśampāyana said:
"I grant you the kingdom; I am true to my word.
Before him, the king [placed] his own bows.
Desiring to know what he would do, he took up many bows that were long, beautiful, strung, and endowed with power.
Then Arjuna spoke words even more dejected:
"O Lord, my bow has never been wielded in such a manner,
nor has a bow such as this ever been seen by me anywhere."
"There are no archers like me on earth.
Arjuna said:
"I sing, I dance, and I play musical instruments;"
"I am skilled in dance and proficient in song. O god among men, give me yourself to Uttarā; I shall become the dancer for the queen."
"But what is the use of proclaiming this form of mine, which only increases my intense grief?
O god among men, know me indeed as Bṛhannaḍā."
"Whether it be a son or a daughter, provided they are devoid of father and mother," Virāṭa said,
"I grant you this boon, O Bṛhannaḍā!"
"Teach my daughter to dance, and those others like her;
for there is no one in my house,
whether man or woman, who acts as an adversary."
"But this deed of yours is not, in my opinion, equal [to your status];
you deserve the earth bounded by the ocean.
Then Virāṭa himself called for his daughter.
And the lord of men spoke with a joyful heart to that beautiful woman of slender waist:
"Let this one be your friend, named Bṛhannaḍā."
O fair-limbed one, you are bound by a friendship of great affection; O lady, you are always as dear to me as my own life,
beautiful, and adorned with garments, ornaments, and abundant food.
Having wandered among all people without restriction,
this form of hers could not belong to one of low birth; nor would such a person be one who breaks her conduct.
Having spoken thus, the king, after having her examined by men in due order, commanded that his daughter— who had arrived with the women— be made to dance.
Having observed Bṛhannalā, who was perceived as a eunuch, in the palace,
the lord of men thus commanded his daughter:
"Let her be properly ushered into your house."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having beheld Bṛhannaḍā, the King of the Matsyas [observed her] in the arts,
as well as in dance and instrumental music.
Having consulted with his various ministers and having quickly tested him with women, the king confirmed that his impotence was indeed permanent.
Then the lord Dhanañjaya sent him to the maidens' quarters; there he instructed Virāṭa’s daughter in singing and instrumental music.
He became a friend to her attendants and likewise their beloved;
thus did Dhananjaya dwell there in that sacrificial session.
While the self-possessed one was performing pleasant acts together with them,
the people there— whether they moved outside or moved within— did not recognize him as the Tathāgata.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then another lordly Pāṇḍava appeared,
as King Virāṭa was inspecting his horses.
Ordinary people beheld him as he approached,
like the orb of the sun released from the clouds; indeed,
they gazed upon those horses here and there.
And as he was looking on, the king of the Matsyas saw him; then that slayer of enemies spoke to his followers:
"From where does this man come, possessing the splendor of an immortal?"
Having thus seen that best of the Kurus,
he then questioned all the members of the assembly:
"Who indeed has previously beheld him?"
"This youth who approaches my assembly is indeed dear to me and esteemed even by the mere sight of him. Let someone say whether they have seen him before."
"He is gazing intently at my horses;
he is certainly an expert horseman and discerning.
Let him be brought quickly into my presence."
The hero shone indeed like an immortal;
approaching the king, the slayer of enemies said:
"May victory be yours, O ruler of the earth, and may prosperity attend you."
"O King, I am skilled with horses and always esteemed by men; I shall be your expert horse-charioteer. While the King of Matsya was still deliberating thus, [the charioteer spoke].
Hurrying, the bull among the Kurus arrived;
then, having bowed down and approached, that best of the Kurus spoke to King Virāṭa, the ruler of the earth.
"O Lord of the Earth, I have come to your city today seeking to live by means of a wage;
may I become your well-paid horse-keeper."
"Make me the lord of horses, if you so desire.
Virāṭa said:
"I shall give you vehicles, wealth, and a residence."
"You ought to become my horse-charioteer.
From where do you come? To whom do you belong? How have you arrived?
Tell me what craft you possess."
Nakula said:
"O crusher of foes, King Yudhiṣṭhira is the eldest of the five sons of Pāṇḍu; by him I was formerly appointed to the care of the horses."
I know the nature of horses and their training in every respect, as well as the behavior of those that are wayward and the entire science of their medical treatment.
Not one of my mounts would ever be timid.
"I have no she-mule, much less horses;
yet people call me that, and even Yudhiṣṭhira the Pāṇḍava calls me by the name Granthika."
Like Mātali, the charioteer of the Lord of the Gods, or Sumantra, the driver of King Daśaratha,
or Sahasāha, the driver of Jamadagni— so too, by your command, O Indra among kings, shall I guide your horses at the bidding of King Yudhiṣṭhira, the sovereign of men.
"I am the protector of hundreds of thousands of millions of horses.
Virāṭa said:
"Whatever horse-drawn vehicles I possess,"
Let all that indeed be under your control today;
moreover, let whoever are my horse-groomers and my charioteers likewise have you as their refuge.
"O one who resembles a god, if this is indeed what you desire,
tell me what wealth you have envisioned; for the work of horses does not seem suitable for you."
For you shine like a king esteemed by me; indeed,
O one of pleasing appearance, this sight of you is equal to the sight of Yudhiṣṭhira himself.
"But how does that blameless Pāṇḍava live and find delight in the forest, deprived as he is of his servants?
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus that youth, resembling the most excellent of Gandharvas,
was honored by the joyful King Virāṭa;
yet no others knew him at all.
Thus did the Pāṇḍavas dwell among the Matsyas, wandering about charmingly and agreeably,
their vision unfailing according to their vows.
Concentrated in mind, they practiced their life in concealment;
the lords of the earth, bounded by the ocean, were exceedingly distressed.
Janamejaya said:
"O twice-born one, while the Pāṇḍavas of great prowess were thus dwelling there in the city of Matsya, what did they do after that? Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus those descendants of Kuru lived there in concealment, serving the king; hear now what they did. This was by the grace of Tṛṇabindu and of the high-souled Dharma.
Thus Yudhiṣṭhira lived in the city of Virāṭa during his period of living incognito; as a courtier, he became beloved by the members of the assembly,
and likewise by Virāṭa and his sons, O lord of the people.
For that Pāṇḍava, knowing the secret heart of the dice,
made them play at his will in the gambling hall like birds bound by a string;
and the King of Dharma, having won the wealth, remained unknown to Virāṭa.

That tiger among men would distribute [the wealth] to his brothers according to their merit; Bhīmasena, moreover, sold the meats and various kinds of edible foods that had been granted by the fisherman to Yudhiṣṭhira.
Arjuna sold the worn-out garments he had obtained in the inner apartments and gave them to all the Pāṇḍavas. Sahadeva, the son of Pāṇḍu, likewise assumed the guise of a cowherd.

And because he served as the superintendent, Nakula, who was intent on performing auspicious deeds, received from the king and bestowed upon the Pāṇḍavas curds, milk, and ghee; Nakula likewise obtained wealth for having performed the work of the horses.
When that king was pleased and was about to bestow [gifts] upon the Pāṇḍavas,
he saw well-trained bulls consecrated by Sahadeva;
delighted, the king then gave them much wealth.
The ascetic Kṛṣṇā, too, observing all those brothers, moved about as a beautiful woman so that she remained unrecognized. Thus did those great chariot-warriors arrange matters with one another.

O lord of men, at that time the sons of Pāṇḍu lived incognito in the city of Virāṭa, like those still dwelling in the womb; they remained there full of apprehension out of fear of the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
while keeping watch over Kṛṣṇā.

Then, in the fourth month, there was a magnificent festival for Brahmā among the Matsyas, which was prosperous and highly esteemed by the people. O King, thousands of wrestlers gathered there from all directions.
O King, in the assembly of Brahmā as well as of Paśupati,
there were great-bodied and highly powerful Asuras, like the Kālakhañjas, endowed with heroism,
fierce in strength, and honored by the king.
With shoulders, hips, and necks like those of lions, they were fair-complexioned and high-spirited; having repeatedly achieved their mark in the arena in the presence of kings,
one among them was great and challenged all the wrestlers.
As he was leaping about in the arena, no one would come near him;
even Kīcaka could not then overpower that wrestler by force,
for all those wrestlers were despondent and their spirits were broken.
With their faces cast downward, the mallas were terrified and distraught;
others, utterly overwhelmed, seemed as if they wished for death itself.
Some desired to enter the earth, while others, having risen up, seemed as if they wished to go into the sky.
Terrified, exhausted, with dejected limbs, silent and with eyes rolling in agitation—
those wrestlers of King Virāṭa were broken-hearted and shorn of their luster;
slain by the lord of wrestlers, they all said nothing at all.
Looking at those terrified wrestlers, the wrestler spoke these words: "O King,
know me to be the king of wrestlers who has arrived upon this entire circle of the earth,
sporting together with lions, tigers, and elephants."
Having heard the words of Mallendra, which were filled with pride in his strength,
Virāṭa looked at those wrestlers who were terrified and spoke these words:
"What man is capable of fighting with this wrestler?"
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, having heard the words of the lord of the Matsyas, replied:
"O Great King, there is a wrestler whom I have seen, O Yudhiṣṭhira;
he is capable, O Lord of the Earth, of fighting with this wrestler."
“That wrestler whom I previously saw in the city of Yudhiṣṭhira—
he is this very wrestler, O King, who now dwells in your kitchen.
Having heard these words of Yudhiṣṭhira, the king spoke clearly.
"Let him also be summoned quickly to fight with the wrestler in the assembly.
Then Bhīmasena, having been challenged and urged by Virāṭa, spoke these words: "O King, I am able to fight."
O Lord of Men, by your majesty, your splendor, your power, and your command,
O Indra among kings, I shall be able to fight with this wrestler,
once I have learned the feat performed by Yudhiṣṭhira through your glory, O Lord of the People.
"And out of devotion to Mahādeva, I shall bring that wrestler down. Thus urged, Bhīmasena challenged the wrestler to the arena;
then the King of Matsya had him fight with the cook.
A friction arose between the two of them, like that between two mountains rubbing against each other.
Then King Matsya had Kīcaka fight with the wrestler;
being thus urged on, Bhīma made up his mind out of sheer distress.
For he could not openly refuse the lord of men;
therefore, that tiger among men, moving with the relaxed gait of a śārdūla,
entered the great arena, gladdening Virāṭa.
Then the son of Kuntī, gladdening the people, fastened his girdle;
thereafter Bhīma challenged that wrestler, who resembled Vṛtra,
named Jīmūta, whose prowess was renowned.
Seizing the wrestler by the side, he roared upon the earth like a lion.
Both were possessed of great energy and both were endowed with fierce prowess;
they were like two massive-bodied, sixty-year-old elephants in rut.
The two heroic wrestlers, possessing strength equal to bulls and prowess like that of lions,
fell upon each other like two elephants intoxicated with rut.
Then, springing up with speed, he seized the wrestler by the side.
Grasping the side with his hand, he knocked the wrestler down.
Then those two tigers among men engaged in a wrestling match,
both heroes exceedingly joyful and each desiring victory over the other.
The clash was most terrifying, like that between a thunderbolt and a mountain;
both were exceedingly thrilled, both possessed of supreme strength, each seeking the other's weak point and desiring victory over the other.

Both were supremely thrilled, like two great elephants in rut, engaging in various wonderful counter-attacks with their arms in a state of intense conflict, through collisions, shakings, crushing blows,
and violent agitations.
With throws of the arms and with fists, with sounds like those of a boar shaking its head, with slaps of the palms like the falling of thunderbolts, with outstretched hands,
and likewise with strikes of the fingernails and terrible kicks of the feet.
With knees that struck like the crashing of stones and with heads that collided,
that battle became a terrible one, fought without weapons through the power of their arms,
by the strength and vitality of those heroes in the presence of the festive assembly.
O King, all the people were filled with delight, rising up with shouts of acclaim at the encounter of those two powerful warriors, which was like the battle between Vṛtra and Vāsava,
characterized by dragging forward, pulling back, drawing near, and thrusting away.
Then they pulled each other toward one another and struck with their knees;
thereafter, scolding each other with a great roar,
both broad-chested, long-armed, and skilled in wrestling grappled together.
They locked together with their arms like iron clubs;
then Bhīma, the slayer of enemies, uprooted the roaring and shouting wrestler with his two arms,
just as a tiger seizes an elephant.
Lifting him up, the mighty-armed and heroic one whirled him around;
then the wrestlers and the people of Matsya were filled with the utmost amazement.
This drawing back and bringing [the opponent] into one's embrace is described as *prakarṣaṇa*.
Drawing him toward him with ease, he brought him face-to-face;
having whirled him around a hundred times until he was lifeless and unconscious,
the mighty-armed Vṛkodara crushed the wrestler upon the ground.
When that world-renowned Malla Jīmūta had been slain,
Virāṭa, together with his kinsmen, attained supreme joy.
Out of that great delight, the high-minded king bestowed much wealth.
Like Vaiśravaṇa bestowing wealth upon Ballava in the great arena,
so did he, by slaying many wrestlers and men of great strength,
bring supreme joy to the King of Matsya.
When no man at all was found there who was his equal,
he then fought with tigers, lions, and even elephants;
and Virāṭa bestowed upon him various kinds of jewels.
Having given wealth to the men who stood there, Vṛkodara departed;
having returned once more to the inner apartments,
he was made to fight by Virāṭa with lions that were intoxicated and possessed of great strength.
Bibhatsu, the son of Pāṇḍu, also gratified Virāṭa with his singing and well-spoken verses, as well as all the women of the inner apartments, by means of well-trained,
swift horses that were brought together from here and there.
Nakula gratified the king, O best of kings;
pleased, the king bestowed upon him much wealth as a gift.
Seeing those cows, healthy and yielding abundant milk, the lord of men [was delighted].
Delighted, the powerful and great King of Matsya bestowed vast wealth upon Sahadeva, O Lord; and seeing his well-trained bulls,
Virāṭa, that bull among men, gave him many kinds of riches.
In that very manner, the King of Matsya himself bestowed much wealth;
pleased with him, that monarch gave him a vast amount of riches,
including cows with their calves, and Virāṭa was filled with wonder.
At that time, the king, being pleased, gave much wealth to him;
yet, O King, beholding all those great car-warriors suffering because of Draupadī,
he was not at all joyful in mind and became intent on sighing.
Thus those bulls among men lived there in disguise,
performing services for King Virāṭa at that time.
Vaiśampāyana said:
While the Pārthas were living incognito in the city of Matsya, ten months passed by while those great car-warriors remained concealed.
O lord of the people, Yājñasenī served Sudeṣṇā.
O Janamejaya, she who deserved to be served lived in great misery.
While the princess of Pañcāla was living thus in the quarters of Sudeṣṇā,
she gratified that queen as well as the women of the inner apartments.
When that year had almost passed, the mighty Kīcaka,
the commander-in-chief, returned from battle after conquering the gateway; there,
the general of Virāṭa beheld her whose face was like a lotus.

Seeing her, who was like the offspring of a god, moving about like a deity, Kīcaka— afflicted by the arrows of love— desired her, even as a dog might covet the sacrificial oblation purified by mantras that lies beside the altar.
But he, tormented by the fire of desire, approached Sudeṣṇā and,
as if laughing, the commander of the army spoke these words:
"Never before has she been seen here by me."
In the palace of King Virāṭa,
that beautiful woman greatly intoxicates me with her form; by her fragrance, that passionate lady is like wine itself.
"O auspicious one, who is this woman of divine form who has entered my heart? Tell me, who is she and from where does this beautiful lady come?
For, having churned my mind, she brings me under her sway."
And I do not consider any other medicine for this to be effective today.
Oh! This beautiful attendant of yours appears to me as one of exceptionally fresh beauty.
For you perform actions that are improper; therefore,
let me rule over whatever I possess—
abounding elephants, horses, and chariots, and great wealth.
Let this [woman] adorn my great house, which is endowed with prosperity, filled with abundant food and drink, enchanting, and decorated with variegated golden ornaments.
Then, having taken leave of Sudeṣṇā, Kīchaka approached the daughter of the king and spoke to Kṛṣṇā, attempting to conciliate her.

"Like a jackal toward the daughter of the king of beasts in the forest—Who are you, whose are you, O auspicious one? From where have you come, O lovely-faced one? Tell me the truth, O beautiful lady, as to why you have arrived at the city of Virāṭa."
Your form is supreme, as is your luster and your unsurpassed delicacy. Your face shines with such radiance, stainless like the moon;
your large, auspicious eyes, O lady of beautiful brows, resemble the petals of a lotus.

O lady whose every limb is beautiful, your speech is like the song of the cuckoo. O woman of lovely hips, such a woman as you, O blameless one, has never before been seen by me anywhere on this earth.
"O slender-waisted one, are you Lakṣmī whose abode is the lotus, or are you Bhūti?
Are you Hrī, Śrī, Kīrti, or Kānti—whichever among these are you, O fair-faced one? For you possess an exceeding beauty, sporting as you do with the limbs of the Bodiless One."
O fair-browed one, you shine exceedingly with a splendor unsurpassed even by the moon;
and your beautiful eyelashes, radiant like the moonlight of a smile,
are encompassed by divine rays of light, possessing celestial beauty and charm.
Beholding your moon-like face endowed with incomparable splendor,
who in this entire world would not fall under the sway of desire?
Both your breasts are exceedingly beautiful and worthy of being adorned with pearl necklaces.
O fair-browed one of lovely smiles, your two breasts are well-formed, symmetrical, endowed with beauty, full, rounded, and close together; shaped like the buds of lotuses,
they prick me like the goads of Love.

O slender-waisted one, this waist of yours is measured by the tips of the fingers, elegantly marked with folds and bent down by the weight of your breasts; and having seen your beautiful hips, which resemble the sandy banks of a river, [I am filled with longing].
"O beautiful lady, this incurable disease of passion assails even me; and the fire of love blazes like a merciless forest conflagration,
intensified by my longing for union with you."
O lady of excellent limbs, extinguish the blazing fire of passion with the rain of self-sacrifice from the cloud that is our union;
for the volleys of Cupid’s arrows are maddening my mind.

O moon-faced one, these sharp and intense arrows of hope for union with you— cruel, violent, fierce, and harsh— have entered my heart after piercing it mercilessly and with great speed, O lady with dark-cornered eyes.
These undertakings of yours, which cause me such extreme intoxication and bring about a madness of joy,
you ought to fulfill here by granting me the enjoyment of surrendering yourself;
for you are wearing wonderful garlands and garments, adorned with every ornament.

"O playful one, enjoy yourself with me as much as you desire; you ought not to dwell in unhappiness, for you are worthy of happiness yet deprived of it. O lady of languid gait, receive from me the highest bliss."
Drinking various delicious drinks that were like nectar, they took delight in those pleasing things as they pleased;
they enjoyed diverse articles of luxury and unsurpassed good fortune.
"Drink, O illustrious lady, and enjoy unsurpassed and auspicious pleasures! This beauty of yours and this prime of youth, O beautiful woman, are now entirely without purpose."
"O beautiful one, though you are naturally radiant, you do not shine like a supreme garland that has not been worn;
I shall abandon those who were my former wives."
"O lady of lovely smiles, let them be your slaves;
and I too, O beautiful one, shall always remain like a slave, subject to your will, O fair-faced one."
O beautiful one, my mind is captivated by the quality of your beauty; your birth has been rendered purposeless,
for you were never seen by me here before.
In the beautiful residence of King Virāṭa, you delight my mind with your beauty. O fair-limbed one, whose are you? From where have you come? And who are you?
"O you with wide copper-hued eyes, I am your slave; O you who walk with the playful gait of an elephant, I follow your will;
O blameless one, I have been struck by the force of Kandarpa."
Like a bird intoxicated by flowers in the springtime,
you whose appearance is thus encompassed by proper conduct do not deserve to serve other women.
"O dark-eyed, long-eyed beauty, why do you yourself arrange your hair in the royal palace, O passionate lady?
For other women would surely perform this task for you."
O you of lovely eyes, your visible form is like a cluster of blossoms that, though not being held by people,
withers away, O fair-limbed one of beautiful smile.
"I renounce those who were my wives in the past;
I shall become your slave and remain obedient to you.
O fair-limbed one, I swear this to you by my own good deeds."
Just as you are established in my heart,
O lady of blameless eyes, so are you worthy of me;
therefore, reflect upon yourself here in that same way.
This is evident to you, O lady of lovely appearance:
just as our ages are equal, so too are our bodies;
for here is a beautiful vessel filled with abundant jewels.
Indeed, even today, others have built for me a supreme residence,
a palace with a series of upper stories and wide gateways,
resembling the abodes of Kubera and Parjanya.
Whatever is in that dwelling belongs to me; whatever has come to me through the power of my wealth, all that I give to you, O lady of tremulous eyes.
O lady of beautiful limbs, you are the vessel for all of this—
abundant beds, seats, drinks, and food;
having entered therein, dwell there happily for a long time.
I take refuge in the God who has the bull as his banner,
the three-eyed one, the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice—
Hara, Bhava, Sthāṇu, the Lord of Umā, the Sovereign.
O fair-browed one, may he grant me union with you today;
having united with you, O lovely-eyed one,
[I shall behold] the six-faced one with twelve blazing eyes.
O you of excellent limbs, I, being pleased by this boon, shall gratify you who are worthy of boons, the giver of boons, and the lord of boons;
for this king is a restrainer of enemy armies.
O beautiful lady, because of my affection for my sister-in-law and for you today,
this man shall fulfill his desire as he wishes;
for I am indeed the one who holds the tip of his bowstring at the forefront of the battle.
But if I do not attain you today, O beautiful one—
like a sinner failing to reach abundant prosperity—
I shall go to the abode of Indra, O auspicious lady.
For, dispatched by you, he has indeed attained the state of no-more-rebirth, having abandoned his beloved wife along with her children, his family, wealth,
fame, renown, and even life itself.
I renounce all my merit that has been performed;
for the sake of you, my beloved, I wish to live,
even though I am unable to endure this rising grief.
Like one afflicted by the violent force of the ocean, I am deeply distressed;
favor me today with a gracious mind, so that I may not wither away nor fall unconscious.
"O large-eyed one, act today in such a way that I do not go to the abode of Yama;
for, O beloved, my life is dependent upon you."
"Separated from you, I do not wish to live for long," said the faultless-limbed lady to the evil-minded Kīcaka. Thus spoke she of blameless limbs.
Draupadī, wearing the guise of a Sairandhrī, said this to him.
Draupadī said:
"O son of a Sūta, you desire me here, though I am not to be desired."
"With this very wealth and effort, you can obtain another woman who is beautiful, who increases her own caste and family, and who is not a low-caste *sairandhrī*, loathsome, or a hairdresser."
A wise man exerts the highest effort regarding his own wife;
for a man devoted to his own wife quickly beholds auspicious things,
whereas a mortal devoted to another's wife does not behold auspicious things.
One shall not be stained by unrighteousness, nor shall one incur infamy;
finding delight in one’s own wife is dharma even for the deceased, there is no doubt—
this is the duty of a mortal toward his own kind of wife, both in this world and in the next.
They perform the funeral rites for the deceased and satisfy them with *nivāpa* offerings;
the wise declare that this is inexhaustible, righteous, and leads to heaven. Sons who are born of wives of their own caste are honored by the family.
It is heard that those born of the field (*kṣetraja*) and other sons increase the lineage;
therefore, virtuous men remain devoted to their own wives. May you be blessed; it is not appropriate for you now to approach another's wife.

O charioteer, with a mind consumed by lust, you desire to touch and behold me; O son of a charioteer, harboring such thoughts toward me, you shall perish quickly this very day, before long, along with your sons, cattle, and kinsmen.
Wives are dear to living beings; reflect well upon dharma. Your mind must never, under any circumstances, be directed toward another's wife.
For the avoidance of such improper acts is the vow of virtuous men.
For a man who is greedily attached to falsehood, being evil-minded and established in delusion,
shall incur terrible infamy and encounter very great fear;
for the progeny of a man who takes pleasure in another's wife perishes.
The ancestors fall as well, and he himself falls down afterwards.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus addressed by Sairandhrī, Kīcaka was deluded by lust.
Though he knew of the many evils— life-threatening and condemned by all the world— that lie in violating another's wife, that man of wicked intellect, his senses unsubdued, spoke thus to Draupadī.
O lady of beautiful hips, O lovely-faced one, you ought not to reject me in this way— I who am possessed by love for your sake, O sweet-smiling one—
especially since I am submissive to you, speaking endearments, O timid one.
"Surely you will feel remorse later, O lady with dark-cornered eyes;
for I, O fair-browed one of slender waist, am the master and the sustainer of this entire kingdom, and my prowess is peerless on earth."
"On this earth, there is no other man here equal to me in beauty, youth, and good fortune, nor in unsurpassed and auspicious enjoyments; here,
amidst enjoyments that fulfill every desire and are beyond compare."
"O auspicious lady, why are you intent on serving me when there are things to be enjoyed? O fair-faced one, this kingdom has been given by me; I am your master.
O woman of excellent limbs, enjoy me and partake of unsurpassed pleasures."
Thus addressed with these wicked words by Kīcaka, that virtuous woman replied to Kīcaka, censuring his speech:
"O son of a Sūta, do not rejoice; today you shall lose your life."
Thinking me difficult to attain and protected by heroes,
you shall fall helplessly and swiftly, like a palm fruit from its stalk,
touched by that wicked mind whose limbs are agitated by the force of passion.
Nor can you, with your wicked mind, touch me, for my husbands are the Gandharvas;
you whose limbs are agitated by the force of passion.
They, being enraged, would surely slay you; enough, do not bring about your own ruin!
Who is this who wishes to cross the ocean by binding a stone around his neck?
By whom could poison be consumed? You are a base man who merely spits at it.
O fool of cruel appearance, just as Rāma, for the sake of Sītā, shall cause the ten-necked one to fall along with his kinsmen, so shall you fall into the netherworld;
and when Rāma has slain you, he will be joyful, as will my husbands.

You wish to travel a path with men who are incapable of it, just as a senseless child standing on one bank desires to cross to the opposite shore; like that dull-witted soul, you desire to do the impossible.
Whether you fly into the interior of the earth or soar upward,
or even if you rush to the far shore of the ocean,
even then you shall find no release from them.
For my excellent sons, the Pramathas, are indeed the children of the gods;
you are like a sick man facing the Night of Doom— why do you now so persistently solicit me, Kīcaka?
For those who long for their beloved, neither going to the earth nor ascending to heaven will provide refuge; O Kīcaka, no auspicious sight awaits you there.
She who would seek to bring him back to life— O evil-minded one, you do not perceive the sin nor the law,
O base Kīcaka of wicked intellect!
Why do you treat me as if I were a child lying on his mother’s lap,
desiring to seize the moon? For you speak these incoherent words out of ignorance, afflicted by passion for me.
But a man who lacks the power ought not to attempt to leap over the mountain;
for if he were to fall into the mouth of the great ocean at the bottom of the earth,
even if he were to spring upward again from within the ground, [he would still fail].
Whether he has fled to the quarters of the sky or to mountain caves,
entered a cavern or gone to the depths of the earth, or whether he is offering oblations, chanting prayers, or falling from a mountain precipice—
Even if he has attained the state of fire or the sun,
a man who insults the wives of great-souled men shall never be released from his fate, however he may try to avoid it.
This word of yours will be in vain,
like attempting to weigh a great mountain on a scale;
for you are like a child [weighing] the Lord of the Stars.
"You shall not obtain me by force, for I am a virtuous woman difficult to attain. A man who violates the wife of a high-souled one finds no refuge even after going to the gods."
O Kīcaka, abandon this intent toward those who desire; do not destroy your own dear life,
like a blazing fire in a great forest.
Like one suffering in the midday heat of summer,
you yourself desire to enter [the fire] for your own destruction and for the ruin of your entire lineage.
Neither in the presence of gods, gandharvas, and great seers,
nor in the world of the nāgas, nor in the abode of asuras and rākṣasas— disregarding me who stand here with your mind— [you have acted thus].
For the sake of your life, you shall not find refuge with me,
just as a certain sick man might not seek the Night of Doom. Why do you now entreat one such as me, O Kīcaka?
"Having cast the noose of Time around your neck, you now wish to enter that which is difficult to enter.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Rejected by the princess,
Kīcaka entered the king’s palace and stood before his sister;
looking upon his beloved sister Sudeṣṇā, who possessed beautiful hair, he spoke.
Overwhelmed by a terrible and boundless passion, he—
struck by delusion like an ocean tossed by the wind— quickly placed his joined palms upon his head at his sister's feet.
Afflicted by extreme sorrow and sighing repeatedly, he spoke to his sister in a voice that was faint, soft, and gentle, yet parched again and again:
"O Kaikeyī, let it be so arranged that I may be reunited with Sairandhrī."
"O Sudeṣṇā, by whatever means that woman who moves with the gait of an elephant might favor me, seek her out; let me not lose my life,
if she, O lady of faultless limbs, does not desire me today."
Vaiśampāyana said:
"With my consciousness surrendered [to him], I went to the abode of Yama.
Embracing her beloved brother, Sudeṣṇā spoke to him.
"This woman of beautiful hips has come for refuge, and I have granted her safety.
Her conduct is virtuous; may you be blessed. I do not dare to speak ill of her here, for she cannot be touched by anyone with a sinful mind."

"Five Gandharvas indeed guard her and delight her; thus she described it to me during our first union. In that very same way, she whose thighs are like an elephant's trunk spoke the truth in my presence."
For those high-souled ones, when enraged, could surely destroy one's very life;
and the king, having perceived this, fell into a state of confusion here,
though he was entreated by me with words of truth, O lord of the earth.
He too, having gazed upon her incessantly, rejoiced in his mind alone;
yet, out of fear of the leaders of the Gandharvas who would destroy his life,
the king did not even think of her in his mind.
For when those high-souled ones are enraged, possessing the splendor of Garuḍa and the wind,
they could consume even the three worlds like suns at the end of the eons;
indeed, Sairandhrī has described this great power of theirs to me.
Out of affection, like a kinsman, I shall tell you this secret:
do not go to a miserable state that is most difficult to traverse; for the powerful might inflict suffering upon you, as well as upon your family and people.
"Therefore, if your life-breaths are dear to you, do not set your mind upon her;
do not think of her, nor go to her, if you desire what is pleasing to me.
Thus addressed, the evil-minded Kīcaka spoke to his sister.
Whether it be a hundred, a thousand, or even tens of thousands of Gandharvas, I alone shall slay them— how much more so five? Furthermore, you do not understand the supreme secret of women.

I have heard that when a high-minded woman sees here in secret a man adorned with various perfumes— whether it be her son, her grandson, or even her brother— the womb of unchaste women swells with desire.
"Therefore, if you wish for my life, speak these words firmly to her.
Thus addressed, Sudeṣṇā, overwhelmed by grief, cried out:
"Alas, what misery! Alas, what hardship! Alas, what a sin!"
Seeing the ripening of that [deed], she wept, afflicted by intense grief:
"Lamenting, he shall fall into the netherworlds at the mouth of the submarine fire;
because of you, my brothers and friends will perish."
What indeed can I do, since you are thus overwhelmed?
You do not recognize what is beneficial; you merely follow after your desires. O wicked one, it is certain that your life has reached its end, since you are so deluded by passion.
"O lowest of men, you seek to separate me from this sinful act which ought not to be done.
Moreover, this was declared of old by wise and supreme men:
'He alone commits the sin; by that, his own kin are destroyed.'"
"You have gone to the domain of Dharmarāja; of this there is no doubt. You will cause all these innocent kinsmen to be slain.
But this is even more painful for me, that out of brotherly affection—"
"Having understood the matter, I shall do so; be satisfied with the destruction of your lineage. Go quickly from here to your own auspicious abode.
Having heard those words of his as he lamented thus many times at that time...
The wise queen, the chief consort of Virāṭa, felt compassion;
having considered her own interests and reflecting upon his welfare,
Sudeṣṇā spoke to the charioteer regarding the distress of Kṛṣṇā.
"Having designated a festival day, prepare wine and food.
Once the food and wine are prepared, you shall send word to me again;
then I will send her to you as a bearer of the wine."
There, in a secluded place where she is unrestrained, you should soothe her as she is sent forth, according to her desire; if, being so consoled, she should find pleasure,
then all this has been immediately accomplished— consider what remains to be done here.
Then, having gone home at his sister's word, Kīcaka had wine brought that was fit for a king and well-distilled. Thus addressed by Sudeṣṇā, Kīcaka was impelled by Time (fate).
Hurrying, he departed from the royal palace for his own home;
having reached his beautiful house, he prepared wine and food,
including abundant and excellent mutton and many various kinds of wild game.
He had skillful cooks prepare most excellent food and drink. When that was prepared, Queen Sudeṣṇā, having been entreated by Kīcaka, sent the Sairandhrī to Kīcaka’s dwelling.
Hurriedly bound by the noose of Time around his neck like a beast,
the deluded soul does not perceive that death has arrived. When the wine has been brought and the well-prepared food is set out, [he remains unaware].
Kīcaka,
having returned once more, spoke these words to Sudeṣṇā:
"Various kinds of honeyed meat and many sorts of prepared foods have been made ready."
"Sudeṣṇā, speak to Sairandhrī so that she may come to my house.
On some pretext today, urge her quickly to do what is pleasing to me.
For I take refuge in the god whose banner is the bull."
"Either my reunion with the Sairandhrī or my own death shall be indicated," said Vaiśampāyana. She,
sighing deeply, said to him, "Return to your own home."
"I shall also quickly command Sairandhrī for the sake of wine. Thus addressed, the evil-minded Kīcaka immediately entered his own house again, his mind fixed entirely on Sairandhrī.
Knowing that Kīcaka had gone, Sudeṣṇā hurried to her own house;
then, having summoned the Sairandhrī, she spoke these words. Sudeṣṇā said:
"Rise up, go, Sairandhrī, to Kīchaka’s residence;
bring me some drink, O blessed lady, for thirst oppresses me.
— Vaiśampāyana said.
Thus addressed by Sudeṣṇā, the princess sighed and,
tormented by grief, replied: "I will certainly not go there,
O blessed lady, for the son of a charioteer, being possessed by lust, covets me."
Draupadī said:
"O princess, I would not go to his dwelling;
O queen, you yourself know how shameless he is."
"O lady of faultless limbs, O beautiful one, I shall not act according to my own lust in your house by being unfaithful to my husbands. And you yourself,
O Queen, know how that agreement was made."
O beautiful lady with lovely hair, since Kīcaka previously entered your house while I was there, that fool, arrogant with lust,
will surely insult me upon seeing me; therefore, O radiant one, I shall not go there.
"How indeed could he tolerate me there, having gone to him as one who has no kinsman? O princess, you have many female servants who are obedient to your will;
send another—blessings be upon you—for he would surely treat me with contempt."
"O Queen, trembling with fear, I will not go to Kīcaka's abode.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"If there is any other task, however exceedingly difficult it may be, I shall perform it for you."
When the princess of Pañcāla had spoken thus, Kaikayī, the queen of Virāṭa, being incensed by the turn of fate, commanded her yet more sternly. Sudeṣṇā said:
"He shall never indeed harm you once you have been sent forth from here by me. But go instead to Kīcaka, urged on by force; there is no other equal to you, so depart with all possible speed."
"One must certainly go; why do you delay me?
Go quickly, hasten, and act out of regard for my pleasure! For there is no brother like me—why do you entertain such doubts?"
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus to her and having compelled her by his authority,
he gave her this golden vessel with its lid.
"Bring that well-made, fragrant *surā*," he said. Filled with apprehension and weeping, she sought refuge in destiny and set out for Kīcaka’s residence to fetch the liquor.
Draupadī said:
"As surely as I know no man other than the Pāṇḍavas,
by that truth, may Kīcaka not bring me, who have come here, under his power."
"As surely as I have never gone to anyone other than the five sons of Pāṇḍu,
by that truth, may Kīcaka not bring me under his power upon seeing me.
Vaiśampāyana said:
The woman of beautiful hips praised Dharma, Śakra, Divākara,
Māruta, the two Aśvin gods, Kubera, Varuṇa, Yama,
Rudra, Agni, Bhaga, Viṣṇu, Skanda, and Pūṣan.
She praised Brahmā together with Sāvitrī;
thus did that fawn-eyed woman of beautiful hips, a practitioner of dharma,
worship the Sun for a moment as a weak woman.
The Sun understood everything concerning that slender-waisted woman;
he then assigned a Rakshasa to guard her from within,
and that spirit did not leave her side in any circumstance while she remained blameless there.
She, with her beautiful hair, set out in haste again and again,
yet she lingered helplessly at the residence of Kīcaka. Seeing that dark-complexioned woman approaching like a terrified doe, [he seized her].
The charioteer Kīcaka, deluded by passion, rose up with joy like one who has reached the further shore after finding a boat; and he spoke these smooth words.
Kīcaka said:
"Welcome to you, O lady with beautiful hair! My night has dawned brightly.
You have arrived as my mistress; do what is pleasing to me. Bestow your affection upon me and bring me under your control."
"Accept from me these enjoyments prepared for your sake:
golden garlands, conch shells, earrings of refined gold,
bright jewels produced in various cities, and beautiful precious gems."
"Bring silken garments and deerskins;
accept them—may you be blessed—and dwell here as you wish.
O lotus-eyed one of lovely appearance, out of love for me, grant me your favor."
"I have a splendid bed prepared for your sake;
come there with me and drink the honey-sweet wine," said Vaiśampāyana.
Seeing the lotus-eyed Draupadī arrived there, that foolish and evil-minded Kīcaka, who was conceited in his own estimation, spoke to her.
"O large-eyed one, accept me, for I am indeed a husband worthy of you.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Approach me, O lady of beautiful hips, as the light of the sun approaches Mount Meru."
Thus addressed by Kīcaka, the princess of Pañcāla, who speaks with grace, replied:
"You ought not to speak such words regarding my conduct;
I cannot be touched by you, just as a Brāhmaṇī cannot be touched by a dog-cooker."
O evil-minded one, you shall not go to the destination that lies between the depths of misery— the destination where many who violate the wives of others go,
men who have shattered the bounds of propriety and dwell in caves like insects.
Draupadī said:
"The princess sent me to your presence to fetch wine;
I shall bring the liquor for her, for your sister is thirsty."
"Bring me a drink quickly; I am thirsty," she said.
"O son of a charioteer, let the *surā* be given to me at once; I am going away.
Kīcaka replied:
"O blessed one, others shall carry away the wine of the princess;
why will you go, O fair-hipped lady? You have come here for my sake.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus the Sūta’s son seized her by the right hand.
Draupadī said:
“Just as I have never been unfaithful, [so may this curse fall upon you].”
If I have never, even in my mind, been overcome by passion for my husbands,
by that very truth I shall behold you, O wicked one, brought under control and dragged away.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having gazed upon that large-eyed woman who was rebuking him, he desired to seize her.
He seized her by the edge of her upper garment;
that Kīcaka violently dragged her as she was being forcibly grasped with great speed.
Sighing repeatedly, the princess struck that wicked man with her body; he fell like a tree whose roots have been severed.
Unable to endure him, the lady of beautiful limbs, trembling with intense rage, struck him violently; yet,
seized by Kīcaka, she shook him off and cast him down upon the ground.
She ran for refuge to the assembly hall where King Yudhiṣṭhira was;
but Kīcaka seized her by the hair as she fled,
and even as the king looked on, he threw her down and struck her with his foot.
While the high-souled King Virāṭa looked on in the assembly hall,
and while the elders among the Brāhmaṇas and the Kṣatriyas were watching,
blood flowed from her mouth as it was scorched by his feet.
Then, O Bhārata, that Rākṣasa who had been commissioned by Arka carried Kīcaka away with the force of the wind;
struck down by the power of the Rākṣasa, he fell to the ground.
Reeling and motionless like a tree whose roots have been severed, the members of that assembly, seeing him there, cried out "Alas! Alas! from all sides;
the men exclaimed, "O son of a Sūta! O Kīcaka! This is not right!"
"Why is this young woman, so pitiable and without kinsmen, being struck? Thus they spoke.
Then Bhīmasena and Yudhiṣṭhira, sitting there, beheld her;
unable to endure Kīcaka’s assault of Draupadī with his foot, they looked upon her.
Upon seeing her, tears flowed from Bhīmasena out of anger;
he began to sigh like smoke, his eyelashes bristled,
and a fierce, sweat-drenched frown appeared upon his forehead.
Then the high-minded Bhīma, desiring to slay the evil-souled Kīcaka, ground his teeth against his own teeth in rage;
and that slayer of enemy heroes rubbed his forehead with his hand.
Furthermore, in a great hurry and filled with rage, he suddenly desired to rise up;
he looked toward the tall tree and glanced back at the king,
who was longing for the slaughter of the evil-minded Kīcaka.
By his very appearance, Yudhiṣṭhira restrained that formidable man;
the sinless King, son of Kuntī,
gradually restored the consciousness of the wise Bhīmasena, who was possessed by rage.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, whose name was Kaṅka, told this narrative:
"O cook, do not commit such violence; this lord of the forest has borne fruit."
No dry wood at all needs to be prepared here;
if you have any need for wood, go outside the city and cut down a tree by its roots, and you will not experience any fatigue.

And for that tree whose cool shade one might take refuge in while it is still fresh, one should not harm even a single leaf, remembering its former service. This is no time for anger, O cook; do not act with rashness.
