"This side of ours is incomplete; it is not sufficient for those who possess great strength.
Then, O King, the Lord of Dharma (Yama), fearing that Bhīma might wake up, pressed his thumb with his own thumb and restrained him.
How could one who is not patient with even a single part of the *Triśaṅku*, which has twelve limbs, twenty-four joints, and three hundred and sixty spokes— how could he endure it?
Behold him looking at the lord of the forest like an elephant in rut.
Yudhiṣṭhira restrained Bhīmasena, saying:
"O cook, why do you look at the tree?
If you have need of wood, let the trees be cut down outside."
Vaiśampāyana said:
But Bhīmasena, the conqueror of enemy cities, having heard those words,
restrained with fortitude the sudden surge of his anger by force.
Understanding his brother’s gesture, Vṛkodara remained silent; yet,
seeing Bhīma’s resolve and the King’s actions,
Draupadī became even more incensed and wept again and again.
Her long, copper-hued eyes reddened from being pursued by Kīcaka,
she reached the door of the assembly hall and, weeping, spoke to the King of Matsya while looking toward her dejected husbands, O lady of beautiful hips.
Protecting her appearance and her promise consistent with dharma,
the daughter of Drupada, as if burning him with her fierce gaze,
spoke these words and brought the king under her control.
For kings of immeasurable splendor, whose nature is to protect their subjects, there is indeed [no lapse] because they constantly abide in dharma and truth through the fulfillment of their duties.
To those who perceive no distinction between their own offspring and other offspring,
who have established equanimity toward both the beloved and the hateful,
and who observe with impartiality when disputes have arisen—
"By a king seated upon the seat of justice, both worlds are conquered.
O King, you are seated upon the seat of justice; protect me, who am innocent.
For I, though blameless, have been [harassed] by the evil-minded Kīcaka."

O Great King, while you were looking on, she was struck with your foot like a slave; O best of men, she was crushed upon the surface of the earth right before your eyes. Protect me, a woman who is innocent and deserving of compassion.

Protect me, who am afraid of Kīcaka; protect righteousness, O lord of men! O ruler of the Matsyas, protect your subjects like a father protects his own biological sons. For that king who, out of delusion, conducts affairs unjustly—
Before long, enemies will bring that evil-souled one under their control. For you are born of the Matsya lineage, the very refuge of truth;
indeed, you were born into such a family devoted to righteousness.
Therefore, O lord of men, I cry out to you for the sake of refuge;
protect me today, O Indra among kings, from Kīcaka, that sinful man.
Knowing me to be helpless, Kīcaka, the lowest of men—

A base-minded person strikes out indeed and does not regard righteousness. By refraining from what should not be done and by maintaining what should be done, those rulers of the earth who are of virtuous conduct among their subjects go to heaven.
Kings who know the distinction between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, yet act according to their own whims,
go headlong into hell after inflicting suffering upon their subjects;
neither by sacrifices, nor by gifts, nor by service to their teachers can they be saved.
They attain such righteousness as results from the fulfillment of their duties.
Furthermore, in ancient times, Brahmā spoke this to Indra when he questioned him regarding how,
in the worlds, there came to be the supreme distinction between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done.
Furthermore, dharma and adharma were joined as a pair for both action and non-action, for the attainment of merit and demerit; indeed,
this was proclaimed of old when living beings were being created.
O humans, this triad of pairs is what you must properly attend to on this earth: in this world, through good conduct or bad conduct, one receives the fruit born of action;
the doer of good reaps good, while the doer of evil reaps evil.
"By that [association] they go to union with either heaven or hell.
Having spoken these supreme words, he dismissed Śatakratu;
and Śakra, having taken leave of Brahmā, protected the kingdom of the gods.
As it was spoken by the God of gods, Brahmā Parameṣṭhin, so too,
O Indra among kings, you should remain steadfast regarding what ought and ought not to be done. Thus said Vaiśampāyana.
While the princess of Pañcāla was thus lamenting, Virāṭa, the bull among the Matsyas,
being unable to punish Kīcaka— who was arrogant in his strength—
restrained the charioteer with gentle words alone.

Having seen Kīcaka, who had committed an offense against the King of Matsya, punished by that blameless king with a penalty not commensurate with his crime, the daughter of the King of Pañcāla, who resembled a daughter of the gods, [was filled with grief].
The knower of dharma,
mindful of the highest law, spoke again to the king regarding Kīcaka, who had committed a crime,
while looking upon all those present in the assembly, O lady of beautiful limbs.
And the princess of Pañcāla, her mind overwhelmed with grief, spoke to Virāṭa.
Draupadī said:
"Those whose enemy does not sleep while touching the earth with his feet..."
The son of a Sūta has trampled with his foot me, their proud wife—
those who would give but never beg, who are devoted to Brahmanas and speakers of truth;
the son of a Sūta has trampled with his foot me, their proud wife.

The son of a charioteer has kicked me, a proud wife, with his foot— those whose drum-beats and the twang of bowstrings were heard incessantly, and by the sound of whose bow-strikes the very earth trembled.
Those who were radiant, self-controlled, powerful, and full of pride—
by a son of a charioteer, my proud wife was struck down by their feet. They were great archers, heroes in battle, arrogant and devoted to their own honor.
For those to whom no one is equal in vigor, truth, strength, and self-restraint—
those for whom no man on earth is a peer in the abundance of their wealth— the son of a charioteer has struck down my beloved wife with his foot.

O King, lord of the earth, while you were looking on and especially while you, who desire the welfare of all creatures, were present, that son of a charioteer struck down my beloved wife with his foot. Thus was she slain here by him.
Those who, bound by the noose of Dharma, might slay this entire world— by them,
the son of a Sūta has struck down me, their proud wife, with his foot.
They who become the refuge for those seeking shelter who have come to them for protection.
Where indeed are those great chariot-warriors now, who move about the world in disguise?
How could they [remain indifferent] while their beloved, virtuous wife was being slain by the son of a Sūta?
Surely one who uses righteousness as a mere pretext does not even honor dharma itself.
He who, seeing me being struck by the evil-minded one,
endures it— just as powerful men of immeasurable splendor endure like eunuchs—
where indeed does their indignation, heroism, and brilliance reside?
Those who do not seek to protect their wife when she is being struck by a wicked man— what can I possibly do here against Virāṭa, this defiler of dharma,
who looks on while I, though innocent, am being beaten?
When dharma, pierced by adharma, enters an assembly,
and if it is not extracted as a barb, all the members of that assembly are themselves pierced.
For where dharma is struck down by adharma, and truth by falsehood, [the members are likewise struck].
"While they look on, he is being slain; the members of that assembly are themselves destroyed.
O King, you do not act at all like a king regarding Kīcaka;
your conduct is like that of bandits, for it does not shine in an assembly."
Kīcaka does not abide by his own duty, nor does the King of Matsya in any way;
even the members of the assembly who wait upon him are ignorant of righteousness.
Kīcaka knows nothing of dharma, and the king’s servants are likewise the same.
"The king does not speak of discipline, nor do his ministers understand it;
O King Virāṭa, I do not reproach you in this assembly of people.
Vaiśampāyana said:
With such words as these, that woman of excellent complexion, Kṛṣṇā, her eyes filled with tears, then reproached the king of the Matsyas:
"O Matsya, it is not right for me to be killed by him in your presence."
"Let the members of the assembly behold the transgression of Kīcaka,
who, though a king, causes fear to the realm in this world—
just as even a father or a mother might administer poison."
Those various bodies of Varuṇa blaze forth greatly;
what refuge can there be for one in that fearful world? O King Virāṭa, behold me, helpless and innocent!
Conciliation does not bear fruit with the wicked; toward the wicked, punishment is employed.
A king who punishes those who should not be punished, and fails to punish those who deserve punishment, shall not remain a king in this world, nor be worthy of the title "king."

The lord of the earth should protect those who are miserable, blind, wretched, helpless, lame, humpbacked, or dull-witted; as well as those without protectors— whether men or women— including children and the elderly, and those oppressed by wicked thieves.

The king should be a protector of the protectorless, a father to those without fathers; he should be a mother to those without mothers, and a teacher to those without teachers. The king is the refuge for those without refuge, and the king is the ultimate resort for men.

O best of men, you should especially protect a virtuous woman who is helpless and has been violated by wicked others, as if she were your own daughter; O King, she has resided in your house for this length of time.
"Moreover, look at me, your daughter-in-law, struck down by Kīcaka.
Virāṭa said:
"I do not know of any dispute between you two out of my sight."
"Without understanding the true nature of the matter, what indeed would be for my welfare?
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard that piteous lamentation of the Sairandhrī, [he spoke].
Then the members of the assembly, recognizing Kṛṣṇā’s state, honored her once more;
they cried out, "Excellent! Excellent! and censured Kīcaka.
Some praised Kṛṣṇā, while others reviled Kīcaka.
Some of those men censured the king, and some the queen.
The members of the assembly said:
“If only one had this wife of long-lashed eyes, with all her limbs so beautiful!”
He shall obtain supreme gain and never grieve;
for such a woman of excellent complexion, with every limb faultless, is not easily found among men— we consider her to be a goddess.
Her body is beautiful and full, and her face surpasses the lotus;
her gait is like that of a swan and her smile like the *kunda* flower—such as she is, she does not deserve even a foot-dust.
She possesses thirty-two teeth, white and set firmly in their sockets.
Her hair is glossy and soft; she does not deserve to be struck with a foot.
Upon the palm of her hand there are the lotus, the wheel, the banner, the conch, the palace, and likewise the sea-monster;
she does not deserve to be struck with a foot.
Indeed, she has four spirals, all turning to the right;
her limbs are even, beautiful, and smooth, such that they do not deserve to be touched by foot; and she has no gaps between her hands and feet, nor any gaps between her teeth.
How can this maiden, with eyes like lotus petals, deserve to be struck by a foot? She is endowed with all auspicious marks, her face resembles the full moon;
being so beautiful and fair of countenance, she is not fit to be struck by a foot.
"Fortunate as a goddess among gods, beautiful as the queen of Śakra,
and possessing such exquisite beauty like an *apsaras*, she is not fit to be slain by a foot.
Vaiśampāyana said:
While the members of the assembly were thus honoring her upon seeing Kṛṣṇā there,
sweat broke out on Yudhiṣṭhira’s forehead from his anger.
Then the Kaurava spoke to his beloved queen, the princess:
There, assuming the form of a wandering mendicant, he said to Kṛṣṇā in the presence of the king:
"Go, Sairandhrī; do not remain here, but go to the residence of Sudeṣṇā.
For this King Virāṭa is righteous in character and fearful of the world beyond."
Since truth does not protect you, even though you stand firm in dharma and vows,
the wives of heroes suffer while remaining devoted to their husbands; yet,
by enduring such hardship through service, they conquer the world of their husbands.
I think that your husbands do not perceive the proper time for anger;
therefore, those Gandharvas, radiant as the sun, do not rush toward you.
O lady with beautiful hair, listen now to these discourses based on the Dharma of Liberation.
Just as the duty of women of noble family is seen to consist in following the law,
there is no sacrifice for a woman, nor a funeral rite (*śrāddha*), nor even a fast; rather,
that service rendered to her husband leads to heaven.
The father protects her in childhood; the husband protects her in youth; and the son protects her in old age. A woman does not deserve independence.
Devoted to their husbands, the wives of heroes are seen [to follow them even in death].
Enduring hardships through their service, they indeed conquer the world of their husbands;
likewise, wives never become angry with their husbands,
even when subjected to many afflictions and remaining unrecognized by their enemies.
Through service characterized by undivided devotion, they indeed conquer the world of their husbands;
your husbands never perceive a fixed time for anger,
and even the slayer of Vṛtra would not approach your husbands when they are enraged.
Therefore, the Gandharvas, who can assume any form at will, do not pursue you;
for if some agreement was made by you, O large-eyed one,
remember it, O lady of patient virtue, for forbearance is indeed the supreme dharma.
Forgiveness is dharma; forgiveness is truth; forgiveness is charity; forgiveness is austerity.
[This is] Vaiśampāyana’s [recension] of the twelve-limbed [Veda] with two parts and twenty-four sections.
"Who could endure the axle of this wheel with sixty-three hundred spokes that has lost its rim?
When this was said, the Lord of Dharma spoke again to her as she stood there:
"O Sairandhrī, you do not know the proper time; like an actress, you run about in vain."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus addressed, Bhadrā looked up and spoke these words:
"You are creating an obstacle for the Matsyas as they gamble in the royal assembly."
"Go, Sairandhrī; the Gandharvas will do what is pleasing to you. They will remove your sorrow from him who has done you this wrong.
Draupadī said:
"Out of extreme compassion for those who practice dharma, I am devoted to their welfare;
in this world, those among them whose eldest brother is a gambler are to be slain.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus, Kṛṣṇā ran toward the quarters of Sudeṣṇā;
having loosened her hair, the fair-hipped woman, her eyes red with agitation,
shone even as she wept, though her tears had then subsided.
Like the orb of the moon in the sky released from a streak of clouds—having spoken thus, the woman of excellent hips wiped her beautiful face.
Vaiśampāyana said:
[Thus spoke the woman of excellent hips, having wiped her beautiful face.]
Having bound up her disheveled hair, which was stained with blood, her entire body smeared with dust, she— whose thighs were like the trunk of a lordly elephant— set forth,
obeying the command of her husband.
The fawn-eyed woman with full breasts is now liberated,
like the radiance of the king of stars (the moon) shrouded by dark clouds—
she for whose sake the sons of Pāṇḍu would even sacrifice their lives.

Seeing her thus distressed, those patient practitioners of dharma did not transgress their agreement, just as the great ocean does not overstep its shore. Trembling, she entered the residence of Sudeṣṇā.
Then she, whose every limb was beautiful, stood weeping before her.
Virāṭa’s queen, resorting to deceit, spoke to her.
Sudeṣṇā said:
What is this, resembling a lotus, with its well-proportioned teeth, lips, eyes,
and nose; shedding tears as it weeps, possessing a radiance like that of the full moon,
and emitting a most beautiful luster from its black pupils, heated by its vapors?
"Water flows from your eyes, which are not squinting;
who has struck you, O lady of beautiful hips? Why do you weep, O lovely one?
Who is being separated from his wife, along with his sons, cattle, and kinsmen?"
"Whose happiness is not yours today, O blessed lady? By whom has something unpleasant been done for you?
Vaiśampāyana said:
Tell me, what shall I do that is pleasing to you? Whom shall I abandon, or whom shall I have slain?"
Sighing deeply, Kṛṣṇā said to him: "Knowing my name, you ask it;
having sent me after your brother, why do you boast in this manner?
Draupadī said:
"Kīcaka killed me there while I was going to fetch wine for you,
even as the king looked on in the assembly hall as if it were a secluded place.
Sudeṣṇā said:

"O lady with beautiful hair, if you agree, I shall have Kīcaka killed. Even though he is clearly my brother by birth, this man, intoxicated by lust, considers you— who practice righteousness— to be an object of his desire, though you are unattainable."
Draupadī said:
"Others indeed will slay him for whose offense he acts;
I believe it is quite evident that he shall go to the next world this very day."
Janamejaya said:
"Alas! Draupadī, the most excellent of women, devoted to her husbands and highly fortunate, has fallen into even greater misery, having been struck down by Kīcaka."
She who, out of respect for her husband’s virtuous sister Duḥśalā,
did not curse the King of Sindhu even when she was forcibly violated by him— why has she arrived here with the wicked-souled Kīcaka?
The illustrious Kṛṣṇā did not curse him, though she was struck by his foot;
for this goddess is a mass of splendor, a knower of dharma, and a speaker of truth— yet,
having been seized by her hair, she will endure it like one who is powerless.
"This reason is not small, for I am desirous of hearing it, O best of beings;
my mind is deeply pained by the sufferings of Kṛṣṇā.
In whose lineage was that ill-behaved man born, O sage?"
How was Kīcaka, the brother-in-law of the King of Matsya, intoxicated by power, even after seeing his beloved wife struck by the son of the Sūta? Vaiśampāyana said:
The heroes did not waver at all; what did they do toward him?
This is a follow-up question posed by you, O enhancer of the Kurus' fame.
O King, I shall relate all of this to you here in detail.

O King, one born to a Brāhmaṇa woman from a Kṣatriya father becomes a Sūta; among those born through the inverse order (prātilomya), he alone is indeed considered twice-born (dvija). For this Rathakāra is regarded as a twice-born man endowed with [specific] ritual functions.
They say that [the Sūta] is inferior to the Kṣatriya but superior to the Vaiśya; however,
because he was previously made an associate with the charioteer by former kings,
the title "King" (rājan) cannot be properly applied to him through such an inverse order.
The domain of those Sūtas was established by name as the territory of the Sūtas; and whatever means of subsistence the Kṣatriyas had previously obtained from the Sūtas,
the king known as Kekaya became the sovereign over those Sūtas.
Born of a princess, he became peerless as a charioteer. O best of the Kurus, O Bhārata, six hundred and one sons, known as the Kīcakas, were then born to him by a Mālavī woman.

O Lord, among them was Kīcaka, the best of warriors and a conqueror of all; he was the eldest brother, intoxicated by his own strength, and because of him there were six hundred charioteers. O descendant of Kuru, Mālavī herself was born there as their younger sister.
Of that Kekaya king, Sudeṣṇā was the daughter;
the Kekaya king joyfully gave her to Virāṭa of the Matsyas.
This occurred after Surathā had died, leaving Kausalyā as Śveta’s mother.
When Śveta was destroyed and Śaṅkha had gone to his maternal uncle’s house,
the king obtained Sudeṣṇā as his queen and dispelled his sorrow;
and [he likewise obtained] Uttarā and Uttara from Virāṭa, O lord of the earth.
O King, the queen Sudeṣṇā gave birth to that blameless daughter of his maternal aunt for the prosperity of the Kaikeya lineage; and Kīcaka,
constantly attending upon her with affection, lived happily in Virāṭa’s service.
His brothers were valiant and all were devoted to him;
they, being highly delighted, increased the strength and the treasury of Virāṭa himself.
There were Daityas known as the Kāleyas, who were for the most part famous throughout the earth.
O King, the Kīcakas were born; Bāṇa was the eldest among them.
For he was endowed with all weapons, powerful, and possessed of terrible prowess.
Kīcaka became one who had destroyed all moral bounds and was a source of terror to men.
Having obtained him who was intoxicated by his own strength, Virāṭa, the lord of the earth,
conquered all his enemies— just as Indra conquered the Dānavas in ancient times—
as well as the Mekhalas, the Trigartas, the Daśārṇas, and the Kaśerukas.
The Mālavas, Yavanas, Pulindas, Kāśis, and Kosalas;
the Aṅgas, Vaṅgas, Kaliṅgas, Taṅgaṇas, and Parataṅgaṇas;
those who pay tribute and those who are exempt, as well as the Śivas and Macchillikas.
And many other heroes, lords of various realms,
broken by Kīcaka in battle, fled in the ten directions;
for he was thus endowed with such prowess and equal in strength to many thousands.
There, Virāṭa made himself the commander of the army;
and his ten brothers, who were like the sons of Daśaratha,
followed those Kīcakas, who were even more powerful.
Bhīma possessed such strength, as did those Kīcakas;
they were the high-souled brothers-in-law of King Virāṭa, seeking his welfare.
All this regarding the prowess of Kīcaka has been told to you.
Listen as I tell you why Draupadī did not curse him: sages, even when their ascetic power flows forth due to anger, do not utter curses;
knowing this according to the truth, Draupadī did not curse him.
Forgiveness is dharma; forgiveness is charity; forgiveness is sacrifice; forgiveness is glory.
Forgiveness is truth; forgiveness is conduct; forgiveness is fame; forgiveness is supreme.
Forgiveness is merit; forgiveness is the sacred ford; forgiveness is everything—so says the Veda.
"This world belongs to the patient, and the next world belongs to the patient.
Knowing all this, she practiced patience,
having understood the intention of her husbands, who were forbearing and practitioners of dharma.
O Bhārata, though she was capable, the large-eyed Satī did not curse him;
and all those Pāṇḍavas, beholding Draupadī so distressed,
were consumed by the fire of wrath, yet they refrained out of regard for their sense of shame.
Then the mighty-armed Bhīma, wishing to slay Kīcaka,
was restrained by the son of Dharma like the great ocean by the shore;
suppressing his wrath within his mind, he sighed day and night.
Then, with great difficulty, he slept that night in the kitchen.
"Quickly give him the *jīvaśrāddha* today for your brother;
look upon him well, for I do not think he will retain his life-breaths."
For among those five husbands of mine who practice righteousness,
Durmarṣaṇa alone is exceedingly difficult to withstand and peerless in strength upon this earth;
were he angry, he would leave this world devoid of men this very night.
The Gandharva, who can assume any form at will, did not become angry for a while,
thinking, "He shall surely know of this kick of my foot.
At that very moment, the wicked Kīcaka, along with his sons, brothers, and kinsmen, [perished].
That evil-minded one will perish, just like one who has performed wicked deeds.
Furthermore, this was previously declared by the skillful, the best of men:
"But one person, having fallen under the power of the noose of Time, commits a sin."
"For it is through the transgression of a base person that a family is destroyed.
Having spoken thus to Sudeṣṇā, the Sairandhrī, bewildered by grief,
undertook a vow for the sake of killing Kīcaka.
Though entreated by the women and honored by Sudeṣṇā,
she neither bathed nor ate, nor did she wipe away the dust;
with her garments soaked in blood, her eyes became sunken.
Seeing her thus tormented by grief, the women wept aloud;
they all longed in their hearts for the slaying of Kīcaka.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Struck by the son of the Sūta, that princess blazed with fury;
desiring the death of Senāvāha,
the beautiful daughter of Drupada then went to her quarters.
Having performed her purification according to the rules, the slender-waisted Kṛṣṇā washed her limbs and her garments with water;
weeping, she reflected upon the resolution of that sorrow.
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? How might my purpose be accomplished?"—having reflected thus, she turned her mind toward Bhīma;
for there was no one other than Bhīma who could now fulfill her heart's desire.
Then, rising in the night and leaving her own bed,
the large-eyed Kṛṣṇā, though she had protectors, ran forth seeking a protector to Bhīmasena’s palace.
Afflicted by great mental anguish,
that high-minded woman of pure smiles, having reached Bhīmasena in the kitchen,
was like a three-year-old cow born in the forest, entirely white in hue.
The princess of Pañcāla approached the unshakable Bhīma, the descendant of Kuru,
as a female elephant approaches a proud bull in a forest waterfall;
she approached him like a cow approaching a great elephant in rut.
Like a creeper embracing a great flowering *śāla* tree growing on the banks of the Gomatī,
the blameless Pāñcālī embraced the middle son of Pāṇḍu;
and having encircled him with her arms, she awakened him.

Like a lioness embracing the king of beasts, she clung to Bhīmasena as he lay asleep like a lion in a difficult forest thicket; and touching her husband with both hands, she awakened him from his sleep.
Like Śrī [awakening] another of great energy, or like [the goddesses] awakening Viṣṇu as he slept upon the ocean,
she awakened the bull-eyed one as he lay upon a bed white with fine linen—
just as Śacī awakens the King of the Gods, or Rudrāṇī awakens Śaṅkara.
As Sāvitrī awakened Brahmā, as Ṣaṣṭhī awakened Guha,
and as a female elephant awakens an elephant resembling a world-elephant,
so did his beloved awaken Bhīma, just as Lakṣmī awakens Dāmodara.

Resplendent like the offspring of a god, the blameless Pāñcālī, dear to her beloved, addressed Bhīmasena with words of affection; sweet as a lute, she spoke with a voice perfectly modulated in the Gāndhāra scale.
"Arise, arise! Why do you lie there like one who is dead, O Bhīmasena? For no one who is not dead lives after seizing the wife of a most wicked man.
While that most sinful leader of my army, my enemy, still lives..."
"Having performed that deed today, how can you indulge in sleep?
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus, the high-minded woman then entered the hall.

In that hall where Bhīma then lay, hissing like the king of beasts, O Kauravya, that chamber— by virtue of the form of the high-souled Bhīma— seemed as if it were swooning and yet blazed forth with splendor.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard that sound while sleeping soundly, Vṛkodara was awakened by the best of the Kurus, like a great elephant prodded by goads.
Awakened by the princess, he abandoned his bed; then,
resembling a cloud,
the invincible one sat upon a cushioned couch and addressed her, the enhancer of the Pāñcāla lineage.
Then the Kuru prince spoke to his beloved queen, the princess:
"For what purpose have you come to me so hurriedly?
Your complexion is not its natural self; you appear emaciated and pale."
Whether it be public or secret, you ought to tell me everything.
Explain it in its entirety so that I may know it all—
whether it be happiness or suffering, whether it be hateful or dear.
"Tell me everything exactly as it is; having heard it, I shall know what is best.
For I alone, O Kṛṣṇā, am to be trusted by you in all undertakings;
even in times of calamity, I shall deliver you again and again."
"Speak quickly as you wish whatever you intend to say;
go indeed to your bed before anyone else awakens."—
Vaiśampāyana.
Then, ashamed and afraid, with her face cast downward and her eyes clouded by tears, she did not utter a single word.
Thereupon, the powerful one of terrible prowess spoke:
Vṛkodara, who is esteemed by the foremost of the Pāṇḍavas, said:
"Tell me, O beautiful one, what may I do for you? O beloved, O woman with the graceful gait of an elephant in play, tell me what is pleasing to you."
Draupadī said:
"How could there be anything not to be grieved for her whose husband is Yudhiṣṭhira? Knowing all my sorrows, why do you ask me?"
O Bhārata, that the Prātikāmī brought me into the assembly hall in the midst of the courtiers with the accusation that I was a slave— that burns me even now;
I was dragged away in the city of Hastināpura into the royal assembly.
While she was in her menses, Duḥśāsana seized her by the hair;
she was seen there by the Kṣatriyas led by Karṇa and others, as well as by Duryodhana,
and by her two fathers-in-law, Bhīṣma and the wise Vidura.
O mighty-armed one, O scorcher of foes, by Droṇa and by Kṛpa,
I was seized by the hair and dragged into the assembly hall while my two fathers-in-law and my husbands were present— yet all this happened while you were still alive, O Pāṇḍava.

Then, having been released from that new kingdom, I went to the forest. Dwelling there in the forest in difficult conditions, exhausted by the journey, I encountered great terror due to the harassment of Jaṭāsura.
"O Lord, what woman other than Draupadī could continue to live after experiencing such intense suffering as I have,
including that endured by the daughter of the King while dwelling in the forest at the hands of the evil-minded Saindhava?"
And who indeed could endure a second such insult? O Pāṇḍava, while you were alive, I traveled on foot through regions situated in difficult terrain— impassable lands teeming with wild beasts.
Then, in the twelfth year, subsisting on wild roots and fruits,
I arrived at this city as an attendant to Sudeṣṇā;
though established in the path of truth and dharma, I served another's wife.
O Pāṇḍava, as long as you were alive, Virāṭa constantly ground gośīrṣaka, padmaka, and hariśyāma sandalwood for you; yet,
for your sake, I have not counted these many sorrows.
"In the very presence of the King of Matsya, while that rogue looked on, I was touched by Kīcaka with his foot; what woman like me could continue to live?
Thus, O Bhārata, I am being tormented by many kinds of afflictions."
"O son of Kuntī, you do not know me; what fruit is there for my living?
I am the daughter of Drupada and the younger sister of Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
Born from the fire-pit, O sir, I have never walked upon the earth."
If you do not kill Kīcaka, I shall die by binding a stone to myself and casting it into the water; I shall drink stirred poison, or else I shall enter the fire;
I shall destroy myself by climbing a tree and leaping down.
"I shall cut my own limb with a weapon; what is the use of life to me?
O Bhārata, tiger among men, this man named Kīcaka, the commander of King Virāṭa’s army and his brother-in-law, is exceedingly wicked-minded."

O slayer of enemies, while I was living in the royal palace in the guise of a *sairandhrī*, that evil-minded man constantly said to me, "Become my wife. Thus was I addressed by him, who deserved to be slain.

Like a fruit ripened by time, my heart is bursting asunder. O son of Kuntī, crusher of enemies, become my refuge; do not join with Yudhiṣṭhira, who is devoid of effort, devoid of indignation, and devoid of prowess.
"May no woman ever give birth to such a son as you!
O Pāṇḍava, I recognize your indignation, your strength, and your heroism;
therefore, O mighty one, I lament before you."
Just as a sixty-year-old elephant, intoxicated and the leader of the herd,
might trample and crush with its feet a *bilva* fruit fallen upon the ground,
even so did he strike his head down upon the surface of the earth.
O tiger among men, O Pāṇḍava, crush him with your left foot! If Kīcaka, having risen in the morning, should see the rising sun after the night has passed, I shall not venture to live.
"You are sworn by my life, by the merit of Arjuna,
by the feet of Yudhiṣṭhira, and by the lives of the twins—
that you shall today take the vow to slay Kīcaka, O Bhārata."
Reproach your eldest brother, that wicked gambler,
by whose deed I have come to this endless suffering; for he,
though the eldest, is the foremost among these [brothers] and a disgrace to the family.
Those brothers of modest intellect also followed him in haste;
for who else, save a wicked gambler, would abandon a kingdom and all his possessions along with himself to play for the sake of the religious life?
If one were to worship the gods morning and evening for many years with a thousand gold coins and whatever other wealth is substantial—
namely, gold ornaments, bullion, garments, vehicles, draft animals, goats, and sheep.
He would never have brought about the depletion of his herds of horses and mules;
yet now, having been stripped of his royal fortune through the pretext of gambling,
he sits in silence like a fool, reflecting upon his own deeds.
Ten thousand elephants, adorned with golden garlands and resembling lotuses, follow him as he goes; yet this man lives by gambling.
Likewise, there are hundreds of thousands of men of immeasurable splendor [who follow him].
They wait upon the great king Yudhiṣṭhira at Indraprastha. He has one hundred thousand slave-girls who, with vessels in hand, feed guests day and night in his kitchen.
This best among givers, having bestowed thousands of gold coins,
is now overwhelmed by this great misfortune born of the gambling match;
for many bards and panegyrists, endowed with melodious voices, [are praising him].
Every morning and evening, they waited upon him, adorned with polished jeweled earrings:
a thousand Vālakhilyas, a thousand who dwell in water,
a thousand who grind with stones, and a thousand who subsist on air.
A thousand wives on earth, a thousand celibate students,
a thousand forest-dwellers, and a thousand householders—
these are the twice-born who are *haṃsas*, *paramahaṃsas*, and *yogins*.
There were *kuṭīcaka* wandering mendicants and others who lived as forest-dwellers;

many were constantly devoted in spirit and possessed sublimated vital energy (*ūrdhvaretas*). These Brahmins were knowers of the four Vedas and were firm in their mastery of phonetics (*śikṣā*) and hermeneutics (*mīmāṃsā*).
The Brahmins who were experts in the Pada and Krama recitations, as well as those who studied the Sāman chants—
thousand ṛṣis such as these were his constant courtiers, endowed with austerity and sacred learning, and provided with every object of desire.

Yudhiṣṭhira supported eighty-eight thousand householders who were *snātakas*, each of whom was provided with thirty maid-servants; he also supported ascetics who had sublimated their vital energy (*ūrdhvaretas*) and would not accept gifts.
And ten thousand others as well— this very lord of men sits here;
he in whom all these qualities reside— kindness, compassion, and likewise a sense of sharing— is this lord of men who sits here.
Yudhiṣṭhira, steadfast and of true prowess, always supports with an undistracted mind— out of compassion— all those in his realms who are blind, aged, helpless, or otherwise destitute.
Always intent on sharing his wealth,
this very man has fallen into hell as the attendant of the fisherman;
Kaṅka, the gambler at the king’s assembly, speaks as Yudhiṣṭhira.
He for whom all the kings were once time-bound givers of tribute while he resided in Indraprastha, now seeks sustenance from others;
he under whose control the kings, the protectors of the earth, formerly lived.
That king who once lived under his own control now lives today under the control of others;
having scorched the entire earth with his splendor like the sun with its rays,
this very Yudhiṣṭhira is now a courtier in the assembly hall of King Virāṭa.

O Pāṇḍava, behold today that other Pāṇḍava whom kings together with sages used to attend upon in the assembly hall— now see him sitting as a courtier, attending upon another and speaking pleasant words to his master.

Seeing Yudhiṣṭhira— who does not deserve this, who is possessed of great wisdom, and who has resorted to such a state for the sake of life— whom would sorrow not undoubtedly enter? Seeing the righteous-souled Yudhiṣṭhira, whose heart is set on dharma, in such a plight, who would not feel pain?
"O hero, behold now that descendant of Bharata, O Bhārata, who was once attended upon in the assembly hall by the entire earth, yet today sits there attended by another.
Thus she is tormented by manifold miseries like one who is helpless."
"O Bhīma, do you not see me standing in the midst of an ocean of grief?
Draupadī said:
"O Bhārata, this which I shall speak is a great sorrow of mine."

"You should not harbor resentment toward me; I say this out of sorrow. O Bhīma, bull among the Bharatas, since you are unequaled in the art of cooking, whose grief would you not increase by claiming to be of the Ballava caste?"
People know you as Ballava, the cook of Virāṭa;
having fallen into the state of a servant, what indeed could be more painful than that,
when you wait upon Virāṭa in the kitchen with the food prepared?
When the cook Ballava speaks thus, my mind sinks;
when the Emperor, being delighted, makes you fight with elephants,
the women in the inner apartments laugh, yet my heart trembles.

"O Bhīma, you are the most powerful among all the strong and possess great strength. When you fight with tigers, buffaloes, and lions in the inner apartments while Kaikeyī looks on, I am overcome by faintness."
Then, rising up, Kaikeyī replied to them all; and having risen from her seat,
the faultless-limbed Kaikeyī spoke to those women, appearing as if struck by dejection upon seeing me.
I believe that this woman of pure smiles feels affection for the cook born of their long association,
and that this lady of lovely laughter feels toward the cowherd a devotion directed toward him alone;
therefore, she grieves with such emotion, for it is difficult for one of lovely smiles to endure.
Having perceived him indeed fighting with deer and tigers,
he grieves for him out of affection and because he is free from fear;
he grieves for this one as he fights against those of great prowess.
The *sairandhrī* is of beautiful form, and Ballava is exceedingly handsome; the minds of women are difficult to fathom, and in my opinion, these two are well-suited to one another.
Due to their constant living together, the *sairandhrī* is ever sensitive to his kindness.
"And these two have been residing in this royal household for the same length of time"—
speaking such words, she constantly informed me;
and seeing me become angry, she suspected me of having feelings for you.
While she was speaking thus, great sorrow entered me:
"When you, so terrible and of such formidable prowess, have fallen into this hellish state,
he did not utter a single word, his eyes red with fury."
But perceiving Bhīma to be enraged, Draupadī spoke again:
"Immersed as I am in grief for Yudhiṣṭhira, I have no desire to live—
[that man] who, on a single chariot, conquered gods, humans, and serpents alike."
This very youth, who was once the dancer for King Virāṭa’s daughters—
he by whose twang of the bowstring the earth trembled—
is today Pārtha, the dancer for Virāṭa’s daughters.
He of immeasurable soul, who gratified the god of fire in the Khāṇḍava forest—
that Pārtha, now entered into the inner apartments, is like a fire concealed within a well.
From that bull among men, his enemies always stand in constant fear.
Dhananjaya remains there in a guise that is held in contempt by the world;
he whose arms, resembling iron clubs, were once hardened by the striking of bowstrings—
that Dhananjaya now sits grieving, with his two conch-like arms covered in dust.
Seeing Arjuna— who, by the twang of his bowstring, made his enemies tremble— now assuming the form of a eunuch and performing song and dance, my mind can find no peace.
Joyful women attend upon him as he listens to the sound of song;
he whose head once shone with a crown radiant as the sun now has his hair ends fashioned into braids— this is that very Dhananjaya today.
In that great-souled one all divine weapons reside;
he who is the repository of all branches of knowledge wears the two earrings.
He, indeed, whom thousands of kings of incomparable splendor [could not overcome].
In battle they cannot be overcome, just as the great ocean cannot overstep its shore.
This very youth, who was a dancer for King Virāṭa’s daughters,
now remains disguised in dress as an attendant to the maidens.
At the mere sound of whose chariot the earth used to tremble,
and upon seeing him charging in battle, his enemies would fall into a state of panic—
upon hearing that such a man has met this fate, Kuntī will be overcome with grief.
O Bhīma, that illustrious younger brother of yours, at whose birth the grief of Kuntī vanished along with the mountains, forests, and all things mobile and immobile, now causes me to grieve today.

Seeing him approaching, adorned with ornaments, earrings of refined gold, and a conch-shell bracelet upon his arm— Arjuna, who wields the formidable bow and whose hair is bound in a braid— my heart sinks.
Seeing Dhananjaya surrounded by maidens, O Bhima, my heart sinks; for there is no archer on this earth equal to him in prowess, yet today he sits here singing, encircled by young women.
He who was esteemed by the world of living beings for his righteousness, heroism, and truth—
seeing Pārtha transformed into the guise of a woman, my heart sinks. He who, having reached his own kingdom, had brought down his fierce enemies and was skilled in weapons.
Displaying supreme heroism, he should stand there, gladdening his own army;
for when they see him, godlike in form, surrounded by maidens like a rutting elephant encircled by female elephants.
Seeing Matsya, Arthapati, Pārtha, and Virāṭa standing together,
my mind was then plunged into the deepest sorrow; as I beheld him seated in the midst of the musical instruments, the very quarters of the sky seemed to vanish from my sight.
Surely the noble lady does not know that Dhanañjaya has fallen into distress—
he who is concealed by a disguise unfit for him, like fire covered by ashes;
nor does she know Ajātaśatru, the Kaurava, who is submerged through playing at a ruinous game of dice.

Satisfying the fires with oblations dedicated to Indra, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Brahmā, Agni, and Viṣṇu, Pārtha— whose nature is inconceivable and who is the destroyer of all enemies— conquered them all on a single chariot by means of his divine weapons.
Displaying the divine Gāndharva weapon, as well as the Vāyavya, Vaiṣṇava, Brāhma, Pāśupata, and Sthāṇukarṇa weapons,
[he struck] the great Asuras, the Paulomas and Kālakeyas, the enemies of Indra.
On a single chariot, he conquered the terrible Nivātakavacas;
then Pārtha, having entered the inner apartments, was concealed like fire within a well,
like a great bull seen among the pens when it has entered the maidens' quarters.
"O Pārtha, my mind is troubled seeing you disguised in women's clothes;
likewise, O Bhārata, seeing the youngest of us, Sahadeva, the lord of warriors,
approaching the cattle dressed as a cowherd, I have turned pale."
O Bhīmasena, reflecting again and again upon the deeds of Sahadeva, I find no sleep; how then could I find any pleasure? He is a youth, a bull among kings, and proficient in all the scriptures.
Seeing him in the guise of a cowherd, my mind is utterly bewildered. O mighty-armed one, I do not perceive any misdeed of Sahadeva,
he who is of true prowess, for whom such suffering as this should befall.
"I am distressed, O best of the Bharatas, seeing your beloved brother—
resembling a bull among cattle— overpowered by Matsya,
enraged, dressed in red garments, and leading the cowherds."
Then, as Virāṭa offers his greetings, a fever arises within me.
For my noble lady always praises the hero Sahadeva, saying,
"O Kṛṣṇā, out of respect for my words, he must always be protected by you."
"How indeed will he, separated from me, dwell in suffering in the forest—
he who is endowed with a noble lineage, possessed of good conduct, virtuous,
restrained by a sense of shame, sweet-spoken, righteous, and dear to me?"
O Yājñasenī, you must recognize him even in the forests and during the nights;
he is both delicate and brave, and remains devoted to the king.
O Princess of Pañcāla, you yourself should feed this man who honors his elder brother.
"Thus did Kuntī speak to me, weeping and longing for her son,
as she stood embracing him who was departing for the great forest;
she saw him occupied with the cattle, sleeping at night upon a calf-skin."
Seeing Sahadeva, the best among warriors, standing there disguised as a cowherd among the cattle— O Pāṇḍava, how can I continue to live?
He who was always endowed with the three qualities of beauty, weaponry, and intelligence.
Behold the reversal of time brought about by Kāla: that very man who was Virāṭa’s horse-keeper—
those princesses, courtesans, and daughters of the common folk,
all women endowed with beauty, have now fallen under the power of Damagranthin.
Crowds gathered, gazing intently at Damagranthi as he was training the horses with speed while the great king looked on;
there I beheld that illustrious and most radiant Matsya.
Seeing Virāṭa approaching and the horses being presented, [Kṛṣṇa said]:
"O Pārtha, O scorcher of foes, do you think that I am happy?
Thus am I beset by hundreds of sorrows on account of Yudhiṣṭhira."
I saw that illustrious one, the leader of Virāṭa.
O Bhārata, descendant of Kuntī, other sorrows even more distinguished than these have befallen me; I shall speak of them as well, so listen.
While you are still living, these various sufferings are withering my body; what indeed could be more painful than this? For a woman who has but one husband lives in nothing but sorrow.
"I have five husbands; my suffering is endless.
Draupadī said:
"I am moving about in the royal palace in the guise of a *sairandhrī*."
"O scorcher of foes, I am the servant of Sudeṣṇā for the sake of one who is a rogue at dice;
behold my intense transformation as a princess. I sit waiting for my time, enduring all this misery as if I were truly afflicted."
"The success of mortals' aims, as well as victory and defeat, is indeed impermanent. Thinking thus, I await the renewed rise of my husbands;
for like a wheel, both the fortunes and the misfortunes of mortals revolve.
"That very cause which brings victory to a man is also the cause of his defeat"— I observe this principle closely. Why do you not acknowledge me, Bhīmasena, as if I were dead?
A person acts in such a way that he encounters the very causes of his own downfall:
having given, men beg; others, having killed, are themselves slain;
and having caused others to fall, they are in turn cast down by others—so have I heard.
"There is no burden too heavy for destiny, nor can one transcend destiny"—
thus I further uphold the traditional teaching regarding destiny.
Where water once stood, there it remains once again.

Thus, desiring a change of fortune, I await my rise once more; for it is said that even a well-executed purpose may fail through destiny. Therefore, a wise person must exert effort toward the attainment of destiny.
"Ask me, who am sorrowful, what the purpose of these words I have spoken is; or even if unasked, I shall tell it to you. I am the queen of the sons of Pāṇḍu and the daughter of Drupada."
"O Bhārata,
subduer of enemies, having reached this state after insulting all the Kurus, the Pañcālas,
and the sons of Pāṇḍu, what woman other than I would wish to live?"
O slayer of enemy heroes, what other woman could be so afflicted as this lady, who is thus surrounded by many brothers, fathers-in-law, and sons? Surely,
in my youth, I must have committed something displeasing to the Creator.
O bull among the Bharatas, it is through his grace that I have fallen into this misfortune;
O Pāṇḍava, look at the state of my complexion, such as it has become,
which was not even like this when I was in that supreme misery.
O Bhima, you alone know what happiness I once had, O Partha;
now that I have fallen into slavery, I find no peace against my will.
O Vrikodara, what joy can there be for me today in this life of mine?
I do not consider this to be anything other than divine, that Pārtha Dhananjaya—
the one with the formidable bow and mighty arms— should remain as if extinguished like a fire.
O Pārtha, the course of living beings is indeed impossible for men to understand.
I consider this downfall of yours to be something unimagined,
for you who were always like Indra used to look toward my face; yet now, though I am the most excellent of women, I must look toward the faces of others who are inferior.

"Behold, O Pāṇḍava, my condition; it is indeed such as I do not deserve, even while you all are still alive. Behold the reversal of time, for she who once held the earth bounded by the oceans under her command—"
Today I am terrified and have become subject to the will of Sudeṣṇā;
she for whom there were once attendants walking before her and followers behind her,
now I myself must walk both before and behind her.
But hear this, O son of Kuntī, which is a sorrow unbearable for me:
she who never grinded her own body-paste,
except for Kuntī— blessings upon you— she today grinds sandalwood.
"Behold my hands, O son of Kuntī; they are not at all as they were before.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus, he showed him both his hands, which were covered with calluses.
Draupadī said:
"I, who was never afraid of Kuntī or of you all at any time,
now stand here as a terrified servant before Virāṭa."
At that time, I stood before Virāṭa like a maidservant, thinking:
"What will the Emperor say to me regarding this well-prepared cosmetic paste? For it is said that the King of Matsya does not approve of sandalwood ground by anyone else."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Recalling her sorrows,
the beautiful Kṛṣṇā wept softly while gazing at Bhīmasena.
Sighing again and again with a voice choked with tears,
she spoke these words, striking at the heart of Bhīmasena:
"King Yudhiṣṭhira, however, will surely reproach you for this."
“If he were to hear it, O auspicious lady, he would give up his very life—
Dhanañjaya, O fair-hipped one, and the twins as well, O lady of radiant smiles.
She wept softly, and Kṛṣṇā spoke these words again:

"O Bhīma, I have not committed a small offense against the gods in the past; yet, O Pāṇḍava, that I still live when I ought to die is due to my own misfortune. If you do not kill Kīcaka, I shall destroy myself."
I shall stir up poison and drink it, or else I shall enter the fire;
for I am unfortunate, meritless, perpetually sorrowful, and distressed. What is the use of my life, now that I have been cast down by sin?
Then Vṛkodara, the slayer of enemy heroes, brought the swollen, calloused hands of that trembling woman to his face and wept. And taking hold of those two hands, the valiant son of Kuntī shed tears.
Then, afflicted by supreme sorrow, he spoke these words.
Bhīmasena said:
"Listen, O blessed lady of beautiful hips; what was thought there in my anger—"
"Having seen you presiding over the assembly and desiring to bring about the great slaughter of the Matsyas— blessings be upon you— I looked toward a tree; however,
there the King of Dharma restrained me with a mere glance."
Having reflected on that, I remained silent with my face turned downward in the kitchen.
Listen, O beautiful lady, to another promise that I shall now declare here—
Vaiśampāyana said.
Consoling the princess of Pañcāla, Bhīmasena said:
"Fie upon the strength of my arms and upon Phalguna’s Gāṇḍīva bow, since both your hands, which were once tender and red, have now become calloused!"
"O timid one, that which I did not do previously now causes me remorse: that I did not bring about the destruction of the evil-doing Kurus in the gambling match.
In the assembly hall of Virāṭa, I would have wrought a great slaughter."
In this matter, the reason why the son of Kuntī waits seems clear to me;
otherwise, I would have crushed the head of Kīcaka with my foot,
as a great elephant in play tramples one intoxicated by the pride of power.
O Kṛṣṇā, when I saw you struck by Kīcaka with his foot,
at that very moment I desired to carry out a great slaughter of the Matsyas;
however, the King of Dharma restrained me there with a mere glance.
Having understood his intention, O beautiful lady, I remained right there;
as did the fall of the Kurus from their kingdom,
and the non-slaughter of Suyodhana, Karṇa, and Śakuni, the son of Subala.
"O auspicious lady, that I have not yet taken the head of the wicked Duḥśāsana burns my heart like an arrow lodged within it.
Moreover, O woman of beautiful hips, you shall remember these words of mine."
When we had gathered together on the auspicious bank of the Sarasvatī,
O Kṛṣṇa, I spoke there, recollecting our former sufferings:
"I will not follow Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira."
O Pāñcālī, having set my mind upon Dhanañjaya, the two sons of Mādrī,
and Yudhiṣṭhira,
I then spoke harsh words to Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, after hearing my speech.
The modest King Yudhiṣṭhira, speaking words of undiminished meaning,
led all his brothers away while the sage Dhaumya looked on:
"Do not weep, O Queen, you who are endowed with the virtues of all sacred scriptures and the worlds."

We must always protect the truth, which is peerless on this earth. Since we have been conciliated, you too should be conciliated; do not abandon the Dharma, O fair-hipped one, and abandon your anger, O high-minded lady.
O auspicious one, if King Yudhiṣṭhira were to hear this entire reproach from you, he would give up his life;
or Dhananjaya, O fair-hipped one, or the twins, O slender-waisted lady.
"If they have gone to another world, I shall not be able to live.
Listen to the dharma, O Pāñcālī, which I shall speak to you, O beautiful lady.
Śāryātī, named Sukanyā, [attended] Cyavana of the Bhṛgu lineage in the forest."

The passionate Nāḍāyanī Indrasenā— of whom you have likely heard for her beauty— followed her husband as he became like an anthill and grew old, even though he was a thousand years of age. She attended upon him as he lay dying.
If you have heard of Vaidehī, the daughter of Janaka,
Sītā followed her husband who dwelt in the great forest;
though she suffered capture by a rākṣasa, she remained the beloved queen of Rāma.
Sītā was abducted by Rāvaṇa and threatened by the rākṣasīs;
though she was being tormented, that woman of beautiful hips remained devoted only to Rāma. Likewise, O timid one, Lopāmudrā, endowed with youth and beauty, [remained faithful].
Having abandoned all superhuman desires,
the blameless and high-minded Sāvitrī followed Agastya; she alone followed the heroic Satyavān, the son of Dyumatsena, even unto the realm of Yama.
Just as these women who have been celebrated—
beautiful and devoted to their husbands— followed King Nala in the midst of the forest, O Kṛṣṇā, even so did you follow your husbands in former times.
"In the same way, O auspicious lady, you too, endowed with all virtues,
must endure this time for no longer than one month and a half.
When the thirteenth year is complete, you shall become the queen of the king."
"I swear to you by truth that this shall not be otherwise;
you ought to establish your authority over all supreme women,
and you shall stand at the head of all kings, O beautiful lady."
Through devotion to your husband and through your conduct, you shall obtain enjoyments difficult to attain;
and when your vow is fulfilled, you shall obtain great enjoyment. Knowing this, devote yourself to your husband, and you shall stand at the head of queens.
Draupadī said:
"O Bhīma, it was out of distress that I shed these tears;
being unable to endure my sorrows, I do not reproach the king."
"O Bhīmasena of great strength, having spoken of what is past,
O son of Kuntī, understand this sorrow of mine which is unbearable:
that this Kīcaka is the king Virāṭa’s son of a charioteer."
The one known by the name Syāla was a Bhoja born in the country of Trigarta;
he had abandoned righteousness, was cruel, yet was beloved in all worldly matters. That evil-minded man constantly said, "Become my wife, O beautiful one."
"O Bhīmasena of great strength, that undisciplined and wicked-souled one thinks, 'He is without a protector. Therefore, by means of what has been liberated and passed away,
become the immediate successor to the task whose time has arrived."

"O Bhīma, here Kaikeyī is constantly anxious for fear that her beauty might be eclipsed by me; she wonders how the King might take her away. Knowing her disposition, and being myself one whose vision is untruthful,"
"O Bhīma, this Kīcaka is evil-minded and constantly lusts after me.
Though I was angry with him, O Bhīma, I restrained my wrath once more and spoke to that man deluded by passion: 'Protect yourself, Kīcaka!'"
"I am the wife of the five Gandharvas, their beloved queen.
Those invincible heroes, who act with reckless daring, will surely slay you.
Thus addressed, the evil-minded Kīcaka replied:
"O Sairandhrī of pure smiles, I am not afraid of the Gandharvas.
Whether it be a hundred or even a thousand Gandharvas assembled in battle, I shall slay them; O timid one, grant me a moment."
When he had spoken thus, I spoke again to the charioteer, who was overcome by passion:
"You are no match for those illustrious Gandharvas;
I am always established in dharma, endowed with noble lineage and virtuous conduct."
"I do not wish for anyone to be killed; therefore, you live, Kīcaka.
When he was addressed thus, that evil-minded man then laughed loudly. Then Kaikeyī sent me there with this message.

Previously urged by him out of a desire to do what was pleasing to his brother, [he said]: "O Sairandhrī, bring wine from Kīcaka’s residence. But when the son of the charioteer saw me, he offered me great consolation.
When her conciliatory words were rejected, he became enraged and set his mind on violating her.
Having understood the intention of that evil-minded Kīcaka,
I ran with all speed to the king for refuge.
But while I was in the presence of the king, the son of a charioteer seized me;
having thrown me down, that evil-souled one struck me with his foot,
even as Virāṭa, Kaṅka, and many people looked on.
Charioteers, courtiers, elephant-riders, and merchants—
having repeatedly reproached the king and Kaṅka as well, I was neither restrained by the king nor did he correct his lack of discipline.
This man named Kīcaka, who is King Virāṭa’s charioteer—
though he has abandoned righteousness, is cruel, and impetuous— is highly esteemed and dear [to the king]. He is a hero, arrogant, evil-minded, and deluded regarding all matters.
O illustrious one, he who violates another's wife obtains even many riches;
he may even seize the wealth of others while they cry out in protest.
He does not abide on the path of the righteous, nor does he desire to practice dharma.
Evil-natured, possessed of a sinful disposition, and subject to the power of sensual passion—
unrestrained and wicked-souled—
he would strike me down at every sight; therefore, I shall abandon my life.
For those striving for dharma, great dharma will perish;
for those guarding their agreements, there will be no wife for you.
When a wife is protected, offspring are protected.
When offspring is protected, one's own self is protected;
for it is within her that one’s own self is born—therefore the wise know her as *jāyā*. But how can the husband be protected by the wife? [She asks: "How shall my husband be born from my womb?"
"I have indeed heard from the Brāhmaṇas, who speak of the duties of the castes,
that for a Kṣatriya there is always no duty other than the destruction of enemies.
While Dharmarāja looked on, Kīcaka struck me with his foot."
O mighty Bhīmasena, while you were present, the son of a Sūta struck me down with his foot— me, your proud wife— though my mind never slumbers even when dwelling amidst the six objects of the senses.
"For by you indeed was I rescued from that terrible Jaṭāsura;
likewise, you have conquered Jayadratha along with your brothers. Therefore, slay even this wicked man who treats me with contempt."
O Bhārata, Kīcaka, because of his royal favor, has caused me great sorrow;
shatter him, who is thus intoxicated by lust, like a jar against a stone—
he who is the cause of my many misfortunes, O Bhārata.
If the sun should rise tomorrow morning while he is still alive, I shall stir up poison and drink it; let me not fall under the power of Kīcaka. For death before you, O Bhīmasena, is better for me.
04,020.034 Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus, Kṛṣṇā wept while leaning against Bhīma’s chest;
and Bhīma, embracing her, offered her great consolation.
Having consoled the slender-waisted daughter of Drupada— who was deeply distressed— with many words consistent with the truth of causes and reality,
he wiped her face, which was covered in tears, with his hand.
And Bhīma, overcome by rage and licking the corners of his mouth, spoke to her who was afflicted with grief,
his mind fixed upon Kīcaka.
Bhīmasena said:
"O blessed one, I shall do exactly as you say, O timid lady.
Today I will destroy that Kīcaka along with his kinsmen.
Make your union with him this very evening."
"O Yājñasenī of pure smiles, having shaken off both suffering and grief,
this is the dancing hall indeed constructed by the King of the Matsyas;
here the maidens dance by day and go to their respective homes at night."
"There, O timid one, is a bed with sturdy limbs and well-established;
there I shall show him his deceased ancestors and grandfathers,
who are deluded by the passion of desire arising from the sight of you."
"O lady of beautiful countenance, arrange a secret signal with the son of the charioteer,
so that they do not see you making this appointment. O auspicious one, act in such a way that he will be present."
"O timid one, O daughter of a king, act in such a way that mortals do not perceive our union, nor the destruction of Kīcaka.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus, O timid one, that slender-limbed woman, having taken leave of him in the kitchen and desiring his death, returned to her own home; and so,
having conversed in that manner, the two of them, filled with grief, shed tears.
When Bhīma had thus vowed the slaughter of Kīcaka,
Draupadī returned once more to the house of Sudeṣṇā;
they both spent that remainder of the night with hearts filled with intense anxiety.
Then Virāṭa, having learned that Kīcaka was a friend of Kṛṣṇā, spoke to his doorkeeper: "Bring Kīcaka here. Sent by Virāṭa, the doorkeeper went to Kīcaka’s residence.
Having gone to that charioteer, he said, "The King of Matsya wishes to see you.
At the king's command, Kīcaka also went to the palace of the Matsya;
having entered and bowed down to the King of Matsya, he spoke.
"I have come, O Great King, at the word of Virāṭa.
Virāṭa said:
"Speak, if there is something to be said; having heard it, I shall indeed go home."
Whether it be toward a wife, a friend, a servant, or even a king,
when happiness or sorrow is shared, there is true joy, O Kīcaka.
You alone are my refuge, and by your favor, I possess this kingdom.
"Or perhaps you are my very own friend; for that reason, I perceive you. Day and night I see distress, yet the [stellar] mandala appears inverted;
I perceive the fire as if smoky and the horses as dejected."
At night, I hear the cries of jackals, both auspicious and inauspicious, as they utter their voices; and I see the orb of the sun hidden by swarms of crows.
Furthermore, O Kīcaka, the astrologers speak thus to me.
"O Kīcaka, I see Saturn in its twelfth house in your birth sign; O Kīcaka, I foresee the collapse of your palace even without the rainy season.
By these great portents, which resemble the end of an eon, I know this for certain."
"O Kīcaka, it is the truth that your death shall come at my hands; or rather,
O hero, I have heard that the Sairandhrī has five brave Gandharva husbands who perform daring deeds and are beloved by the Lord of the Gods."
"O child, you desire to make Sairandhrī the wife of those sages who, having been cursed by some ascetic, roam this earth while protecting their own devoted wife,
Sairandhrī."
She cannot be enjoyed by you while she is protected by a Gandharva;
you are excessively afflicted by passion and do not perceive this duty. O gentle one, you will certainly have to die because of these lightning strikes.
And what other woman of such a kind could walk upon the circle of the earth,
except for Sairandhrī— blessings be upon you— who is protected by the Gandharvas herself?
Whether she be an old man, a master, or even the husband of a sister.

"O son of Kaikeyī, the king must always be honored and respected; you must carry out my word. Abandon that talk of Sairandhrī, O Kīcaka; she appears as a great object of desire because of her exceeding beauty."
"Having abandoned desire for the Sairandhrī, you shall become the commander of my army.
Kīcaka said:
"O son of Kaikeyī, protect [her] with confidence according to my word."
"In every way, your word must be carried out by me;
nevertheless, this slender-waisted woman must certainly be enjoyed by me, if this passionate Sairandhrī remains clinging to my side with affection."
O King, that fish does not lie upon its bed; I think it has died of its own accord.
O lord of men, desire for the sake of Sairandhrī torments me intensely;
having cast my life away like a blade of grass, I must indeed enjoy that auspicious woman.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O lord of the people, the Gandharvas were not capable of doing even the slightest thing against me.
Afflicted by love, he then went to the king.
O king of kings, having disregarded the words of the monarch and desiring union with the daughter of Drupada,
he was reconciling himself while knowing that his death was certain.
When that night had passed, Kīcaka rose in the morning,
went to the royal palace, and spoke thus to Draupadī:
"In the assembly hall, while the king looked on, I threw you down and struck you with my foot."
And you did not find any protection when attacked by one more powerful;
for it is only by common report that this man is called the king of the Matsyas by name.
Indeed, I alone am the king of the Matsyas and the commander of the army.
"Attain happiness; O timid one, I shall become your slave.
For without you, O timid one, I cannot bear to live for long.
O lady of beautiful hips, I shall give you a hundred gold coins this very day."
I shall give you a hundred female slaves and another hundred male slaves;
let there be a chariot yoked with mules for us, O timid one—let there be a union between us.
I will give you all these things and other items worthy of a king as well.
Draupadī said:
"O Kīcaka, accept this one condition of mine today,
if you indeed desire union with me now."
Neither a friend nor a brother would recognize you as being united with me;
through such discovery, there would be disaster and great infamy.
Indeed, I am afraid of being discovered by the illustrious Gandharvas.
"Promise this to me, and then I shall be under your control.
Kīcaka said:
"O lady of beautiful hips, I will do exactly as you say."
"O blessed one, I shall go alone to your empty dwelling for the sake of union with you, O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, for I am infatuated by passion;
so that the Gandharvas, radiant as the sun, shall not perceive you."
Draupadī said:
"This dancing hall which has been built by the King of Matsya—
here the maidens dance by day and go to their respective homes at night."
"Go there in the darkness; the Gandharvas will not perceive you.
There, any fault will be avoided, of this there is no doubt. Being alone, go to the dancing hall at night according to the appointment."
Kīcaka said:
"In that matter, I shall come under your control; of this there is no doubt. O blessed lady, I shall do exactly as you desire, O timid one."
"O beautiful one, being alone, I shall come to the dancing hall for the sake of our union; O fair-hipped one, I swear it by my own merit,
so that the Gandharvas do not perceive you, O woman of excellent complexion."
"I promise you truly: you shall have no fear from the Gandharvas. Today I shall adorn myself for the sake of our union; I shall also provide you with various beautiful garments."
"O Sūta, Draupadī said:
'I shall delight with you in such a way that you will never abandon me;
indeed, O charioteer, I shall show you happiness.'"
"O Kīcaka, that which has never been experienced by you since birth...
Vaiśampāyana said:
While Kṛṣṇā was thus speaking these words to Kīcaka, [Kīcaka seized her].
O King, half a day passed as if it were equal to a month; there, she informed Bhīmasena of that matter. Then Kīcaka, having gone home, was overwhelmed with great joy.
Deluded, he did not recognize that he was Death himself in the form of Sairandhrī;
especially intent upon perfumes, ornaments, and garlands, he,
infatuated by desire, quickly adorned himself.
As he performed that task, time seemed to stretch out for him as he brooded upon that very large-eyed woman;
and even as he sought to abandon his own splendor, his majesty became even more exalted.
At the time of his own destruction, like one wishing to burn the wick of a lamp,
Kīcaka— deluded by lust and full of confidence in that matter—
was so preoccupied with thoughts of their union that he did not realize the day was passing away.

Then the auspicious Draupadī, having gone to the kitchen, approached her husband Bhīma, the descendant of Kuru, from nearby. She, whose hair was beautiful, said to him: "I have [dealt with] Kīcaka..."
"O scorcher of enemies, as you have said, their meeting in the dancing hall was destined by time; Kīcaka has been bound by fate and overpowered by desire. He will come to that empty dancing hall."
"O mighty-armed one, alone at night, destroy that Kīcaka.
O son of Kuntī, O Pāṇḍava, go to the dancing hall and deprive that son of a Sūta, Kīcaka— who is arrogant with pride— of his life."
Out of pride, that son of a Sūta disregards the Gandharvas;
O best among strikers, uproot him like a reed, O Naga!
Wipe away the tears of me who am overwhelmed by grief, O Bhārata.
"Display today your prowess and valor in accordance with the strength of your arms;
may you be blessed, act for the honor of yourself and of your lineage.
Bhīmasena said:
"Welcome to you, O lady of beautiful hips, for you have informed me of what is dear to me.
Indeed, O woman of excellent complexion, I do not desire anyone else as a companion.
The joy that I feel at the prospect of meeting Kīcaka was described by you."
"O woman of excellent complexion, after slaying Hiḍimba, that was my joy;
truly, placing truth, my brothers, and dharma before me, I tell you this:
I shall slay Kīcaka just as the Lord of the Gods slew Vṛtra."
"I shall forcibly destroy him, just as Keśava destroyed Keśin; whether in the thicket or in the open, I will crush Kīcaka. O blessed lady, I shall slay Kīcaka, who is intoxicated with passion."
But he whose soul is overcome by desire regards you, who are so difficult to attain;
yet if they should realize it, I shall certainly slay even the fish.
Furthermore, if they perceive that the Sūta’s son has been killed by me...
"I shall rid this abode of fish of all its inhabitants;
then, having slain Duryodhana, I shall take possession of the earth.
But if the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra learns that the Matsyas have been slain by me..."
"Then, having slain Duryodhana along with his followers and kinsmen,
O beautiful lady, I shall recover the entire kingdom of the Kurus.
I shall not be able to persuade Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī."

Let Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, serve Matsya as he pleases; let others likewise, being humble and practitioners of dharma, serve him as they wish. But I cannot bear to neglect you, who have fallen into this misery.
"O Pāñcālī, be at peace once more through the slaying of Kīcaka.
Draupadī said:
"O Bhīma, if the citizens learn of the slaying of Kīcaka..."
O mighty-armed one, because of what you have done, I am able to continue living;
O Lord, so that you do not abandon the truth on my account,
O hero, strike down Kīcaka while remaining hidden.
For Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī and King of Dharma, having awakened to his duty,
will surely go back to the forest again, surrounded by his younger brothers;
and who, O Bhārata, could transgress one so supreme and devoted to righteousness?
O Bhīma, I am terrified; please do not act rashly. O Kauravya, O powerful crusher of enemies, act in such a way that no one discovers that you have slain the Sūtaputra.
"Remaining invisible, O subduer of enemies, destroy his life-breaths.
Bhīmasena said,
"O timid one, I shall do exactly as you say."
"O blameless lady, today, while remaining unseen in this darkness, I shall slay Kīcaka along with his kinsmen. Today,
like a serpent attacking a wood-apple fruit, I shall crush his head."

O Pāñcālī, regarding that evil-minded Kīcaka who desired what was unobtainable, what I said to the son of Dharmarāja— what else could anyone have done but follow the King out of anger? Who indeed would not obey a monarch?
Vaiśampāyana said:
By the grace of Dharma, however, the son of the Wind-god transformed his appearance and assumed the form of a cowherd.
Terrible, fierce, and intoxicated by his strength like Death itself,
he stood there like a lion for the purpose of slaying an elephant.
Having spoken thus, the mighty-armed joy of the Pāṇḍavas remained there.
Then, at midnight, that courageous man of formidable prowess rose up;
covered then with a clean, soft cloth and placing Draupadī behind him, he went to where the dancing hall was located.
Then Bhīma, having gone there first, sat down hidden in the night;
invisible like a lion waiting for a deer, he awaited Kīchaka,
longing for the slaughter of that evil-minded man.
In the meantime, when the sun had set,
the charioteer Kīcaka, having adorned himself according to his desire,
arrived and quickly went to the trysting-place, an open, empty chamber.
At that time, in the dancing hall, anticipating a meeting with Pāñcālī,
he entered that chamber, thinking it was the appointed place;
and having entered that great dwelling enveloped in darkness, he remained there.
Then, the evil-minded one approached Bhīma, who had arrived there earlier and was standing in a secluded spot, possessing incomparable splendor;
having come near Bhīma, the wicked-minded one addressed him.
As he lay there upon his bed, the charioteer seized Death,
who was blazing with the fury born of Kṛṣṇa’s assault, just as a small animal might seize a flaming moth or a lion.
Having approached him, Kīcaka, deluded by lust and his mind and soul agitated by joy, spoke with a smile:
"I have brought you wealth of many forms and infinite quantity."

O fair-browed one, he built a house and an inner apartment rich with wealth and jewels, attended by hundreds of female servants, adorned with young women endowed with beauty and grace, and resplendent with play and pleasure.
All of this has come upon you suddenly for that very reason. It is not without cause that the women in our homes always praise me, saying:
"There is no other man like you—well-dressed and handsome."
Endowed with beauty, adorned with baths and aloe-wood paste, I was always beloved by women; through my good fortune, I was pleasing to behold.
O lotus-eyed one, this is the fruit I have obtained because of that beauty.
Bhīmasena said:
"By good fortune you are handsome; by good fortune you praise yourself.
Even by you, such a woman—endowed with beauty, character, and virtue—"
"O son of a charioteer, behold this woman whom you have never seen before, from whom you were born. In a moment you shall see her, endowed with such virtues;
you ought to look upon her quickly, for you will be freed from desire."

But such a touch as this has never before been experienced by you. You understand the nature of touch; you are clever and skilled in the ways of love. There is no other man here who brings such pleasure to women as you do.
04,021.047 Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus to him, the mighty-armed Bhīma of terrible prowess,
the son of Kuntī, leapt up and laughed at that lowest of men.

"Today, O wicked one, as you are being dragged upon the ground by me, your sister shall see you, who resemble a mountain, like a great elephant by a lion. Once you are slain, Sairandhrī will roam about free from all affliction."
"Then the husbands of the *sairandhrī* will indeed live in happiness.
Having heard those words of Bhīma,
that one of great strength then spoke these words to him who was enraged at night:
"O great hero, you are undoubtedly a Gandharva;
today I shall slay you along with your allies and your kinsmen. Thus was he addressed by that evil-minded Kīcaka.
Those two, both possessed of great prowess, suddenly fell upon him;
Bhīma seized them by their fragrant, garlanded hair.
Thus was that foremost of the strong grasped by the hair with force by the powerful one.
Seizing his hair with force, he grabbed the Pāṇḍava by the arms;
a wrestling match ensued between those two enraged lions among men,
like that of two powerful elephants over a female in spring.
Roaring like two tigers, as haughty as Tārkṣya and the serpent,
Bhīma and Kīcaka fell down effortlessly yet with equal fury;
like two elephants intoxicated with rut, they roared as they fell to the earth.
Like two bulls trampling an anthill, those two of equal prowess pressed forward;
the chief of the Kīcakas and that most excellent of men were enraged with one another, each seeking the other's death.
Like the two lion-like monkeys, Vālin and Sugrīva, the brothers, as before; then, raising their arms like five-headed serpents,
they struck one another with claws and fangs, intoxicated by the poison of their wrath.
Struck with force by the powerful Kīcaka, Bhīma—
firm in his vow— did not move even a single step from his position in the battle.
As they grappled with one another, each dragging the other toward himself, they locked together.
Both shone forth like two full-grown bulls;
for between them there occurred a most tumultuous and exceedingly terrible clash,
like that of two proud tigers armed with claws and teeth.
Then, rushing forward in indignation, he seized him with his arms like one rutting elephant attacking another with temples and mouth flowing with ichor;
and the heroic Bhīma likewise received him then.
Then Kīcaka, the best among the strong, violently seized her by force.
From the crushing pressure of the arms of those two powerful men,
a terrible sound arose in the struggle, like the cracking of bamboo.
Then Vṛkodara, having seized him by force in the middle of the house,
shook him violently, like a fierce wind shaking a tree;
and being grasped in battle by the mighty Bhīma, he became weak.
He struggled with all his might and dragged the Pāṇḍava toward him;
though he stood with trembling feet, slightly reeling from rage,
the powerful Kīcaka threw Bhīma to the ground with his knees.
But Bhīma, having been thrown to the ground by the stronger Kīcaka,
then sprang up with speed like a snake struck by a staff;
for both those men, the Sūta and the Pāṇḍava, were intoxicated by their strength and driven by rivalry.
