At midnight, those two strong men dragged each other about in the lonely night; then that best of palaces trembled again and again,
and the two, filled with intense rage, roared at one another.
Struck on the chest with both palms by Bhīma, the powerful Kīcaka,
though consumed by rage, did not move even a single step from his place.
Having endured that unbearable force for a moment upon the ground, he remained there.
Then, oppressed by Bhīma’s strength, the charioteer was forcibly driven back.
Perceiving him retreating, the immensely powerful Bhīmasena drew him toward his chest and, with great force, crushed the unconscious man.
Overcome with rage and sighing deeply, Vṛkodara,
the best among victors, then seized him firmly by the hair.
Having grasped Kīcaka, the mighty Bhīma roared aloud.
Like a tiger longing for flesh that has seized a great deer,
the exceedingly powerful Kīcaka, arrogant in his strength and difficult to overcome, continued to struggle there with the energetic Pāṇḍava.
Struck violently on the head with his fist by Bhīmasena, Kīcaka, his eyes turned red and bulging, fell lifeless to the ground. Then, perceiving him to be exhausted, Vṛkodara—
With his two arms, he bound him as one binds an animal with a rope;
though he was crying out with a great roar, sounding like a burst bherī drum,
he whirled him around for a long time while he writhed, deprived of consciousness.
Then Vṛkodara, seizing his throat with both arms with great force,
squeezed it to appease Draupadī’s anger.
Thereupon, all his limbs were broken, and his eyes and garments were disarrayed.
Having stepped upon the waist of the base Kīcaka with his knee,
he crushed him with his arms and killed him like an animal. Perceiving that Kīcaka was dying, the son of Pāṇḍu—
He whirled him about upon the surface of the earth and spoke these words:
"Today, having become free from debt to my brother by slaying this thorn in the side of Sairandhrī, I shall attain supreme peace."
Having spoken thus, that hero among men,
his eyes red with rage, [beheld] Kīcaka,
whose garments and ornaments were slipping off as he quivered.
With his mind bewildered and deprived of life,
he was cast aside; having crushed hand against hand, the powerful one, biting his lips,
being the best among the strong, stepped forward with force in a state of rage.
Leaping up with great force onto Kīcaka’s chest, the valiant one struck him with his knees; seizing Kīcaka’s feet,
he whirled him around with speed and dashed him against the ground.
Bhima, too, of great prowess, quickly releasing his feet and leaping upward,
fell upon Kīcaka’s head;
seizing him by the hair and pulling him up, he dragged him about in every direction.
Seizing Bhīma’s hands, Kīcaka, arrogant in his strength,
released the hair of Draupadī and grabbed the Pāṇḍava by the throat;
with their throats thus gripped, they both threw each other down in the combat.
Like two enraged cats hissing and hissing with their breaths,
the son of Kuntī was upon Kīcaka and Kīcaka was upon the son of Kuntī;
thus the Sūta and the Pāṇḍava threw each other down for a moment.
Rising once more, those two heroes, both possessed of mighty arms and incensed by their mutual provocation, engaged in a wrestling match,
striking one another with their feet, knees, and fists.
As Bhīma and Kīcaka were thus striking each other,
a sound arose in the night like the crash of a thunderbolt;
then the powerful Bhīma, finding an opening, seized Kīcaka with both his hands.
Seeing him faltering, he clasped him in the middle and broke him;
having thrown him face-upward, he stood upon his chest with both feet. The one of firm form wiped away the dust with his right hand.
Seizing his fist, he struck him violently upon the head.
By that blow of the fist, his tongue was forced out, his eyes rolled from their sockets,
and he discharged excrement and urine, braying like a buffalo.
He thrust his feet, hands, head, and neck entirely into his body,
just as the wielder of the Pināka bow [Śiva] did with a sacrificial animal.
With all his limbs crushed, he was made to resemble a single mass of flesh.
There, having himself kindled a fire,
the mighty Bhimasena showed the *kīcaka* to Kṛṣṇā;
and the son of Pāṇḍu, possessed of great splendor, spoke to Draupadī.
"Come, O Pāñcālī, look at him— see how this lustful man has been made!
Having spoken thus, O Great King, Bhīma of terrible prowess pressed down upon the body of that evil-minded one with his foot.
Then, having kindled a fire there and shown Kīcaka to her,
that hero spoke again to the princess of Pañcāla:
"O lady of beautiful hair, those who desire you, who are endowed with virtue and good character— "
"O timid one, in this way they shall be slain so that Kīcaka may be made to look beautiful. Having performed that most difficult task, the supreme favor of Kṛṣṇā,
he who struck you down with his foot after throwing you to the ground, O blessed lady— "

Having spoken thus, the mighty-armed one, having slain Kīcaka, ceased from the great battle in order to inform the others of what had occurred. Thus, having killed Kīcaka, he attained the pacification of his wrath.
Having taken leave of Draupadī Kṛṣṇā, Bhīma of terrible prowess quickly went to the kitchen;
having bathed, applied unguents, and fulfilled his heart's desire,
he sat comfortably upon his bed.
Then, when Kṛṣṇā realized that Bhīma had gone to the kitchen,
Draupadī— the best of women— having caused Kīcaka to be slain,
was filled with joy and, her distress vanished, spoke to the hall-keepers.
"Here lies Kīcaka, slain by my Gandharva husbands;
he who was intoxicated with lust for another's wife—come and behold him!
Having heard those words of hers, the guards of the dancing hall...
Suddenly, thousands of people arrived carrying torches;
hearing that roar of his, Kīcaka’s brothers then went to that house and found Kīcaka struck down.
They saw him lying dead on the ground, drenched in blood;
neither his neck, nor his feet, nor his hands, nor his head could be found.
Seeing him deprived of both hands and feet, they were overcome with distress.
Then they all gazed upon him and were struck with supreme wonder;
seeing that superhuman deed performed, he had been struck down.
Then, O bull of the Bharatas, they quickly became afraid, taking up their weapons.

Then, their hair standing on end with wonder as they gazed upon Kīcaka, they examined him who had been slain by the Gandharva, wondering: "Where is his neck? Where are his feet? Where are his hands, and likewise, where is his head?"
Seeing the commander of the army slain at night, those who were facing the forces of King Virāṭa thought that he had been given as a gift by Uṣādhidevī.
A lump of flesh mixed with sweet wine.
Vaiśampāyana said:
At that time, all his kinsmen gathered there together.
Seeing Kīcaka, they wept, surrounding him on all sides;
with their hair standing on end and terrified at the sight of Kīcaka,
whose every limb was thus contorted like a tortoise pulled out onto dry land.

Having heard that Kīcaka— that bull among men, intoxicated by his strength, unassailable by anyone, and like a Dānava slain by Indra— had been killed by Bhīmasena, who was himself a Gandharva, [the king was overcome].
Desiring to prepare her for the marriage rite, they set out to lead her outside;
then the assembled sons of the Sūta beheld Kṛṣṇā from nearby,
standing with faultless limbs as she leaned against a pillar.
When the Sūtas had assembled, Upakīcaka spoke to them,
as if laughing yet burning with indignation at them with his eyes:
"Let this unchaste woman be slain quickly, for whose sake Kīcaka was killed!"
"Alternatively, she should not be killed here; let her be burned together with the lustful man.
Even for one who is dead, every effort must be made to do what is pleasing to the son of the Sūta.
For this woman of wicked conduct was an enemy to my brother."

"Because of whom he met his death, she ought not to live. O Sūtas, having taken leave of the lord of men, I shall endure being burned; for even though Kīcaka has been slain by the Gandharvas, this would be pleasing to him."
Then they said to Virāṭa: "Kīcaka has been killed on her account;
he should be burned today along with this [body]. You ought to grant permission for that.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then the charioteers, having approached Virāṭa with palms joined in reverence, said:
"This Kīcaka lies here slain by Gandharvas who can assume any form at will."
"She was killed by Sairandhrī in the night; let us burn her along with her.
For she has been honored by you, O King; therefore, you ought to grant permission.
Having considered the prowess of the Sūtas, the king consented.
O lord of the people, regarding the burning of Sairandhrī together with the son of the Sūta—
having encountered the lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇā there while she was terrified and bewildered,
those Kīcakas seized her violently.
Then, having placed that slender-waisted woman upon it and bound her,
they all lifted her up and went toward the cremation ground.
Then all his kinsmen there were permitted to depart.
Seeing Kīcaka, the female attendants standing all around wept;
then, having placed Kṛṣṇā upon him, Kīcaka bound her by her hair and her feet.
And those charioteers, having looked toward Kṛṣṇā and addressing her with these words, spoke:
"It was for her sake that this great-souled one was slain."
Therefore, indeed, she was pursued along the path by Kīcaka,
that ignoble being;
thus says Vaiśampāyana.
Sundarī, though her life had departed,
lay upon the bed bound to it; so too did the wise and illustrious Kṛṣṇā.
O King,
that woman of beautiful limbs and irreproachable character was being carried away by the sons of the Sūta; helpless and dragged along, she lingered right there upon her excellent couch.
Seeking a protector though she already had one, Kṛṣṇā cried out;
with her limbs bound by the dead man, she was then hopeless of life. Led toward the cremation ground, she wailed like a female elephant.
Draupadī said:
"Jaya, Jayanta, Vijaya, Jayatsena, and Jayadbala—let them understand my words; the sons of the Sūta are carrying me away."
The great sound of their kettledrums and the twang of their bowstrings were heard;
the roar of their bowstrings and palms, like the crashing of a thunderbolt,
was heard as a terrifying sound from those swift warriors in that great battle.
The powerful sound of the chariots of the illustrious Gandharvas— let them understand my words; the sons of the Sūta are leading me away,
they whose prowess is incomparable and whose strength and fame are like those of Śakra.
"May those foremost lions among kings know me to be deeply distressed.
Vaiśampāyana said:
These were the piteous words of lamentation uttered by Kṛṣṇā.
Upon hearing this, Bhīma rushed from his bed without hesitation.
Bhīmasena said:
"O Sairandhrī, I hear your words as they were spoken by you."
"Therefore, O timid one, you have no fear from the sons of the Sūta.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus, that mighty-armed one yawned, desiring to slay them.
Then, having made his attire loose-fitting and changed his appearance,
Bhīmasena leaped down through a non-doorway and went outside. Having violently uprooted a tree from the wall, he [proceeded].
Facing the cremation ground, he proceeded to where those Kīcakas had gone;
having leaped over the wall and emerged from that best of cities,
Bhīma then sprang forward with speed ahead of the charioteers.
Having gone near the funeral pyre, O lord of the people, he saw there a great tree, as tall as a palm, with a massive trunk, dried at the top;
approaching it like an elephant and embracing it with both arms, he [fell].
The scorcher of enemies hoisted upon his shoulder a tree ten fathoms long; that powerful man, lifting up that massive trunk and branches of the ten-fathom tree, whirled it with great speed.
Seizing his staff, he rushed toward the charioteers like Death himself;
then, by the force of his thighs, the *nyagrodha*, *aśvattha*,
and *kiṃśuka* trees fell to the ground and lay there in heaps.
Seeing that Gandharva approaching like an enraged lion,
the charioteers trembled on all sides, shaken by despair and fear.
Beholding that Gandharva then coming toward them like the God of Death himself, they were struck with terror.
Then the Upakīcakas, desiring to burn their eldest brother,
spoke to one another, trembling with fear and despair:
"A powerful Gandharva approaches, enraged and uprooting a tree."
"O highly fortunate Gandharvas, radiant as the sun, you have awakened;
let Sairandhrī be released quickly, for a great danger has come upon us.
But they, seeing that tree brandished by Bhīmasena, [were struck with fear].
Having released Draupadī there, they fled toward the city.
Then Bhīma, springing up, fell before those who were running away. Seeing him, they stood motionless, agitated by fear.
Seeing those [enemies] numbering in the hundreds like Dānavas, that Vajrin-like Bhīmasena (Vṛkodara) struck down twenty-seven, thirty,
and fifty-four of them with a single blow.
Beholding them rushing forward like Dānavas,
the formidable wielder of the thunderbolt sent one hundred and five of them to the abode of Yama with this tree, O King of kings, for the mighty son of the Wind-god was indeed powerful.
Equal to the force of the wind, the illustrious and mighty-armed Bhīmasena of great strength, having slain all those charioteers without exception,
then comforted Kṛṣṇā by releasing her, O lord of the people.
And there, the mighty-armed and invincible Vṛkodara spoke to the princess of Pañcāla, Draupadī, whose face was flooded with tears and who was distressed:
"Do not grieve, O Yājñasenī; you remain steadfast in the vow of devotion to your husband."
A woman established in devotion to her husband should always protect her own vow.
Long ago, there was a woman named Śiromaṇi, who was beloved by her husband;
one day, that virtuous lady was abducted by a *rākṣasa* in the form of her husband.
Having settled her on the shore of a certain lake, that Rākṣasa abandoned his form as her husband and assumed a most dreadful demonic shape;
yet when she would not consent through conciliation, bribery, or sowing dissension, he acted.
Then, having cast her down, he proceeded to have sexual intercourse with her;
thereupon, she summoned her fortitude and did not yield an opening. Then, drawing his sword, he terrified that virtuous woman.
Having cast aside all fear, the virtuous woman, firmly resolved to give up her life,
made this vow before Kṛṣṇa, being wholly devoted to her husband:
"If I have ever honored my husband, who is my great deity..."
"By deed, by mind, and by speech, my gurus have been satisfied by me;
by that truth, let my womb today become a firm rock. When she had thus made her vow, her womb became that very rock.
Everything between her navel and her knees became as hard as stone;
then, drawing his sword, he swiftly severed her head.
She became a companion named Jayā to Pārvatī, like the flesh on her fingernails.
Therefore, for a devoted wife, suffering is slight and happiness is great.
Thus, O timid one, those who afflict you though you are innocent shall be slain. Go back to the city, O Kṛṣṇā; no fear exists for you.
"Go quickly by another path to the residence of Sudeṣṇā. Having been addressed thus by Bhīmasena, she vanished at that very moment,
fearing that someone might see her as she withdrew.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"So that they might not recognize us while we were thus situated during the night,
Kṛṣṇā, having been comforted by Bhīmasena, proceeded toward the city."
Having accomplished her purpose, she of auspicious marks entered the palace of Sudeṣṇā, just as Śacī entered Triviṣṭapa when Nahuṣa had been cursed.
Bhīma, too, was of immeasurable prowess, powerful, and a crusher of enemies.
Having slain all those Kīcakas there, the younger brother of the son of Dharma—
Rāma, having destroyed the Kīcakas without exception like the Rātriñcaras—
then entered the city, his enemies conquered and his spirit undaunted.
"I shall go by another way to Virāṭa’s kitchen;
and those one hundred and five [warriors] have been slain there, O Bhārata,
lying like a great forest cut down with its trees fallen."
"Thus, O King, those one hundred and five Kīcakas were slain, as well as that former commander; this makes six hundred Sūtas.
Out of fear of the Gandharvas, the kinsmen of Kīcaka did not dare to speak."
Unable even to look upon her there out of fear,
all the Matsyas gathered in the city of Virāṭa saw those five hundred charioteers slain at dawn.
O King, having witnessed that great marvel, the men and women gathered together,
as well as the citizens, were filled with supreme wonder.
Having reached a state of extreme amazement, O Bhārata, they said nothing at all.
Vaiśampāyana said: Then,
when the night had passed and dawn had broken, the king rose with his retinue and heard that one hundred and six Kīcakas had been slain at daybreak.
Having seen those charioteers slain by Bhīmasena, O Bhārata, they went and reported it to the king,
as did all the citizens gathered together.
O King, more than a hundred Sūta sons were slain by the Gandharvas;
they appeared scattered upon the surface of the earth like the great peak of a mountain shattered by a thunderbolt.
"And this Sairandhrī, having been liberated, will return to your house;
O King, your entire city will fall into danger,
for such is the nature of Sairandhrī and the Gandharvas are possessed of great power."
There is no doubt that the object desired by men for sexual union is you;
O King, act with such policy that this city does not swiftly go to destruction because of your disguise as a *sairandhrī*.
For those who gaze with unblinking eyes upon that auspicious woman, endowed with the excellence of all her limbs and radiant with beauty and charm,
there is no obstruction of either the mind or the sight.
Therefore, that foolish man who, having seen her whose beauty is peerless on earth,
should fall under the power of desire, will be slain by the Gandharvas.
Drive her out from the palace and especially from the city.
"Desire, having entered through Sairandhrī, will surely destroy the city.
Having heard those words of theirs, Virāṭa, the commander of the army, said:
"Let the highest funeral rites be performed for these charioteers."
Let all those Kīcakas be quickly consumed in that very same single, well-kindled fire, together with jewels and perfumes from every side.
Let them all be burned in that very same single, well-kindled fire.
Having burned all the Kīcakas and performed their funeral rites in every way,
the king, overcome with trepidation, spoke to his queen Sudeṣṇā:
"When the Sairandhrī arrives, speak these words to her in my name."
"Go, Sairandhrī; may it be well with you. Wander as you please, O weak one. O lady of beautiful hips, the king fears defeat at the hands of the Gandharvas.
Indeed, I do not venture to speak to her myself while she is protected by the Gandharvas."
"However, women are not at fault in speaking thus; therefore, I tell you this.
Then Kṛṣṇā, freed from fear and having cast off the sons of the Sūta, was liberated by Bhīmasena and proceeded toward the city.
Like a young doe terrified by a tiger,
that high-minded woman washed her limbs and her garments with water;
seeing her, O King, the men fled in the ten directions.
Terrified by the fear of the *gandharvas*, some closed their eyes;
others likewise fled, while still others,
bewildered, covered their eyes with their hands.
"Do not look at her!"— saying this,
the people cried out in a state of great distress;
for who today could behold her, so full of beauty?
"Let him lie here broken, just like the *kīcaka* reeds," they cried, their consciousness overwhelmed by the force of fear and bewildered by the terror caused by the *gandharva*.
Then, O King, the princess of Pañcāla saw Bhīmasena standing at the door of the kitchen like a great elephant in rut; gazing at him in wonder,
she spoke these words slowly with signs of recognition.
Homage to the King of the Gandharvas, by whom I have been delivered from the Kīcakas— me,
who was faultless yet dwelling helplessly in their house. Homage be to you, the Gandharva, who protects me while I am terrified.
Bhīmasena said:
"O woman, those men who here in this world move about under your control—
you should always remain subject to them and conduct yourself as you please."
"Having heard her words, they indeed move about free from debt.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Having heard those words of theirs, other people did not give birth [to such offspring]."
Then the daughter of the Pāñcāla king also went there;
in that dancing hall,
the princess of King Virāṭa beheld the long-armed Dhanañjaya as he was teaching her to dance.
Then, having emerged from the dancing hall together with Arjuna,
those maidens beheld Kṛṣṇā approaching— distressed, though she was innocent.
The maidens said:
"By good fortune, O Sairandhrī, you have been liberated; by good fortune, you have returned.
By good fortune, those Sūtas who tormented you though you were innocent have been slain.
Bṛhannaḍā said:
"O Sairandhrī, how were you released? And how were those wicked men slain? I truly wish to hear all of this from you exactly as it happened.
Sairandhrī said:
"Bṛhannaḍā, what business do you have today with a *sairandhrī*, you who,
O blessed one, always dwell happily in the maidens' quarters? For you do not experience the suffering that a *sairandhrī* must endure."
"You live here in happiness; that suffering has not been encountered by you. Therefore, you ask me, who am thus distressed, as if laughing.
Bṛhannaḍā said:
"O auspicious one, Bṛhannaḍā too experiences unsurpassed suffering; O foolish girl, you do not realize that she has entered the womb of an animal.
I have lived with you, and you have lived with all of us."

O lady of beautiful hips, when you are suffering, who indeed would not feel sorrow? Yet, it is certainly impossible for anyone anywhere to know the heart of another completely; it is for this reason that you do not understand me.
"O lady, I would have to live in a dwelling more difficult than this because of you.
Indeed, whose heart can truly be known by whom?
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, together with the maidens, Draupadī entered that royal palace and approached Sudeṣṇā without retreating.
At the word of Virāṭa, the princess spoke this to her:
"Sairandhrī, go quickly wherever you wish to go. May you be blessed; the king fears defeat by the Gandharvas.
And you too, O fair-browed one, are young and peerless in beauty upon this earth."
Sensual objects are desired by men, and the Gandharvas are exceedingly prone to anger; furthermore, the minds of men, O radiant one, are attached to the pleasure born of touch.
Therefore, I have great fear of you for my kingdom and my city.
"Go this very day from the city wherever you please;
for your sake, O auspicious one, all my kinsmen have been slain. Truly, your intellect is cruel, since you have caused the death of my brothers."
"Therefore, a danger from the Gandharva kings arises today.
Go as you please, Sairandhrī, so that there may be safety for you here."—
Vaiśampāyana.
Having heard the words of Sudeṣṇā, the Sairandhrī spoke as follows:
The Sairandhrī said:
"O beautiful lady, let the king forgive me for only thirteen days more."
The Gandharvas will have accomplished their purpose; of this there is no doubt.
Then they will lead me away and do what is pleasing to you.
And the king, together with his kinsmen, will surely be united with prosperity.
Having spoken thus, Kaikeyī then addressed the king;
her desires fulfilled, she remained there, having been gratified by the son of Vāyu,
O auspicious one, for those who have received favors from a king are always grateful.
The virtuous, when intoxicated by power, desire only to retaliate for what has been done to them. I am a petitioner; consider whether this is right or wrong. — Vaiśampāyana.
"Support her for just that length of time, and it will be for your own welfare.
Having heard those words of hers, Kaikeyī, distressed and bewildered by grief,
spoke to Draupadī, who was herself emaciated by the calamity that had befallen her brother.
"O blessed lady, dwell here as you please; I have come to you for refuge. Protect my husband and especially my sons.
Having thus related the account of the year spent in secret residence by the Pāṇḍavas, the son of Parāśara [Vaiśampāyana] spoke.
In this [section], ending with the slaying of Kīcaka, for thirteen days, for the sake of dispelling the remaining impressions of their ignorance,
and indeed for the purpose of investigating the affairs of the Lord of the Kurus and attaining the fruit sought through long search, [the events concerning] Suyodhana and the others [are described].
In order to describe their movements and counter-movements,
Vaiśampāyana said:
"When Kīcaka had been slain, King Virāṭa, the slayer of enemy heroes..."

O lord of the people, upon the slaughter of Kīcaka along with his younger brothers, the king, together with his ministers and his domestic priest, experienced intense grief; and reflecting on that great calamity, the common folk were struck with wonder.
In that city and throughout the countryside, there was a universal rumor:
"Kīcaka is indeed the king’s favorite because of his heroism;
he is a great being, renowned for his prowess in battle, powerful, and invincible in combat."
"He was a slayer of men, a wicked-minded violator of others' wives;
that evil-souled and depraved man has indeed been slain by the Gandharvas," so they cried out, O Great King, as they struck down the enemy host.
In various places, people spoke of Kīcaka as being invincible;
meanwhile, those spies employed by the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra had searched through many villages, kingdoms, and cities.
Having made arrangements as instructed and according to the directions shown,
they returned toward Nāgapura with their minds fixed on their task;
having reached Hāstinapura, they approached the subduer of enemies, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
There, having seen the king, the Kuru descendant Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son,
seated upon a supreme golden throne that shone like the sun, he bowed his head to the ground and honored him with blessings of victory.
He was being attended by his ministers, like Vāsava by the Maruts,
together with Droṇa, Karṇa, Kṛpa, and the high-souled Bhīṣma,
as well as by learned men, singers, poets, and reciters of hymns.
Accompanied by many kṣatriyas with their retinues,
and joined by his brothers as well as the great car-warriors of Trigarta,
they spoke these words to Duryodhana as he sat in the midst of the assembly hall.
"O Indra among men, we have always exerted the greatest effort in searching for those Pāṇḍavas in that vast forest,
which is desolate, teeming with wild beasts, and covered with various trees and creepers."
In this place abounding with spreading creepers and covered with various shrubs,
we do not know by which path the sons of Pṛthā, those of firm prowess, have gone,
even as we search for their footprints here and there.
O lord of men, we have searched extensively on lofty mountain peaks, in various provinces,
in regions crowded with people, in market towns, and in cities;
yet we do not know the whereabouts of the Pāṇḍavas.
They have perished utterly; may it be well with you, O bull among men!
[They were lost] in the peaks and thickets of the mountains, within the caves, on the ridges, by the river-springs, and in the lakes and ponds.
In deep ravines, in inaccessible places, in villages, and in groves— their movements are difficult to discern, for they are sought out by us alone,
even in the vicinity of elephants and serpents, amidst lions, and among *śarabhas*.
O best of chariot-warriors, though we have searched along the tracks of the chariots, O best of men, we do not know their destination nor their dwelling place;
for a certain time, O lord of men, we followed the track of the charioteers.
"O scorcher of foes, having searched according to the rules and understood the matter in its true essence, we have reached Dvāravatī, O King, without the sons of Pṛthā;
for there are other people in the countryside who are disguised as Pārthas."
"O King, we have searched throughout the entire circle of the earth;
yet there, O lord of men, neither the Pāṇḍavas nor the devoted Kṛṣṇā are to be found. We do not know the Pāṇḍavas at all, despite our efforts."

"Be at peace; they are destroyed. Be well, O scorcher of foes! They have utterly perished; salutations to you, O bull among the Bharatas! For we do not know the destination or even the dwelling place of those great-souled ones."
We know neither the movements of the Pāṇḍavas nor the deeds they have performed;
yet the entire earth in its totality— with its mountains, forests, and groves,
along with its kingdoms, cities, villages, and towns— is [within our reach].
"We have searched for all of them, yet we do not see the Pāṇḍavas.
Therefore, O lord of men, O ruler of the people,
instruct us as to what further we should do in the search for the Pāṇḍavas."
And behold this dear, auspicious, and beautiful speech of ours,
O King, by which the Trigartas were defeated by the great power of the high-souled Kīcaka, the charioteer of the Matsya king.
Slain by the Gandharvas at night, O Bhārata, he lies fallen—
Virāṭa’s brother-in-law, the noble-minded commander of the army,
the great elder brother of Sudeṣṇā, a hero, a warrior free from distress.
He was energetic, possessed of great heroism, wise in policy, and powerful; skilled in battle, a slayer of enemy heroes, and equal to a lion in prowess;
he was expert in protecting his subjects and capable of subduing his foes.
Having conquered his enemies in great battle, fierce yet devoted to honor, he gladdens the hearts of men and women; steadfast, eloquent, and fond of combat,
this best of men is a vessel for merit, virtue, wealth, and pleasure.

O lord of men, he was slain at night by the Gandharvas on account of a woman; for there is a certain broad-hipped queen among the Gandharvas named Sairandhrī, whom that powerful, arrogant, and evil-minded man desired.
"O Acyuta, while remaining invisible, that evil-minded one, together with his brothers,
has slain our friends and killed the foremost warriors here;
thus have we heard that he was struck down by the Gandharvas in the night."
Together with many kinsmen, Kīcaka has been slain.
O Indra among kings, from this day forward, it is our intention that you dispatch spies everywhere to search for the Pāṇḍavas.

At night, that evil-minded one was slain along with his brothers by the Gandharvas. Having heard this welcome news of the defeat of our enemies, we have learned only this much; may it be well with you, O lord of men.
"O descendant of Kuru, having accomplished your task, determine what must be done next.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then King Duryodhana, having heard those words of theirs at that time...
Having remained deep in thought for a long time, he replied to the members of the assembly:
"O Great King, although he knew [the truth], with his inner self pierced by a thorn,
he did not show any sign of emotion upon hearing of Kīcaka’s slaughter."

Relying solely on his valor, the powerful son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the Kaurava, having been like one whose life-force had departed and was merely gasping, now regained his strength; upon hearing their words, he reflected for a moment.
"Indeed, the ultimate course of actions is very difficult to discern.
Therefore, all of you should look out for where the Pāṇḍavas might have gone;
for the greater part of the time has passed, and only a small portion remains."
If, during this thirteenth year of their life in concealment,
those Pāṇḍavas should pass the remainder of this year here— having fulfilled their agreement and being devoted to their vow of truth— then [they shall reveal themselves].
Like lordly elephants exuding rut, all of them resemble venomous serpents;
if provoked against the Kauravas, they will certainly become a source of suffering. O lord of men, these kings must be understood through well-guided reasoning.
By means of clever, wise, and skillful spies who were well-guarded,
those who had previously been identified as having assumed difficult disguises were recognized before their time;
then, having conquered their anger, they entered the forest once again.
"Therefore, desire to learn quickly so that our kingdom may remain for a long time absolutely imperishable, free from dualities, undisturbed, and without rivals.
Then Karna said, "O Bhārata, let them go at once."
"May these [weapons], which are endowed with truth, dharma, and purpose, not go back again to Karṇa."
"Others are more cunning, skillful, discreet, and effective.
When these words had been spoken by Duryodhana, who was exceedingly distressed, [he said:
"Let them wander through various countries, well-disguised, in regions teeming with prosperous populations."
There, in various social gatherings, among perfected ones and renunciants,
in places of service, at sacred fords, in villages, and in cities;
in places of service, at sacred fords, and in various mines.
They must be identified by men through well-disciplined reasoning,
by those who are variously devoted to that task, who truly know them, and who are skillful and discreet;
the Pāṇḍavas living in concealment must be diligently sought out.
In river thickets, at sacred fords, in villages and cities,
in delightful hermitages, on mountains, and in caves—
then the younger brother [addressed] his elder brother, who was devoted to sinful inclinations.
Then his elder brother Duḥśāsana said to his brother:
"O King, O lord of men, let those spies in whom we have confidence go forth again after they have been provided with their rewards, in order to search for them further."
"I shall dispatch them, who are striving with firm devotion;
O Great King Priyadarśin, this is my opinion.
Let other spies go there, moving in disguise."
And all that Karṇa has said, we see to be exactly so:
"Animals see with their noses; Brāhmaṇas see with the Vedas;
kings see with their spies; and other people see with their eyes."
"Let all the spies search here and there exactly as instructed;
let these and many others go from region to region according to the rules.
Yet, their movement, their dwelling, and their activities cannot be discovered."
Either they have met with disaster, or those fools have gone to the far shore of the wavy sea;
or else, being deluded, they have perished on the way,
or those who imagined themselves heroes have been devoured by wild beasts in the great forest.
Having reached a supreme island, or mountain fastnesses, or forests,
their pride humbled and their hopes destroyed, they have either been devoured by *rākṣasas*, or having encountered a perilous place, they have perished for all eternity.
"Therefore, O joy of the Kurus, making your mind undistracted,
perform the task according to your resolve and as you deem fit, O lord of men.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then the highly heroic Droṇa, who perceives the truth of reality, said:
"Such as they are do not perish, nor do they suffer defeat;
for they are brave, accomplished in learning, wise, and masters of their senses."
They were knowers of dharma, grateful, and devoted to the King of Dharma; they knew the true essence of policy, dharma, and worldly purpose, and regarded him with the same composure as a father—
he who was established in dharma, firm in truth, the eldest, and one who honored his elders.
O King, those brothers were devoted to their high-souled brother Ajātaśatru, who was modest and likewise devoted to them; they were obedient, humble,
and great-souled.
"For what reason would the wise son of Pṛthā act for their benefit?
Therefore, they await with effort the arrival of the rising of Time;
indeed, I perceive through my intellect that they shall not meet with destruction."
"Now, whatever task must be done, let it be performed quickly and without delay;
let it be well-considered, and let their dwelling be prepared.
To the Matsya king who spoke thus, the Kauravas replied individually.
With palms joined in reverence, all of them, led by Yudhiṣṭhira, said:
"O lord of the people, we all rejoice in your words,
which accord with the needs of the sons of Pāṇḍu, who are steadfast in soul in all their undertakings."
Let such a policy be adopted so that their movements may be observed;
strive by every possible means to find the Pāṇḍavas as you see them.
Indeed, those heroes are difficult to track, for they are sinless and protected by their ascetic power.
"O Pārtha, he is pure-souled, virtuous, truthful, ethical, and pure;
he is an immeasurable mass of splendor who might even pluck out our eyes.
Therefore, having recognized him, let this be done, and let us search for him further."
By Brahmins, spies, perfected ones (siddhas), and other people who were knowledgeable of that;
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu and grandfather of the Bharatas...
Learned, knowing the proper place and time, a knower of reality, and conversant with all duties,
he— upon the conclusion of the teacher’s speech—
joined his own words to it and spoke these words for the sake of their welfare to the Bharatas.
Bhīṣma then addressed these words, which were focused entirely on Yudhiṣṭhira, the knower of dharma who is grounded in righteousness— words that were ever composed and never distracted,
difficult for the wicked to obtain, yet always cherished by the virtuous.
There Bhīṣma spoke words honored by the virtuous:
"Just as this Brāhmaṇa Droṇa, who knows the true essence of all matters, has spoken, so do I applaud those words; I have no hesitation in this regard."
Without doubt, it is exactly so; understand this further:
endowed with all auspicious marks, the Pāṇḍavas do not deserve destruction.
They are perfected in learning and conduct, and are possessed of the vows of the virtuous.
Immersed in the instructions of their elders and devoted to the vow of truth,
those who know the proper conduct and maintain their agreements, being pure in their vows and bearing the burden of the righteous, ought not to perish.
Always devoted to the duty of the Kṣatriya and ever following Keśava,
those great-souled and mighty heroes—
the Pāṇḍavas— were indeed protected by righteousness and by their own prowess.
"It is my firm conviction that they shall not meet with destruction;
therefore, O Bhārata, I shall direct my intellect toward the Pāṇḍavas.
For the policy of one who conducts himself with sound statesmanship cannot be fathomed by others."

"However, that which is possible for us to say here regarding those Pāṇḍavas, having reflected upon them with our intellect—not out of malice, but out of wisdom—I shall speak; listen to that. Yet, this policy should never be spoken by those like me to him under any circumstances."
"But this must be spoken properly, and never unrighteously,
O dear one, for you who abide by the instruction of the elders and are of truthful character.
However, it was improper for me to speak [thus], for the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas are equal to me."
Having reflected upon the dwelling place of the sons of Pāṇḍu, I speak; what is the use of much idle talk? Where there is dharma, there is victory.
However, a wise man who desires to speak here among the virtuous must necessarily [speak with restraint].
One should speak according to one's understanding in every way out of a desire for the Dharma; however,
in this thirteenth year, I do not think of the dwelling place of the King of Dharma in the same way as these other people.
In this matter, my dear father, it is not fitting for those kings to act improperly. O lord of men, hear now of the dwelling place of the sons of Pāṇḍu,
who are highly illustrious, accompanied by their heroic brothers and Kṛṣṇā.
"For what purpose would that great king not achieve his own welfare? You already know exactly how the Pāṇḍava was previously treated with deceit,
and how he has been constantly tormented in the city by those desiring the kingdom even now."
Therefore, that king, being naturally wise in policy, moves about in disguise; having dwelt for one year in this most excellent and well-concealed residence,
he will arrive when the time has come, and you shall soon behold the son of Pāṇḍu.
O scorcher of enemies, O mighty-armed one, take measures together with his brothers and Draupadī so that no source of happiness may arise for that hero,
that best among the upholders of truth, while he dwells there in concealment as a king.
The people there will be free from passion and delusion; for there shall be neither mental anguish nor physical disease, O Great King, O bull among Kṣatriyas,
in whatever city or countryside King Yudhiṣṭhira resides.
In the land where King Yudhiṣṭhira reigns, the people will be charitable, virtuous, generous, modest, and restrained by a sense of shame;
they will be pleasant-spoken, ever self-controlled, auspicious, and devoted to truth.

Where King Yudhiṣṭhira resides, the people will be joyful, well-nourished, pure, and skillful; they will be free from malice, envy, slander, and jealousy, remaining devoted each to their own respective duty.
There will be many resonant chants of the Vedas (*brahmaghoṣa*) and likewise full oblations (*pūrṇāhuti*); there will be numerous sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees (*bhūridakṣiṇā*).
And there, without a doubt, the rain-god (*parjanya*) shall always pour down rain properly.
The earth shall abound with crops and be free from calamities;
the grains shall be full of flavor and the fruits excellent in quality;
the garlands shall be fragrant and the speech of people auspicious.
The wind is pleasant to the touch, and the sight is free from obstruction; no diseases exist there, nor are there killings or imprisonments;
there are no thieves, no deceptions, and no afflictions whatsoever.
Where King Yudhiṣṭhira is, there are neither the powerless nor the wicked;
where King Yudhiṣṭhira is, fear does not enter.
There, the cattle are numerous, neither emaciated nor difficult to milk.
Milk, curds, and clarified butter—nutritious and wholesome;
clear waters and all auspicious things;
drinks endowed with excellent qualities and foods rich in flavor.
In that region where King Yudhiṣṭhira shall be,
the tastes, touches, smells, and sounds will be endowed with excellence;
and wherever King Yudhiṣṭhira is, all visible things will be serene.

And in that thirteenth year, O dear one, in that region inhabited by the Pāṇḍavas, the various religious duties will be seen being practiced by the twice-born, each perfectly endowed with its own specific qualities.
The people there were full of affection, contented, pure, and steadfast; they were devoted to honoring the gods and guests, possessed of love for all beings,
generous in giving what was desired, full of great energy, and ever dedicated to dharma.
Where King Yudhiṣṭhira is, there the people will be haters of evil and seekers of the auspicious, constantly performing sacrifices and observing virtuous vows;
they will be ever-rejoicing in festivals, eternally joyful, and endowed with prosperity.
"O dear one, this shall be our dwelling where King Yudhiṣṭhira resides— he who has abandoned falsehood in speech, who is auspicious, prosperous, and blessed;
he who desires auspicious goals and possesses an auspicious mind."
Endowed with compassion for all beings and always possessing a pure mind,
that righteous-souled one will be beyond description even by the twice-born, O Bhārata;
and the people there will be constantly devoted to their desired vows.
O dear one, even that righteous-souled one was difficult to perceive by the twice-born;
how much less, then, can Pārtha be fully known by ordinary people?
In him reside truth, fortitude, generosity, supreme peace, and constant forbearance.
Modesty, prosperity, fame, supreme splendor, compassion, and likewise straightforwardness—
therefore, I am unable to describe otherwise the dwelling of that wise one, which was hidden by his sacrifice, nor his supreme destination.
Having reflected thus upon what you consider to be beneficial,
perform it quickly, O Kauravya, if you indeed place such faith in me. For that which I tell you, my dear, is what is truly appropriate for the family.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Kṛpa, the son of Śaradvat, spoke these words at that time:
"What has been spoken by the elder regarding the Pāṇḍavas is both appropriate and timely."

"Listen now to my words here as well, which are consistent with dharma and artha, gentle, truthful, and reasoned, and appropriate for this occasion— spoken by Bhīṣma. Let their course and their place of residence be considered through the sacred fords (tīrthas)."
Furthermore, let a policy be adopted now that would be beneficial.
My dear son, one who desires prosperity must not despise an enemy, even if he is an ordinary man; how much less so the Pāṇḍavas, my dear son, who are all skilled in weapons in battle?
Therefore, while the high-souled Pāṇḍavas have entered into a sacrificial session (sattra),
remaining hidden and concealed, and when the time for action has arrived,
one must ascertain the strength of oneself both within one's own kingdom and in the kingdoms of others.
When the time for the rise of the Pāṇḍavas has arrived, there is no doubt;
we seek to see the dwelling place of the sons of Pāṇḍu,
for the high-souled and mighty Pārthas have completed their period of concealment.
"The Pāṇḍavas will indeed become highly energetic and possessed of exceeding splendor. Therefore, let military force, the treasury, and policy be duly prepared,
so that when the opportune time arrives, we may properly form an alliance with them."
"Dear father, I believe you should ascertain all that strength of yours—
certainly among all your friends, whether they be strong or weak—
and having recognized their various degrees of power, as well as those who stand neutral, O Bhārata."

Whether they are joyful or not joyful, we shall likewise reconcile them with their enemies by means of conciliation, sowing dissension, bribery, punishment, and tribute; and we shall subdue the strong against others through justice, and the weak by force.

Having conciliated your friends, let your army be addressed with kind words; then, augmented by your treasury and forces, you will achieve complete success. You shall also be able to fight against powerful enemies when they appear before you.
Or even with the other Pāṇḍavas, whose own strength and mounts are inferior;
having thus resolved everything according to your own duty and with firm resolve,
O lord of men, you shall obtain long-lasting happiness in due time.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Duryodhana, having heard the words of those high-souled ones and having reflected for a moment as it were, spoke this to his ministers:
For I have previously heard this in the assemblies of people in their discourses:
that the wise, learned in the scriptures, and those of firm resolve among the intelligent,
discern the essential from the trivial by means of the eye of policy.
In strength of arm, fortitude, vital energy, and physical prowess— now in the world of men, including the daityas, humans,
and rākṣasas— there are four tigers among men who are equal to Śakra in power on this earth.
Among living beings, they are the most excellent; there is no one equal to them in strength.
They are always possessed of equal vital power, with their strength and prowess ever complete—namely Baladeva, Bhīma, and the heroic King of Madra.
Of them, Kīcaka was the fourth; we have not heard of a fifth.
Each possessed strength immediately following the other, and each desired victory over the next.
Always with minds agitated by passion, they longed for a wrestling match.
By that sign, I am convinced that Vṛkodara is still alive; it is clear to my mind that the Pāṇḍavas are living,
and I believe Kīcaka was killed there by Bhīmasena.

I believe this Sairandhrī is Draupadī; there is no need for further deliberation on this point. I suspect that it was for the sake of Kṛṣṇā that the mighty Kīcaka was slain by Bhīmasena at night under the pretext of being a Gandharva.
For who else besides Bhīma is capable of slaying Kīcaka by his sheer might,
crushing all his limbs with the strength of his arms without the use of weapons,
so that he is instantly ground into a powder of skin, flesh, and bone?
"Assuming another form, this was surely an act of Bhima;
undoubtedly, for the sake of Krishna, the son of a Suta has been slain by Bhimasena under the pretext of being a Gandharva during the night— of this there is no doubt."
Those virtues of the country and its people which were described by my grandfather have been heard by me many times regarding the kingdom of Matsya;
I believe that the Pāṇḍavas are living in disguise in the city of Virāṭa.
"They dwell in that delightful city; let an expedition be undertaken there. We shall go to the kingdom of Matsya and seize their wealth of cattle.
Once the cattle-wealth is seized, those Pāṇḍavas will surely come to fight."
Even if we see the Pāṇḍavas before the time has expired,
they shall enter the forest once again for another twelve years;
therefore, by either outcome, there will be gain for us.
"In this way, there will be an increase in our treasury and the destruction of our enemies;
how could Suyodhana, who was previously supported by Yudhiṣṭhira, now approach us?
Furthermore, this Matsya speaks thus out of contempt for me."
"Therefore, this indeed must be done; let the journey toward him be undertaken. I consider this well-guided course of action for all, if it pleases you.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Suśarman, the king of the Trigartas and a leader of chariot-divisions,
having first conversed with Karṇa as well as Duḥśāsana,
spoke these words appropriate for the occasion with great haste.
O Lord, he has been repeatedly humiliated in the past by the Matsyas along with the Sālveyakas,
and again and again by the charioteer Kīcaka;
and he has been forcibly oppressed, together with his kinsmen, by that powerful man.
Then, looking toward Karṇa, he addressed Duryodhana:
"The King of Matsya has repeatedly oppressed my kingdom with his might;
in former times, the powerful Kīcaka was his commander."
Cruel, intolerant, evil-minded, and renowned on earth for his prowess—
that wicked-doer, a man of ruthless deeds, was slain there by the Gandharvas.
And when he had been killed, O King, [the enemy] was stripped of pride and left without refuge.
"It is my conviction that Virāṭa will become dispirited;
therefore, O sinless one, an expedition there is my opinion, if it pleases you,
for the sake of all the Kauravas and the high-souled Karṇa."
"I consider this to be the urgent and beneficial task that has now arrived:
let us quickly invade his kingdom, which is filled with abundant grain,
and seize his various jewels and riches."
We shall seize his villages or kingdoms, dividing them among ourselves; or else, having scattered his forces, we shall enter the city by force and carry off many thousands of beautiful cattle.
"O lord of the people, having joined with the Kauravas and the Trigartas, we shall besiege the city by force and carry off his various cattle, all of us acting together in perfect unison."
Or, having made an alliance with him, we shall curb his prowess;
and having destroyed his entire army, we shall bring him under our control. Having brought him into subjection through proper means, we shall dwell in happiness.
"And there will be an increase in your strength, of this there is no doubt.
Having heard those words of his, Karṇa said to the king:
"The speech uttered by Suśarman is well-spoken, timely, and beneficial for us."
"Therefore, let us depart quickly after marshaling the army,
if this is pleasing to you, for it is indeed my own wish as well; or else, O sinless one, do as you think best regarding the division of the forces."
"This elder of the Kurus, our grandfather, is possessed of wisdom; likewise are the preceptor Droṇa and Kṛpa, the son of Śaradvat. Let the expedition be undertaken exactly as they all deem fit."
"Having consulted together, let us go quickly for the sake of accomplishing the king's purpose.
Moreover, what business have we with the Pāṇḍavas, who are deficient in wealth, strength, and prowess? They have either utterly perished or have reached the abode of Yama."
Therefore, O King, surrounded by a great fourfold army,
let us go without anxiety to the territory of Virāṭa;
for we shall seize his cattle and various kinds of wealth.
Duryodhana said:
"O sinless one, these words spoken by you are indeed worthy of being carried out; for this was reported to me here by spies who had been dispatched."
The end of the powerful Kīcaka, the son of a Sūta, occurred;
for at that very moment, a great anxiety arose in his heart regarding the sons of Pāṇḍu,
thinking that no one other than Vṛkodara could slay Kīcaka, who was endowed with such strength.
For Virāṭa always desires what is pleasing to the sons of Pṛthā;
they too dwell there in confidence, staying for certain.
And as for the sign spoken by the Grandfather regarding the discovery of the sons of Pṛthā—

"For it is said that such [abundance] is indeed heard of within the domain of King Virāṭa. Therefore, having gone there quickly, we, joined by our own forces, shall seize his wealth of cattle and crush his kingdom, O Karṇa."
And they, seeking the welfare of Virāṭa, will follow us;
there we shall recognize them and, having understood their true nature,
send them back to the forest before our term of exile is complete.
"Even having slain them right there, we shall enjoy the earth in happiness;
for this time is short and the opportunity appears clear to me.
Let us mobilize our armies for the march when tomorrow has dawned."
Karna said:
"O best of kings, even if those sons of Pritha were there,
and even if both sides had achieved success, you would still have gone [to that place]."
Because of their defeat by Virāṭa, the awakening of the Pāṇḍavas,
and because they are wretched, deprived of their treasury, and emaciated by their forest exile,
they deserve to be killed with ease; therefore, let them indeed be sent into exile.
Then King Duryodhana, having accepted those words of Karṇa, the son of Vaikartana, himself quickly issued an order to Duḥśāsana,
who was ever devoted to his command.

"Having consulted with the elders, quickly mobilize the army so that we may proceed together with all the Kauravas to the designated location. Let the great car-warrior Suśarman go to the place as directed."
Accompanied by the Trigartas and with his entire army and vehicles, the king has already set out well-prepared toward the territory of Matsya;
we shall follow behind him there on the following day.
The very prosperous territory of the Matsya king [was seized] by the well-united [Trigartas].
Now that the cattle-wealth of the Matsya king has been taken by Suśarman,
Virāṭa will take his army and fight with the Trigartas.

On another day, let the Kauravas seize the cattle there; for the sake of the cattle, the Pāṇḍavas will fight there with the Kurus. Having set out swiftly toward the city of Virāṭa, they shall go there.
"Having quickly approached the cowherds, let them seize the vast wealth—
the hundreds of thousands of cows that are both beautiful and excellent.
We too shall seize [the rest], having divided our army into two parts."
Through the fault of associating with the wicked, the virtuous undergo transformation.
Due to his association with Duryodhana, Bhīṣma went to the cattle-raid.
All the chariot-warriors, accompanied by a vast force of infantry, were fully armored.
Desiring to take revenge, the enemies fell upon the cattle. Then King Suśarman, having gone toward the direction indicated by Agni,
seized the cattle on the seventh day of the fortnight of the summer solstice.

On another day, O King, all the Kauravas gathered together on the eighth lunar day and seized those herds of cattle by the thousands. The highly heroic Kauravas, however, were within the territory of the Matsyas.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, O great king, while those high-souled Pāṇḍavas of immeasurable splendor remained right there, having entered into disguised forms, [the following occurred].
The period of time has passed properly for those dwelling in that excellent city while performing the services of King Virāṭa, the lord of the earth;
and now that Kīcaka has been slain, King Virāṭa, the slayer of enemy heroes—
The powerful son of Kuntī, together with his ministers, made a counter-array against them.
Then, O Bhārata, at the end of that thirteenth year,
a great quantity of cattle was forcibly seized by Suśarman.
Then there arose a great clamor, and a cloud of dust reached the heavens;
there was the blaring of conchs and kettledrums, and the mighty sound of war-drums, along with the noise of cattle,
horses, chariots, elephants, and men on foot.
Thus, having set out, while the cattle-wealth of the Matsya king was being seized by the Trigartas, the cowherds resisted them.
Then the many Trigartas, having surrounded a vast amount of wealth, [proceeded].
O Bhārata, having surrounded them with swift horses and multitudes of chariots,
they fought against the cowherds in battle, setting their hearts on victory;
those cowherds were being struck down by many who held spears and lances in their hands.
The cowherds of Gokula, filled with devotion, warded them off with vigor using battle-axes,
clubs, slings, and mallets; the cowherds struck the horses from all sides with various types of plows.
Being struck, those enraged Trigarta chariot-warriors released showers of arrows and put the cowherds to flight in battle;
then the young men, terrified, gasping for breath, and covered in dust, [fled].
Then, with great speed, the cowherds returned to the city;
having reached Virāṭa’s city, those men, adorned with earrings, leaped down from their chariot and spoke to the king of Matsya.
Surrounded by heroic warriors wearing earrings and armlets,
together with his virtuous ministers and the Pāṇḍavas, those bulls among men, he—
the great king and increaser of the realm— was seated in the assembly hall.
Approaching Virāṭa, he then spoke with a bow:
"Having defeated us in battle and humiliated us along with our kinsmen,
the Trigartas are driving away hundreds of thousands of your cows."
"O lord of men, seek to recover them; let not your cattle perish.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard those words of the cowherds, the subduer of enemies [the king]...
Having heard that, the king marshalled the army of the Matsyas— an array thick with chariots, elephants, and horses, and crowded with infantry and banners—
after the king, the slayer of enemy heroes, had then given his orders to the Matsyas.
There, kings and princes donned their armor—
resplendent, variegated, and easy to handle— each according to his share.
Separately, they yoked horses to chariots equipped with golden trappings.
Having unfastened their bowstrings, the heroes fixed them upon their bows.
Then Śatānīka, the beloved brother of Virāṭa, donned a golden armor that was as bright as molten gold and contained an inner core of adamantine iron.
Madirāśva, the younger brother of Śatānīka, donned a firm armor made entirely of iron, adorned with auspicious plates;
it possessed a hundred suns, a hundred whirlpools, a hundred spots, and a hundred eyes.
The king of the Matsyas donned an impenetrable armor;
upon its surface were a hundred fragrant lotuses,
and Sūryadatta fastened it on— a backplate of gold with the brilliance of the sun.
The heroic Śaṅkha, the eldest son of Virāṭa, donned a firm, white coat of mail with a hundred eyes, made of iron within;
and the great car-warriors likewise put on their respective armor by the hundreds.
Intending to fight, those strikers of divine form girded themselves for battle;
upon great chariots equipped with excellent gear and shining bright, the great car-warriors harnessed horses clad in separate golden trappings.
Then the majestic fish-banner, resembling the sun and moon and made of gold, was hoisted upon the divine chariot. Furthermore,
various other banners, adorned with gold and of diverse forms, were raised.
The brave Kṣatriyas harnessed various swift horses, adorned with ornaments of refined gold, to their respective chariots.
While the chariots were being yoked, Kaṅka spoke to the king.
"I too have obtained the fourfold weapon from the best of sages;
clad in armor and mounting my chariot, I shall go forth to the place of the cattle.
And here, O sinless one, is seen the powerful and heroic Valala."
"Yoke the cowherds and the horse-keepers to the chariots;
it is my conviction that they would never fail to fight for the sake of the cattle.
Then King Matsya spoke to his youngest son, Śatānīka.
Kaṅka, Ballava, Gopāla, the powerful Dāmagranthin, Tantipāla, and Gosaneya— these bulls among men,
it is my conviction that they would fight; of this there is no doubt.
Let these also be given chariots adorned with banners and flags;
let them put on their bodies various armor— both firm and supple— and let weapons also be bestowed upon them.
"These men, possessing the physical form of heroes with arms like the trunks of elephant kings—
my mind is made up that they would never fail to fight. Having heard these words of the king, he became hurried in his thoughts.
O King, Śatānīka then assigned chariots to the sons of Pṛthā—
to Sahadeva, to the king [Yudhiṣṭhira], to Bhīma, and to Nakula.
Thereupon, those charioteers, filled with joy and motivated by devotion to the king, [prepared them].
They quickly yoked the chariots as directed by the god among men;
Virāṭa then assigned to those of unwearied deeds various armor, both beautiful and strong, yet flexible.
Having quickly accepted those, the Pāṇḍavas—
heroes of lion-like prowess, powerful and high-minded— girded themselves;
and having fastened them upon their bodies, those subduers of enemies put on their armor.
Mounting chariots well-equipped with horses, those best of men,
the sons of Pṛthā— crushers of enemy hosts, swift, skilled in battle, and all disguised in their forms— set forth joyfully.
Mounting chariots adorned with gold, those great car-warriors,
the Pāṇḍavas— those best of kings— set forth joyfully, clad in armor.
Following behind Virāṭa, those bulls among the Kurus marched together.
The four heroic Pāṇḍava brothers, whose valor is truth,
drew back the long and sturdy bowstrings according to their strength and fixed them upon their bows.
Then all those heroes, well-dressed and anointed with sandalwood paste,
being urged on by the lord of men, quickly drove their horses.
Those horses were covered in gold, large in stature, and excellent at drawing the chariot.
Driven forward, they appeared like rows of birds;
and there were formidable, rutting elephants with temples and faces streaming [ichor],
resembling clouds pouring rain— fine-tusked beasts sixty years of age.
Mounted by well-trained elephant-riders skilled in battle,
they followed behind the king like moving mountains—
those confident, obedient, and joyful followers.
Twenty thousand men as followers,
eight thousand chariots, ten hundred elephants,
and sixty thousand horses of the Matsyas marched forth.
O Bhārata, two full hundred thousand foot soldiers—
this limitless force of the Matsyas marched forth.
O bull of the Bharatas, that army of Virāṭa shone resplendently.
O Great King, that foremost army of Virāṭa, setting out as if desiring to follow the tracks of the cattle, shone like a forest rich in many flowers, variegated in the springtime.
04,030.030c Crowded with men bearing firm weapons, and teeming with elephants, horses, and chariots.
04,031.001 Vaiśampāyana said:
04,031.001a Having marched out from the city, the heroes, skilled strikers, drew up their forces in battle array.
When the sun had set, the Matsyas attacked the Trigartas;
previously, those great car-warriors, the Trigartas, had already attacked the Matsyas.
Then those Trigartas and Matsyas, enraged and intoxicated by battle, [encountered one another].
Roaring at one another, those mighty and fearsome elephants, greedy for the cattle and urged on by lances and hooks,
were mounted by skilled elephant-riders who were village chiefs.
Their encounter was terrible, tumultuous, and hair-raising—
a horrific clash as they struck one another, swelling the realm of Yama.
O King, as the sun hung low, it was like the battle between the gods and the asuras.
Possessing a vast force consisting of foot soldiers, chariots, elephant-riders, and horsemen,
as they charged at one another and struck each other down,
a cloud of dust rose from the earth so that nothing could be discerned.
Birds fell to the ground, shrouded by the dust raised by the army;
the sun was hidden by the converging arrows,
and the sky shone as if filled with fireflies.
With gold-feathered arrows, possessing extremely sharp points and a brilliance like that of fire or a thunderbolt,
the gold-backed bows of the archers were interlaced as those world-heroes fell, discharging their weapons with both left and right hands.
Chariots encountered chariots, and foot soldiers with foot soldiers; horsemen met horsemen, and great elephants met great elephants.
Here, the chariot-warriors and the horsemen engaged in combat.
O King, enraged in battle, they struck one another with swords, spears, lances, pikes, and even javelins;
and they beheld those whose movement was in the air being slain.
Striking one another in battle, those heroes with arms like iron clubs were unable,
despite their fury, to turn the other warriors away from their valor.
[He beheld him] with well-formed upper lip, a beautiful nose, well-groomed hair, and adorned.
A severed head, covered in dust and adorned with earrings, was seen; there,
the limbs of Kṣatriyas were seen cut into pieces by arrows in that great battle, resembling the trunks of *śāla* trees.
The earth there was strewn with arms smeared with sandalwood paste that resembled the coils of serpents, and with heads adorned with earrings;
meanwhile, a fierce clash took place between chariot-warriors and their opponents.

Just as a youthful, dark-complexioned woman shines while wearing two smooth garments dyed with great gold, so too did the Earth shine there, surrounded by horsemen with their horses and foot-soldiers with their infantry.
The dust of the earth was laid by the spreading blood; a terrible dejection took hold, and everything proceeded without restraint. Then, violently pierced by arrows, they reviled one another.
Their movement was in the intermediate space, and even their sight could not be obstructed;
they struck [the enemy] violently, like bulls among cattle.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, whose soul is dharma, together with his brothers—
Having formed the *vyūha* of Virāṭa, the son of Pāṇḍu fought;
having made himself like a hawk, Yudhiṣṭhira became the beak. The two Yamas became the wings, and Vṛkodara was the tail.
There, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, slew a thousand;
and Bhīmasena, the most excellent of all wielders of weapons, being greatly enraged,
the hero sent two thousand chariots to the other world.
Nakula slew three hundred, and Sahadeva four hundred;
Śatānīka, having slain one hundred, and Viśālākṣa four hundred—
those two great car-warriors entered the vast army of the Trigartas.
Having entered that great army, those two powerful and illustrious warriors,
highly enraged, engaged in a hand-to-hand struggle, grappling hair against hair and nail against nail.
Having observed the Trigartas, they both entered the circle of chariots.
Sūryadatta and Madirāśva followed behind;
then Śaṅkha, the son of Virāṭa, a mighty archer of great strength,
entered the vast army while slaughtering his enemies in battle.
In that battle, Virāṭa, having slain five hundred chariots and hundreds of horses there,
as well as five great car-warriors,
moved through various maneuvers on his chariot, O leader of chariot-divisions.
In that battle, he encountered Suśarman of the Trigartas, who possessed a golden chariot. Those two high-souled and mighty warriors contended there,
roaring at one another like two bulls in a cow-pen.
Then Suśarman, the king of the Trigartas, who is fierce in battle,
that bull among men, encountered the King of Matsya— who had prepared his horses— for a single combat of chariots; he was the chief of the Trigartas and possessed great strength.
Then those two lions among kings, bulls among men, highly agitated and impatient, engaged each other in a duel of chariots and shone forth resplendent.
In that battle, heroic warriors with arms like iron clubs fought as valiant men.
In the battle, headless trunks (*kabandhas*) set out to slay the great warriors; "Kill! Kill! they cried, even as heads fell, urging on the trunk-like bodies with shouts of "Hum" and other cries.
And Virāṭa, having witnessed that great marvel, was filled with curiosity;
the king attained supreme joy, thinking, "Such men as these belong to me.
By Kabandha, a hundred warriors were struck down at the head of the battle.
Then Kabandha fell down along with a rain of flowers;
a celestial chariot, impelled by the gods and surrounded by Apsarases, arrived,
and having ascended it in the sight of all the warriors, he went to heaven.
Enraged, the heroes were unable to turn their backs;
then the two chariot-warriors, having maneuvered their chariots around each other from all sides,
swiftly discharged arrows like two clouds pouring down torrents of rain.
Highly enraged and intolerant of one another, they moved about,
both skilled in weapons, striking with sharpened arrows and wielding swords, spears, and maces.
Then the king pierced Suśarman with ten shafts.
With five arrows each, he pierced his four horses;
with two he struck the charioteer, and with three swift shafts, the standard.
In the same manner, Suśarman, who is fierce in battle, [struck] the King of Matsya.
The master of supreme weapons pierced him with fifty sharp arrows.
Then, having surrounded the armies of the King of Matsya and Suśarman,
they could no longer recognize one another at that hour of night, as everything was shrouded in dust.
Vaiśampāyana said:
O Bhārata, when the world was overwhelmed by darkness and dust,
those strikers stood for a moment with their armies drawn up in battle array.
Then the moon rose, dispelling the darkness and making the night clear, gladdening the kṣatriyas in battle. Thereupon, having attained light, the battle commenced once more.
Then, beholding that terrible form, they could not look at one another.
Thereupon Suśarman of Trigarta, together with his younger brother,
rushed from all sides against the king of the Matsyas with a multitude of chariots.
Then, leaping down from their two chariots, those two brothers, bulls among Kṣatriyas,
rushed furiously toward the horses with maces in hand.
And so it was with their respective forces as well.
Then, enraged, they rushed at one another with maces,
swords, and axes,
and with spears that had sharp points and well-polished edges.
But King Suśarman,
the lord of the Trigartas, having overwhelmed and forcibly conquered the Matsya king along with his entire army by means of his own strength;
He rushed toward the powerful Virāṭa like two rutting bulls, like two elephants intoxicated with pride,
like two lions seizing an elephant, or like Śakra and Vṛtra risen up in conflict.
Both were equal in strength and energy, both equal in prowess;
both were equal in the discharge of weapons, and both were experts in battle.
Having slain those two principal warriors separately, as well as both rear-guard charioteers, [he prevailed].
Let alone those two who were equally skilled in wielding the bow, as arrogant as Viṣṇu and Kaṃsa;
Suśarman, the slayer of enemy heroes, powerful and heroic, armed with a mace,
captured the King of Matsya alive after he had been deprived of his chariot.

Having overpowered him like a weeping bridegroom, Suśarman placed him upon his own chariot and departed with swift horses. When that exceedingly powerful Virāṭa had been captured and deprived of his chariot—

All their strength was shattered; devoid of energy and hope, the Matsyas, severely afflicted by the Trigartas, fled in fear. They scattered in all directions and intermediate points, fleeing and departing.
While they were being terrified, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī,
addressed the mighty-armed Bhīmasena, the subduer of enemies:
"The King of Matsya has been seized by Suśarman of the Trigartas."

"O mighty-armed one, rescue him; let him not fall under the power of his enemies. O mighty-armed Bhīmasena, we have all lived happily, well-honored with every object of desire, until he was captured by Suśarman."
"Save him, deliver him quickly—this king who brings us joy!
O Bhīmasena, you must repay him for his hospitality.
Vaiśampāyana said:
To him who was speaking thus, the invincible and mighty Bhīmasena addressed Yudhiṣṭhira in the midst of the battle. Bhīmasena said:
"O King, I shall protect him from your command;
behold my great feat as I fight with the enemies. Relying on the strength of your own arms, remain here together with your brothers."
"O King, standing at one side, behold my prowess today!
This great tree with its sturdy trunk stands like a mace;
having uprooted it, I shall put the enemies to flight."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Beholding that hero, his brother Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, spoke to him as he was gazing at the lord of the forest like an elephant in rut.
"Do not, O Bhīma, commit such a rash act; let this lord of the forest remain.
Lest people, seeing you performing superhuman deeds with the tree, should recognize you and say, 'This is Bhīma,' O Bhārata."
"Do not grasp this tree, and do not roar a lion's roar.
Having grasped this tree, do not charge at this army. O hero, if you were to carry off the tree, people would surely know [your identity]."
"O Bhīma, take up some other human weapon—
whether it be a bow, a spear, a sword, or an axe—
whatever may be human and unobserved by others."
"Taking up that very weapon, quickly liberate the lord of the earth.
And let the two mighty twins become the protectors of your wheels,
O dear one, as you form a battle array in the encounter, desiring to rescue the King of Matsya."
Having understood his brother's words and having cast aside the tree, Bhīma,
the Pāṇḍava, took up his bow and, mounting his chariot, arrived.
Having spoken thus to Bhīmasena, Yudhiṣṭhira himself followed with swift horses, desiring to rescue the best of the Matsyas.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus addressed, the mighty Bhīmasena, possessing great speed,
seized that excellent bow and, with extreme velocity,
released showers of arrows like a rain-cloud discharging its waters.
Then Bhīma, the doer of terrible deeds, rushed toward Suśarman;
seeing Virāṭa nearby, he cried out, "Stay! Stay!
Suśarman gazed upon him, who resembled Yama, the Destroyer at the end of time.
"Stay! Stay! cried the bull among chariot-warriors from behind, as they beheld that great deed and saw that a mighty battle was at hand;
then Suśarman turned back with his brothers, seizing his bow.
In the mere twinkling of an eye, those chariots were struck down by Bhīmasena near Virāṭa; indeed, the chariots,
elephants, and horses along with their riders were felled by Bhīmasena.

Hundreds of thousands of throngs of brave warriors with formidable bows, along with their foot-soldiers, were slain by that high-souled one as he took up his mace. Having witnessed such a battle, Suśarman, who was fierce in combat, [was struck with awe].
He reflected in his mind: "What indeed remains of my army? Another [warrior] is seen in the host who was previously submerged in that great force; he now appears with his bow drawn back to his ear."
Suśarman repeatedly discharged sharp arrows.
Then all of them together urged on their horses,
displaying divine weapons in their indignation against the Trigartas.
Seeing those Pāṇḍavas who had turned their chariots back,
that great army and the daughter of Virāṭa, filled with supreme rage, fought most wonderfully;
while the Trigartas, having bypassed them, fought on, desiring victory.
Then Bhīmasena, the best among all wielders of weapons, being greatly enraged,
slew a thousand of them there; and Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī,
[slew many], while Bhīma showed seven hundred warriors the world beyond.
Nakula also dispatched seven hundred with his arrows; and the powerful Sahadeva, that bull among men, commanded by Yudhiṣṭhira, slew three hundred heroes.
Then, having pierced through that vast army of the Trigartas, O bull among men, that most formidable hero rushed toward Suśarman, who stood with weapon raised,
agitating all the troops like a lion among small deer.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, that great car-warrior, acting with haste,
rushed toward Suśarman and pierced him deeply with arrows.
Suśarman, also greatly incensed, quickly rushed toward Yudhiṣṭhira.
Piercing [his opponent] with nine arrows, he struck down the four horses with four;
then, O King, Vṛkodara, the son of Kuntī,
acting with swift prowess, having approached Suśarman, crushed his horses.
Then, having slain his two rear-guards with supreme arrows,
he furiously struck down the charioteer from the seat of the chariot;
and [he also slew] the wheel-protector, the hero renowned by the name Śoṇāśva.
Seeing that duel, he then abandoned the Trigarta king out of fear. Thereupon, the mighty Virāṭa leaped down from Suśarman’s chariot,
seized his mace, and struck him with it.
Though old, he moved about with mace in hand like a youth.
Having witnessed that feat of the two, Matsya and the Pāṇḍava,
in battle, he hurriedly abandoned his chariot and fled from the fray on foot.
Seeing the Trigarta fleeing, Bhīma addressed him:
"With such valor as this, how can you seek to seize the cattle by force?
O prince, turn back; flight is not fitting for you."
"And why, having abandoned your followers, do you despair in the midst of the enemy?
Thus addressed by Pārtha, the powerful Suśarman, a leader of chariot-divisions, cried out "Stay! Stay! and suddenly rushed toward Bhīma.

The powerful one swiftly struck Bhīma with five arrows in that battle. Having rendered those shafts useless, Suśarman, desiring life, then fled quickly and composedly from the field of combat, seeking to save his own life.

But Bhīma, of terrifying appearance, leaping down from his chariot while adorned with earrings, seized the king of the Trigartas as a lion seizes a small deer. The valiant Bhīmasena then rushed after him as he fled.
Leaping up and approaching with speed, he fell upon Suśarman’s chariot and seized the head of Suśarman as he was still fighting;
having rushed toward Suśarman, he grasped him by the hair.
Raising him up in rage, the mighty-armed one crushed him against the surface of the earth; as he was wailing, he struck him on the head with his foot,
and Bhīma pressed his knee into him and beat him with his elbow.
Afflicted by the severe blow, the king fell into a swoon. Then,
as Bhīma was being restrained by the twins in that battle against the Trigarta king,
Bhīma became enraged and destroyed his pride.
Just as a cat, springing upward in rage, seizes the head of a mouse, so too,
when that great car-warrior of the Trigartas was deprived of his chariot and captured, the entire Trigarta army, overcome with fear, broke and fled.
Then, having turned back all the cattle and having completely defeated Suśarman and seized his wealth, the mighty sons of Pāṇḍu—
endowed with the strength of their own arms, restrained by modesty, and firm in their vows— proceeded on their way.
Having liberated Virāṭa, those Pāṇḍavas, who had slain their enemies,
were the high-souled destroyers of Virāṭa’s afflictions;
