and as they all stood before him, Bhīma then addressed him.

"This man of evil conduct does not deserve to live by my hand. What indeed can I do, since the King is ever compassionate? Having seized the King by the throat, I shall bring him, helpless, under my control."
Then Vṛkodara, the son of Pṛthā, having bound him as he struggled—
unconscious and covered in dust— placed him upon his chariot and approached Yudhiṣṭhira, who stood in the midst of the battle.
Bhīma showed him that condition of Suśarman;
then that tiger among men spoke to Bhīma, who shines in battle.
Seeing this, the king laughed and said, "Let this lowest of men indeed be released."
Thus addressed, Bhīma spoke to the mighty Suśarman:
"O fool, if you wish to live, listen to the condition you must state:
you must declare, 'I am a slave,' in assemblies and in public halls."
"In this way I shall grant you your life; such is the rule for one conquered in battle.
Then his eldest brother spoke these words with affection:
"Release this man of base conduct, if we are an authority to you."
"For he has entered into the state of a slave to King Virāṭa.
Go as one who is no longer a slave; you are released. Do not act in this manner ever again.
When this was said, Suśarman stood with shame, his face cast downward.
Once released, he approached the king, paid his respects, and departed.
Having set Suśarman free, those Pāṇḍavas— whose enemies had been slain,
who were endowed with the strength of their own arms, devoted to modesty, and firm in their vows— remained there.
Having slain his enemies in battle, that high-souled Bhīmasena dwelt happily that night in the midst of the forefront of the fray for Virāṭa.
The powerful and indignant one roared with joy,
like a lion after slaying a small deer;
then Virāṭa [beheld] the sons of Kuntī, whose prowess was superhuman.
Filled with joy, he honored those great chariot-warriors with wealth, respect, kind words, affection, and delight. Virāṭa said:
"Just as these jewels are mine, so indeed are they yours.
All of you, perform your tasks with them as you desire and as it brings you pleasure.
I shall give you adorned maidens and various kinds of wealth."

O destroyers of enemies, whatever was desired by your minds has been fulfilled; through your prowess, I have today been released here in safety. Therefore, you all are indeed the lords of the Matsyas.
Vaiśampāyana said:
To the King of Matsya, who had thus offered his salutations, all the Kauravas, led by Yudhiṣṭhira, spoke individually with their palms joined in reverence.
"O Lord of the People, we welcome all your words.
We are truly satisfied by this very fact—that you have today been released from your enemies. That you are freed from your foes is indeed for our own benefit."
"We have no task to perform, nor do we seek wealth.
Then the King of Matsya, his mind filled with joy, spoke to Yudhiṣṭhira with words faltering from delight and overflowing with affection.
Once again, the mighty-armed Virāṭa, the best of kings, said:
"Come, I shall consecrate you; may you be our king of the Matsyas.
And whatever else is desired by your heart, O destroyer of enemies, [that too I shall grant]."
I shall bestow all of that upon you; your honor deserves everything from us.
O jewel, cattle, gold, gems, pearls, or whatever else—O Vaiyāghrapadya, chief of Brahmins, salutations to you in every way!
"Indeed, it is because of you that today I behold both my kingdom and myself.
Thus addressed by the Matsya king, the Pāṇḍava spoke to him:
"The source from which this agitation arose—that enemy has been brought under control."
When the king spoke thus in that assembly, saying "with discipline," the King of Dharma, O Great King, addressed him with fitting words;
then Yudhiṣṭhira spoke once more to the Matsya.
"I rejoice in your words; O fish, you speak what is pleasing to me. Always devoted to compassion, may you be forever happy.
Then King Virāṭa spoke again to Kaṅka.
"O best of the twice-born, oh, what deeds of the Śūdra Valala!
It is by that Śūdra Valala that I have been protected in battle.
O sinless one, all this has come to pass for me because of you."
"Choose a boon—may it be well with you! Speak, what may I do for you?
With great joy I shall give you various kinds of jewels, as well as beds, seats, vehicles, and adorned maidens."
Multitudes of elephants, horses, and chariots, as well as various kingdoms—
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Accept these from me out of affection for me."
To him who was speaking thus, the Kaurava replied:
"This alone is my joy, O sinless one, that you have been released from your enemies; if you are confident and satisfied, then enter once more."

Embracing my wives and sons, that affection of mine is indeed incomparable. O Indra among kings, O best of men, release Suśarman along with his servants, troops, and mounts; this is the boon I choose.
Thus addressed by Kaṅka, Virāṭa, the best of kings, replied to Kaṅka: "Let Suśarman go and exert himself;
let messengers go quickly to your city, O King."
"Let them announce what is pleasing to their friends and proclaim your victory.
Then, at those words, the King of Matsya commanded his messengers:
"Go to the city and announce my victory in battle."
"Let the princes, having adorned themselves, come forth from my city,
along with all kinds of musical instruments and well-adorned courtesans.
Having heard this command, they were then urged by King Matsya.

Having received that command with their heads bowed, they set out with joyful hearts. And let all those citizens indeed return [safely]. Having traveled for the entire night, they then arrived at the rising of the sun.
Having been addressed thus, those messengers departed alone during the night; then,
having stayed overnight in that interval, the swift-following messengers entered the city when the sun had fully risen.
In the vicinity of Virāṭa’s city, messengers proclaimed the victory;
the city was like an incomparable one, enriched with rows of raised banners.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When he had departed for Trigarta, Duryodhana, together with his ministers, then approached Virāṭa, desiring to recover those cattle of his own;
[with him were] Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Karṇa, and Kṛpa, who was a knower of the supreme weapons.
The son of Droṇa, Saubala, and likewise the lord Duḥśāsana;
Vivimśati, Vikarṇa, and the heroic Citrasena; Durmukha, Duḥsaha, and whoever other great car-warriors there were.
Having approached the cattle-stations of Virāṭa, the lord of the earth,
these Kurus swiftly drove away the guards and seized the wealth of cattle by force;
they are driving away sixty thousand cows.
Surrounded on all sides by a vast multitude of chariots,
a tremendous clamor arose from the cowherd settlements as they were being slaughtered by those great car-warriors in that terrifying conflict.

But the superintendent of cattle, terrified, mounted his chariot and went quickly toward the city, crying out piteously like one in distress. Having entered the city, he then proceeded to the king's palace.
Quickly descending from the chariot, he entered to report [the news].
Seeing the proud son of Matsya named Bhūmijaya,
he told him everything regarding the plundering of the kingdom's cattle.
"The Kurus are driving away sixty thousand cows;
arise to win back that wealth of cattle which increases the prosperity of the kingdom.
O prince, desiring our welfare, set out yourself at once."
For King Matsya has appointed you here as the guardian of his empty city;
that lord of men boasts of you in the midst of his assembly, saying,
"My son is worthy of me, a hero, and the upholder of his lineage."
"My son is a warrior skilled in the use of bows and missiles, ever heroic,
and capable of fighting in battle against such Kauravas;
let those words spoken by that lord of men come true."
Victory in battle is certain, and the Kauravas are surely slain. Having conquered the Kurus, turn back, O best among those who possess cattle!
Burn their armies with the fierce energy of your arrows, O Bhīma.
With gold-feathered, straight-jointed arrows released from his bow,
pierce the ranks of the enemies like a leader of elephant herds.
[Pierce] that great-sounding [bow], which has the bow-staff for its body, the string for its lute-strings, and the noose for its pillow.
"Play the bow-lute, which has the color of arrows, in the midst of the enemy!
O prince, depart quickly from the city; why do you remain here?
Let white horses, resembling silver, be yoked to your chariot."

O Lord, let them raise for you a golden banner bearing the emblem of a lion. Released by your skillful hand, let your arrows— gold-feathered and with bright points— cover the sun and bring an end to the lives of rival kings.
Having conquered all the Kurus in battle, like the wielder of the thunderbolt against the Asuras,
and having attained great glory, you shall enter this city again; for you,
O son of the Lord of Matsya, are the supreme refuge of the kingdom.

Just as Arjuna is the foremost among victors among the sons of Pāṇḍu, so indeed are you surely the refuge for those dwelling in this realm. May all who dwell in this realm today become possessed of a secure refuge.
Vaiśampāyana said:
In the presence of a great multitude, and especially in the midst of women,
the superintendent of the cattle spoke these words that increase one's splendor.
Having been addressed by him in the midst of the women, Uttara, praising those words which grant fearlessness within the inner apartments, spoke this speech: Uttara said:
"Today, armed with my firm bow, I would follow the tracks of the cattle,
were there some charioteer skilled in horses to be found for me;
yet I do not find such a man who might serve as my driver."
"Behold quickly my charioteer, who is ready for me as I set forth.
Whether it be twenty-eight nights or even a month at most,
since that great battle occurred, my charioteer has been slain there."
"If I could find another man skilled in the management of horses and vehicles,
I would go today with haste to that enemy army, crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots, and having raised my great banner high, I would plunge into it."
Having conquered the Kurus— who were rendered powerless by the heat of his weapons— he brought back their cattle;
he encountered Duryodhana, the son of Śantanu, Karṇa the son of Vaikartana, Kṛpa,
and Droṇa along with his son— all those great archers assembled together.
Having terrified them in battle like the wielder of the thunderbolt against the Dānavas,
I shall bring back the cattle again in this very moment;
for the Kurus, finding the place empty, are departing while taking the wealth of cattle.
"What indeed could have been done by me had I been there?
Today those assembled Kauravas might have witnessed my prowess.
Is this Partha Arjuna himself who oppresses us?"
Vaiśampāyana said:
As he spoke those words again and again regarding the women,
Pāñcālī could not endure that mention of Bībhatsu.
Then, having approached him from the midst of the women, that ascetic woman,
as if feeling bashful, slowly spoke these words.
Having heard those words spoken by Uttara, Arjuna—
Recalling those words in secret, Arjuna addressed his beloved wife at a later time: "O Pāñcālī,
daughter of King Drupada, renowned for your beauty."
"O Pāñcālī of pure smiles, go quickly and say to Uttarā— who is endowed with the virtues of truth and uprightness and who desires the welfare and pleasure of her husband:
'In former times, during the battle at Khāṇḍava, this [bow] indeed belonged to Savyasācin.'"
The charioteer of Pārtha, the son of Pāṇḍu, was Bṛhannalā.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"If Bṛhannalā is the driver, there will be a great victory in battle."

Then, urged by that Arjuna, the daughter of Pañcāla, who possessed a radiant smile, approached Uttarā’s quarters; and having learned that the time had come, she was released like the moon from the mouth of Rāhu.

Unable to endure that suffering, the lotus-eyed Draupadī, graceful and radiant, spoke these words to Uttarā in the midst of her friends, regarding Yudhiṣṭhira, who is devoted to dharma and established on the path of truth and uprightness.
He who resembles a large elephant, a youth of most pleasing appearance—
this youth who is like the leader of a herd of elephants— is Draupadī’s [husband].
"I am Bṛhannalā," he addressed the people;
for formerly, I believe, he was the charioteer of Pārtha,
the foremost among archers.
Known as Bṛhannaḍā, he was the charioteer of Pārtha.
With him as his charioteer, Arjuna [then] [conquered] the gods, Gandharvas, great serpents, and Asuras.
That heroic one conquered all beings and also gratified Hiraṇyaretas (Agni),
even as he observed his own destruction in battle.
Standing in the midst of the enemy host, I recognized their prowess;
then, the valiant one, having gathered the reins and restrained them,
took up his bow and set forth while remaining seated in the chariot.
Neither all living beings, nor the gods and dānavas,
nor even all the assembled Kurus,
though they be archers, could ever take away your wealth.
If Bṛhannalā was Uttara’s charioteer,
he was a disciple of that high-souled one and was no inferior in archery;
O hero, I have seen him before while I was traveling among the Pāṇḍavas.
When the Fire-god consumed the great Khāṇḍava forest,
it was then that Arjuna’s excellent horses were guided by him;
with him as his charioteer, Pārtha [conquered] all beings in every way.
He conquered Khāṇḍavaprastha, for there was no such driver.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Uttarā, together with Sairandhrī, spoke to her brother.

"O hero, quickly request this Bṛhannalā for the office of charioteer; for she is highly trained in charioteering, as well as in dancing, singing, and playing musical instruments. Thus spoke the Sairandhrī, O wise one, praising Bṛhannalā.
Having heard the successive words uttered by Sairandhrī and having reflected upon them thoroughly in his mind, Uttara spoke again to Sairandhrī.
"Sairandhrī, you know well my vow;
this man is indeed not a eunuch himself. O auspicious lady, I shall not reveal Bṛhannalā."
"Restrain the horses yourself," he said.
At that time when fear had arrived, there was neither religious observance nor its absence.
"A wise person should act in such a way that they cross over suffering;
thus have those who know the Dharma said. Therefore, Bṛhannalā must be told:
'This maiden with beautiful hips is your younger sister.'"
O hero, he will undoubtedly carry out her command;
if he indeed becomes the charioteer, there is no doubt that after conquering all the Kurus and recovering the cattle, his return will be certain.
Thus addressed by the Sairandhrī, he replied to his sister:
"Go, O lady of faultless limbs, and bring that Bṛhannaḍā here.
Sent by her brother, she went quickly to the dancing hall.
"Where that mighty-armed Pāṇḍava dwells, concealed by a disguise.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Wearing a golden garland, she ran forth.
Sent by her illustrious elder brother, the renowned Sudakṣiṇā— whose waist was slender as the middle of a sacrificial altar,
whose complexion resembled the petals of a lotus, and who wore a crest of hair— arrived.
Slender and beautiful-limbed, with a girdle variegated with jewels,
the daughter of King Matsya,
endowed with splendor and arched brows, entered that dancing hall.
Like a flash of lightning following a cloud, she—
whose thighs were as firm as an elephant’s trunk,
who was irreproachable, possessed of beautiful teeth, and slender-waisted— followed after him.
Having approached that Pārtha, who wore excellent garlands, that auspicious woman— like a female elephant approaching a bull elephant—
was a jewel of a woman, beloved and honored by his mind.
The daughter of Virāṭa, who possessed the splendor of Indra,
was beautiful to behold and renowned; with long,
wide eyes, she spoke to Arjuna with affection.
Then Pārtha addressed that maiden, who had well-rounded thighs and skin radiant as gold: "O wearer of golden garlands, why have you come?"
O fawn-eyed one, O passionate lady, why are you in such a hurry?
O beautiful one, why is your face not serene?
O woman, tell me the truth quickly.
Having heard her brother’s command,
the fair-browed one of auspicious countenance— adorned with ornaments of gold and gems,
and wearing earrings of gold, diamonds, pearls, and jewels— [prepared to depart].
Gentle in her gait, urged by the command of her brother, she whose body turned in a clockwise direction, who possessed a crest of hair,
whose face was like a lotus, and whose eyes were as broad as lotus petals.
Vaiśampāyana said:
O King, having seen that large-eyed princess, his friend,
he spoke with a smile, asking, "Whence have you come?"
Approaching that bull among men, the princess,
manifesting her affection in the midst of her friends, spoke these words with urgency and sweet syllables: "O Uttara, speak."
"O Bṛhannaḍā, the cows of our kingdom are being driven away by the Kurus;
my brother, bearing his bow, will set out to conquer them.
And before long, his chariot-driver was slain in battle."
"Therefore, there is no charioteer equal to him who might perform his driving.
To him, O Bṛhannaḍā, as he was striving for the position of charioteer,
Sairandhrī declared your skill in the knowledge of horses."
"O Bṛhannaḍā, you were formerly the beloved charioteer of Arjuna;
with you as his companion, that bull among the Pāṇḍavas conquered the earth.
Therefore, O Bṛhannaḍā, perform the duty of my brother’s charioteer well."
"For long ago our cows were carried away by the Kurus from a great distance;
yet today, though thus enjoined by me, you will not carry out these words of mine. Since you speak thus despite my affectionate entreaty, I shall give up my life."
Thus addressed by that fair-hipped friend, the scorcher of foes went into the presence of the prince of immeasurable prowess.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Her earrings were fashioned from diamond and beryl; she possessed the fragrance of the petals of blooming lotuses and water lilies;
and her face resembled the serene countenance of the Lord of Stars (the Moon).
The maiden spoke these words to Pārtha:
"O Bṛhannalā, the Kurus are carrying away my father’s wealth—
a hundred thousand cows."
"Restrain your brother's horses before others carry our cattle even further away;
Sairandhrī tells you this, O Bṛhannalā."
Well-trained in the management of chariots and horses,
I shall die; of this I have no doubt,
if you do not go there as chosen by me.
Thus enjoined by the daughter of the king of men,
Dhananjaya, that best of men, with a joyful mind,
spoke with auspicious and gentle words, O Pārtha.
"O lady of beautiful countenance, with white teeth and a pure smile, O sweet-smiling one, I shall go wherever you desire;
or I shall enter the blazing fire."
"O lady of excellent limbs, I desire your life;
O beautiful one, what dear thing shall I do for you today?
My beloved, you shall not see that city because of me."
"Of Vaivasvata, the Lord of the Departed, who brings great terror"—
having spoken thus, that bull among the Kuru heroes addressed Vilāsinī, who had white teeth and a pure smile.
With his face adorned in the form of Bṛhannalā,
he approached the presence of Virāṭa’s son;
as he drew near, he was arrayed in excellent ornaments.
Possessing great radiance like the leader of a herd of elephants,
with arms like those of a lordly elephant and eyes as broad as lotuses,
he has a chest like a door-panel and uplifted shoulders.
Then the son of Virāṭa addressed Bṛhannalā regarding that Pārtha, the crusher of enemies, who had arrived with great strength like a maddened elephant.
Desiring to lead the cows back, Uttara spoke;
she, the large-eyed one, followed him as he went swiftly like an elephant in rut,
just as a young female elephant follows her lord.
But seeing him from afar, the prince addressed him:
"With you as his charioteer, Pārtha gratified the fire-god at Khāṇḍava; with you as his charioteer, Dhanañjaya, the son of Kuntī, conquered the entire earth."
"Sairandhrī has spoken to you, for she knows the Pāṇḍavas. Therefore, O Bṛhannaḍā, restrain my horses as I prepare to fight with the Kurus and seek to recover the wealth of cattle."
"O you who were formerly Arjuna’s beloved charioteer,
by your assistance that bull among the Pāṇḍavas conquered the earth. You are Mātali, the heroic charioteer of the Lord of the Gods, renowned for your valor."
Suhotra was the charioteer of Viṣṇu, the son of Jamadagni, and Dāruka was the driver of Aruṇa, the charioteer of the Sun; Sumantra was the charioteer of Daśaratha.
All these renowned charioteers were not equal to Bṛhannalā.
"Having been addressed thus by the Sairandhrī, I am indeed calling you;
come with me to fight, O Bṛhannalā!
The cattle, carried off by the Kurus, have gone further and further away."
Thus addressed, Bṛhannaḍā replied to the prince:
"What power do I have to act as a charioteer at the head of battle?
Whether it be song, dance, or various kinds of instrumental music..."
"I shall do that; may you be blessed. But as for charioteering, how could it be possible for me? Uttara said:
"O Bṛhannaḍā, you may rather become a singer or a dancer."
Quickly mount my chariot and restrain these excellent horses. Whether you be a dancer or even a singer,
quickly put on your radiant armor.
"04,035.016d*0637_001 They constantly speak of your manly deeds;
04,035.016d*0637_002 women praise them even in my presence today," said Vaiśampāyana.
Having spoken thus, the best of princes then smiled and greeted Arjuna; thereafter,
Uttara [struck] the iron statue with a hundred eyes.
Then the son of Virāṭa himself took up that radiant object, variegated with gold, and gave it to Bṛhannalā,
the slayer of enemy heroes.
Then, by the command of the son of Matsya, the heroic Bṛhannalā took up [the bow] as if she had no desire to act.
"If there is valor in battle and the power to slay the enemies,
then I shall follow you, O sir, wherever you go.
Vaiśampāyana said:
There, that Pāṇḍava, the subduer of enemies, knowing everything, performed many jests in the presence of Uttarā;
lifting up his armor, he put it on his body.
Seeing him there, the large-eyed maidens laughed;
as he took it up, the hero, with his face cast downward, struck out at the women.
Then the slayer of enemies,
whose valor is truth, although fully aware [of the situation], pulled down the armor that had been fastened crosswise and was turned downward.
As if unaware, the hero among all Kurus,
that best of warriors, cast his weapon upward and struck;
then Dhananjaya again with effort fastened his armor.
While he was performing many such feats,
the young maidens and women laughed;
but seeing him thus bewildered, Uttara himself then [intervened].
He equipped Bṛhannaḍā with a highly precious coat of mail;
yet Uttara could not overcome Dhananjaya, who was thus transforming himself as the crusher of his enemies.
The prince himself equipped him with beautiful armor made of refined Jāmbūnada gold,
radiant and resembling the heat of a blazing fire.
Blazing like the thousand-rayed sun himself,
wearing a preeminent armor that possessed a radiance like his own,
he raised a banner bearing a lion and appointed him to the position of charioteer.
Then, having quickly inspected him,
he yoked to the chariot horses covered with golden nets,
whose harnesses were adorned by ornaments set within golden lattices.
He took refuge on the chariot with a golden lion,
and he placed there upon the seat of the chariot many precious bows, numerous beautiful arrows, and various weapons.
Taking them, the hero set forth with Bṛhannaḍā as his charioteer.
Then Uttarā and her maiden friends said to him:
"O Bṛhannaḍā, please bring us some beautiful garments."
Having defeated the Kurus led by Bhīṣma and Droṇa in battle, he won for the sake of the Pāñcālikā various fine and variegated garments.
Then, as those maidens were speaking together, the son of Pāṇḍu [addressed them].
Pārtha, whose voice was like the roar of clouds or a kettledrum, replied with a smile:
"If Uttara conquers these great chariot-warriors in battle,
then I shall bring back celestial and resplendent garments."
Having spoken thus, the heroic Bībhatsu then urged on his horses toward the Kurus, who were adorned with various banners and flags.
Then Uttara [donned] the armor of great power.
Having fastened on a firm chariot adorned with gold and lapis lazuli, the hero set forth,
taking Dhananjaya as his charioteer.
Beholding him standing upon that excellent chariot,
the mighty-armed one accompanied by Bṛhannaḍā,
the women, the maidens, and the twice-born of firm vows [gazed upon him].
Then the women circumambulated him and said:
"That auspicious event which occurred long ago at the burning of the Khāṇḍava forest for Arjuna, who moves like a bull— "
"O Bṛhannaḍā, having encountered the Kurus in battle today, may that auspiciousness be joined with Uttara!
Vaiśampāyana said:

Having departed from the royal capital, Vairāṭi Pṛthivījaya said to his charioteer, "Drive to where those Kurus have gone. Having indeed conquered the assembled Kurus who were desirous of victory, [he proceeded].
"Having quickly taken their cows, I shall return again to my own city.
Then the son of Pāṇḍu urged on those excellent horses;
those steeds, possessing the speed of the wind, were driven by that lion among men.

Wearing golden garlands, they bore along as if painting the very sky. Then, having traveled not very far, the son of Matsya and Dhanañjaya, those slayers of enemies, beheld the army of the mighty Kurus.
Having gone around the cremation ground, he then approached the Kurus. They both gazed upon that *śamī* tree and the troops arrayed on all sides.
That great army of theirs shone forth with a roar like the ocean.
O best of men, as that [army] glided through the sky like a forest thick with trees,
the king beheld the dust it raised;
reaching up to the heavens, it obscured the vision of all living beings.
Having beheld that vast army, crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots,
protected by Karṇa, Duryodhana, Kṛpa, and the son of Śantanu,
as well as by the wise and great archer Droṇa together with his son;

Seeing that incomparable army, which increased their fear, the son of Virāṭa, his hair standing on end and agitated by terror, spoke to Pārtha: "I do not dare to fight with the Kurus; indeed, look at my hair standing on end."

I am not able to fight against the Kuru army, which possesses many heroes, is exceedingly fierce, is difficult even for the gods to approach, and is infinite. I do not hope to enter the Bharata host, with its terrifying bows.
Even by the gods together with Indra it would not be possible, much less by men;
for upon merely seeing the enemy in battle— thick with chariots, elephants, and horses, and crowded with infantry and banners— my very soul seems to tremble.
Where Drona and Bhishma, Kripa, Karna, and Vivimshati;
Ashvatthaman, Vikarna, Somadatta, and Bahlika;
as well as the heroic King Duryodhana, the best among chariot-warriors, [are stationed].
Radiant and great archers, all of them skilled in battle,
like rutting great elephants, equipped with banners and flags;
possessed of policy and great archery, they were certain in the use of all weapons.
Invincible by all armies, even by the gods led by Vāsava;
elephants with banners and great chariots with standards;
and horses adorned with variegated ornaments, though exerting themselves, were scattered about.
It was for the sake of conquering those heroes in battle that I, evil-minded as I am, came here.
Indeed, upon seeing these Kurus with their ranks arrayed and ready to strike,
my hair stood on end and a faintness came over me.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Though unskilled, he was deceived by the skill of that rogue through his own folly as the latter looked on;
for he had seen the vast army of the Kurus, those firm bowmen.
The dull-witted one lamented in the presence of Savyasācin:
"My father has gone against the Trigartas, leaving me behind in an empty place;
he has taken the entire army with him, so I have no soldiers here."
"Being but a single youth, untrained in weapons, I shall not be able to fight against these many who are skilled in arms. Turn back, Bṛhannaḍā!
Vaiśampāyana said.
To him who was speaking thus,
Bībhatsu, that great chariot-warrior (*mahāratha*) of all the worlds, replied with a smile;
Arjuna said:

"You appear dejected with fear, increasing the joy of your enemies; yet the foes have not yet performed any deed upon the field of battle. Moreover, you yourself said to me: 'Carry me toward the Kauravas.'"
Therefore, O mighty-armed one, I shall lead you there where these many banners stand—
in the midst of the Kurus, those murderous aggressors who are greedy for the prize—
and I shall lead you even among those fighting upon the earth.

O subduer of enemies, having made a vow in the presence of women while men were listening, you have now departed from the Kurus' army— which is as deep as the ocean— boasting; tell me, what is it that you do not understand in this matter?
Having thus boasted of your manliness before women and before men,
why do you not wish to fight after having set out?
For if you do not conquer them and win back those cows, you will surely return home in shame.
O hero, men and women gathered together will laugh at you;
I too have been praised here by the Sairandhrī for my skill in the art of charioteering.
Indeed, I shall not be able to return toward the city without having won back the cattle.
"Because of the praise of Sairandhrī and because of those words of yours, how could I not fight all the Kurus? Be firm!
Uttara said:

Let the Kurus take as much wealth from the Matsyas as they wish; however, these six are indeed desperados: the arsonist, the poisoner, the one with a weapon in hand, the robber of wealth, and the one who seizes land and wives.

Even if an assailant approaches who is well-versed in the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, a man who kills him while he intends to kill would not become a slayer of a Brahmin. I have no need for battle; let my cows depart as well.
"My city is empty, and I am even afraid of my father;
I shall drink neither milk, nor curd, nor ghee, nor buttermilk. Indeed, I shall drink sour gruel, for I have no need for cows."
"And as you look on, O Bṛhannalā, I shall enter the city;
turn the chariot back quickly, for my heart is breaking. It is better to live even for a short time than I have any need for cattle."
"If I go toward the city while still alive,
O Bṛhannaḍā, let the women and men laugh at me; from now on,
my food shall be devoid of dairy products, consisting even of sour gruel."
"I shall eat with many people, or else I will go away out of fear of death.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus, the boy, adorned with earrings, leaped down from the chariot and fled in terror.
Casting aside his pride and discarding his bow and arrow, that dull-witted man,
Bṛhannaḍā, said:
"This flight is not the duty of a Kṣatriya as remembered by those of old."
"Death in battle is better for you than fleeing in fear.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus, the son of Kuntī leaped down from his excellent chariot.
Dhananjaya pursued the prince as he fled,
shaking his long braid and his two fine red garments,
appearing as if he were bending the very earth with his powerful strides.
Seeing Arjuna running with his braid disheveled, some soldiers, not recognizing him at that time, laughed upon beholding him in such a state. Seeing him rushing forward so swiftly, the Kurus said:
"Soldiers!
Who is this who runs away without attachment, having previously abandoned his excellent chariot?
Who is he, disguised by his appearance like fire concealed by ashes?"
"Some resemble a man, some resemble a woman"—
thus did the soldiers speak, and Droṇa said this to them:
"The preceptor of the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas is in wisdom equal to Śukra and Aṅgiras."
What need have you for deliberation, or indeed for following after this? Like one running fearlessly after another who is fleeing in terror,
that bull among men shines forth, having shaken off his mass of matted hair.
He bears a form like that of Arjuna, yet assumes the appearance of a eunuch;
in appearance he resembles Pārtha, though adorned in female attire.
This very head and neck, these two arms like iron maces—[are they his?]
His prowess is exactly like that; he is none other than Dhanañjaya. Just as Devendra is among the immortals, so is Dhanañjaya among men.
Who else in the world but Dhanañjaya would advance against us alone?
When Droṇa had spoken thus, the wise Karṇa replied:
"The one son of Virāṭa was present in the empty city;
it is said that he has gone out merely out of childishness, not from any display of prowess."
"Having appointed a eunuch as our charioteer, we have gone out from the city;
surely it is Pārtha Arjuna who is moving about here, concealed by a disguise. For they would certainly not be able to withstand us in battle."
"How could one among them fight all the Kurus together?
Having made Uttara his charioteer, he has gone out from the city;
I think that upon seeing our banners, he is fleeing in fear."
"Surely this Dhanañjaya wishes to seize him as he runs;
he pursues us alone, for there is no one else in the world besides Dhanañjaya.
Having made Uttara his charioteer, he desires to fight here himself."
Thus all the Kurus reflected individually,
yet they were unable to determine any further course of action.
Then Duryodhana spoke these words to the soldiers, the best of chariot-warriors:
Neither Arjuna nor Vāsudeva, nor Rāma, nor even Pradyumna could possibly fight against us in battle;
how then could any one of them fight all the Kurus?
"O Bhārata, if another should come to the path of the cattle disguised as a eunuch,
I shall strike him with sharp arrows and cast him down to the earth—
having seen that Pāṇḍava thus concealed by the sacrificial canopy."
"Let us not lead Arjuna away," they said; thus all those great car-warriors, the Kurus, deliberated again and again.
He is a firm archer, possessed of great being, and equal to Śakra in prowess.

If he comes to fight, the entire army will be thrown into doubt; moreover, they do not consider anyone there to be a match for Dhanañjaya. But Dhanañjaya, having pursued Uttara as he fled, [overtook him].
Having run a hundred paces quickly, he seized her by the hair.
"Do not seize me! May you be blessed! I am your slave, O Bṛhannalā!"—even as she spoke thus, he swiftly caught up with her as she was running away with speed.
The powerful Bībhatsu, the crusher of enemies, seized the son of Virāṭa; being thus assailed by Arjuna, he lamented like one in distress:
"Do not kill me! May you be blessed! Release me; I am going to my home."
Saying, "Release me! Release me! Release me! he grasped his feet.
Then, having shown himself to everyone, O King, he bit his finger. Thus entreated by Pārtha with the words, "Do not fear," he lamented.
Then Uttara, the son of Virāṭa, spoke much that was piteous;
he said:
"O auspicious Bṛhannaḍā of slender waist, you should indeed listen."
"Turn the chariot back quickly; one who lives sees prosperity.
I shall give you fourteen villages filled with wealth and herds of cattle; I offer this wealth to you—release me, O Bṛhannaḍā!"
"Release me, O Bṛhannaḍā, along with two thousand bright horses adorned with golden garlands and endowed with all auspicious marks."—
Thus spoke Uttara.
"Whatever you desire of gold, jewels, and pearls, I shall give to you. Elephants, horses, chariots, cows, and well-adorned women—
I give to you a hundred *niṣkas* of pure gold."
"I shall give you a hundred *niṣkas* of the finest silver; release me, O Bṛhannalā!
And I will give you eight great-lustered *vaiḍūrya* gems set in gold."
"O Bṛhannaḍā, release me; give me a chariot covered with a golden pole and yoked with excellent horses, ten rutting elephants,
sixty well-adorned maidens, and a village."
"Release me, for I am deeply distressed, overwhelmed, and trembling with fear.
O eunuch, I shall go to the city to see my afflicted mother.
I am the young son of the King of Matsya, and by him I have been well cared for."
"Lying by my mother's side, untouched by sun or wind, and having never seen the battle of armies, where are those Kurus for me? Where are they?
I shall go to my mother's side; release me, O Bṛhannalā!"

The Kuru army appears like the ocean at the time of universal dissolution. Out of ignorance, in the midst of women, I spoke words marked by prowess and heroism out of pride: "Who could possibly conquer the Kurus?"
"Or, if you do not release me but carry me away, I shall die before you. Take all this wealth and let me go, Bṛhannaḍā;
I shall live on sour gruel, for I have no need for cattle."
Arjuna said:
"O Bṛhannaḍā, turn back; while living, I shall obtain other cows.
For fame is the sole witness for hundreds of aeons."
"O son of a king, life is as flickering as the ear of an elephant; do not enter the midst of the arena.
Uttara said:
We are ashamed of breaking our resolve on the stage of battle;
as for that fame which rises up even at the destruction of the body— fie upon it, for it brings only suffering and destroys its very root!
"Who indeed, having sold their body for wealth,
would perform a pilgrimage to a temple?
Vaiśampāyana said:

Laughing at him as he thus lamented these words, senseless and distressed, that tiger among men brought him near to the chariot. Then Pārtha spoke to him, who was afflicted by fear and deprived of his senses.
Arjuna said:
"I shall fight the Kauravas; you, Uttara, must restrain the horses. Why do you take up [these weapons] and yet become intent on flight?"
"Fight together with the Kauravas; victory shall be yours,
for he with whom I act as charioteer in battle—
whether he be a king or a prince— his victory is certain and eternal."
"Fight by all means against the Kurus with me as your ally;
having conquered the earth and attained glory, you shall enjoy this entire world. Even if slain, you will attain heaven; flight is not for your welfare."
"Today, having conquered all the Kurus, you shall obtain victory;
I shall strive for this end, for I am considered your ally here. I shall restrain the horses of whichever [chariot] he mounts, so that he does not flee in fear."
"O crusher of foes, if you do not dare to fight with the enemies, come and guide my horses while I battle them. Protected by the strength of my arms, advance against this division of chariots."
"Most invincible, formidable, and protected by heroic great chariot-warriors—do not fear, O foremost of princes; you are a Kṣatriya, O scorcher of foes.
Why, O tiger among men, do you despond in the midst of the enemy?"

"I shall indeed fight with the Kurus and I will win back your cattle. Having entered this unassailable and difficult-to-approach array of chariots, O best of men, you be my driver; I shall fight with the Kurus."
"I shall lead the heroes, fierce in battle, to the abode of Yama.
Speaking thus, O bull of the Bharatas, the undefeated Bībhatsu comforted Uttara, the son of Virāṭa, for a moment.
Then Pārtha, the best among strikers, placed him— who was struggling, unwilling, and oppressed by fear— upon his chariot;
and with swift steeds, Pārtha proceeded toward the Kurus.
Just as Indra proceeds with Mātali to slay the Dānavas,
so did Dhanañjaya, having placed him upon the seat of his chariot as he was lamenting,
approach that Śamī tree to take up the Gāṇḍīva bow.
Having comforted Uttara and made him his charioteer, Arjuna—
Vaiśampāyana said:—
beheld that bull among men standing upon the chariot in the guise of a eunuch.
Having placed Uttara upon the chariot as it proceeded toward the śamī tree,
all those foremost car-warriors of the Kurus, headed by Bhīṣma and Droṇa,
became terrified in their minds out of fear of Dhanañjaya.
Beholding them with their enthusiasm destroyed and observing those wonderful portents,
Bhāradvāja, the preceptor and best among weapon-bearers, spoke:
"The winds blow unsteadily, harsh and with a rough sound."
The sky is shrouded in darkness with the appearance of the color of ashes;
clouds of harsh hue, wondrous to behold, are seen;
and various weapons emerge from their scabbards.
These fierce jackals howl in the blazing quarter,
and the horses shed tears while the banners tremble though unshaken. Such are the many portents that are seen here.
"Be alert and remain standing; a battle is at hand. Protect yourselves as well, arrange the army in formation, await the slaughter, and protect the wealth of cattle."

Having spoken these words, he looked toward Bhīṣma and said: "O son of the River, the son of the enemy of mountains (Indra) is named Nagāhvaya; he is the banner of the enemy of Laṅkā’s lord (Rāvaṇa)."
With a gait like that of a celestial nymph, the lord of the gods moved about;
then the preceptor spoke those very same words.
Having spoken thus, O lord of the people, Droṇa remained silent by means of a sign.

Having heard the words of Bhāradvāja, the son of Gaṅgā (Bhīṣma) replied with a sign: "Our time has passed; they have entered another territory, for the deadline that was declared by us in the assembly hall has expired."
"You need have no fear of the enemy; cast away your apprehension, O bull among men.
Then, looking toward Duryodhana, Droṇa spoke by means of a sign. When these beneficial words had been spoken by Devavrata, [Droṇa addressed him].
This hero, a great archer and the best among all wielders of weapons,
is Savyasācin, the scorcher of foes who has displayed his prowess for the sake of the cattle; he whose banner bears the enemy of the Lord of Laṅkā’s grove, O Son of the River.
This son of the mountain-lord named Naga,
wearing a crown and disguised as a woman,
will defeat you and lead away your cattle today.
Pārtha has arrived in the guise of a eunuch; there is no doubt about this.
This is that valiant Pārtha, Savyasācin, the scorcher of foes;
he would not turn back from battle even by all the hosts of Maruts.
By him many conquerors of kings have been slain;
in him all that great splendor has fully and intensely burst forth,
by whom Drupada was bound with might and my sacrificial fee was bestowed.
Having pierced the target situated in the sky and having utterly defeated the kings,
by him the princess of Pañcāla was previously won at her *svayaṃvara*;
by him, having conquered gods and asuras, the Fire-god was gratified at Khaṇḍava.
By him Subhadrā was won after defeating the Yādavas;
by him the enemy of Tripura, the destroyer of Smara, was conquered in battle;
and having gone to Triviṣṭapa, the Dānavas were defeated in war by him who overcame Indra.
O King, thirty million Nivātakavacas, the Dānavas,
as well as the Kālakeyas who dwell in Hiraṇyapura, were all conquered by him;
it was he who released you when you were bound by Citrasena in that forest.
By whom, having gone to the northern side of Mount Meru, great wealth was brought back;
who caused the son of Dharma to perform sacrifices after conquering all kings; and in whom resided heroism, valor, splendor, fortitude, and prowess.
Majesty, profundity, modesty, glory, righteousness, compassion, and uprightness—
he who is endowed with such qualities as these is undoubtedly this son of Pṛthā;
though he suffered in the forest, this hero was trained by Vāsava.

Overcome by indignation, he will fight; of this there is no doubt. O Kauravas, I do not see anyone here who can withstand him in combat—even Mahādeva himself is said to have been gratified by Pārtha in battle.
"The Lord, disguised in the dress of a Kirāta on Mount Himavat"—
to Droṇa speaking thus, Karṇa, filled with rage, spoke these words.
Karṇa said:
"You always boast to us of the virtues of Phalguna,
yet Arjuna is not worth even a sixteenth part of me or Duryodhana.
Duryodhana said:
"O son of Rādhā, if this is indeed Pārtha, my purpose will be accomplished;
for they shall have to live known once more for another twelve years.
But if this is some other man in the guise of a eunuch,"
"With well-sharpened arrows, I shall strike him down to the surface of the earth.
Vaiśampāyana said:
While that scorcher of foes, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, was speaking those words,
Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, and the son of Droṇa praised that manliness.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having approached that *śamī* tree, Pārtha spoke to the son of Virāṭa.
"You are known to be delicate and not very skilled in battle.
Come, O Bhūmijaya, O son of Virāṭa, climb this great *śamī* tree. Commanded by me, O Uttara, quickly fetch the bows."
For these [tusks] of yours will not be able to endure my strength— neither to carry a heavy burden, nor to crush an elephant,
nor to withstand the movement of my arms as I conquer my enemies here.
O mighty-armed scorcher of foes, with these weapons of yours— which are all exceedingly fine, short, and soft— I am indeed unable to perform any victorious deed here.
"Therefore, O conqueror of lands, ascend this leafy *śamī* tree;
for upon it are placed the bows of the sons of Pāṇḍu—
those of Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīma, Bībhatsu, and likewise those of the twins."
The banners, arrows, and divine armor of the heroes are here;
and here too is this bow of great power, Pārtha’s Gāṇḍīva,
which alone is equal to a hundred thousand and increases the prosperity of the kingdom.
Exceedingly capable of enduring exertion, equal to the great king of grasses (śara), a great vessel for all weapons, and a cause of distress to enemies;
it was divine, fashioned with gold, smooth, long, and without blemish.
It is capable of bearing a heavy burden, both formidable and beautiful to behold;
all such [limbs] are powerful, firm,
preeminent, distinguished, and indeed difficult to look upon.
Thus addressed by Arjuna, the son of Virāṭa replied.
Uttara said:
"We have heard that a corpse was indeed tied to this tree."
"How could I, being a prince, touch this with my hand?
It is not fitting for me, born of the Kṣatriya lineage, to seize such a thing, especially as I am a great prince who knows the mantras and the sacrifice."
“If I were to touch her body here, even though I am free from grief,
how could you, O Bṛhannaḍā, allow me— who have touched her body like an impure corpse-carrier— to engage in social intercourse?”
Then the heroic Pārtha, the conqueror of enemy cities, spoke to him—
the heir of all the Matsyas, born of noble lineage, and highly skilled.
"I know you, O man of great wisdom, to be auspicious by birth and lineage;
how then, O scorcher of foes, could I speak an evil word to you?
Bṛhannaḍā said:
"O Indra among kings, you shall be fit for social intercourse and indeed pure;
do not fear these bows, for no physical body exists here.
[I am] the heir of the King of Matsya, born in his lineage, and possessed of a high mind."
"How could I make you perform such a censurable task, O prince?
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having been addressed thus by Pārtha, he, adorned with earrings, leaped down from the chariot.
Then the son of Virāṭa, being helpless, climbed the *śamī* tree.
Standing upon his chariot, Dhanañjaya, the slayer of enemies, commanded him:
"Descend these bows from the top of the tree; do not be afraid."
"Quickly remove their wrappings. Having taken away the costly bows of those broad-chested men and having loosened the leaf-wrappings, he brought them forward.
Likewise, having loosened their bindings on all sides,
he saw the Gāṇḍīva bow there along with four others; as those bows, radiant as the sun, were being unfastened, [he beheld them].
A divine radiance burst forth like that of the planets at their rising;
beholding their forms, which were like those of yawning serpents,
his hair stood on end and he became instantly agitated with fear.
Then, his body trembling,
the prince was comforted by Arjuna; somewhat emboldened, he [spoke].
He practiced looking at them, practicing touching them again and again;
closing his eyes and opening them once more, and touching them repeatedly,
he finally beheld them clearly and was comforted.
Having heard that, Śatrughna then said to Arjuna:
"O charioteer, what is this? Is it a lord of elephants, or perhaps a bow?
Having touched those bows, which were radiant and massive, he spoke.
O King, the son of Virāṭa spoke these words to Arjuna:
Uttara said,
"Such a wonderful form of a bow has never been seen nor heard of before."
On which a hundred drops of gold have been set—
this supreme bow, adorned with ten billion golden [ornaments], belongs to whom?
Upon its back, golden elephants appear as if armored.
Whose is this supreme bow with beautiful sides and a fine grip? Whose is this excellent bow, upon whose back sixty pure, refined golden insects (*indragopaka*) shine, beautifully arranged?
Where three golden suns shine,
armored and blazing with splendor— whose is this supreme bow?
Where there are golden Śāla trees, variegated with refined gold.
To whom does this supreme bow belong, variegated with gold and jewels?
And to whom do these thousands of feathered iron arrows belong,
their tips polished with silver and kept in a golden quiver?
Whose are these broad arrows, fletched with vulture feathers and sharpened on stone;
these yellow-hued, well-nosed, golden shafts made entirely of iron?
Whose is this dark quiver, marked with the signs of five tigers?
Intermingled with boar-eared arrows, he carries ten [types of] shafts.
Whose are these broad, long arrows, entirely made of iron, seven hundred in number— these *nārāca* arrows that feed on blood?

Whose are these divine arrows, capable of bearing a heavy burden and terrifying to enemies, which have beautiful feathers like parrot wings on their front halves, while their rear halves are made of iron, yellow, with golden shafts, and sharpened on stone?
Whose is this long arrow, with a golden shaft and vulture feathers, terrifying to enemies, with a stone-edged back and a stone-tipped point;
this great weapon, with its hilt adorned with gold, is placed within a scabbard made of tiger-skin?

Whose is this great, divine sword with a golden hilt, perfectly free of blemish, possessing a beautiful sheath, excellent blades, and adorned with tiny bells? Whose is this stainless sword set within a cowhide scabbard?

Whose quiver holds this golden-hafted, invincible arrow of the Niṣadhas, the accomplisher of great feats— this weapon with its golden body, endowed with perfect proportions and form, yellow like the sky?
In whose case is this heavy, yellow sword— made of steel, perfectly flawless, and glowing like fire— kept in a well-refined golden scabbard? Whose is this dark sword, covered with spots of gold?
With a touch like that of a venomous serpent, it pierces the bodies of others; capable of bearing heavy burdens, divine, and a source of terror to rivals—
this is the superior [bow].
"Charioteer, what is this divine sight? Is it a serpent, or perhaps a bow?
Here are golden lotuses with a hundred petals, distributed in parts, glowing like fire on *kuśa* grass, radiant and vast."
And here, golden drops strung with jewels shine all around;
adorned with gold, they gleam upon the back with the radiance of the moon and sun.
Here, too, are golden flowers, lotuses of a hundred petals, arranged in their respective places.
Whose [chariot] is of a wondrous form, terrifying and fearsome to behold,
resembling a blue lotus, adorned with gold,
and upon whose back stand golden bulls with horns?
Whose is this palm-tree-sized [staff], adorned with jewels and gold? It is made of refined gold, upon which ten monkeys sit;
it is difficult to bend, great, long, beautiful, and invincible.
Whose is this such wondrous bow, and why are all these men clad in armor? Whose is this [chariot] whose radiance is as pure as the moon and sun, which is beautiful and lovely to behold,
and upon whose back rest swans with flames resembling the fire of *kuśa* grass?
"O charioteer, whose bow is this that resembles the Śārṅga and Gāṇḍīva?
This fourth bow, with its golden body, shines like a mass of lightning;
it is made of flawless blue lotus-stalks and possesses the luster of gold."
O charioteer,
whose is this divine bow, resembling Indra’s rainbow,
which stands raised like a long serpent’s hood, difficult to bend because of its strength, upon the back of which fish are piled up in heaps?
There are golden iguanas by the thousands and fourteen leopards;
here too are peacocks made of gold, adorned with hundreds of moons and suns.
Whose is this fifth bow, its limbs variegated with Jāmbūnada gold?
To whom do these razor-tipped iron arrows belong, a thousand in number that shave the hair?
To whom do these birds with sharp-pointed beaks belong, and to whom do these sharpened shafts?
To whom do these broad *vipāṭa* arrows belong, fletched with half-vulture feathers?

Whose are these beautiful arrows with boar-ears and sharp points? Whose are these seven hundred arrows, whose touch is like the thunderbolt and whose flames are like fire, with golden feathers and sharp tips?
Whose is this long arrow, sharpened in a sheath of cowhide?
Whose is this firm, smooth, and beautiful staff that shines so brightly?
Whose is this divine, great-splendored sword with its tiger-skin scabbard?
Whose is this sword for sowing, marked with the sign of five tigers?
Whose is this stainless sword, encased in leopard skin?
Whose is this broad and great sword, the color of a blue lotus?
Whose is this great sword, sharp-edged and perfectly polished, sheathed in the skin of a lion king? Whose is it, encased in a scabbard of bull-hide, upon whose hilt five adorned suns are seen?
Whose is this vast sword, so captivating with its hilt and scabbard? It lies within a sheath made of parṣata leather, polished with oil and well-maintained.
Whose is this great sword, endowed with such perfect proportions and color?
No elephant whatsoever could survive if pierced by this [arrow]. These sharp-tusked arrows, yellowish-green in color, five hundred in number, have been placed in a golden quiver; whose are they?

"O Bṛhannaḍā, being questioned by me, explain according to the truth: whose [bow] has a touch like that of a venomous serpent, which is straight in flight and firm; and upon its closing, beautiful golden tigers are seen?"
"Supreme wonder has arisen in me upon seeing all this great [display].
Bṛhannaḍā said: Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus addressed by Uttara, Pārtha spoke to the son of Virāṭa with gentle words, reassuring him as he was terrified and overcome by fear:
"Regarding that which you previously asked me here concerning the destroyer of enemy armies— "
This is the bow Gāṇḍīva, renowned throughout the worlds as belonging to Pārtha;
it is impenetrable, ageless, glorious, divine, indestructible, and without flaw—
the preeminent among all weapons, adorned with gold.
This was that supreme weapon, the Gāṇḍīva, which belonged to Arjuna;
it was equal to a hundred thousand [other weapons], the enhancer of kingdoms,
by means of which Pārtha overcomes both gods and men in battle.
Variegated with diverse colors, smooth, long, and without blemish,
it has been worshipped by gods, dānavas, and gandharvas for eternal years; indeed,
Brahmā formerly wore this for a thousand years.
Immediately thereafter, Prajāpati then maintained [the office] for three hundred and fifty years; Śakra [did so] for eighty-five years;
King Soma for five hundred years; and likewise Varuṇa for one hundred.

And from that Varuṇa, Agni affectionately brought forth that auspicious weapon; by Agni, through a reciprocal agreement, the Gāṇḍīva was given to the son of Pṛthā. For sixty-five years, the son of Pṛthā, whose horses are white, wielded it.
This great, divine, and supreme bow of great power—
beautiful to behold, resembling a blue lotus— was obtained by me from Varuṇa for the sake of the high-souled Kuru king.
Golden drops were skillfully fastened upon its back;
honored among gods and mortals, it bore a most excellent form.
As tall as a palm tree, Bhīma’s [bow] was adorned with jewels and gold.

The bow of Bhīmasena was difficult to bend, great, long, beautiful in form, and invincible; it had excellent sides and was adorned with gold. There were also a thousand golden arm-guards and fourteen leopards.
And golden bulls with horns stand upon his back;
by means of these, Pārtha, the scorcher of foes, conquered the entire eastern quarter.
Adorned on their backs, they shine, refined as if by fire and well-proportioned.
O son of Virāṭa, this excellent bow with its beautiful form, variegated like an *indragopaka* insect, belongs to King Yudhiṣṭhira; on it,
radiant golden suns shine forth.
Blazing indeed with splendor, this is the weapon of Nakula;
where there are golden locusts, variegated with refined gold—
this is the bow of Sahadeva, the son of Mādrī.
And O Vairāṭi, this bow made of horn, variegated with refined gold, belongs to Nakula. And these thousands of feathered arrows,
resembling razors and like the venom of serpents, belong to Arjuna, O Vairāṭi.
Blazing with splendor in battle and moving swiftly, these [arrows] become inexhaustible for the hero as he arrays them against his enemies in combat;
they possess terrible tips and long forms, capable of splitting even mountains.
These broad and long arrows, shaped like half-moons, are Bhīma’s sharpened shafts that destroy his enemies;
and these yellow-colored ones, with golden feathers and whetted on stone, are likewise his.
This is Nakula’s quiver, marked with the sign of five tigers;
by means of it, he conquered the entire western quarter in battle.
For this was indeed the quiver belonging to that wise son of Mādrī.
These arrows, which have the appearance of the sun and are made entirely of iron,
are the variegated and skillfully crafted weapons of the wise Sahadeva.
And these sharp, yellow, broad, and long-feathered shafts—

"These great arrows of the king have golden feathers and three joints. But this long arrow, with its back like a stone and its point like a bee, is Arjuna’s; it is firm and capable of enduring heavy burdens in battle."
The great arrow of Bhīmasena has a scabbard made of tiger-skin;
it is divine, capable of bearing heavy weight, and terrifying to his enemies. It possesses an excellent blade, a variegated sheath, and a gold hilt, and is unsurpassed.
This is the sword of the wise Dharmarāja, the Kaurava;
and this, which is sheathed in a scabbard made of five-tufted [leather] and adorned with variegated work,
is Nakula’s firm sword, capable of enduring heavy burdens.
But this stainless sword, sheathed in a cow-hide scabbard—know it to belong to Sahadeva; it is firm and capable of bearing every burden.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus did Pārtha, the scorcher of foes whose prowess is truth, then describe his own weapons there to the son of Virāṭa.
And here were peacock-feathered arrows made of gold, adorned with hundreds of moons and suns.
This bow, however, belongs to Nakula, the wise son of Mādrī;
this variegated bow is similar to that of his younger brother.
And this turmeric-colored bow belongs to the high-souled Kuru king.
These arrows of Bhīmasena, capable of splitting even mountains,
are radiant, massive in size, sharp-tipped, well-crafted, and firm; indeed,
dispatched by Bhīma, they are the warders-off of the elephants.
Golden-hued, radiant, auspicious, and resembling the staff of Death—
these are indeed Nakula’s arrows, possessing a brilliance equal to the thunderbolt and lightning;
they are long, with even blades, and perfectly balanced, about which you have asked.
Those sharp-pointed arrows with boar-ears belong to Sahadeva; but this divine shaft, sheathed in a cowhide quiver,
is Pārtha’s— this great and terrible weapon capable of enduring every strain.
This stainless sword, sheathed in a leopard skin,
belongs to King Yudhiṣṭhira, the wise son of Kuntī;
it has a scabbard made of tiger skin and bears the marks of five tigers.

The sword of the wise Pārtha, which has the luster of a blue lotus, is trained to strike down the shoulders of even the most arrogant elephants; it is covered with a lion’s skin, possesses a sharp edge, and is perfectly balanced.
This beautiful sword with its extremely sharp point belongs to the wise son of Kuntī;
this is Arjuna’s scimitar, the destroyer of the vanguard of enemy armies.
As for this one with the radiant hilt, which has been placed in the sheath belonging to the son of Pṛṣata—
This sword of Nakula, possessing a radiance equal to Vaiśvānara, is indeed formidable; and this tawny sword, variegated with a hilt made of jewels,
is the sword of Sahadeva— capable of bearing great weight and exceedingly sharp.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"This is Bhīma’s great mace, the destroyer of all enemies;
for Arjuna quickly related this truthfully through his spies."
Weapons, quivers, and swords of incomparable luster— where indeed are those, including the excellent bow of the mighty Sahadeva,
belonging to the high-souled Pāṇḍavas who dwell in concealment?
"04,038.058d*0722_002 Here lie the highly precious [remains] of those who have attained the perfection of their vows.
04,038.058d*0722_003 Thus did Arjuna speak all that was further regarding the truth.
Uttara said:
These weapons, fashioned from gold, belonging to those high-souled sons of Pṛthā who act with swiftness, shine brilliantly. Vaiśampāyana said:
In the meantime, the dull-witted son of Virāṭa did not recognize Pārtha; standing before him, he asked once again:
"Where indeed is Arjuna Pārtha, or Yudhiṣṭhira the Kaurava?"
Nakula, Sahadeva, and Bhīmasena the Pāṇḍava—
where indeed are those heroic Pāṇḍavas, unconquered in battles?
These divine [weapons] of theirs shine and gleam with splendor.
In what region do those knowers of dharma, who are so affectionate toward their kin, dwell?
Where is Yudhiṣṭhira, the Kuru king, the son of Dharma;
and where are Bhīmasena and Arjuna—all of whom are my maternal uncles?
Either Nakula or Sahadeva is skilled in all weapons in battle;
he is virtuous in character, righteous in soul, possessed of dharma, a knower of dharma, wise,
the overseer of dharma, devoted to the vows of dharma, a knower of dharma, and the very embodiment of dharma.
Established in dharma, a performer of dharma, a protector of dharma, and a doer of excellent dharma;
a support for truth, uprightness, and forbearance, compassionate, and devoted to dharma—
all these high-souled ones are destroyers of all enemies.
Having lost their kingdom at dice, they were never heard of again;
where is Draupadī, the princess of Pañcāla, renowned as a jewel among women? When they were defeated at dice, Kṛṣṇā followed them into the forest.
Having renounced the kingdom of dharma, they have gone to the forest; if you know of the Pāṇḍavas, those practitioners of dharma—where are they now?
And where do they dwell today? Tell me the truth, Bṛhannalā.
Then Bībhatsu, the son of Kuntī who rides white horses,
laughed and said to that prince Uttara, "Listen to my words."
"For what purpose have the weapons and missiles of the high-souled ones come here?
How were they recognized by you? Tell me this, O beautiful one.
Then, smiling, the son of Kuntī spoke to the prince.

"Do not fear, O tiger among kings; I shall describe everything to you. There is no need to be afraid here even now, O prince, however it may be. We are the Pāṇḍavas by name, who have reached the end of our forest exile."
"Twelve years ago, they lived here in concealment;
therefore, O most exalted one, listen with an unhesitating mind.
Arjuna said:
"I am Arjuna, the son of Pṛthā; Yudhiṣṭhira is the courtier. Bhīmasena is Ballava, your father’s cook of savory dishes.
Nakula is the horse-keeper, and Sahadeva is in the cow-pen."
"Know that Sairandhrī is Draupadī, for whose sake the wicked Kīcakas were slain by Bhīmasena along with their brothers in battle. Upon hearing these words of Jiṣṇu, his eyes widened with amazement.
Gazing at Pārtha with unblinking eyes, he spoke these words slowly.
Uttara said:
"The ten names of Pārtha which were previously heard by me—"
"If you would have faith in all of them, I shall explain them to you.
Arjuna said:
"Indeed, I shall declare to you those ten names which belong to me."
O Vairāṭa, listen to those things which you have heard before;
having become one-pointed in mind, listen to everything with a concentrated spirit. The Lord, the god who is the sovereign of the triple heaven, ordained it in the sky.
Listen now, O Vairāṭa, to the truth regarding those names as they are used in the world:
Arjuna, Phalguna, Jiṣṇu, Kirīṭin, Śvetavāhana,
Bībhatsu, Vijaya, Kṛṣṇa, Savyasācin, and Dhanañjaya.
"These names of mine were established by the best of the gods.
Uttara said:
"O Pāṇḍava, these ten names are united according to their qualities."
O sinless one, these renowned titles are well known to me as they circulate in the world: by what means are you named Vijaya? By what means are you Śvetavāhana?
Why are you named Kirīṭin? And how is it that you are Savyasācin?
"Arjuna, Phalguna, Jishnu, Krishna, Bibhatsu, and Dhananjaya—by what [names] am I [known]? Tell me the truth of this.
I have heard only the etymological origins of that hero's names."
"If you were to tell me all of that, I would believe everything you say.
Yet this fickle mind of mine wanders here and there regarding you;
tell me quickly, O Bṛhannalā, are you Arjuna or someone else?"
Arjuna said:
"Having conquered all the inhabited lands and seized their wealth entirely, I stand in the midst of that wealth; therefore they call me Dhanañjaya."

"When I set out for battle, I do not turn back until I have conquered those who are intoxicated with war; because of this, they know me as Vijaya (the Victorious). White horses, equipped with golden trappings, are yoked to my chariot."
Because I fought in battle with him, I am known as Śvetavāhana;
my crown, which resembles the sun,
shines upon my head as I stand upon my chariot in the midst of the fray, glowing like the sun or fire.

I was born by day on the back of the Himavat under the two *Pūrvaphalgunī* and the two *Uttaraphalgunī* constellations; therefore, they know me as Phalguna. Whoever should inflict a wound upon my body while my elder brother looks on—
If he should ever show me the blood of Yudhiṣṭhira, I would bring about his downfall within his lineage; of this there is no doubt.
Long ago, while I was fighting the foremost of the Dānavas, Śakra granted this to me.

A crown, radiant as the sun, rests upon his head; because of it, they call him Kirīṭin (the Diademed One). It is indestructible, beautiful, variegated, adorned with gold, given by Indra, and cannot be taken away.
"Even while fighting, I would never perform a loathsome act in any way; therefore, among gods and men, they know me as Bībhatsu. Both my hands are dexterous for drawing the Gāṇḍīva."
Equipped with my bow, I discharge a rain of arrows;
my two arms prevail in battle for the destruction of the enemy host.
Because of this, among gods and men, they know me as Savyasācin.
On this earth bounded by the four oceans, my equal in complexion is hard to find;
I perform pure deeds, and for that reason they know me as Arjuna. I am difficult to attain, difficult to overcome, a subduer, and the son of Indra.

Because of that, I am renowned among gods and men by the name Jiṣṇu. My mother’s name was Pṛthā; therefore, they call me Pārtha. [I have conquered] the gods, dānavas, gandharvas, piśācas, uragas, and rākṣasas.
In the past, having conquered in battle, I gratified Agni in the Khandava forest;
and after gratifying the Consumer of Oblations together with the wielder of the Śārṅga bow,
I beheld the Grandfather and Maheśvara as they had gone to the third heaven.
Seeing those two best of gods, the givers of boons, who had arrived when he had fallen to the ground in a swoon, he first regained consciousness and rose; then,
bowing his head to the earth, he paid homage to those two givers of boons.
Out of affection for me, they both bestowed upon me the eleventh name, "Kṛṣṇa. Satisfied with my prowess and gratified by my deeds,
they, surrounded by all the gods, spoke to me once again in person.
"O dear one, choose a boon—whatever you desire, O Pāṇḍava—from that [I shall grant it];
thus I obtained divine and powerful weapons:
the Brāhma, the Pāśupata, and the invincible Sthūṇākarṇa."
Belonging to Indra, Varuṇa, Agni, Vāyu, and indeed Viṣṇu—
having made Mātali my charioteer, I then repeatedly conquered the invincible Nivātakavacas in battle with that chariot of Indra.

Having alone conquered in battle thirty million great asuras— Dānavas who never retreat in combat and whose armor cannot be pierced even by the gods— because they had been granted boons, I further gratified the gods.
Then the Blessed Lord Indra himself gave me a diadem;
and the gods gave me a conch shell that wards off the armies of enemies. I [stood] on the far shore of the ocean against those dwelling in Hiraṇyapura.
Having slain sixty thousand, I achieved victory;
standing undaunted upon my chariot amidst hundreds and thousands,
I remained invincible in the midst of the enemy, and the cardinal directions did not grow dim for me.
O dear one, while Suyodhana was being carried away by the king of the Gandharvas, I—
having defeated him along with his brothers and the Gandharvas in battle and having slain fourteen thousand [of their followers]— liberated him.
"Do not fear; be free from terror before these assembled Kurus—
while Suyodhana, Karṇa, and Kṛpa look on,
and while Bhīṣma the grandfather, the son of Droṇa, and Droṇa himself are present."
"Having conquered all the Kurus, I shall bring back your cattle. My father gave me my tenth name, "Kṛṣṇa," because I was dark-complexioned yet pure, and because I was so dear to him as a child.
"I stand alert in battle, O son of Virāṭa; let your fear depart.
Having heard this, his soul thrilled with joy and his eyes wide with wonder, Vaiśampāyana said:
Then the son of Virāṭa approached Pārtha from nearby and paid his respects.
Upon hearing those words of his, O best of the Pārshatas, the son of Virāṭa was thrilled;
his hair stood on end, he was filled with joy, and his eyes widened with wonder.
Beholding that high-souled Arjuna, the joy of the Matsyas joined his palms in reverence, saluted him, and then spoke these words:
"I am known by the name Bhūmijaya, and my name is also Uttara."
"By good fortune, O Pārtha, I behold you; welcome to you, Dhanañjaya!
O red-eyed one, O mighty-armed one, whose arms resemble the trunks of the king of elephants, you ought to forgive me for whatever I said to you out of ignorance."
O best of men, because you did not take all of this to heart out of negligence,
you previously performed various difficult deeds.
Therefore, my fear has passed away and my joy in you is supreme.
I shall become your slave; look upon me with compassion. This was the promise made by me previously for the sake of serving as your charioteer.
Peace of mind has arisen within me, and great fortune has come to me,
O Dhanañjaya, that what I spoke to you out of ignorance should now be forgotten,
as long as I do not know you in truth, O Bhārata.
"O Father, I had such fear of the Kurus, of this there is no doubt;
but when I recognized you in truth, O Bhārata,
I was struck with wonder, O Great Being— destroyer of all enemies!"
Sprinkled with the water of your words, my heart— like a lotus scorched by the heat and devoid of water in a lake— is as if it were a withered lotus; yet,
O Arjuna, this vow of mine is not fulfilled, and joy arises within me.

"O you who are fierce in battle, we previously made this vow: 'May I be the charioteer here in the great conflict for the son of the Lord of Gods. That vow of mine has been fulfilled by reason of my acting as your charioteer."
"O hero, you should not be angry with me, for you are equal to a world-protector. O mighty-armed one, I seek your favor regarding my previous transgression.
O Pārtha, as long as I did not behold you, such was my fear."
"Seeing you, I am filled with fear; who, desiring to live, would fight against you?
Thus spoke the son of Matsya to Arjuna, his hair standing on end, as he stood before him with palms joined in reverence, like Vāsava before Brahmā.
Then Arjuna, having comforted the Matsyan prince Vairāṭi,
spoke to him joyfully at that time, like the sun after destroying the darkness;
having consoled the son of the Matsya king, he strung his bow, Gāṇḍīva.
Having become most worthy of being beheld, he stood radiant like the sun.
Uttara said:
"O hero, having mounted this vast chariot with me as its driver..."
"To which army will you go? "I shall go as commanded by you," he said.
Arjuna replied:
"I am pleased, O tiger among men; no fear exists for you."

"I drive away all your enemies in battle, O you who are skilled in combat! Be at ease, O one of great intelligence; behold me together with the foes, fighting fiercely and performing great and terrible deeds in this struggle."
"Quickly fasten the Gāṇḍīva bow, the Devadatta bow, and these arrows adorned with gold— all these quivers— to my chariot;
and bring this sword decorated with gold."
"Mount Gaṇḍīva, Devadatta, and likewise the two inexhaustible great quivers upon this chariot;
I shall bring back your cattle to you.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard Arjuna’s words, Uttara then quickly descended from there,
swiftly taking up Arjuna’s weapons.
Arjuna said:
"I shall indeed fight with the Kurus; I will win back your cattle.
I will satisfy the king and enter the city again—[that city] whose wings are the resolve [of its inhabitants], and whose walls and gateways are my arms."

It was crowded with triple-staffs and quivers, thronged with many banners; it was filled with the striking of bowstrings and the wrathful roars of combat, with the sound of drums like the rattling of rims,
rich with canopies of arrow-nets, and loud with the clamor of shouting warriors.
"O son of Virāṭa, this chariot shall become a city protected by me;
presided over by me in battle, this chariot of the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow shall be invincible to the enemy armies— let your fear depart."
Uttara said:
"I do not fear them; I know you to be firm in battle, equal even to Keśava himself or Indra in person."
What is the use of much talk? Listen to my final words:
O son of Kuntī, I do not fear even Śatakratu himself, nor Yama, Varuṇa, or Kubera, nor even a hundred Droṇas and Bhīṣmas.
But as I reflect upon this, I am utterly bewildered;
being of dull intellect, I cannot arrive at any certainty whatsoever regarding one who possesses such heroic limbs and form, and who is endowed with all the auspicious marks.
By what ripening of karma has this state of impotence come upon you?
I suspect that you, though moving about in the guise of an eunuch, are the trident-bearing Śiva,
or perhaps a god like the king of the Gandharvas, or even Indra, the performer of a hundred sacrifices.
Arjuna said:
"By the command of my eldest brother, I am observing this vow of celibacy for one year; I tell you this truly."
"O mighty-armed one, I am not a coward, nor am I subject to another's will;
yet, being bound by righteousness, I formerly went to the abode of the gods at my elder brother’s command. There, in the Sudharmā hall, I beheld Urvaśī."

I beheld her dancing, possessing a supreme form, in the presence of the wielder of the thunderbolt; I gazed at her with unblinking eyes as she stood firm within my lineage. At night, she came to my bed, desiring to take pleasure with me.
Having saluted her, I paid her the respect due to a mother.
She, however, being enraged, cursed me, saying, "You shall become a eunuch.
Having heard that, Indra said to me, "Do not fear the eunuch, O Pārtha."
"O sinless one, Indra, the bull, sent me forth after bestowing his favor upon me, thinking: 'In the past, while living incognito, you might have been of service to him.
That very vow has now come to pass, and it has been fulfilled by me."
"O prince, know that this impotence which has come upon me was born of Urvaśī’s curse; know that I have now completed my vow and emerged from it. Uttara said:
"This is the supreme favor shown to me today, that my deliberation has not been in vain;
for such superior men as you do not appear here in the form of eunuchs.
With you as my ally, I could fight even the immortals in battle."

That fear of mine has vanished; tell me, what shall I do? I shall hold your horses, you who shatter the chariots of your enemies, for I have been trained in charioteering by a master, O bull among men.
"O bull among men, know me to be as trained in charioteering as Dāruka is for Vāsudeva, or Mātali for Śakra.
O Pāṇḍava, [I am skilled] in these five modes of driving horses on a chariot."
The enemies will flee in all directions as you advance here and there.
O mighty-armed one, these horses of yours are indeed invincible in battle;
they are fit for this excellent chariot, full of vitality, and have conquered all fatigue.
That horse who, when he moves, does not let his hoofprints be seen upon the ground as they reach the earth,
and who is yoked to the right pole like Sugrīva; and this beautiful one, the best of draft-horses, who carries the left pole.
I consider that beautiful horse with its golden armor, who carries the left flank of the army, to be equal in speed to Meghapuṣpa; indeed, I think it is even stronger in its swiftness.
"This horse that carries your right flank, with its neck arched and uplifted,
is considered even more powerful in speed than Balāhaka.
This very chariot is worthy of carrying you, an archer, in battle."
"And you, having mounted this chariot, are in my opinion worthy to fight against all the enemies who have arrived, like the King of the Gods against the Asuras.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, leaping down from his chariot, that heroic crusher of enemies bowed to the gods, took up the Gāṇḍīva bow, and shone with splendor. Then, that powerful hero removed his bracelets from his arms.
In the midst of the variegated sound of kettledrums, he put on his auspicious leather arm-guards;
having lifted and removed his two divine earrings given by Indra,
he tied back his dark, curling hair with a white cloth.
Then, facing the east, pure and with a disciplined mind,
the mighty-armed one meditated upon all the weapons within his excellent chariot;
and all the weapons, with palms joined in reverence, spoke to Pārtha, the son of the king.
"O son of Pāṇḍu, we are these most noble servants.
Then Pārtha, having prostrated and touched them with his hand,
addressed them all, saying, "May all your desires be fulfilled here."
Having received those weapons, his face became radiant with joy;
then that bull of the Bharatas duly recalled the divine weapons,
O best of men, and those great weapons then approached the highly blessed Arjuna.
Quickly stringing the bow Gāṇḍīva, he drew it back;
as that bow was being drawn, there arose a great sound,
like that of a massive mountain struck by another mountain.
The earth shook with a thunderous roar, and a fierce wind blew in all directions;
a great meteor fell, and the quarters of the sky were no longer visible. At that time, the heavens were filled with bewildered birds, and the great trees trembled violently.
The Kurus did not recognize that sound, which was like the crash of a thunderbolt;
hearing it, they were terrified with dejected minds, as if they had heard the cry of Tārkṣya,
just as the powerful Indra [once] cast aside the terrifying crash of a thunderbolt.
Like the great sound of a thunderbolt or the mighty twang of a bowstring, Arjuna,
standing firm on his chariot and restraining his enemies and heroes,
drew that best of bows with both arms upon the chariot.
Uttara said:
"O best of the Pāṇḍavas, how will you alone defeat these many great chariot-warriors in battle, who have mastered all weapons and missiles?"
"You are without allies, O son of Kuntī, while the Kauravas have allies.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"For this very reason, O mighty-armed one, I stand before you in fear."
