Then Pārtha, laughing with a resonant voice, said:
"O hero, when I was fighting with the exceedingly powerful Gandharvas during the cattle-expedition, who was my companion? Who was my friend at that time?"
Likewise, when I was fighting in that terrifying Khāṇḍava forest, crowded with gods and dānavas— against the Nivātakavacas and the mighty Paulomas— who then became my friend?
When he fought for the sake of the King of the Gods, who then became his ally?
And when he fought against many kings in the battle at the self-choice ceremony (*svayaṃvara*) of the Princess of Pañcāla, O dear one, who then became his ally?
Having lived under the tutelage of the preceptor Droṇa, and of Śakra, Vaiśravaṇa, Yama,
Varuṇa, Pāvaka, Kṛpa, and Kṛṣṇa Mādhava,
as well as the wielder of the Pināka bow himself— how could I not fight these?
"Drive my chariot quickly; let the fever of your mind depart.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having made Uttara his charioteer and having circumambulated the Śamī tree, he departed.
Then, having taken up all his weapons, Dhanañjaya set forth;
that great car-warrior, having removed the lion-standard from that chariot and placed it at the foot of a *śamī* tree, proceeded with Uttara as his charioteer.
Having yoked to his chariot the divine illusion fashioned by Viśvakarman,
he mentally envisioned a golden banner marked with the sign of a monkey and a lion’s tail, as well as the favor of the Fire-god.
And he, knowing that thought, summoned the spirits upon his banner;
having raised a monkey upon the banner and brandishing the Gāṇḍīva bow,
Uttara rose up, O dear one, having returned here after remembering [his former life].

Having comforted him, Bībhatsu, the great car-warrior, hastened to advance. From the sky, a divine and beautiful chariot with banners, variegated parts, and quivers swiftly descended upon his own chariot.
Seeing that chariot arrive, he then made a circumambulation;
then Bībhatsu, the son of Kuntī, whose horses are white, mounted the chariot,
girt with a sword, clad in armor, and grasping his bow.
Then he whose banner bears the foremost of monkeys set out toward the north;
having reached the vicinity of the army,
that powerful crusher of foes took up his great, resonant, and most excellent conch.
Summoning his strength, he exerted a force that caused the hair of his enemies to stand on end;
the son of Vāsava placed into his mouth [the blade] as white as the moon or a kunda flower,
its surface covered with veins and its two cheeks quivering.
With eyes sunken and deep-set, with a short and thick neck, with chest and belly pressed closely together, and adorned by a face turned askance,
he seemed as if shaking the three worlds to their very foundations according to the full extent of his own power.
The subduer of enemies blew [his conch] along with the ten Maruts;
that sound of his conch was heard exceedingly like a dark rain-cloud.
By the sound of that conch and the resonance of his bow—
With the roar of the monkey and the sound of the chariot wheels,
the son of Indra (Arjuna) struck terror into the moving host.
Then those swift draft-animals fell to the earth upon their knees.
And Uttara, seized with terror, sank down upon the floor of the chariot.
Having steadied the horses and gathered them in with the reins, the son of Kuntī shone upon the floor of the chariot like the sun atop Mount Meru in the north.
Terrified by the sound of the conch and fainting from the strike of the bowstring, Uttara was embraced and comforted by Arjuna:
"Do not fear, O foremost of princes; you are a Kṣatriya, O scorcher of foes!"
O tiger among men, why do you despair in the midst of the enemy?
Have you not heard the sounds of conchs and the loud blasts of kettledrums,
and the trumpeting of elephants standing in battle arrays?
"How is it that you, being terrified by this sound of the conch here,
have become dejected and frightened like an ordinary man?
Uttara replied:
"I have heard the sounds of conchs and the loud blasts of kettledrums,
and the trumpeting of elephants standing in battle arrays;
yet never before have I heard such a sound of conchs."
"Never before have I seen such a form as this banner,
nor have I ever heard anywhere the roar of such a bow.
By the sound of this conch and the resonance of this bow..."
My mind is utterly bewildered by the cries of non-human beings dwelling upon the banner, and by the roar of the chariot;
all the directions are agitated, and my heart seems to ache.
"Covered by the banner, all the directions are no longer visible to me;
my ears have been deafened by the sound of the Gāṇḍīva. To Uttara, who was thus speaking in reproach, he who was fierce in battle replied:
When he had traveled for a moment, Pārtha spoke to the son of Virāṭa.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Again and again [he blew] the banner, the conch, and the bow."
With his mind utterly bewildered, the son of Virāṭa gazed up at Arjuna.
Arjuna said:
"Be firm, O mighty-armed one, and regain your composure."
Arjuna said:
"Mounting the chariot in a secluded spot, press down with your feet and hold the reins firmly; I shall blow the conch shell once again."
No other fear exists while I stand in this battle; behold, O hero, the strength of my arms as I fight with the enemies. Steadfasten your heart so that a great roar may arise.
Having spoken thus, the mighty-armed Savyasācin, the scorcher of foes,
blew his supreme great conch, Devadatta;
and making the twang of his bowstring and the sound of his palms, he bewildered all living beings.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then that powerful one once again blew that conch shell,
which produces sorrow for enemies and increases the joy of friends.
Then he blew his conch shell, as if splitting the mountains,
the caves of the hills, the quarters of the sky, and the peaks themselves;
and Uttara, shrinking back, sat down upon the floor of the chariot.
Then Arjuna blew his conch shell with a sound that was exceedingly unbearable;
by the blast of that conch, the rattling of the chariot wheels,
and the roar of the Gāṇḍīva bow, the earth trembled.
Hearing that sound, Droṇa then spoke these words to the son of Gaṅgā:
"Seeing Uttara on the chariot, who was bewildered by the blast of the conch, he remembered that chariot; thus the one with the monkey-banner arrived."
Dhananjaya comforted him once again;
then Drona, the highly intelligent one and the best among all wielders of weapons,
spoke in the midst of the Kurus as if to awaken them all.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Hearing that sound of the conch, which was like the roar of a cloud,
his eyes widened with wonder at the very sound of the Gāṇḍīva bowstring.
Then Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Droṇa, the son of Bharadvāja and the best among all wielders of weapons,
looked toward King Duryodhana, the subduer of enemies, and spoke to him.
Droṇa said:
O son of the River, he whose banner bears the enemy of the Lord of Laṅkā’s grove, who is named after a mountain,
is the son of the enemy of mountains (Indra).
This energetic one, wearing the guise of a woman,
will conquer all the heroes of the Kurus;
she is not a woman, for if she were a woman, she would be such a one.
She herself, the slayer of Śumbha and Niśumbha,
assumes a body consisting of an illusory woman; or rather, it is the Ancient Puruṣa who performs this sport.
Just as Indrajit [conquered] the Kṣatriya women, so too did this son of Aṅgana;
indeed, the teacher spoke these words:
"As is the roar of a chariot, as is the sound of a conch being blown."
"The earth trembles; this is none other than Savyasācin.
O King, this is an omen of portents occurring here for us.
For I do not see victory for our army, O scorcher of foes."
The weapons do not gleam, the horses are not spirited, and the fires, though well-kindled, do not shine; that is not auspicious. Furthermore, all our beasts are crying out dreadfully toward the sun.
Crows are perching upon the banners; that is not auspicious. Furthermore, birds on our left portend great danger. This jackal is howling and running through the midst of the army.
And when the unstruck sound has emerged, it portends great fear; I perceive that the hairs on your bodies are standing on end. Surely the destruction of the kṣatriyas through war is now foreseen.
The celestial bodies do not shine, and the beasts and birds are fierce;
various terrible portents are seen that signal the destruction of the Kṣatriyas,
and especially here, these omens point toward our own ruin.
Your army is being tormented by blazing meteors,
O Lord of the People; your mounts are joyless and seem to be weeping,
while vultures hover around your troops on all sides.
You will grieve upon seeing the army oppressed by the arrows of Pārtha; the elephants will have cold limbs, be covered in sweat, and yawn repeatedly,
while the horses shed tears.
They constantly discharge urine and excrement again and again;
the earth is drenched with blood, and all the quarters of the sky are filled with smoke.
The sun does not shine, and it portends a great terror.
The elephants were terrified, and the warriors were also struck with fear;
your army was utterly defeated, and no one wished to fight.
With their faces mostly pale, all the warriors were distraught.
All of them gaze again and again toward the southern quarter;
even the deer and the birds fly away keeping us to their left;
and the sounds of our musical instruments, though loudly sounded, do not resonate deeply for us.

Like the deep and far-reaching roar of a cloud, this rattling of chariots is heard; it belongs to no one other than Dhanañjaya. This is the sound of the horses neighing as they carry the son of Pākaśāsana.
The great monkey-banner is ever-present and flutters unattached;
by the sound of Pārtha’s conch, my ears have been deafened.
The entire army is terrified; this cannot be anyone other than Dhanañjaya.
Placing King Duryodhana, the subduer of enemies, at our head,
let us set the cattle in motion and stand ready to strike with our ranks drawn up in battle array. Having divided the army into three parts and raised our banners high, we shall advance.
"Let outposts be established in all directions so that we may fight Arjuna with vigilance;
for this Dhananjaya, scorching this army with his sharp arrows,
will place his left foot upon the heads of all the lords of men."
"For this Bībhatsu cannot be conquered even by the gods and asuras together.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Then King Duryodhana spoke to Bhīṣma on the battlefield."
Droṇa, that tiger among chariot-warriors, and Kṛpa, the great car-fighter—
this matter has been stated by me to the preceptor and to Karṇa repeatedly;
yet I shall say it once more, for I am not satiated with speaking of it.

"For those who are defeated must dwell for twelve years in the forest, unknown in inhabited lands; this indeed is our wager. For them, that period has not yet ended, as the thirteenth year is still ongoing."
Bībhatsu has come together with us while living in concealment;
yet, if Bībhatsu has arrived before the period of exile has ended,
the Pāṇḍavas shall dwell in the forest for another twelve years.
Either they do not know [the truth] out of greed, or delusion has taken possession of them;
Bhīṣma ought to discern what is deficient or excessive among these men. Furthermore, when there is a conflict of interests, doubt always arises.
Even those people who are knowers of the Dharma become utterly deluded regarding their own true interest;
for an objective intended in one way turns out quite differently.
This was seen by those seeking the northern path who desired to fight the army of Matsya.
"If Bībhatsu has arrived, who among them would turn his back?
We have come here for the sake of the Trigartas to fight the Matsyas;
they recounted to us many instances of the injuries inflicted by the Matsyas."
To them, who were overcome by fear, seeking protection from their terror, and entreating us for safety, we gave this promise.
First, they were to seize our great wealth of cattle and fish; indeed,
they agreed with us that this would take place on the afternoon of the seventh day,
while on the eighth day, we were to act at the rising of the sun.
"When the fish has departed, these cows must be seized at the cow's footprint"— this was our firm resolve and our counsel regarding one another in the city named after the Naga,
for the purpose of identifying all the Pāṇḍavas.
Either those cattle do not see us, or perhaps they have been defeated; or else, having deceived us, they may have made an alliance with the Matsya king.
Or perhaps the Matsya king has approached them together with his provincial subjects.
Accompanied by his entire army and surrounded by those of terrifying form, he has come to fight us,
having arrived throughout the entire night.
Among them, some one of great prowess must have come forward as a leader;
he has arrived here to conquer us, whether it be the King of the Matsyas himself or Bībhatsu.
Whether this be the king of the Matsyas, or whether it be Bībhatsu who has come.
"It was our established agreement that we must all fight together;
I shall strike him down to the earth with my well-sharpened arrows.
Why then do these best of chariot-warriors remain stationed upon their chariots?"
Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, Vikarṇa, and the son of Droṇa—
all these great car-warriors have their minds agitated at this time; indeed,
there is no good for them other than battle, so let yourselves be resolved accordingly.
Whether it be a battle with the entire world or with the gods including Indra,
even if our wealth of cattle were seized by the thunderbolt-wielding god or by Yama in combat, who would return to Hastinapura?
For among foot-soldiers who have been struck down by arrows and broken in the dense forest, who indeed could survive? There would be doubt even regarding the horses.
Therefore, let such a policy be adopted as places the Teacher behind us.
Having heard the words of Duryodhana, the son of Rādhā spoke these words:
"He indeed knows their intention; therefore, he seems to terrify us. I perceive that his affection for Arjuna is exceedingly great."
For indeed, seeing Bībhatsu approaching, he praised him, saying:
"Let such a policy be enacted so that the army does not break;
for while Droṇa was listening to the neighing [of the horses], everything has fallen apart."
"Like a leaderless army in a vast forest during the summer, fallen under the power of its enemies, let such a policy be enacted so that the host does not go astray;
for the Pāṇḍavas have always been dear to the Teacher, especially so."
04,042.022d–0813_001 He himself spoke thus, intending no benefit for others:
"Upon hearing the neighing of horses, what praise could there be for another?
Whether standing still or moving along, horses always neigh."
The winds blow constantly and Vasava rains perpetually;
likewise, the roar of thunder is frequently heard,
terrifying all these people of yours as well as the sons of Pāṇḍu.
Standing at the head of the entire army, he speaks much that is nonsensical,
just as those seeking horses and desiring to catch them hear only the sounds of neighing; such might be the case with you.
"What is Arjuna’s duty in this matter, or how is he praised?
It can only be out of desire, hatred, or sheer anger toward us.
For teachers are indeed compassionate, wise, and perceivers of what is harmful."
When a great danger has arisen, these should not be consulted under any circumstances.
In variegated palaces, in social gatherings, and in dwellings,
it is the wise who shine there while engaging in diverse conversations.
Performing many wondrous feats in the assembly of people,
they were experts in archery and the beautiful aiming of weapons; they were skilled in discerning the vulnerabilities of their enemies and in the conduct of men.
In the management of elephants, horses, and chariots; in the work involving donkeys, camels, goats, and sheep;
in the care of cattle herds, city streets, and the gates of the main entrances—wherever there are defects in the preparation of food, the wise excel in those matters.
Setting aside those wise men who speak of the virtues of the enemy,
let such a policy be adopted so that the foe may indeed be slain. Let the cattle be secured and let the army be arrayed without delay.
"Let defensive measures be established where we shall fight the enemies;
O hero, you must consider how our victory may be secured.
Karṇa said:
I perceive all of you, O long-lived ones, as if terrified and trembling; your minds are averse to battle, and you are all unsettled—
whether it be this son of Jamadagni or Indra, the destroyer of cities.
"Whether this be the king of the Matsyas, or whether it be Bībhatsu who has arrived,
I shall hold him back as the shore holds back the ocean, the abode of sea-monsters.
Against my straight-knotted arrows released from my bow..."
There is no turning back for those who advance, like slithering serpents. Let these gold-feathered, sharp-pointed arrows, released by my skillful hand, cover Pārtha like locusts covering a tree.
From the bowstring striking firmly against the nocks of the arrows,
let the sound of his palms be heard like that of two drums being beaten;
sometimes he would strike one, four, five, sixty, or even a hundred at once.
Behold the chariot-warriors among the fishers slain by my arrows—
one, two, four, five, sixty, and in some places a hundred;
behold the elephants struck down and strewn about by me with a single shaft.
With feathered arrows released from my arms, cleansed with oil,
the sky shone as if covered with fireflies;
for Bībhatsu had remained concentrated for thirteen years.
Feeling affection for me, he will strike out in battle;
and having become a worthy recipient, like a virtuous Brahmin, let the son of Kuntī receive the thousands of showers of arrows released by me.
And this great archer is renowned throughout the three worlds; nor am I, O best of the Kurus, in any way inferior to Arjuna. When my straight-knotted arrows are released from my hand—

There is no turning back for those who go forth, possessing splendor equal to Vaiśvānara. Today, let the sky be seen as if covered with fireflies— by golden vultures released here and there, their wings like those of hawks.
Let the tumultuous roar be heard, like that of singing bees,
of my straight-knotted arrows released from my bow;
who could withstand them while standing before me, even with all the gods and asuras combined?
Today I shall discharge that inexhaustible debt previously promised by my word;
having slain Arjuna in battle, I will pay it to the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
As the feathered shafts are being severed in mid-air and scattered about, [let them fall].

Let the movement of my arrows be seen like a swarm of locusts in the sky. With a touch like Indra’s thunderbolt and a splendor equal to Mahendra himself, I shall afflict Pārtha as one might strike an elephant with firebrands.

From his chariot, I shall seize the heroic Atiratha, the best among all wielders of weapons— the helpless son of Pṛthā— just as Garuḍa seizes a serpent. Him who is as difficult to withstand as fire, with swords, spears, and arrows as its fuel.

I shall extinguish the blazing Pandava-fire, which seems to consume its enemies, with a great cloud of arrows; the speed of my horses will be the preceding wind, the multitude of my chariots the thunder, and I myself the downpour of rain.
I shall extinguish the fire of Arjuna as it consumes the ranks,
by means of my various small and broad-headed arrows falling upon him;
with his mind thus bewildered, the son of Kuntī will not know what he ought to do.
Let the arrows released from my bow, resembling venomous serpents, rush toward Pārtha like snakes into an anthill— well-sharpened,
gold-feathered, well-polished, and with straight joints.
Behold Kaunteya covered [with arrows], like a mountain with *karṇikāra* flowers;
the sound of the falling, falling, falling steeds— like peacocks, like peacocks, like peacocks— is as if they are all falling down.
"For the weapon that was obtained by me from the best of sages, the son of Jamadagni—
relying upon that and my own prowess, I could fight even Vāsava himself.
That monkey standing at the tip of the banner has been struck down by me with a broad-headed shaft."

This very day, let the sound of the spirits dwelling upon the enemy’s banner— those who, being assailed by me, cry out with terrible roars as they fall to the earth and flee in all directions— reach up to the heavens.
If I were to discharge this weapon in anger, it would consume this entire earth;
how much more so Pārtha, standing alone at the head of the battle?
Today, I shall extract the dart that has long resided in the heart of Duryodhana.
I shall uproot Bibhatsu by toppling him from his chariot; today let the Kauravas behold Partha— his horses slain, deprived of his chariot, yet standing firm in his manliness— sighing like a serpent.
Let the Kurus go as they please, taking all their wealth;
or let them remain in their chariots and witness my battle.
Let them behold my prowess here today!
"O people, let the hosts of gods and *siddhas* grant their approval!
Even though the son of Śakra has been deprived of his chariot in battle,"—
thus Kṛpa spoke, and then he ceased.
Kṛpa said:
Having heard those words of his, Vaiśampāyana, who was an expert in the treatises on political ethics (nītiśāstra), [replied].
Kṛpa, the son of Śaradvat and preceptor of the Kuru heroes, said:
"O Rādheya, your mind has always been more cruel in battle;
you do not understand the true nature of matters, nor do you consider their consequences."
For there are many courses of action that have been contemplated by relying upon various treatises;
yet those who know the past declare that war is the most sinful among them.
However, when joined with the proper place and time, war becomes the giver of victory.

That very same action, if performed at an improper time, does not bear fruit here; however, when exertion is applied at the right place and the right time, it leads to prosperity. Therefore, let the interval between actions be managed with favorable coordination.
"For the wise do not attempt to bear the burden of a chariot-maker;
yet, having reflected, we find that a confrontation with Pārtha is not possible for us. For he alone is capable of repelling our enemies in battle."
One protected the Kurus, and one gratified the fire;
one observed the vow of celibacy for five years;
and one, having taken Subhadrā onto his chariot, challenged Kṛṣṇa to a duel.
In this very forest, Kṛṣṇa fought Śarva, who stood in the form of a Kirāta, and won back the abducted Draupadī; and alone,
he learned weapons from Śakra for five years.
Alone he conquered the Lord of the Gods and obtained the king of weapons;
alone, having conquered Saṃyaminī, he established the fame of the Kurus; alone, that subduer of enemies [conquered] Citrasena, the king of the Gandharvas.
He swiftly conquered his most invincible army in battle;
having defeated the Kṣatriyas at the svayaṃvara, Pārtha obtained the illustrious princess of Pañcāla and departed with her— where indeed had you gone then?

Likewise, the Nivātakavacas and the Kālakhañjas, those Dānavas who were incapable of being slain even by the gods, were struck down in battle by you alone. O Karṇa, what indeed have you accomplished here in the past by yourself?
Just as each one of them has brought those rulers of the earth under his control,
even Indra himself is not fit to fight Pārtha in combat.
For whoever dares to challenge him to battle, a remedy must be applied to him.
Raising your right hand against an enraged venomous serpent,
you wish to seize its fang with your forefinger without due reflection; or else, wandering alone in the forest, you seek to confront a rutting elephant.
Mounted upon a goadless elephant, you wish to enter the city;
O fool, clad in garments of kusha grass, you imagine yourself able to leap into a blazing fire fed with offerings of clarified butter, fat, and marrow.

Anointed with ghee and clad in rags, you wish to cross over by swimming through the middle; what manliness indeed is there in one who, having bound himself and tied a great rock to his neck, would attempt to swim across the ocean with his bare arms?
O Karṇa, that evil-minded man who wishes to fight such a Pārtha— one who is unskilled in weapons against one skilled in weapons, and utterly weak against one who is strong— is surely deluded.
This man has been humiliated by us here for thirteen years.

A lion released from its bonds will leave nothing remaining of us. Having rashly attacked Pārtha while he sat in seclusion, like a fire concealed in a well, we have fallen into supreme danger through our ignorance.
"How could one man extinguish a fire cast upon a heap of cotton?
How shall we fight together against Pārtha, who has arrived intoxicated with the pride of battle?
Let the soldiers stand ready, armored, with their ranks arrayed, prepared to strike."
"O Karṇa,
do not act rashly! Droṇa, Duryodhana, Bhīṣma, yourself, the son of Droṇa, and all of us shall fight Pārtha when that son of Indra has arrived standing ready for battle."
"For we shall not defeat Pārtha in battle unless we unite;
if we stand together as a compact force, even six chariot-warriors could fight against Pārtha, who is as resolute as the wielder of the thunderbolt with his weapon raised."
04,044.022a "With our armies drawn up in battle array, we supreme archers, prepared for combat, shall fight Arjuna in the fray, just as the Dānavas fought Vāsava.
04,044.022c Vaiśampāyana said:
O King, having heard the words of Kṛpa, Karṇa, the lord of warriors,
spoke again in great anger, censuring the brahmin Kṛpa:
"I perceive that you, O Teacher, have succumbed to fear regarding the enemy out of partiality."

One who is terrified should not fight; I shall fight Dhananjaya. Surely you possess the Vāruṇa, Āgneya, Yāmya, and Vāyavya weapons, as well as the Brahmāśiras; yet, being devoid of courage, they are useless to you.
This service to a friend has been performed by you, great chariot-warriors who are like fathers and sons;
the maintenance provided by your master has been fulfilled, so you may now depart as you please. You, however, should always take alms and attend to the sacrifices.
"Come now, eat; do not terrify us with war. The Bhārgava weapon released by me would consume this entire earth—how much more so Arjuna alone, the son of Pāṇḍu, in battle?"
"The Matsyas, having taken refuge with the Pāṇḍava, will follow in his footsteps;
I shall slay them. You may go home.
Having heard those words of his, the powerful Aśvatthāman [replied].
The best among speakers, looking toward Duryodhana, said:
"All of you, being prepared, surround that foremost of chariot-warriors on all sides;
let six chariot-warriors disperse around him, as the Asuras did around the wielder of the thunderbolt."
Aśvatthāman said:
"The cattle have not yet been won back, nor have they crossed the boundary;
they have not even reached Hastināpura, yet you, O Karṇa, boast."
"O best of the twice-born, you recite many treatises on dharma;
have you seen among them anything such as this, that a king should be defeated at dice after having conquered many battles and acquired vast wealth?"
Having conquered the highest realm, they say nothing at all regarding their own prowess. Fire cooks without speaking; the sun shines in silence;
and the earth silently sustains the worlds, including all things mobile and immobile.
The duties of the four social orders have been prescribed by the wise:
by which means wealth is to be acquired, and what one may do without incurring fault.
Having studied the Vedas, a Brāhmaṇa should officiate at sacrifices for others and perform sacrifices himself.

A Kṣatriya, relying on the bow, should only perform sacrifices for himself and not officiate at the sacrifices of others; a Vaiśya, having acquired wealth, should cause the Vedic rites to be performed;
and a Śūdra should always perform service toward the three other castes.
Adopting the conduct of a reed through the rules of the yoga of salutation,
those highly fortunate ones, conducting themselves according to the scriptures even while ruling this earth, show honor to their gurus, even if they are devoid of good qualities.
"What caste produced this [lineage] among them? What were their other mantras and what were their rites?
Vaiśampāyana said:
"What is this [caste] among the social orders (*varṇa*) that belongs to the king, who is the speaker, the enjoyer, and the controller?"
Looking toward Duryodhana and Karṇa in the assembly of the Kurus,
Aśvatthāman, filled with intense rage, rebuked Duryodhana:
"Having obtained a kingdom through gambling, what Kṣatriya could possibly be satisfied?"

In such a cruel manner, like any other ordinary person, he acted; yet when wealth is obtained, what wise man would boast of that which is practiced by the vulgar and censured by the virtuous in this world?
Whether he be a king, a Kṣatriya, or someone else, if that intelligent and wise man acts with deceit and fraudulent stratagems like a hunter,
what was that duel in which you defeated Dhanañjaya?
In what [encounter] were Nakula and Sahadeva— those whose wealth was seized by you—
and Yudhiṣṭhira defeated? And in what battle was Bhīma, the foremost of the strong,
and Indraprastha formerly conquered by you?
Likewise, what kind of battle was that in which Kṛṣṇā was defeated by you— she who,
wearing but a single garment and in her courses, was brought into the assembly hall by you of wicked deeds?
You have cut down their great root, just as one seeking heartwood cuts down a sandalwood tree.
"O hero, you caused labor to be performed; what did Vidura say about that?
We observe that among human beings, as well as among other creatures—even down to insects and ants—there is a limit to their capacity for peace according to their strength."
The Pāṇḍava does not deserve to endure that suffering of Draupadī;
Dhanañjaya has appeared for the misery of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Yet you, acting as a wise man, desire to speak such words here.

The victorious one, the ender of enmity, will leave nothing remaining for us. This Dhananjaya, the son of Kuntī, would not refrain from fighting here out of fear, whether it be against the gods, the Gandharvas, the Asuras, or the Rākṣasas.
Whomever he attacks in battle while filled with rage,
he will strike down like a tree with the speed of Garuḍa;
superior to you in prowess, he is equal to the King of the Gods in archery.
Who would not honor that Pārtha, who is equal to Vāsudeva in battle?
One should fight divinity with divinity and man with man;
one should strike weapon with weapon—who is a man equal to Arjuna?
Having addressed the son of Rādhā in this manner, he then spoke to Duryodhana:
"Those who know the law understand that a disciple is next only to a son;
for this reason as well, the Pāṇḍava is dear to Droṇa."
"Just as you played at dice, just as you seized Indraprastha,
and just as you brought Kṛṣṇā to the assembly hall, so now fight the Pāṇḍava!
This uncle of yours is wise and skilled in the duty of a warrior."
Let Śakuni, the King of Gāndhāra, who is skilled at dice, fight here.
The Gāṇḍīva does not cast dice; it casts neither the Kṛta nor the Dvāpara [dice].
The Gāṇḍīva hurls blazing, sharpened, and keen arrows.

For the well-sharpened, vulture-feathered arrows released from the Gāṇḍīva do not stop midway, even when they strike mountains, for they are capable of splitting them asunder. Death, the Destroyer, the Bringer of Peace, as well as the fire of the submarine mare’s mouth— [all these cannot withstand it].

A razor’s edge, poison, a serpent, and fire— these may leave something remaining in some cases, but not so Dhanañjaya when he is enraged. Just as you played at dice with your maternal uncle in the assembly hall...
"Fight thus in battle, well-protected by the son of Subala.
Let the preceptor fight as he pleases; I will not fight Dhananjaya.
For it is the King of Matsya whom we must combat, should he come to the place where the cattle are."
Karna said:
"This son of Drona is always evil-minded and of sinful prowess;
what need is there for Partha here, or how is he praised?"
Except for mere desire, delusion, or greed toward us,
he praises that evil-souled Pāṇḍava of sinful prowess solely out of malice,
and he constantly reviles me as well, driven by the very wish of his enemy.
Therefore, let this man of evil intellect behold my prowess while I am watching.
Aśvatthāman said:
"Brahmins are said to be heroes of speech, and Kṣatriyas are heroes of the arm."
Karṇa said:
"The hero Arjuna is a hero by means of his bow; Karṇa is a hero by his desires. But the Brahmin preceptor always strikes terror into the entire army."
Out of affection for the sons of Pāṇḍu, he displayed his hostility toward you;
consequently, the winds always blew favorably and Indra constantly sent down rain,
as he achieved great victory by defeating Arjuna in battle.
"Then, O lowest of Brahmins, I shall cut off your head with my sword.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When these words had been spoken by Karṇa, O slayer of enemies...
Then, O King, Aśvatthāman took up his sword and shield;
having grasped his stainless sword and taken up his radiant shield,
he rushed to fight Karṇa like a lion against a small deer.

When that sword had been seized, Karna, the best of chariot-warriors and a man of great prowess, quickly leapt down from his chariot while grasping his own sword. Then those two of great heroism, wielding their weapons and intoxicated by battle, [encountered one another].
Seeking to slay one another like two lions fierce with rut,
those two of great prowess were seen standing ready for battle;
then the impetuous Duryodhana quickly descended from his chariot.
Approaching the preceptor’s son, Aśvatthāman, he said:
"O Aśvatthāman, son of the preceptor, O best of the twice-born, please forgive this;
Karṇa did not know how to speak, and Brahmins are prone to great anger."

"The burden of this battle is placed upon you; this is the firm resolve. Thus addressed by the king, O monarch, and being restrained by him, he reached his own chariot quickly and said nothing at all.
Karna also quickly mounted his own chariot by the king’s command. Then, Vaiśampāyana said:
thereupon the son of Śantanu [Dhṛtarāṣṭra] spoke words that were beneficial and skilled in matters of dharma and artha.
In the assembly of the Kurus, Bhīṣma spoke these words to Duryodhana:
"Droṇa indeed perceives correctly; Kṛpa likewise perceives correctly."
The son of the preceptor speaks what is innate, certain, and virtuous;
Karṇa, however, desires to fight according to the duty of a Kṣatriya as is proper. A man who possesses discernment should not harbor malice toward his preceptor.
It is my opinion that one should fight only after carefully considering both place and time.
How could a wise man not become bewildered when five adversaries, who are like the sun and skilled strikers, rise against him?

Even those people who are knowers of the Dharma become utterly deluded when it comes to their own interests. Therefore, O lord of men, the evil-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra does not perceive the truth regarding what must be done, even though he beholds Dhanañjaya.
"The fool, having fallen under the sway of anger, neither sees nor smells.
Having spoken thus to the king, Vaiśampāyana said again to the son of Droṇa:
With palms joined in reverence, that best of the Bharatas and foremost among the wise spoke with gentle words:
"O King, if it pleases you, I shall speak these words to you.
That which Karṇa addressed us was intended to provoke our fiery spirit."
"May the son of the preceptor forgive; a great task has presented itself.
This is not the time for hostility now that the son of Kuntī has arrived.
Everything must be forgiven by you, and by the preceptor Kṛpa as well."

The wise and learned call these the calamities of power; among them, however, the wise consider dissension at the outset to be the most evil. Indeed, your mastery of weapons is like the radiance within the sun.
Just as the mark of the moon is never removed in any way,
so too is Brahminhood and the Brahmā-weapon established in you. On one side are the four Vedas, and on the other side, the power of the Kṣatriya is seen.

"We have never heard of these two qualities combined in anyone else, except for the preceptor of the Bharatas together with his son; such is my conviction. This is confirmed by the Vedāntas, the Purāṇas, and the ancient Itihāsas."
"O King, who could be superior to Droṇa, except for the son of Jamadagni? Neither the Brahmā weapon nor the Vedas are seen anywhere else [but in him].
Let the preceptor’s son forgive us; this is not the time for internal dissension."

"Let us all join together and fight the son of Pākaśāsana who has arrived. Among the calamities of an army described here by the wise, dissension among the leaders is indeed considered the most wicked."
Aśvatthāman said:
"O bull among men, it is not at all right for this to be said of us;
however, the virtues were spoken of by our preceptor while he was overcome with wrath."
"The virtues of even an enemy should be acknowledged, and the faults of even a teacher should be spoken.
Duryodhana said:
"In every way and with every effort, one should speak what is beneficial for a son or a pupil."
"Let the Teacher himself forgive this; let peace be established here.
For when the Guru is being provoked, such conduct is caused by anger.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, O Bhārata, Duryodhana, together with Karṇa, Bhīṣma, and the high-souled Kṛpa, sought forgiveness from Droṇa. Droṇa said:

"By that very first speech which Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, uttered, I am indeed pleased; let the supreme course of action be determined here. So that, while Duryodhana is negligent, the serpent does not touch the soldiers."
Whether out of rashness or delusion, let such a policy be adopted so that Dhananjaya does not reveal himself while our forest exile is still unfulfilled; for,
failing to obtain wealth here, he will not forgive us today.

"Let such a policy be devised so that he may not, by any means, enter into alliance with the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and so that he may not defeat them. Such words were also spoken previously by Duryodhana."
"Remembering that, O son of Gaṅgā, you ought to speak accordingly.
Bhīṣma said:
"O dear one, the divisions of time—kalās, muhūrtas, and days—are joined together."
The half-months and months, the lunar mansions and the planets,
as well as the seasons and the years, are likewise joined together;
thus, by means of the divisions of time, the wheel of time revolves.
Due to the lapse of time for them and the deviation of the celestial bodies,
every fifth year two extra months arise;
these [extra] months of theirs amount to five months and twelve nights.
"It is my conviction that thirteen years have passed;
for Bībhatsu arrived on the very day before yesterday,
after two years, five fortnights, and two days had elapsed."
In the eighth part of the day, one intercalary month falls away.
Having understood with certainty that everything they have heard was practiced exactly as it is, Bibhatsu then arrived.

All of them are indeed great-souled, and all are experts in dharma and artha; since Yudhiṣṭhira is their king, how could they ever transgress against dharma? [Only] out of desire, anger, greed, or even from desire, anger, and fear.
Whether out of affection or through delusion, the son of Dharma does not transgress the law; the sons of Kuntī are free from greed and have performed what is difficult to do,
nor would they desire sovereignty by any improper means.
At that very moment, those descendants of Kuru desired to display their prowess;
yet, bound by the fetters of dharma, they did not deviate from the vow of the kṣatriyas. For it would have been called a falsehood, and one would have met with defeat.
The sons of Pṛthā would choose death rather than untruth under any circumstances;
for when the time has come, those bulls among men will not abandon what must be attained,
even if it were guarded by the wielder of the thunderbolt, for such is the prowess of the Pāṇḍavas.

"O King, let us all fight in battle against Phalguna, the best among all wielders of weapons, who has arrived here; of this there is no doubt. Therefore, let us perform whatever auspicious deed is practiced by the virtuous in this world."

"Let that be prepared quickly, lest our purpose fall into the hands of our enemies. For I do not see absolute victory in battle at any time, O Kaurava; yet Dhananjaya has already arrived, O Indra among kings."
When battle has commenced, existence and non-existence, victory and defeat—undoubtedly one of these two must inevitably touch [the combatants]; this is seen without doubt.
Therefore, whether it be the conduct of war or action consistent with dharma, [one must proceed].
"O Indra among kings, act quickly, for Dhanañjaya has arrived!
Even Pārtha alone could consume the earth with his arrows in battle;
O dear one, how much more so when he is joined by his brothers against the Kauravas in the fray?"
"Therefore, O best of the Kurus, make peace if you so deem it right.
Duryodhana said:
"O Grandfather, I will not give back the kingdom to the Pāṇḍavas."
"O Lord, let the village, the army, the female slaves, even the small amount of wealth,
and whatever is required for the expedition of war, be quickly prepared.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When Bhīṣma and Duryodhana had ceased speaking,
and when Droṇa, the best of the twice-born, had spoken words that were appropriate and meaningful,
Bhīṣma said:
Whether it be for the sake of war or in accordance with dharma, who in this world is equal to you? You ought to speak further;
hear here what my own thought is, if it pleases you.
"In every way, O joy of the Kurus, I must speak what is for your ultimate good:
take one-fourth of the army and go quickly toward the city;
then let another fourth part go, taking the cattle with them."
"We, however, with half the army, shall fight against the Pāṇḍava. Drona, Karna, Ashvatthaman, and likewise Kripa— we shall all fight back against Bibhatsu, who has arrived having made his resolve."
In this way, the king shall be well-protected and shall not experience any weakness,
even if a fish or even Indra, the performer of a hundred sacrifices, were to return; I shall hold him back, as the shore holds back the ocean, the abode of sea-monsters.
"Let us fight together in unison against the son of Pākaśāsana who has arrived.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When Droṇa had ceased speaking, the wise Bhīṣma spoke.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Those words spoken by the high-souled Bhīṣma were pleasing to them;
for the king of the Kauravas acted accordingly immediately thereafter.
Having sent the king ahead and immediately thereafter that wealth of cattle, Bhīṣma,
having stationed the army commanders, proceeded to form the battle array.
"Let the Preceptor stand in the center, while Aśvatthāman stands on the left."
Let the wise Kṛpa, son of Śaradvat, protect the right flank;
and let the highly heroic Vikarṇa, Durmukha the scorcher of foes,
Śakuni the son of Subala, and the mighty Duḥsaha do the same.
"Let the unconquered great car-warriors protect Droṇa's flank;
let Karṇa, the son of the Sūta, stand armored at the front.
As for myself, I shall stand at the rear of the entire army, protecting it."
"All are great chariot-warriors, heroes, mighty archers, and possessed of great strength.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Let them fight with all effort against the best of the Pāṇḍavas who has arrived in battle."
Having formed an impenetrable array against the enemy forces—
the Vajragarbha, the Vrīhimukha, the Padma, and the Ardhacandramaṇḍala—
the best of the Kurus, Bhīṣma, stood at the rear of that formation with his weapons raised.
Raising a golden palm-tree banner, he shone while standing upon his chariot.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When the armies had been thus arrayed by the great car-warriors of the Kuru lineage...
By means of his skillful stratagem, Arjuna quickly caused the earth to resound with the roar of his chariot;
they beheld the tip of his banner and heard the clatter of the chariot,
as well as the sound of the *gāṇḍīva* bow being violently shaken.
Having gone only three *krośas*, Pāṇḍava Śvetavāhana,
Pārtha, looked toward the front of the army and said to the son of Virāṭa:
"I do not see the king here, stationed within this array of chariots."
Taking the right flank, the Kurus are advancing toward the north. Leaving behind this division of chariots protected by great archers,
proceed toward the vanguard of the cattle so that I may behold my enemy.
"Go quickly to the edge of the cattle-pen and swiftly drive the cows back, O lord,
so that by the time these Kurus have returned at full speed,
I shall have brought all the animals back under your control."
Having spoken thus in battle, the unconquered Pārtha,
reaching the left flank of the son of Virāṭa, urged the horses forward with speed.
Then Pārtha paid his respects to Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu, and to Kṛpa.
With two sharp arrows each, he likewise greeted his preceptor and Droṇa;
with shafts, he paid homage to Droṇa, Kṛpa, and Bhīṣma.
Then, having observed all that, Droṇa spoke these words.
No one would wish to fight him, nor would anyone protect their own life [against him];
for he is a hero, a warrior, and truly invincible in combat.
Seeing the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, that great car-warrior, approaching,
this tip of Pārtha’s banner shines forth from afar;
and here is the roar of the monkey, sounding like a rain-cloud.
Standing firm, he advances in his chariot, brandishing the *gāṇḍīva* bow;
the sound of the horses neighing as they carry the son of Pākaśāsana is heard,
as terrible as the roar of a rain-cloud.
Like the son of Vāsava, this radiant one seems to tear asunder the earth;
here comes that noble one, the best of chariot-warriors,
standing upon his excellent chariot, impelled by the foremost of car-drivers.
Having seen this array of chariots, that subduer of enemies,
the son of Pāṇḍu— modest, generous, and steadfast— is honoring it;
he draws his supreme bow, Gāṇḍīva, which sounds like a thunderclap.
For these two arrows, with their variegated feathers and straight shafts, are fixed together at my feet; they are buried deep with their points facing upward.
Furthermore, two other arrows have passed beyond, having grazed my ears.
Having touched him and inquired after his health with great intensity as they passed by, [they said]:
"This wise Dhananjaya, son of Pāṇḍu, who is dear to his kinsmen, has not been seen by us for a long time; he is exceedingly radiant with splendor."
Having indeed dwelt in the forest and performed superhuman deeds, Pārtha now offers his salutations; he inquires after my hearing and,
having asked after my welfare, those clad in heron-feathered garments have departed.
Filled with indignation and awakened by sorrow,
he will surely destroy this Bharata army alone today,
after having dwelt for more than twelve years.
Unrecognized by his own kin, the diadem-wearing Arjuna, mounted upon his chariot, blazes forth like the sun dispelling the darkness born of night; this is the thirteenth [chapter].
Charioteer, archer, with beautiful palms, equipped with quiver,
conch, banner, armor, and diadem;
bearing sword and bow, Pārtha shines resplendent.
Like a crested fire surrounded by ladles and sprinkled with clarified butter—
Vaiśampāyana said:
Seeing that Pāṇḍava Arjuna approaching from nearby, [he spoke].
The Nārāyaṇas were unable to look upon him as he performed his ascetic penance, just as one cannot look upon the sun.
Seeing that array of chariots, Pārtha spoke to his charioteer.
Arjuna said:
"O charioteer, restrain the horses at the range of an arrow-shot from the army,
so that I may observe where that lowest of the Kuru lineage is within this host.
[Behold him] adorned with jewels and beryl, and embellished with the finest gems."
I recognize his banner raised high from afar;
if I see this evil-minded and excessively arrogant man here,
I shall send him to Yama, even if the Lord himself be his ally.
Disregarding all others and seeing that excessively arrogant man, I shall fall upon his head; then these [foes] will be defeated.
Here stands Drona, and immediately behind him is the son of Drona.
"Bhīṣma, Kṛpa, and Karṇa—the great archers—are stationed here.
I do not see the king; he is departing, taking the cattle with him. Following the southern path, I suspect he is intent on saving his own life."

"Abandoning this array of chariots, go where Suyodhana is; there alone shall I fight, O son of Virāṭa, for there can be no battle without a prize. Having conquered him, I shall indeed return, taking back the cattle."
Like a lion upon a small deer, I shall fall upon his head; I will swiftly slay him with arrows released from the Gāṇḍīva bow. When he is slain, all [the enemies] will be utterly defeated.
I shall strike down Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son along with Saubala with my arrows—
the speaker of uncivilized words and the very stain upon the Kurus.
I do not see this king here, nor this army, free from carnage.
"Attack the king!"— at these words, Aśvatthāman, the preceptor of the middle rank, stood forth fearlessly immediately thereafter;
while the two great archers, Kṛpa and Karṇa, took their positions in front.
Bhūriśravas, Somadatta, Bāhlīka, and Jayadratha—
those experts in battle— stood taking their position on the right wing,
along with the King of Sālva, Dyumatsena, Vṛṣasena, and the son of Subala.
The Daśārṇas and the Kāliṅgas have taken their positions on the left wing; behind them stands the chief of the Kurus, Bhīṣma, clad in armor,
the powerful grandfather of us all, with half of the army.
"I do not see Duryodhana; where indeed is that king going?
Abandon this array of chariots and go to where Suyodhana is. Having slain him, I shall return; he is taking the cattle as he goes."
"Go toward the herd of cattle where the king will be," said the unconquered Pārtha to the son of Virāṭa in that battle; having spoken thus,
he then proceeded in haste, his fingers touching his divine bow.
Then Bhīṣma, the scorcher of foes, spoke these words in the midst of the Kurus:
"This knower of dharma, who is dear to his kinsmen, has not been seen by us for a long time;
this son of Pākaśāsana, O Acyuta, shines exceedingly with splendor."
This Pārtha, remembering the humiliation, seeks out Duryodhana;
beholding the army, he hastens to seize him with resolve. The son of Pākaśāsana gazes upon him as a lion looks to seize its prey.
"It is my thought that these should be given later.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having been addressed thus, the son of Virāṭa restrained the horses with great effort.
Then, having restrained the reins, he urged the steeds toward where those bulls of the Kuru race were, specifically toward where Duryodhana was;
for when the one with white horses had departed, leaving the line of chariots behind.
Having understood his intention, Droṇa spoke these words:
"Bībhatsu does not wish to stand in the interval without the king;
we shall seize the rear of him as he advances with speed."
For no one else could fight him when he was enraged in battle—
save for the thousand-eyed god, or Kṛṣṇa the son of Devakī,
or even the preeminent teacher, the great car-warrior Bhāradvāja.
"What will our cattle or vast wealth avail us?
Duryodhana is already sinking in the waters of the Pārthas like a boat.
Having spoken thus in the battle, Bhīṣma, the Kaurava, [departed] with his army.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, for the sake of protecting the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, [the charioteer] pursued Pārtha.
Having gone a distance of three *krośas*, Pārtha spoke to the son of Virāṭa.
"O subduer of enemies, station the horses at the distance of an arrow's flight from the army.
O charioteer, drive slowly; this is the foremost herd of cattle that has been sighted.
Proceed along the north of the army, having separated the cattle."
"Having surrounded the herd of cattle, I shall fight Suyodhana here. The cows, along with their cowherds, are fleeing in haste; release them!
Having gone there, O hero, release the animals together with their keepers."
And in the midst of the army, go forward facing the east;
and let all these Kurus, who are great car-warriors, behold my heroism and prowess in battle, just as the Dānavas beheld that of Mahendra.
Having proceeded in that very manner and proclaimed his own name as Bībhatsu,
he released sharp-pointed, keen arrows resembling the God of Death;
he swiftly covered that army with arrows like a swarm of locusts.
The field became devoid of space due to the arrows discharged by Kirīṭin;
and that vast army, oppressed by the arrows of Pārtha,
was being scattered by the floods of shafts impelled by him.
They could not see the earth nor the sky, for they were covered by his feathered shafts;
indeed, they could no longer see the cattle, as they were struck by the straight-flying arrows released by Pārtha.
Arjuna, however, was then filled with joy, displaying his own prowess.
He afflicted the armies with arrows discharged from the *gāṇḍīva* bow. Neither in battle nor in retreat did they have any thought for their own lives;
rather, they honored the swiftness of Pārtha with their minds.

Then he blew his conch shell, which was as white as the moon, ocean-born, and terrifying to the Kuru army; it caused the hair of his enemies to stand on end. And having strung his excellent bow, he summoned the spirits upon his banner.
By the sound of that conch, by the roar of the chariot wheels,
and by the twang of the Gāṇḍīva bow, the earth trembled,
as did those non-human beings dwelling upon his banner.
O King, by that great sound, as well as by the roar of the gods in the sky and of human beings, the vast herd of cattle was terrified;
shaking their tails upward and lowing on all sides, they fled.
The cows returned, taking their stand toward the southern direction.
Then that hero Bībhatsu, the slayer of hosts of enemies, urged on the cowherds in the battle, saying, "Drive the cows! Drive them!"
And Bibhatsu, the joy of the Pāṇḍus, spoke these further words to gladden him:
"Look toward the vanguard of the cattle and quickly turn back the cows,
before these Kurus, having exerted their speed, can overtake us."
"Go northward, O prince, past these cattle and the armies;
let all the Kurus behold my heroism and prowess. Thinking it a great gain, the Kurus will look toward Arjuna in battle."
Seeing him approaching not far away, they quickly rushed forward on chariots,
accompanied by a vast and resplendent retinue of elephants and horses,
and by warriors bearing spears and swords in their hands, with bows and arrows raised as weapons.
Those armies of the Kurus, who were prepared for battle,
shone like lightning-charged clouds gliding through the sky; indeed,
having seen those divisions with their chariots arrayed, they appeared magnificent.
Pārtha, too, like the wind, shook the formidable front of the army with his arrows.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having forcefully repelled that enemy host;
Having conquered those cattle, Arjuna, the foremost of archers,
then advanced toward Duryodhana,
desiring once more to do what was pleasing to him in battle.
When the cows had departed swiftly for the Matsyas,
and considering that Kirīṭin had accomplished his task,
they returned from there taking the cattle with them.
The hosts of cowherds departed for their own kingdoms.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then there were three thousand chariots belonging to those who wielded bows.
O Bhārata, the terrible [weapons] of the Kuru heroes were scattered about;
Karṇa stood against Dhanañjaya with a thousand chariots,
while the wise Bhīṣma, son of Śantanu, was placed at the front with a thousand.
Likewise, surrounded by his brothers and a thousand chariots,
Duryodhana stood at the rear, blazing with splendor and grasping a sword-hilt.
Foot soldiers, together with their horses, took their positions in the open spaces.
And seeing those vast armies of the high-souled warriors, with elephants of terrifying form urged on by lances and goads,
the Pāṇḍava addressed Uttara, the son of Virāṭa.
Armored horses stood there with their mounted riders,
and in various open spaces, thousands of foot soldiers were positioned facing toward Duryodhana as he advanced.
The Kuru heroes suddenly rushed forward.
Uttara said,
"O Pārtha, best among strikers, turn back toward the city."
"These cows have already been won by you; why indeed engage in this futile battle?
One should not fight when the outcome is uncertain, even if one's own strength is abundant. For what is the point of engaging in a conflict with many when you alone are sufficient?"
Having heard these words of the son of Virāṭa, Arjuna, as if terrified, then laughed and said to him again: "Do not fear; behold the spectacle here!
O Uttara, you have previously seen many battles."
Behold this very battle, wherein one man alone [fought] against many;
then, as Arjuna advanced with speed toward Duryodhana,
all the foremost chariot-warriors of the Kuru king suddenly fell upon him.
Seeing their many divisions, densely arrayed and bearing numerous banners,
that slayer of enemies [beheld] the son of Matsya.
Then Arjuna, having addressed the son of Virāṭa, spoke:
"Now, with the reins well-gripped by you..."
"Having restrained the horses and looked on with vigilance,
send him quickly against this hero;
I choose to fight Vaikartana."
That elephant-girth, variegated in many ways,
which you see upon the pillar of the chariot as something beautiful to behold,
revolving and radiant like fire—
This is the foremost division of Vaikartana;
with this, let us quickly drive forward these white horses with their golden reins and yokes.
Exert every effort with all your speed;
attack this host of lions among chariot-warriors!
Like an elephant against an elephant, I shall strike down that evil-minded one.
"Whosoever desires to fight the son of the Suta,
I shall engage him in battle today in the midst of the Kuru heroes; go, therefore, as you have been directed."
O prince, lead me to him alone,
who has conceived such pride through his reliance on Duryodhana; I shall strike him down in the midst of his chariot.
Like the thousand-eyed Indra [slaying] Vṛtra with his thunderbolt,
he pierced the heart [of his foe] with extremely sharp arrows released from the Gāṇḍīva, their tips bright white.
With those large horses, swift as the wind and adorned with golden girths,
the son of Virāṭa scattered that army of chariot-warriors.
Then, in the midst of the battle, he bore the Pāṇḍava away;
seeing Vaikartana rushing forward with supreme splendor, they protected him.
Those throngs of chariot-heroes rushed forward in battle,
like a bull assailed by a tiger—
namely Citrāṅgada and the heroic Citraratha.
Saṃgrāmajit, Duḥsaha, Citrasena,
Vivimśati, Durjaya, Durmukha,
Vikarṇa, Duḥśāsana, and Saubala.
Śoṇa and Niṣedha followed him; those youths, the sons of Vaikartana, and his uterine brothers all went after him with great speed.
Seeing the son of Vikartana approaching Pārtha,
those of great strength took up their bows in battle and overwhelmed Dhanañjaya with floods of arrows.
Their lute-like bows had many strings formed by firm bowstrings, with arrows for the finger-picks and arrow-clusters for the plectrum;
they had the fingertips for mechanical frets and the steady staff of the bow for the neck.
Pārtha quickly began to play the lute; Citrasena, Saṃgrāmajit, Śatrusaha, and Jaya struck him with sharp, broad-headed arrows.
The great car-warriors, desiring to protect Karṇa, went forth to meet the advancing Bhārata;
then that hero among men [stood] before them.
With the flames of his bow and the heat of the speed of his arrows,
that wrath of the bull among the Kurus consumed the throngs of chariots, just as fire consumes a forest.
When that tumultuous battle had commenced,
Vikarṇa, a preeminent hero of the Kurus, approached Pārtha— the great car-warrior (atiratha)— in his chariot with a shower of sharp arrows.
Then Bhīma,
having drawn the bow of Vikarṇa— which was adorned with the finest gold and possessed a firm string— assailed his younger brother.
Having violently struck down his standard, he caused it to fall;
with his standard severed, he too fled away with speed— him, the harasser of the hosts of enemies.
Unable to endure the anger of Śatruṃtapa as he performed superhuman deeds,
[Kṛtavarman] struck Pārtha with a tortoise-clawed arrow.
Pierced by that king, an Atiratha,
as he was plunging into the army of the Kurus,
he quickly struck Śatruṃtapa with five arrows.
Then he struck his charioteer with ten arrows;
thus pierced by that bull of the Bharatas with an arrow that had passed through his body armor, [the charioteer]—
His life departed, he fell upon the earth in battle like a tree blown down by the wind from the summit of a mountain;
those bulls among chariot-warriors [were struck] by that bull among chariot-warriors.
Heroes broken in battle by one more heroic than they trembled like great forests shaken by the force of the wind at the end of time.
Slain by Pārtha, those heroes among men—
youthful, well-attired, givers of wealth, and equal in prowess to Vāsava— slept upon the earth.
Defeated in battle by the son of Vāsava,
those elephants, clad in armor of gold and black iron,
resembled the great serpents of the Himalayas.
Thus, slaying his enemies in battle,
that hero among men, the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow,
moved through all the quarters and intermediate directions in the fray.
Like a fire burning a forest at the end of the heat,
or like the fierce wind scattering and driving away loose leaves in spring as it blows through the sky;
Thus, scattering his rivals, the diadem-wearing Atiratha moved through the battle in his chariot,
having slain the horses of the one whose vehicle was drawn by red steeds.
Then the wearer of the diadem, possessed of undaunted spirit, struck off the head of Saṃgrāmajit, the brother of Vaikartana, with a single arrow.
When that brother had been slain, the son of the Sūta,
Vaikartana, summoning his prowess,
seized [his bow] like the king of elephants baring its tusks.
Like a tiger rushing toward a great bull,
Vaikartana swiftly struck the Pāṇḍava with twelve arrows.
He pierced all the horses in their limbs and struck down the son of Virāṭa with arrows;
as he was rushing forward suddenly, Kiritin [assailed him].
Having impetuously rushed toward the son of Vikartana,
he fell upon him with speed,
like the many-colored-winged Garuḍa swooping down upon a serpent.
Having heard of the battle between Karṇa and Pārtha— those two who were the foremost of all archers, possessed of great strength, and capable of withstanding all enemies— [the people were amazed].
Desiring to see him, the Kurus stood all around;
that son of Pāṇḍu, his wrath suddenly aroused,
looked with joy at Karṇa, who had committed the offense.
In an instant, along with his horses, chariot,
and charioteer, he was concealed by a terrible shower of volleys of arrows; then, the chariots and elephants were deeply pierced.
The warriors of those bulls among the Bharatas cried out; Bhīṣma and his leaders, along with their horses, had vanished,
their chariots strewn with arrows by Kirīṭin.
And Karna, having repelled those arrows released from Arjuna’s arms with his own showers of shafts,
stood there, the high-souled one, with his bow and arrows ready.
Like a fire with sparks, Karṇa acted swiftly;
then there arose the sound of palms and cymbals,
along with the resonant blare of conchs, kettledrums, and the sacred syllable *praṇava*.
Amidst the sound of his war-cries, the twang of his bowstring, and the slapping of his palms, that son of Vikartana was honored by the Kurus,
who raised their tails like great banners aloft.
Beholding the wearer of the diadem, who was terrifying the entire host with his preeminent banner and making a great roar with the sound of the *Gāṇḍīva* bow, Karṇa let out a shout.
And having afflicted Vaikartana with his arrows—
along with his horses, charioteer, and chariot—
the diadem-wearing Arjuna violently showered him with shafts.
Seeing the Grandfather, Drona, and Kripa,
Vaikartana also rained down many arrows upon Partha, like a cloud pouring forth rain.
In that very same way, the wearer of the diadem and garland covered Karṇa with sharp arrows as the two of them discharged volleys of extremely keen shafts.
In that battle where the great torrents of arrows increased like weapons,
the world beheld them through the gaps in the clouds, as if they were the sun and the moon caught within a chariot.
Then Karṇa, acting with haste and unable to endure it, pierced the four swift horses of Kirīṭin with sharp arrows,
and struck his charioteer with three.
He quickly pierced his standard with three arrows; thus deeply pierced, that crusher of enemies in battle was like a lion awakened from sleep.
The wielder of the Gāṇḍīva, the bull among the Kurus, Jishnu,
having struck down that high-souled one with a rain of straight-flying arrows and celestial weapons, advanced toward Karṇa.
He manifested a superhuman feat;
he shrouded Karṇa’s chariot with arrows,
just as the sun covers these worlds with its webs of rays.
Like a lordly elephant struck by another elephant,
he drew his bow back to his ear and, grasping sharpened broad-headed arrows from his quiver, released them.
Then he who crushes his enemies pierced the son of the Suta with arrows—
his arms, thighs, head, forehead,
neck, and the parts of his chariot.
As he stood firm, [Duryodhana] was pierced in battle by arrows released from the Gāṇḍīva, which flashed like thunderbolts;
he was struck down by those shafts discharged by Pārtha.
Like a powerful elephant defeated by another elephant,
the son of Vaikartana, scorched by the arrows of the Pāṇḍava, abandoned the front of the battle and fled.
Vaiśampāyana said: When the son of Rādhā had departed, those led by Duryodhana,
with their respective divisions, assailed the Pāṇḍava with arrows.
As that army, arrayed in many formations, was charging with arrows,
Bībhatsu, the son of Kuntī whose chariot is drawn by white horses, laughed and,
employing a divine weapon, advanced against those best of car-warriors.
Just as the sun covers the earth with its rays,
so do the arrows released from the Gāṇḍīva cover all directions;
[they leave no space] for chariots, nor for horses, nor for banners, nor for armor.
With sharp arrows that pierced through one another, there was an interval of only two finger-breadths between them;
for this was due to the conjunction of fate, the skill and strength of Pārtha, Uttara’s own training, and the mastery of their weapons.
And they said that the banners and the Gāṇḍīva bow were created by divine illusion; whether in the course of the battle here or there, at a distance or nearby,
on difficult terrain, on uneven ground, or on level or low-lying earth.
And his movement could not be obstructed, just like that of a chariot or the mind;
for in battles, the wise, having witnessed those various feats of valor and that most wonderful prowess and strength of Pārtha, [were amazed].

The enemies, terrified, fled even with their chariots turned away; they were unable even to look at Bībhatsu, who was like the fire of cosmic destruction consuming all creatures, blazing like a flaming fire.
Those broken ranks shone under Arjuna’s arrows,
like forest-tops pervaded by the rays of the sun,
or like groves of *aśoka* trees with their gathered, beautiful blossoms.
Pārtha gladdened the army, which was drenched in blood;
by means of Arjuna’s arrows, thousands of various kinds of umbrellas and banners were severed and carried away into the sky by the wind.
For those horses, terrified by Arjuna’s strength, fled in the ten directions; having abandoned the region of the chariot wheels, their yokes severed by Pārtha,
they fell down with their forelegs cut off by his sharp arrows.
First, with their heads, the horses struck the earth; then, with their haunches,
they struck the elephants in their eyes, claws, tusks, gums,
and other vital parts, thus slaughtering those noble beasts.
In an instant, the earth was covered by the lifeless bodies of the Kaurava elephants, like the sky by clouds; meanwhile,
the mighty-armed Arjuna, as if burning them with his divine weapons, continued his assault.
Born from the mouth of Vaḍavā, like the fire of time (kālāgni) on all sides, he—
like a fire of fierce flames at the end of a cosmic age— will burn everything, both stationary and moving, entirely as it has been ripened by time.
In that same way, through the power of his weapons, the resonance of his bow,
and by virtue of both destiny and his own prowess, Bibhatsu, the son of Pṛthā, generally stripped the enemies within that army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son of their capacity for battle.
As night generally brings rest to living beings,
he passed over his enemies with sudden force, having swiftly advanced against them;
for his superhuman weapon was swift, far-reaching, firm, and unfailing.
Covered by those moving through the air like birds dwelling in the sky, Arjuna filled the heavens with blood-drinking arrows released from the *gāṇḍīva* bow by the power of his own weapons.
Like the speed of Tārkṣya in the sky, they did not strike their own bodies or those of others;
they passed through the armor, the charioteers, and even the golden mail of the horses,
as well as the sun-like diadem and the tiger-skin shield.
All his limbs, covered by the arrows of his enemies on the chariot,
shone as if all beings were shrouded by a mist;
the opponents were unable to strike that chariot even once.
For that chariot, being unpracticed by them, sped past those [foes];
just as those arrows did not stick in the bodies of the enemies,
so too the chariot of Bībhatsu did not stick among the enemy ranks.
Having plunged into the enemy host, that chariot-warrior agitated it with infinite speed, like a serpent sporting in the great ocean; likewise,
he who transcends all sound discharged his weapons incessantly and in great abundance.
The constant sound of the bow of the diadem-wearing Arjuna was heard by all beings;
there, elephants were cut down at very short intervals by his arrows,
appearing like clouds pierced by rays of light.
As he roamed through all directions, shooting to the left and to the right,
his circle of the bow was constantly seen in battle; yet his arrows never fell upon anything formless, just as eyes never fall upon such things.
The arrows of the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva did not fall upon non-targets;
his path in battle was even more terrible than that of a thousand elephants trampling a forest simultaneously.
"Surely Śakra, together with all the immortals, is slaying us because he desires victory for Pārtha"—
thus did the enemies think, being tormented by Pārtha himself;
yet they regarded Savyasācin as one who was excessively slaughtering his foes.

Like Time itself devouring all creatures in the form of Arjuna, the bodies of the Kuru army fell— even those not struck by Pārtha— as if they had been slain by him, because they witnessed the deeds of Pārtha.
Like the tops of plants ripened by the passage of time,
the Kurus bowed down through the power of Arjuna’s prowess and out of fear of him; then,
as Arjuna slapped his arms, his conch shell resounded.
Out of wrath, Arjuna turned back even those who were enraged and facing away;
and the vanguard forces, shattered by Arjuna,
once again made the earth red with streams of blood.
With dust raised by the wind, mingled with blood,
and with fine drops of blood scattered by that very wind,
they were drenched and stained with blood, their weapons soaked in gore.
Immersed in blood and slain by Kirīṭin,
those warriors there became as crimson as the rays of the sun;
for an instant, that place became red like the clouds of twilight together with the sun.

Even if the sun were to turn back after reaching its setting, the son of Pāṇḍu would not turn back without having conquered his enemies— so have the wise declared. All those heroes in battle were established in their manly prowess.
With divine weapons, that one of immeasurable soul struck all the archers;
he struck Droṇa with seventy-three small arrows,
Śakuni with eighty, and the son of Droṇa quickly with seven.
Arjuna pierced Duḥṣaha with ten arrows,
Duḥśāsana with twelve, Kṛpa the son of Śaradvat with three,
and Bhīṣma the son of Śantanu with sixty in the center of the chest.
With a sharp, yellowed, barbed arrow, he pierced Karṇa;
and in the midst of his enemies, the son of Vāsava struck down his supreme weapons.
Having pierced Karṇa, who was clad in armor, with those sharpened shafts, he [struck him] through.
Urged on by Dṛḍhadhanvan, he advanced, splitting the earth; then that subduer of enemies struck down his horses with four [arrows] and, with a razor-sharp shaft,
severed the head of the charioteer from his body.
With a crescent-shaped arrow, he severed the bow held in his hand.
When that illustrious Karṇa, who had mastered all weapons, was thus pierced,
Vaiśampāyana said:
When their horses and charioteers were slain and they were left without chariots, the army then broke apart. That entire force, though possessing the strength of a vast flood,
having encountered Bhīṣma, came to a standstill like the great ocean against the shore.
Having comforted them all, that scorcher of foes, the son of Gaṅgā,
the mighty-armed one who is undefeated in battles and skilled in warfare, then formed his battle array and fought amidst a thick mass of chariots, elephants, and horses.
Impenetrable by enemy armies and regarded as formidable even by heroes,
they were protected by the Teacher, Duryodhana, the Suta’s son, Kṛpa, and Bhīṣma.
Knowing that the army was invincible, difficult to approach,
and crowded with men, horses, and elephants,
the son of Virāṭa spoke these words.
"O Jiṣṇu, having mounted this beautiful chariot with me as your charioteer, which division will you go to? "I shall go wherever I am told by you," [he replied].
Arjuna said:
O Uttara, that red-eyed and unassailable one whom you see standing upon his chariot, leaning against a blue banner and clad in tiger-skin—
this is the chariot-army of Kṛpa; bring him right here to me.
I shall show this firm-bowed archer my swift weapon. He whose banner bears a beautiful golden water-pot is the preceptor Droṇa, the best among all wielders of weapons.
"O hero, with a serene mind, perform a circumambulation of him;
for this is the eternal dharma, provided it is done without opposition right here,
if Droṇa strikes my body first."
Then I shall strike him, yet he will feel no anger. Not far from him, whose bow is seen at the top of his standard,
is this preceptor’s son, the great car-warrior Aśvatthāman.
"He is always worthy of my respect, even among all wielders of weapons. Upon reaching his chariot, you shall turn back again and again.
But as for this one in the front of the chariot-host, covered in golden armor—"
He stands at the head of the third division of the army, engaged in the conduct of affairs; on the tip of whose standard is a golden banner supported by an elephant—
this is the illustrious King Suyodhana, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.

"O hero, bring your chariot, which shatters the chariots of enemies, before him; for he is a crusher of splendor and is irrepressible in battle. Among the disciples of Droṇa, he is considered the foremost in the swiftness of his weapons."
"I shall display to him my vast and swift weapons with my arrows. He upon whose banner-top stands a beautiful elephant-girth is this Karṇa, the son of Vaikartana, who has already been known to you."
"Mounting the chariot of this evil-minded son of Rādhā,
you must remain vigilant in battle, for he is always in rivalry with me.
He who [bears] a blue banner marked with five stars..."
The heroic Hastāvāpin, wielding a great bow, stands upon his chariot;
on his chariot stands that excellent banner, variegated with stars and the sun. That white, spotless umbrella which stands over his head—[he is he].
Of this great host of chariots, adorned with various banners and flags,
he who stands at the front like the sun above a mass of clouds—
he whose golden armor is seen, resembling the moon and the sun— [is Bhīṣma].
Wearing a golden helmet, he seems to terrify my mind.
This Bhīṣma, son of Śantanu, is the grandfather of us all;
yet, bound by royal splendor, he follows the will of Duryodhana.
"Only after this [elephant] has been driven away should he advance; let him not become an obstacle to me.
As I fight with him, restrain my horses with care.
Thus was he addressed at that time by Pārtha, the crusher of enemies.
He upon whose banner-top a sacrificial altar made of Jāmbūnada gold is seen,
and who has crimson horses yoked to his chariot— this is Droṇa who shines forth.

The preceptor is skillful, wise, a knower of Brahman, and the best among heroes; he is unrivaled in lightness of hand, a long-range shooter, and a great chariot-warrior. With a serene mind, O hero, perform a circumambulation of him.
And it is precisely within this non-contradiction that this eternal Dharma resides:
"If Droṇa should strike my body as I am about to strike him, then I shall strike him in return; otherwise, there is no battle for me."
"O charioteer, drive slowly for me as I fight with that high-souled Brahmin, the preeminent teacher of the Bharatas;
on the tip of his banner, a lion’s tail shines in all directions."
But that son of the preceptor of the Bharatas, Aśvatthāman, shines forth;
on the tip of his banner is seen [an emblem] with a luster like the rising sun,
making him invincible to all armies, even by the gods together with Indra.

"Therefore, O charioteer, drive slowly while I am fighting him whose banner-top, adorned with a bull, shines in all directions. This great car-warrior Kṛpa is indeed the foremost among the best of teachers."
"He is equal to Droṇa in valor and was my father’s dearest friend. Therefore, O charioteer, drive slowly as I fight with him—
he whose elephant's girth is adorned with golden bells."
From afar, the banner on his chariot shines like a flash of lightning;
this is Karṇa, the son of Vaikartana, the peerless standard among archers.
This one, so difficult to conquer, is indeed always in competition with me.
For this great chariot-warrior Karṇa is indeed the disciple of Rāma, the son of Jamadagni; he is skilled in all weapons, the best among all wielders of arms,
possessed of matchless valor in battle, firm in his aim, and full of prowess.
Today I shall engage in battle with this kinsman of the Sūtas;
you shall behold this combat like that between Bali and Vāsava,
against the heroic son of a Sūta, a great car-warrior and archer.
"Therefore, O charioteer, drive slowly as I fight. And he upon whose chariot-seat stands a jeweled elephant-banner—
this is Duryodhana, the Kuru prince, covered in glory."
He has found his mark, is a firm piercer, light-handed, and full of prowess;
therefore, O charioteer, drive slowly as I fight with him—
he who possesses a banner white and bright, five *tāla*-trees in height.
Shining with a staff of lapis lazuli and a palm-leaf fan,
he stands at the head of the army, gladdening them, wearing finger-guards and wielding a great bow—
he who was formerly defeated in single combat by Rāma, the son of Jamadagni.
Swift, light-handed in piercing the mark, nimble of hand, and full of prowess—
this Bhīṣma, son of Śantanu, is the grandfather of us all,
the preeminent leader of all warriors and the best among all wielders of weapons.
Bound by royal splendor yet following the will of Suyodhana, he must be approached last; let him not become an obstacle for me. While I am fighting with him, restrain my horses with great care.
