Having quickly described these [enemies] to Uttara by their appearance and their distinctive marks, Pārtha then hastened toward the battle;
for he has always been our firm enemy, constantly speaking with bitter words.
"By the power of his very support, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, along with the son of Subala,
having driven us from the kingdom, will yet fight again even today.
Then the son of Virāṭa, remaining unperturbed, carried Savyasācin away.
04,050.023c Where Kṛpa stood, O King, about to fight against Dhanañjaya,
04,050.023d Vaiśampāyana said:
Then the valiant Aśvatthāman, having beheld Karṇa there, [proceeded].
Smiling, he spoke indeed to the son of the Sūta, the subduer of enemies:
"O Karṇa, that which you boasted so much and so improperly in the midst of the assembly—
'There is no one equal to me in battle'— that very thing has now arrived."
Like the enraged God of Death himself, this crusher of all beings yawns like a lion in the midst of the front of the battle;
if you are a hero in combat, show yourself without the assembly hall.
If you are unable [to contend] with the heroic Pārtha of wondrous deeds,
then go once more to the assembly hall and, having quickly taken counsel with the wise son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, deliberate with your maternal uncle as you please.
Thus addressed, Karṇa then rolled his eyes in anger and spoke these words to the son of Droṇa in the presence of the Kurus:
"I do not fear Bībhatsu, nor Kṛṣṇa, the son of Devakī."
Devoted to the duty of a Kṣatriya even more than all the Pāṇḍavas,
for among men of superior spirit who subsist by the science of archery,
pride arises when they roar and their voice does not falter.
"Let the son of the preceptor watch me for a long time fighting with Arjuna, well-prepared; indeed, victory rests with me. Then Bībhatsu, the son of Kuntī who rides white horses, laughed.
Displaying divine weapons against those best of chariot-warriors,
the high-minded but dull-witted son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, sighing deeply out of confidence,
King Duryodhana then spoke, O great king.
"For we did not know that Arjuna was staying there in the palace of the Matsya king;
it was because of him, O Karṇa, that we seized this great wealth of the Matsyas.
If that is so, let us go now, returning this vast amount of wealth."
Infamy would not fail to follow us in both worlds;
moreover, there is nothing that brings greater happiness to Kṣatriyas than battle.
Therefore, let us engage in combat with the son of Pṛthā, and not flee.
Having spoken thus, the king indeed desired to advance;
those five thousand bow-wielding heroes then rushed toward Pārtha like moths into a flame.
There, armored horses were gathered along with foot soldiers;
and elephants of terrifying form were stationed by men skilled in the training of elephants, who were well-prepared and held lances and goads in their hands.
Enraged, they rushed forward with bows in hand and weapons raised;
five preeminent car-warriors swiftly surrounded him—
Droṇa, Bhīṣma, Karṇa, and the heroic Kuru king.
The mighty-armed Aśvatthāman, devoted to the science of archery,
discharged arrows perfectly like clouds in the rainy season;
regarding it as a great gain, they received Dhananjaya.
Raining down showers of arrows and making the ten directions resound,
Vaiśampāyana said:
Those armies of the Kurus, with their fierce archers, were seen there.
Like clouds moving slowly with gentle breezes at the end of the summer heat,
the horses stood nearby, mounted by their riders;
and the elephants of fearsome form were urged on by lances and goads.
Mounted by high ministers, resplendent with various shining coats of mail,
and ridden by skilled and trained elephant-riders expert in warfare;
then Śakra, having mounted Sudarśana along with the hosts of gods, [departed].
Having summoned all the gods, O King, he then approached it, which was covered with armor of lapis lazuli and accompanied by the hosts of the Viśvedevas, Aśvins, and Maruts;
it was crowded with gods, yakṣas, gandharvas, and great serpents.
It shone like the sky when freed from clouds, as if by the planets; at that time,
Vāsava and all the others assembled for the sake of witnessing the power of those weapons being employed against human beings.
The gods, having arrived in their respective celestial chariots, came individually to witness that terrible and great battle at the encounter between Bhīṣma and Arjuna,
where there were hundreds of thousands of golden pillars.
Others, made of precious jewels, supported the palace;
there, the celestial chariot of the king of the gods, which moves at will, is adorned with every kind of gem and shone brilliantly as it traveled through the sky.
There dwell the thirty-three gods together with Vāsava,
as well as Gandharvas, Rākṣasas, serpents, and the Pitṛs along with the great ṛṣis;
likewise King Vasumān, Balākṣa, and Supratardana.
Aṣṭaka, Śibi, Yayāti, Nahuṣa, Gaya,
Manu, Kṣupa, Raghu, Bhānu, Kṛśāśva, Sagara, and Śala—
these highly resplendent ones were seen together in the celestial chariot of the king of the gods.
Of Agni, Īśa, Soma, Varuṇa, and Prajāpati; likewise of Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, of Kubera and Yama;
and of Alambuṣa, Ugrasena, and the Gandharva Tumburu.
The celestial chariots shone forth according to their respective portions and designated places;
and all the hosts of gods, the Siddhas, and the supreme ṛṣis arrived to witness the battle between Arjuna and the Kurus.
Then, the holy fragrance of divine garlands spread everywhere at the onset of spring, like the scent from forests in full bloom;
the red and non-red [garments] of the gods standing there were clearly visible.
Parasols, garments, garlands, and fans [were spread out];
the dust of the earth was stilled as everything became pervaded by rays of light;
and the wind, carrying divine fragrances, attended upon the warriors.
The sky appeared as if illuminated,
adorned with variegated forms by various celestial chariots— both stationary and descending— which shone with diverse jewels and were brought there by the supreme gods.

Seated upon his celestial chariot and surrounded by the gods, the wielder of the thunderbolt shone resplendent there; bearing a garland adorned with lotuses and water-lilies, the one of great splendor,
the slayer of Bala, gazed at that immense battle and could not look away.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Hari-vāhana, having caused all the gods to ascend the palace named Sudarśana, proceeded to where the Pāṇḍava was.
In its center, a thousand rows of pillars were firmly established;
there, upon the path of the sun, stood the stainless assembly hall of Vāsava.
Therein dwelt the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, the two Aśvins, and the hosts of Maruts.
There, white parasols made of gold and crystal,
variegated with precious gems and of various forms,
were seen individually in the sky, radiant and auspicious.
Of Agni, Indra, Soma, Yama, and Varuṇa;
likewise of Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, Mitra and the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada); and of Rudra, Viṣṇu, Savitṛ, and the Thirty-three gods as well.
Golden chains and various kinds of exquisite garlands,
interspersed with celestial flowers, were suspended there as parasols.
And upon that palace, O King, which was adorned with divine jewels, [they shone].
Pervaded by divine fragrances, celestial garlands shone forth;
a divine wind blew, carrying scents from every direction,
and the seasons, O Bhārata, stood present, bringing flowers.
The lords of creatures, the seven great seers,
the celestial seers, and those dwellers of heaven, O King—
all the thirty gods together with Indra— were stationed there.

Neither mud nor dust entered there in any way whatsoever; even the sun did not shine with excessive heat, though its light remained somewhat harsh. And the wind, carrying divine fragrance, blew there.

The sky and all the directions became visible as something beautiful to behold; there, the gods, having ascended that celestial palace which shone on all sides, traveled through the stainless atmosphere in that vehicle that moves at will.
There, royal sages and celestial dwellers had likewise ascended:
King Śveta, Vasumān, Bhadra, Pratardana,
Nṛga, Yayāti, Nahuṣa, Māndhātṛ, Bharata, and Kuru.
Aṣṭaka, Śibi, Pūru, and that king Purūravas; Dambhodbhava, Kārtavīrya Arjuna, and likewise Sagara; Dilīpa, Bharata, Pūru, Śayyāti, and Somaka.
The radiant Hariścandra, as well as Raghu and Daśaratha,
the royal sage Bhagīratha, and all [the kings], O Janamejaya,
and the mighty-armed Pāṇḍu, who was fanned by ten thousand yak-tail whisks.
With a parasol being held over him, surrounded by the splendor of the Rājasūya sacrifice—
these and many others, virtuous in character, pure in their vows,
renowned, and of great prowess, remained there in heaven.
All the hosts of Apsarases and all the Gandharvas as well,
the Daityas, Rākṣasas, Yakṣas, Suparṇas, and likewise the Pannagas,
and all the gods headed by Vāsava together with the lords of their respective hosts.
Desirous of witnessing that battle, they ascended there;
thus, stationed in the sky like those dwelling in palaces,
the denizens of heaven took their places to behold the combat between one and many.
And likewise, O Bhārata, there were variegated umbrellas of divine form.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having seen the armies of the Kurus drawn up in battle array, the joy of the Kurus [Dhṛtarāṣṭra]—
Thereupon, addressing Vairāṭi, the Pāṇḍava spoke these words:
"Go to the right of him on whose banner a sacrificial altar made of gold shines, where Kṛpa, the son of Śaradvat, is stationed."
Having heard the words of Dhanañjaya, the son of Virāṭa then quickly urged on the horses,
which were as white as silver and adorned with golden trappings;
moving them in due order, the hero attained the highest speed.
He urged on those horses, which resembled the moon and appeared as if enraged;
having approached the vicinity of the Kuru army, that expert in horse-lore brought those steeds, swift as the wind, back again.
Having turned clockwise and keeping the mandala to his left,
the Matsya prince, who knew the true principles, bewildered the Kurus with his chariot;
the son of Virāṭa, standing upon Kṛpa’s chariot, was fearless from any quarter.
Having circumambulated him clockwise, the mighty one stood before him.
Then Arjuna, mounting his chariot, blew his excellent conch, Devadatta, which produced a great sound, and proclaimed his own name.
The sound of that conch being blown by the victorious and heroic [Arjuna] in battle was great, like the sound of a mountain splitting asunder;
the Kurus, along with their armies, honored that conch.
Though blown by Arjuna in such a manner that it did not shatter into a hundred pieces,
the sound, having enveloped the heavens, returned and was heard again,
like the thunderbolt hurled by Maghavan as it strikes a mountain.
In the meantime, Kṛpa— possessed of great heroism and prowess, highly indomitable, and a supreme being among the wielders of weapons— arrived there, enraged at Arjuna.
Desiring to fight Arjuna, that great car-warrior, seeking battle,
took up the conch shell born from the great ocean and blew it with force, O hero. That best of chariot-fighters then filled the three worlds with its sound.
Taking up his great bow, he then produced a tremendous sound from its string.
Then Arjuna, leaving the chariot of the son of Droṇa, quickly approached the excellent chariot of Kṛpa, which shone like the sun and the fire.
Those two mighty warriors, standing ready for battle on chariots as radiant as the sun,
shone like two autumnal clouds.
Then Śāradvata quickly struck Pārtha with ten swift arrows.
He pierced that slayer of enemy heroes with sharp arrows capable of cleaving the vital organs.
Pārtha, too, drawing his supreme weapon Gāṇḍīva, renowned throughout the world,
discharged many iron shafts (nārāca) capable of piercing the vital organs.
And Kṛpa, taking up his bow, likewise advanced against Arjuna. Before those blood-drinking iron arrows could reach him, Kṛpa cut them into hundreds and thousands of pieces with his sharp shafts.
Like a cloud at the end of the summer heat, he released a shower of arrows;
gladdening all his friends, he fought back against Phalguna. Drawing his bow with great force, the Pāṇḍava of terrible prowess—
Then the son of Pṛthā, the great car-warrior, filled with rage, displaying various maneuvers, covered the cardinal and intermediate directions with his arrows;
the lord made the sky appear as if it were a single expanse everywhere.
The immeasurable-souled son of Pṛthā covered Kṛpa with hundreds of arrows,
just as a cloud rising at the proper time covers a mountain with torrents of rain.
Pierced by those sharp arrows resembling flames of fire, he became enraged.
Kṛpa became like a smokeless fire blazing in battle;
having swiftly struck the high-souled Pārtha of incomparable prowess with a thousand arrows, Kṛpa uttered a roar in the fray.
Then that hero, taking up his bow, pierced Pārtha with ten swift arrows having golden shafts and straight joints;
in that battle, Pārtha shattered Kṛpa’s excellent standard.
Thereafter, the immensely radiant Pārtha took up iron arrows resembling the sun, and further, many feathered shafts in that battle; with those,
the mighty-armed one then struck Kṛpa’s chariot-guards.
Candraketu, Suketu, Citrāśva, Maṇimān, the valiant Muñjamauli, and the terrifying Hemavarmā— these best of Kṣatriyas, possessed of great strength, were slain while they were fighting.
Suratha, Atiratha, Suṣeṇa, Ariṣṭa,
and Nṛketu, along with their armies, fell down lifeless;
Arjuna, acting with haste, struck down their horses with arrows released from the Gāṇḍīva.
With four supreme arrows, sharp and fierce, he pierced the four horses. Pierced by those whetted shafts that were like blazing serpents,
all the horses suddenly leapt up, and Kṛpa then fell from his position.
Seeing that Gautama had fallen from his position, the joy of the Kurus,
the slayer of enemy heroes, did not strike him, out of respect for his dignity. But Gautama, having regained his position once more, [assailed] Savyasācin.
He swiftly pierced him with ten heron-feathered arrows;
then Pārtha, with a single sharpened broad-headed shaft,
cut his bow asunder and further snatched the bow from his hand.
Then, with sharp arrows capable of piercing the vital organs, he shattered his armor; yet Pārtha did not cause pain to his body.
As he was being freed from the armor, his body shone forth.
Like the slough of a snake being cast off at the proper time,
when his bow was cut by Pārtha, Gautama took up another bow and made it ready; that was like a marvel.

The son of Kuntī, that slayer of enemy heroes, severed even that [bow] of Śāradvata’s son with a straight-knotted shaft; in this manner, the Pāṇḍava, displaying great manual dexterity, cut down many other bows.

His bow having been severed, the powerful warrior then took up a spear and hurled it at the son of Pāṇḍu like a blazing thunderbolt. Then, grasping that spear, which possessed the radiance of the sun and the fire, [he launched it].
Enraged, he suddenly hurled it at Pārtha of wondrous deeds. As that gold-adorned spear approached through the sky like a great meteor, Arjuna severed it with ten arrows.
Cut into ten pieces by the wise Pārtha, that spear fell to the ground.
When his spear was thus severed, Kṛpa was deprived of his chariot and afflicted by arrows;
then, with his bow, he [stood] amidst the yoke-pole, struck by *bhalla* shafts.
Quickly seizing another great bow from his chariot,
he swiftly pierced Pārtha with ten sharpened arrows.
Then Pārtha, possessed of great splendor, [discharged] arrows with the brilliance of fire.
Enraged in the battle, he discharged thirteen stone-sharpened arrows;
having struck them down, O Bhārata, Pārtha, as if in the blink of an eye,
took up another thirteen feathered shafts.
Then, with one arrow, that mighty warrior severed his yoke; with four, the four horses;
with a sixth, the head from the body of the charioteer;
with three, the triple-bamboo pole in battle; and with two, the two axles.
With a twelfth broad-headed arrow (bhalla), he likewise cut down his standard.
Then, as if laughing, Phalguna—
equal to Indra— struck Kṛpa in the chest with a thirteenth shaft that resembled a thunderbolt.
With his bow broken, deprived of his chariot, his horses slain, and his charioteer killed,
that slayer of enemies leaped down from the chariot with mace in hand and swiftly hurled that mace.
He suddenly hurled his mace at Pārtha of immeasurable splendor.
But that heavy, well-adorned mace, once released by Kṛpa,
was struck back along its own path by Arjuna with his arrows.
Then Kṛpa, of swift prowess, having drawn his sword and his radiant shield marked with a hundred moons, desired to slay the Pāṇḍava;
for that son of Śaradvat was a highly trained and great preceptor.
Moving through the air, the powerful Khechara wandered alone, gradually wielding his shield and sword.
Then, as if in the blink of an eye, the son of Kuntī severed both the sword and the shield with ten razor-sharp arrows; it was like a marvel.
With a dejected countenance, his efforts for battle having ceased,
the highly energetic Kṛpa leaped onto the chariot of Aśvatthāman and once again took up his bow for his sister’s son.
Then, with arrows released from the Gāṇḍīva bow, he warded off his sword; and upon the destruction of both sword and shield,
Dīrgha bit his lips with his teeth and grew enraged in his heart.
Having said again,
"So be it," the warriors, seeking to protect the indignant Śāradvata,
then covered Pārtha from all sides in battle with showers of arrows.
Then the son of Virāṭa, having turned his horses to the left and performed a double circle, held those warriors at bay.
Then those bulls among men, taking Kṛpa— who was now deprived of his chariot— [with him],...
Those of great speed carried [the chariot] away from Dhanañjaya, the son of Kuntī.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When Kṛpa had been led away, Droṇa, however, took up a very great bow.
The invincible Śoṇāśva rushed toward Śvetavāhana; but Arjuna, the best of chariot-warriors, seeing his preceptor approaching nearby on a golden chariot, spoke these words to Uttara:
Arjuna said:
There stands this golden altar, resembling the blazing crest of a fire,
erected upon a golden pillar and adorned with banners.
"Carry me there, may prosperity be yours, O noble one—to the division of Droṇa. I shall fight with the son of Bharadvāja, the high-souled preceptor.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Seeing Vaikartana victorious, Pārtha said to the son of Virāṭa:
"Be firm in this battle, O prince; victory shall be ours until I blow my conch shell, which makes the hair of our enemies stand on end."
"Go quickly, undaunted, unconfused, with a steady heart and gaze, to where my preceptor Droṇa, the great chariot-warrior, is;
while Arjuna thus sports upon the field of battle."
His strength, courage, splendor, and agility increased;
and beholding that marvel, Uttara was overcome by supreme fear.
O best of the Bharatas, as you discharge your divine weapons and floods of arrows, my mind is utterly bewildered upon beholding your prowess; my heart is split in two by fear.
Vaiśampāyana said: "I behold the sound of your Gāṇḍīva bow, never heard before,
as well as the great strength of your arms as you draw the bow extensively."
Your splendor is invincible, like that of Viṣṇu during his three strides.
Then Uttara beheld that wonderful Gāṇḍīva bow and the arrows suddenly released by Kirīṭin.
Terrified in the midst of the battle, he said to Arjuna,
"I am unable to control your horses. To him,
Arjuna replied with a slight smile:
The wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, the slayer of enemies—
with me as your ally, from where can you have any fear?
Go, address Uttara’s horses and drive them forward!
Reassured by Dhanañjaya,
the son of Virāṭa quickly urged the horses forward;
and Dhanañjaya, too, drawing his bow, [prepared for battle].
Resembling the great Indra, he drew his bow;
and then Arjuna, the son of Bībhatsu, spoke again to Uttara:
"O dear one, you must not fear while with me at the head of the battle."
"You are a prince; may prosperity be yours! You were born in the great Matsya lineage, into a family of kṣatriyas; you ought not to despair.
O prince, summoning vast fortitude, [mount] my chariot."
"Drive [the chariot] for me as I am fighting with my enemies in battle. Having spoken thus to him, Arjuna Bībhatsu,
the Pāṇḍava and best among chariot-warriors, looked toward the son of Bharadvāja and spoke again.
Large, beautiful-drawn horses, crimson in hue, shine forth;
resembling smooth coral, with copper-colored mouths and pleasing appearance,
they are yoked to his excellent chariot, being experts in every form of training.
On that excellent chariot stood the hero Bhāradvāja, the best among all wielders of weapons,
long-armed, possessed of great splendor, endowed with strength and beauty,
renowned throughout all the worlds, and full of majesty.
For he was equal to Uśanas in intellect and like Bṛhaspati in statesmanship;
likewise, O noble one, he possessed all the divine weapons along with the methods of their withdrawal, as well as the four Vedas and the practice of celibacy.
In him the science of archery (*dhanurveda*) is eternally established in its entirety;
likewise the Purāṇas, the Itihāsas, and the science of statecraft (*arthavidyā*) according to Manu.
Furthermore, therein reside forbearance, self-control, truthfulness, compassion, and straightforwardness.
These and many other virtues reside in that best of the twice-born—
he who is always dear to me, and he who is always dear to me. With that illustrious man, I desire to fight in battle.
"Therefore, O Uttara, drive quickly and take the teacher there.
Behold another wonderful battle between me and him.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus addressed by Arjuna, the son of Virāṭa urged those gold-adorned horses toward the chariot of Bhāradvāja’s son.
As that Pāṇḍava, the best among chariot-warriors, was rushing forward with speed, [Droṇa perceived him].
Droṇa rushed against the son of Pṛthā, like one rutting elephant charging another;
seeing the son of Kuntī advancing toward his golden chariot,
the mighty-armed one addressed these words with joined palms to his preceptor.
Then he blew his conch shell, which resounded like a hundred kettledrums;
the entire army was agitated like a surging ocean.
Then [he urged on] those excellent red horses, swift as thought and white as swans.
Seeing them mingled in battle, the people in the fray were filled with wonder;
beholding those two chariots at the forefront of the conflict, both endowed with prowess— the teacher and the disciple, undefeated, accomplished in learning, and high-minded.
Then, seeing the two mighty warriors Droṇa and Pārtha locked together in combat,
the great army of the Bharatas trembled repeatedly. At that moment,
the heroic Pārtha, filled with joy, seemed as if he were laughing.
Having encountered Droṇa’s chariot with his own, that great car-warrior,
the mighty-armed son of Kuntī and slayer of enemy heroes, saluted him and spoke these words in a gentle voice, preceded by conciliatory greetings.
"We have lived our dwelling in the forest and now desire to take action against you; you ought not to direct your anger toward us, O you who are ever invincible in battle.
But I, O sinless one, shall strike you only after you have struck me first."
"Such is the thought that occurs to me; therefore, you ought to do it.
Then Droṇa discharged more than twenty arrows at him, and Pārtha, with a practiced hand, cut them down before they had even reached him.
Then the heroic Drona, displaying his swiftness with weapons, covered Partha’s chariot with a thousand arrows,
as well as his horses that shone like silver, using shafts feathered with heron plumes and sharpened on stone.
The one of immeasurable soul showered [arrows] upon Pārtha, as if to provoke him;
thus did the battle proceed between the son of Bharadvāja and the Diademed One,
as they both discharged arrows of blazing splendor equally in the fray.
Both of them were renowned for their deeds; both were equal to the wind in speed;
both were experts in divine weapons; and both possessed supreme splendor.
Discharging nets of arrows, they bewildered the kings.
"Who else besides Droṇa is worthy to fight Arjuna in battle?"—
at this, all the warriors assembled there were struck with amazement,
and as he swiftly discharged his arrows, they honored him, crying out, "Excellent! Excellent!"
"Indeed, who else besides Phalguna deserves to fight Droṇa in battle?
This dharma of the Kṣatriyas is fierce, in that one must fight even with a preceptor. Thus spoke the people standing there at the head of the fray.
Those two heroic great chariot-warriors, both enraged and drawn close together, covered each other with showers of arrows; undefeated in battle,
they shone like two suns risen at the end of time.
Then Bharadvāja, enraged, drew his massive, gold-backed, and unassailable bow and fought against Phalguna. He [covered] Arjuna’s chariot with nets consisting of arrows.

With sun-bright arrows polished on stone, that mighty-armed great car-warrior obscured the splendor of the sun; and with sharp, high-velocity shafts, he pierced Pārtha, just as a cloud strikes a mountain with rain.
Like a dark cloud at the end of the summer heat, Phalguna showered him down;
indeed, with sharp arrows made of Jāmbūnada gold released from his bow,
Bhāradvāja completely covered that best of charioteers, Arjuna.
In the same manner, the Pāṇḍava took up the divine bow Gāṇḍīva—
slayer of enemies, swift, bold, and the supreme instrument for accomplishing great tasks— and the long-armed one shone as he brandished that bow, Gāṇḍīva.
The valiant one discharged many variegated arrows adorned with gold,
destroying the showers of shafts released by the son of Bharadvāja;
as they were swiftly loosed from his bow, it was like a marvel.
Moving about in his chariot, that son of Pṛthā, Dhananjaya, was a sight to behold;
he displayed all his weapons simultaneously in every direction.
As the Pāṇḍava took up his terrible arrows and fixed them to the bow, he appeared magnificent.
Because of his lightness of hand, they could not perceive the son of Kuntī as he discharged [his arrows].
With his shafts, he made the sky appear as if it were a single expanse of shadow on all sides;
at that time, Droṇa was no longer visible, as if enveloped by a mist.

O King, the immense form of Pārtha, as he discharged nets of arrows, was like the body of the sun when its rays are fully blossomed; such was the great form of the high-souled son of Kuntī as he cast forth his volleys of shafts.
Enveloped then by those excellent arrows, his form appeared like a mountain blazing on all sides. Having seen Pārtha’s own chariot covered with arrows in the battle, [he was struck with wonder].
Stretching his variegated bow, which resounded like the thundering of clouds,
the Kauravas beheld him in battle as he repeatedly released his arrows;
and as he moved about, a great roar was heard in all directions.
O bull of the Bharatas, the roar of Droṇa’s bow, sounding like the crash of lightning and thunder, caused amazement among the troops as he drew that formidable,
supreme weapon which resembled a circle of fire.
Droṇa, the ornament of the assembly, shattered those arrows;
he shone like the sun dispelling the darkness in the sky. Then there arose a great sound, like that of bamboos being consumed by fire.
With arrows having shafts made of Jāmbūnada gold, discharged from his excellent and variegated bow,
he of immeasurable soul covered the quarters and the radiance of the sun.
Then, [he loosed] those straight-knotted arrows with golden shafts.
In the sky, many creatures moving through the air were seen;
yet the arrows, released from Droṇa’s bow with their feathers joined together,
appeared as a single, long, continuous shaft in the firmament.
In the sky they appeared like rows of swans;
thus those two heroes, discharging great arrows adorned with gold,
made the sky appear as if covered with meteors.
And the arrows of those two, fledged with the feathers of herons and peacocks, shone like rows of swans moving through the sky in autumn. There,
a battle broke out between the two high-souled warriors, filled with intense fury.
The terrible battle between Droṇa and the Pāṇḍava was like that between Vṛtra and Vāsava.
Like two elephants attacking one another with the tips of their tusks,
they struck each other with arrows released from bows drawn to their full stretch.
Those two heroes, enraged and gracing the battlefield,
engaged in combat, each discharging divine weapons in turn.
But the heroic Pārtha, displaying his own prowess in the encounter—
With great weapons, he covered the high-souled Droṇa with arrows;
then Arjuna, the best among victors, warded off with his own sharp shafts the stone-sharpened arrows discharged by that preeminent teacher.

Displaying his own formidable self, the son of Indra, possessed of fierce prowess, swiftly covered the sky with many arrows. He assailed Arjuna, that tiger among men of piercing splendor, who was intent on slaying him.
Droṇa pierced him with sharp, straight-knotted arrows;
the powerful Droṇa, skilled in battle, became filled with joy. In that encounter, Droṇa was the foremost of preceptors and the best among those who bear weapons.
Arjuna played with him using straight-knotted arrows;
as the son of Bharadvāja discharged celestial weapons in that great battle,
Phalguna warded off those weapons with his own and fought him back.

A fierce encounter took place between those two enraged lions among men, as they were mutually intolerant of one another like a god and a dānava. Then Bhāradvāja and Arjuna displayed great weapons against each other in battle.

The Pāṇḍava swallowed again and again each weapon released by Droṇa— whether it was Indra’s, Vāyu’s, or Agni’s— with his own weapon. Thus did those two heroic and great archers discharge their sharpened arrows.
With showers of arrows, the two of them made the sky appear as a single shadow. Then,
the sound of the arrows released by Arjuna as they fell upon the bodies was heard like the roar of thunderbolts striking mountains.
Then, O lord of the people, the elephants, chariots,
and horsemen appeared smeared with blood like flowering *kiṃśuka* trees,
resembling groves of *aśoka* trees covered with fresh blossoms.
O Bhārata, at that time the armies there shone with the arrows of Pārtha,
with arms still adorned with bracelets, with various great chariot-warriors,
and with fallen armor variegated with gold and banners.
With warriors slain there, tormented by the arrows of Pārtha,
the army became utterly bewildered during the encounter between Droṇa and Arjuna. Those two heroes, however, brandished their bows capable of bearing a great burden.
Desiring to strike one another in battle with their arrows,
they covered each other; O bull of the Bharatas,
a tumultuous battle took place between Droṇa and the son of Kuntī, like that between Bali and Vāsava.
Then, with straight-knotted arrows released from fully drawn bows,
they tore into one another as a gamble for their lives proceeded. Then, a roar arose in the sky from those praising Droṇa there.
Droṇa has performed a difficult feat in that he fought Arjuna—
the crusher of foes, possessed of great heroism, firm of grip, and unassailable;
the conqueror of gods, Daityas, and serpents, and a great chariot-warrior.
Beholding Pārtha’s tireless training, his lightness of hand, and his ability to strike from afar in battle, Droṇa was filled with wonder;
thus did that terrible battle between those two great-souled men continue for a long time.
A most terrible conflict, causing the agitation of the world,
unfolded. Then, O bull of the Bharatas, the impatient Pārtha, raising his divine bow Gāṇḍīva, drew it with both arms in the battle.
Seeing that continuous rain of arrows, which was like a flight of locusts, they were all struck with wonder and honored him, crying out, "Excellent! Excellent!
And the wind was not able to pass through the intervals between his arrows.

As he was then incessantly fitting his arrows and discharging them, no interval whatsoever could be seen in Pārtha’s taking up his shafts. Thus did that most terrible battle with swift weapons proceed.
Faster than the swift, Pārtha discharged other arrows; then,
hundreds of thousands of straight-knotted shafts fell simultaneously there, close upon Droṇa’s chariot.
O bull of the Bharatas, as the *droṇa* was being strewn with arrows by the wielder of the *gāṇḍīva*, a great cry of "Alas! arose among the troops;
and Maghavat himself praised the swiftness of the Pāṇḍava’s weapons.
The Gandharvas and Apsarases who had gathered there,
seeing Droṇa submerged in the ocean of battle, [beheld] the powerful son [of Droṇa],
that leader of chariot-divisions, with a great multitude of chariots.
The preceptor’s son, Aśvatthāman, suddenly checked the Pāṇḍava;
he inwardly praised that deed of the high-souled Pārtha, yet he provoked his wrath most intensely.
Overcome by fury, he rushed toward Pārtha in battle,
scattering thousands of arrows like a rain-bearing cloud.
But the mighty-armed one, turning his horses toward where the son of Droṇa was, [checked him].
Pārtha gave Droṇa an opening to withdraw;
having gained that opening, the hero quickly retreated with his swift horses,
his armor and standard shattered and himself mangled by the supreme arrows.
When Droṇa had been defeated in battle, the son of Droṇa arrived;
with bloodshot eyes like Death himself bearing his staff, he stood in the fray.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then the son of Droṇa, possessed of great heroism, advanced toward Arjuna;
Pārtha received him as he rushed like a violent gust of wind,
raining down a vast net of arrows like a cloud.
A great encounter took place between those two, like that between the gods and the asuras,
as they scattered nets of arrows like Vṛtra and Vāsava;
at that time, the sun did not shine, nor did the wind blow.
When the sky was made thick with arrows and turned into shadow on all sides,
O conqueror of enemy cities, there arose a great crackling sound from the two combatants as they struck one another, like that of burning bamboos.
Arjuna has rendered all his horses short-lived;
O King, he is so bewildered that he does not know which direction to take.
Then the son of Droṇa, possessed of great heroism, [will pursue] Pārtha as he moves about.
Having observed a minute opening, he indeed severed the bowstring with a razor-sharp arrow;
seeing that superhuman feat of his, the gods honored him,
for no other man besides Pārtha Dhanañjaya would have been able to stand [in such a position].
Droṇa, Bhīṣma, Karṇa, and the great car-warrior Kṛpa, exclaiming "Excellent! Excellent!", honored that deed of his.
Then the son of Droṇa, having drawn away eight bows from that bull among men, [advanced].
Again he struck Pārtha in the heart with heron-feathered arrows. Then the mighty-armed Pārtha, laughing loudly, powerfully strung the Gāṇḍīva with a new bowstring.
Seeing him approaching in a rage like an elephant in rut,
O Bhārata, the son of Droṇa, filled with anger, challenged him to battle. Then,
drawing his bow into a crescent shape, Pārtha engaged with him.
He severed his bow, as well as the charioteer and the horses of the chariot;
he also pierced him with sharp arrows resembling venomous serpents.
Thereupon, that bull among chariot-warriors mounted another chariot and returned.
Like a rutting leader of an elephant herd against an intoxicated elephant,
a battle then commenced between those two solitary heroes upon the earth;
in the midst of the fray, it was truly immense and hair-raising for both.
All the Kurus, filled with wonder, beheld those two heroes—
those two high-souled ones fighting like two leaders of elephant herds come together.
Those two heroes, bulls among men, struck each other.
With arrows shaped like venomous serpents, blazing like flaming snakes,
the two divine quivers of the high-souled Pāṇḍava became inexhaustible;
by means of them, the heroic Pārtha stood firm in battle like an immovable mountain.

Furthermore, as Aśvatthāman discharged arrows rapidly in battle, they were quickly exhausted; thus, Arjuna became superior to him. Then Karṇa, drawing his great bow with even greater fury, [discharged his shafts].
Then a great sound of "Alas! Alas! arose;
Pārtha fixed his gaze upon wherever the bow was being drawn.
There he beheld the son of Rādhā, and his anger increased all the more.
Overcome by the power of rage and desiring to slay Karṇa,
that bull among the Kurus glared at him with his eyes rolling.
Thus, while Pārtha was turned away, the arrows of Droṇa’s son—
O King, thousands of men quickly brought [the equipment],
while the mighty-armed Dhananjaya, the conqueror of enemies, having left the son of Droṇa, suddenly rushed toward Karṇa himself.
Rushing toward him with eyes bloodshot with rage, the son of Kuntī,
desiring a duel in chariots, spoke these words.
Arjuna said:
"O Karṇa, that which you boasted so much with words in the midst of the assembly—
'There is no one equal to me in battle'— that very thing has now arrived. Today, O Karṇa, having engaged with me in this great conflict,"
"You will know your own inferiority and will no longer despise others.
You spoke harsh words, having utterly abandoned the Dharma;
yet I consider this which you intend to do to be difficult indeed."
"O son of Rādhā, do today in the midst of the Kurus, along with me, that which you previously spoke of when no one else was present;
[that which you vowed] regarding Pāñcālī while she was being tormented by those evil-minded men in the assembly hall."
"You have seen it; now reap its fruit alone. O Rādheya, behold my victory in battle over that anger of yours which was formerly endured by me while I was bound by the fetters of dharma."
O evil-minded one, receive now the fruit of that very hostility for which you endured twelve years in the forest;
come, Karṇa, and engage in battle with me!
"Let all the Kurus, together with their soldiers, become spectators.
Karṇa said:
"O Pārtha, perform in deed that which you speak with words."
For it is well known on earth that action indeed surpasses speech.
That which was previously endured by you was endured out of incapacity; O Pārtha, having now witnessed your prowess, I take back those words.
If you previously endured being bound by the fetters of dharma,
and likewise consider yourself unbound though you are bound; and if you have indeed lived out your forest-dwelling as it was prescribed— then [you have fulfilled your duty].

Therefore, though you know both dharma and artha, you wish to break this agreement out of affliction. O Pārtha, even if Śakra himself were to fight on your behalf, there would still be no cause for my distress as I display my prowess.
"O son of Kuntī, this desire of yours shall be fulfilled before long.
You shall fight with me, and today you shall behold my power.
Arjuna said:
It was only because you fled from my battle just now that you still live, O son of Rādhā; your younger brother has been slain. A firefly shines only so long as the moon has not yet risen.
When the thousand-rayed sun has risen, neither the firefly nor the moon shines;
likewise, O Karṇa, your roaring is in vain after you have defeated mere commoners.
And who is there—having caused his own brother to be slain and having abandoned the front of the battle—who could [speak thus]?
"No man other than you, O virtuous one, would speak thus while established in such a position.
Vaiśampāyana said:
While the unconquered Bībhatsu was speaking thus to Karṇa...
He advanced, discharging arrows capable of piercing body armor;
Karna received those shafts, which resembled flames of fire,
with a great shower of his own arrows, like a cloud pouring down rain.
For having advanced and brandishing his bow Gāṇḍīva, Bībhatsu,
desiring to slay Karṇa in battle, discharged many arrows;
Karṇa received them as a mountain receives the force of the wind.
Like a cloud raining down a great net of arrows,
a massive encounter took place between the two of them, resembling the battle between the gods and the asuras,
as they discharged nets of shafts until there was no space left in the sky.
Terrible nets of arrows rose up on all sides;
dust from the earth rained down during the encounter between Karṇa and Pārtha.
Neither the sun shone nor did the wind blow.
The sky, covered by arrows, became as if it were shadowed;
and the roar of the Gāṇḍīva and likewise of Karṇa’s bow was most terrible, like that of burning bamboos.
Arjuna, however, striking down horses, elephants, and chariots,
threw that army into turmoil and pierced Karṇa repeatedly;
he pierced his horses and struck his two arms and his hand-guard separately.
Unable to endure it, he severed the strap of Karṇa’s quiver with a sharp-pointed, straight-knotted arrow; then,
taking other arrows from his side-quiver, Karṇa—
He struck the Pāṇḍava on the hand, but his fist shattered. Then the mighty-armed Pārtha cut off Karṇa’s bow; Karṇa hurled a spear at him, but Pārtha destroyed it with his arrows.
Then Karna, his bow severed, swiftly hurled a spear. Partha cut that spear down in the battle with sharp arrows.
Thereupon, many followers of Radheya rushed forward.
And with arrows released from the Gāṇḍīva, he dispatched them to the abode of Yama;
those great lords of elephants lay prostrate, covering the entire earth along the paths of Pārtha’s arrows.
With golden girths and variegated with nets of arrows, like mountains entwined by masses of fire,
they [were] the destroyers of the enemy army and its women.
While he was performing superhuman feats,
Vaikartana, unable to endure it,
quickly struck him from afar as if hitting a target.

Then Bībhatsu struck his horses with sharp arrows capable of bearing great weight, released from a draw back as far as the ear; slain by them, they fell to the earth. Then, with another flaming arrow, the mighty-armed one—
The valiant son of Kuntī pierced Karṇa in the chest with a sharp arrow;
having pierced his armor, the shaft entered his body.
Then, overwhelmed by darkness, he was no longer conscious of anything at all.

Suffering intense pain, he abandoned the battle and fled facing north. Then, O King, Arjuna and the great car-warrior Uttara cried out in reproach upon seeing Karṇa retreating from the field of battle.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, having defeated the son of Vikartana, Pārtha spoke to the son of Virāṭa:
"Lead me to that army where the golden palm tree stands."
Here stands our grandfather Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, upon his chariot;
possessing the appearance of an immortal, he awaits battle with me.
There stands that golden palm-tree, adorned with diamonds and lapis lazuli.
Shaken by the wind, he shines exceedingly in battle;
I shall strike terribly, shattering the multitudes of chariots,
and I shall even seize the bowstring of this man in combat.
Then, beholding that vast army crowded with chariots, elephants, and horses,
Uttara— pierced deeply by arrows— spoke to Pārtha:
"O hero, I shall not be able to restrain your excellent horses here."
My vital breaths fail me and my mind seems to reel; yet,
through the power of these divine weapons being employed here by you and the Kurus, the ten directions seem to whirl before me.
I am fainting from the stench of fat, blood, and marrow;
my mind is split in two as I behold this terror. Never before have I seen such a gathering of heroes in a great battle.
By the great slaughter of iguanas, by the blaring of conch shells,
by the lion-roars of heroes, by the trumpeting of elephants,
and by the sound of the Gāṇḍīva bow which was like a thunderbolt— these were all present in abundance.
"O hero, for me whose mind is bewildered, both the Vedas and the Smṛtis have perished as I constantly behold the *gāṇḍīva* bow being whirled in battle by you like a circle of fire."

O hero, my vision wavers and my heart seems to tear asunder; your body in battle is like that of the enraged wielder of the Pināka bow. Even upon seeing you stretching out your arm, fear arises within me.
Though I am looking at you, I am deprived of my senses and do not perceive you taking up, nor aiming, nor releasing those excellent arrows;
my vital breaths fail me, and this earth seems to tremble before me.
Arjuna said:
"I have no power to control either the whip or the reins;
do not fear, O bull among men, steady yourself."
Most wonderful deeds have been performed by you at the head of the battle! You are a prince—blessings upon you—born into the renowned lineage of the Matsyas;
O subduer of enemies, you ought not to despair.
"O prince, slayer of enemies, summoning great fortitude while I fight in battle, restrain my horses on my chariot.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus to the son of Virāṭa,
the mighty-armed Arjuna, the best of chariot-warriors and foremost among car-borne heroes, spoke this once again:
"Lead me quickly to that very vanguard of Bhīṣma’s army."
Behold today my wonderful, divine weapon as I discharge it—
like a flash of lightning approaching from the thundering clouds in the sky.
The Kurus shall behold my Gāṇḍīva bow with its golden back.
"By which side will he strike— by the right or by the left?"—
thus shall all my assembled enemies conjecture regarding me,
as I cross that river difficult to traverse, whose waters are blood, whose eddies are chariots, and whose crocodiles are elephants.
I shall cause to flow a river that carries one to the next world;
with straight-knotted broad-headed arrows, I will cut down the forest of the Kurus, dense with branches of hands, feet, heads, backs, and arms.
Lying in their quivers, well-feathered at the tips, sharpened, and sounding like kettledrums—
these arrows released by me in battle shall consume the Kurus,
as I, the lone archer, conquer the Kaurava army.
There will be a hundred paths, like those of a fire in a forest;
you shall see the entire army pierced by me as if by a wheel.
I shall show you my wonderful skill in the art of archery.
"Stand unperturbed upon the chariot, whether on level or uneven ground.
I shall shatter with my thunderbolts the mountain standing there, covering the very heavens. In the past, at the command of Indra, I struck down [the demons] in battle."
Having made Mātali his charioteer, he then slew all the Nivātakavacas in battle as they were rushing forward from every side to fight;
having destroyed the Nivātakavacas by the thousands with the weapons of the Gāṇḍīva bow.
O charioteer, with the Raudra weapon, I slew hundreds and thousands of fierce Asuras, both the Paulomas and the Kālakhañjas. From Indra I obtained a firm grip, and from Brahmā, manual dexterity.

I shattered Hiranyapura on the far shore of the ocean, having defeated sixty thousand chariot-warriors armed with fierce bows— after Prajapati had unleashed a fierce, tumultuous, and wondrous assault upon me.

Behold indeed the hosts of the Kurus being struck down by me, like cotton-wool scattered by a mighty wind; [a field] where the trees of banners have fallen and the grass of foot-soldiers is strewn, yet filled with throngs of lions that are chariot-warriors.
I shall set ablaze with the fiery energy of my weapons the forest of the Kurus, which is filled with throngs of lion-like chariots and crowded with bow-vines.
With my straight-jointed arrows, I shall strike them down from the seats of their chariots.
Since I alone shall drive back all those exceedingly powerful warriors standing ready for battle, just as the wielder of the thunderbolt [Vajrapāṇi] drives back the Asuras;
for I have received the Raudra weapon from Rudra and the Vāruṇa weapon from Varuṇa.
I know the solar weapon from Sūrya, and the Yāmya weapon from the wielder of the staff; I know the Āgneya weapon from Agni, and the Vāyavya weapon from Mātariśvan;
I know the Gāruḍa weapon from Garuḍa, and the Pāśupata weapon from Paśupati.
I also learned the Naga-weapon from Vāsuki and the serpent-binding weapon from the serpents;
likewise, from the Gandharvas and Guhyakas, I learned the Gandharva and Guhyaka weapons. Having propitiated Mahāmāyā, I also mastered the Māyā-weapon.

From the glorious Sūrya, I received the Cākṣuṣī lore; from the mouth of Brahmā, the Brahmāstra; from the planets, the planetary weapons (grahāstras); and from each of their respective gurus, I obtained the techniques of drawing, aiming, and releasing them.
Furthermore, there are five methods for the introduction to liberation; indeed, those various modes of application for the divine weapons were learned by me from the mouths of their respective gurus.

Behold me as I employ from my arsenal numerous divine weapons— such as the *prasthāpana*, the supreme *saṃmohana*, and those that cause impairment and other such celestial missiles— against the enemy forces through their application.

When the opportunity arrived for those who were engaged in their yogic practices, I was encountered by other gods; what man could withstand me? Today, with showers of hair-raising arrows released from the Gāṇḍīva bow—
I shall strike down the multitudes of chariots of the Kuru archers;
for I have obtained from Śakra weapons such as the thunderbolt by propitiating and serving the guardians of the quarters and the world-protectors through worship.
Having subdued his senses through fierce austerities over a long period of time, devoted to that goal, abstaining from food, motionless like a pillar, and without support,
he endured rain, cold, and heat, and thus obtained the collection of divine weapons.
"O son of Virāṭa, I shall uproot this terrible forest of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's sons, which is guarded by lions among men; let your fear depart. Thus was the son of Virāṭa comforted by Savyasācin.
He plunged into the formidable chariot-force of the wise Bhīṣma.
As the mighty-armed Dhanañjaya approached, desiring to conquer his enemies in battle, the one of cruel deeds, remaining unperturbed, checked him.
Turning back, Jiṣṇu struck down his banner at the base;
pierced by arrows with golden tips, he fell from his chariot.
O bull of the Bharatas, Duḥśāsana then quickly advanced against Arjuna.
Other youths as well, adorned with various ornaments and polished earrings, wearing colorful garlands and decorations, learned and high-minded,
approached Bhīmadhanvā, winding their bowstrings around their arms.
Duḥśāsana, Vikarṇa, Duḥsaha, and Viviṃśati,
having approached, surrounded Bībhatsu, the wielder of the terrible bow;
thereupon Duḥśāsana struck sixty arrows into his left side.

Having aimed and joined his shot, the wise son of Kuntī [pierced him]; but the heroic Duḥśāsana, having pierced Uttara, the son of Virāṭa, with a broad-headed arrow, struck Arjuna in return between the breasts with a second shaft.
Turning toward him, Jishnu cut through his gold-adorned bow with a broad-edged, vulture-feathered shaft;
then he pierced him in the center of the chest with five more arrows from behind.

Afflicted by the arrows of Pārtha, he fled, abandoning the battle. Then Vikarṇa, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, pierced Arjuna— the slayer of enemy heroes— with sharp, straight-flying arrows feathered with vulture plumes.
Then the son of Kuntī quickly struck him on the forehead with a straight-knotted arrow; pierced thus, he fell from his chariot.
Thereupon, Duḥsaha, together with Vivimśati, rushed toward Pārtha.
Desiring to protect his brother in battle, he covered him with sharp arrows;
then Dhananjaya, remaining unperturbed, pierced both of them simultaneously with two sharpened shafts fletched with vulture feathers and slew their horses.
With their horses slain and their bodies pierced by arrows, both sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra were carried away on other chariots by their followers.
In the same way, the son of Subala, filled with rage—
With three sharpened yellow arrows, the hero pierced the archer and let out a roar;
he then struck him again with three more shafts.
Seeing him approaching and roaring at the head of the battle,
the hero took up thirteen sharpened arrows;
with one he struck the bow from his hand, and with four he struck the four horses.
With two arrows he struck his crown upon the head, with one the charioteer,
and with two more Arjuna reduced the chariot to pieces as small as sesame seeds in the battle;
likewise, he struck him in the heart with three straight-flying shafts.
Deeply pierced by the powerful and high-souled Arjuna,
he abandoned his chariot whose horses had been slain and went to where Suyodhana was. There, having conquered the king’s younger brothers in battle, Bībhatsu let out a roar.
Then he put to flight the remaining sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
having routed them in battle, Pārtha illuminated the field of combat.
And the unconquered Bībhatsu rushed toward all directions.
The son of Kuntī, wearing his diadem and garland, possessed of great strength and sure aim,
shone with immense splendor as he struck off hundreds of heads and arms resembling iron clubs from those adorned with golden necklaces.
The earth [was graced] by those with white teeth resembling lotuses, suns,
and moons, and with beautiful faces, eyes, and noses,
adorned with radiant crowns and earrings.
It shone, strewn with human heads—
heads that were handsome with fine noses, with beautiful, glowing eyes, well-groomed beards,
and finely adorned with golden earrings; severed heads were seen scattered across the battlefield.
Thus that army, struck down, fled in all directions out of fear;
toward every quarter and intermediate point around the chariot of the son of Kuntī,
sharp arrows issued forth from Arjuna’s Gāṇḍīva bow.
Like those running to rid themselves of an enemy,
the feathered arrows of Phalguna went forth with the speed of their shafts' tips,
snatching away from the chariots lives, arms, and heads.
In the sky, they appeared like rows of swans;
as he discharged his arrows with lightness and skill, shooting both left and right, Pārtha’s shafts went forth by the hundreds and thousands.
Crushing the lofty heads of the archers,
that bull among kṣatriyas dispatched three hundred attacking Kuru warriors who had emerged from the seats of their chariots.
The son of Kuntī, a man of great prowess who had drawn his bow firmly and achieved his mark, [advanced].
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then all the great chariot-warriors of the Kauravas, having assembled together...
O Bhārata, they united and, being vigilant, fought back against Arjuna. In the meantime, seeing Kṛpa afflicted by Phalguna and defeated in battle, the enraged Bhīṣma then spoke to Droṇa.
"Phalguna defeats each one of us individually in battle—
myself, Droṇa, Karṇa, the son of Droṇa, Gautama,
and many other heroes; yet we shall conquer the son of Vāsava."
That one of immeasurable soul covered those great car-warriors on all sides with nets made of arrows, just as mist shrouds mountains;
while great elephants trumpeted and horses neighed.
With the sounds of kettledrums and conchs, that tumultuous noise arose;
piercing through the bodies of men and horses as well as their iron armor,
the masses of arrows from Pārtha flew forth by the thousands.

Hurrying and discharging his arrows, that son of Pāṇḍu shone in battle like the radiant sun at midday in autumn. All [the warriors] found the arrows released from Pārtha’s bow irresistible in the fray.
Then, terrified, the chariot-warriors fell from their chariots,
the riders from the backs of their horses, and the foot-soldiers also to the ground;
as they were being struck by arrows, the armor of those great-souled men [crashed].
A great roar arose from the copper, silver, and iron [of the weapons];
the entire battlefield was covered with the lifeless bodies of elephants,
horses, and riders, their lives snuffed out by sharp arrows.
The earth was strewn with men fallen from the seats of their chariots— horsemen whose weapons had slipped from their grasp due to exhaustion—
and Dhananjaya, bow in hand, seemed as if he were dancing in the midst of the battle.
That bull among men struck off the heads of the kṣatriyas in battle;
hearing the roar of the Gāṇḍīva, which was like the crash of a thunderbolt,
all living beings were terrified and fled from the great conflict.
Heads were seen fallen upon the front lines of battle, adorned with earrings and turbans and still wearing garlands of gold; likewise,
limbs mangled by arrows and arms still clutching bows.
Covered by others with their hands and ornaments, the earth shone;
O bull of the Bharatas, as heads were struck down by sharp arrows in the midst of the fray, it was like a rain of stones falling from the sky.
Having thus displayed his own fierce form, he of Rudra-like prowess slaughtered warriors in battle by the hundreds and thousands; meanwhile,
Pārtha remained confined, wandering for thirteen years.
The son of Pāṇḍu unleashed a terrible fire of wrath upon the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra. Seeing his prowess as he consumed that army,
all the warriors became intent on peace while the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra looked on.
Just as a sixty-year-old elephant with temporal juice flowing crushes a forest of reeds,
so did Arjuna, by the brilliance of his weapons, utterly overwhelm all others;
having terrified that army, he put the great chariot-warriors to flight.
Arjuna, the best among victors, O Bhārata, moved about the field;
as he traversed its paths and struck down his foes on the battlefield,
he set flowing a terrible river with waves of surging blood.
At the end of the eon, Time has fashioned a terrible river: crowded with bones for its moss, featuring arrows and bows as its rafts, mired in flesh and blood,
choked with armor and turbans, and filled with great elephants, tortoises, and serpents.
Flowing with fat, marrow, grease, and blood, it increases great terror;
it is fierce in form, most formidable, and resounds with the cries of beasts of prey.
It has sharp weapons for its great crocodiles and is frequented by hosts of flesh-eaters.
Churning with waves of pearl necklaces and adorned with various ornaments,
it had great whirlpools of volleys of arrows and crocodiles in the form of serpents; difficult to cross,
of fierce appearance, and most terrifying, it resounded with the roar of arrows like thunderclaps.
He set flowing a terrible river frequented by hosts of *piśācas*,
with swords and scimitars for its pāṭhīna fish, chowries and turbans for its foam, horse-necked steeds for its great whirlpools, and headless trunks for its human beings.
It resounded with the harsh cries of crows and herons, and was filled with the calls of cranes and curlews;
it possessed great chariots and vast islands, and echoed with the blare of conchs and drums;
it was filled with the great roar of lion's roars and crowded with the sounds of shells and trumpets.
Rich with the lotuses that were the heads of the best of heroes, possessing the great fires of arrows and bows, teeming with foot-soldiers as its fish, having elephant-heads for its turtles,
resounding with the cries of jackals and deer, and mired in the mud of flesh and blood.
Pārtha created a great river of flowing blood, a terrible stream frequented by hosts of *piśācas*, shoreless and boundless on all sides,
with its waters consisting entirely of blood.
With the bodies of elephants as its great islands, the bodies of horses as its massive boulders, the multitudes of infantry as its dense thickets, and the rows of chariots as its great trees;
covered with the grassy mats of hair, it was exceedingly terrifying to men.

O King, the son of Indra (Arjuna) thus set flowing that terrifying river, which carries unfathomable blood, flows toward the ocean of Yama, and is difficult for timid mortals to cross but easy for heroes to traverse.
For as he took up his arrows, fixed them, and released them,
and as he drew the Gāṇḍīva bow, not even the slightest interval could be seen.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Duryodhana, Karṇa, Duḥśāsana, and Vivimśati,
along with Droṇa and his son, and the great car-warrior Kṛpa,
returned to the battle highly incensed, desiring to slay Dhanañjaya.
Stretching their powerful and firm bows,
O great king, he whose banner bears the monkey advanced on a chariot of solar brilliance with its pennons fluttering to meet them all.
Then Kṛpa, Karṇa, and Droṇa, the best of chariot-warriors,
surrounding the immensely heroic Dhanañjaya with great weapons,
rained them down in a state of intense fury, like massive clouds upon a mountain.
Discharging volleys of arrows perfectly like monsoon clouds,
they rained down showers of shafts upon Kirīṭin as he was rushing forward,
swiftly with many feathered arrows in that battle.
Stationing themselves nearby, they filled [the air] with devotion;
yet there was no harm to the limbs of the Northern one (Arjuna), nor to his wheels, nor to his horses.
For he was thus completely covered on all sides by those divine weapons.
Not even a space of two finger-breadths was seen to be uncovered on it. Then, laughing, the great car-warrior Bībhatsu fixed the divine Aindra weapon, which resembled the sun, upon the Gāṇḍīva bow.
Having bewildered them all there by the splendor of his weapons,
Arjuna, the victor in assembly, afflicted them with arrows—
he struck Duryodhana with seventy-three and Śakuni with five shafts.
The one of great strength struck Droṇa with a single arrow and Kṛpa with two;
he struck the Sūtaputra with eighty and likewise the son of Droṇa with sixty,
as well as all those headed by Duḥśāsana there, by the power of his weapons.
With those arrows, the Pāṇḍava, the best among wielders of weapons, afflicted [his enemies];
like the sun scorching with its rays, that mighty one blazed in battle, [overwhelming] neither the axle-trees, nor the wheels, nor the chariots, nor the horses.
The son of Kuntī, adorned with his diadem and garland, completely shrouded all the Kurus; just as lightning appears within a cloud or fire upon a mountain peak,
so did the Gāṇḍīva appear, stretched out like the bow of Indra.
Just as when the rain-god pours forth, lightning flashes in the sky,
illuminating all the quarters and the earth on every side,
so did that falling Gāṇḍīva envelop all ten directions.
All the chariot-warriors there became terrified on every side;
all, becoming intent on peace, could not find composure in their own minds.
Thus did those soldiers behave there while the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra looked on.
All those warriors, their hearts despondent, turned their backs on the battle;
thus, O bull of the Bharatas, all the armies were broken and fled in every direction, despairing of their own lives.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then the invincible and majestic Bhīṣma, son of Śantanu,
rushed toward Dhanañjaya while his warriors were being slaughtered.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having thus put that army to flight, Pārtha rushed toward Bhīṣma while all the troops of the high-souled Kaurava were terrified.
As Narasiṃha advanced toward him, desiring to conquer his enemies in battle,
Vṛṣasena quickly rushed at Dhanañjaya, eager for combat.
Then Pārtha swiftly [severed] his bow with a razor-edged arrow.
With a vulture-feathered arrow adorned with gold, he cut [the other’s bow];
then he pierced him again in the middle of the chest with five more arrows.
Struck by Pārtha’s arrows, he leaped down from his chariot and fled.
Duḥśāsana, Vikarṇa, Śakuni, and Vivimśati surrounded the Pāṇḍava, the wielder of the terrible bow, as he advanced. Enraged in battle, Pārtha [assailed] them with straight-jointed arrows.
In that battle, he swiftly cut down their yokes, banners,
and poles. With their banners severed and the bindings of their bows destroyed, they all, tormented by the arrows of Pārtha, fled from the midst of the fray.
Then, laughing, Bībhatsu said this to the son of Virāṭa:
"Now take me to that raised golden palm-tree, so that I may strike it again and again like lightning flashing repeatedly from the midst of the clouds."
"Go there, O scorcher of foes, to that Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu;
I shall display his divine weapons in battle—
terrible in form, variegated, swift, and heavy."
Having heard those words of his, Vairāṭi, the charioteer of Pārtha,
urged on by him, drove the chariot toward Bhīṣma’s chariot.
Then, seeing that excellent chariot of Phalguna thus urged forward, [he advanced].

Like a great cloud suddenly driven by the wind, Bhīṣma, the son of Gaṅgā and conqueror of enemy cities, advanced in his chariot radiant as the sun upon seeing Arjuna approaching. He turned back to face him.
Seeking battle, he went forth to meet him like a great bull meeting a bull;
grasping his excellent bow adorned with gold,
he took up sharp-pointed arrows capable of piercing and crushing the vital organs.
With a white parasol being held over his head,
that tiger among men shone like a mountain at the rising of the sun;
then the son of Gaṅgā, having blown his conch shell, gladdened the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Turning to the right, he intercepted Bībhatsu.
Seeing him approaching in that manner, the son of Kuntī, the slayer of enemy heroes,
the valiant one, blew his great conch shell Devadatta in the midst of the battle.
Then, at that time, those two— the conchs of Bhīṣma and the Pāṇḍava— resounded exceedingly,
making the heavens, the sky, and the earth vibrate in every direction.
With a joyful soul, Bhīṣma received [the challenge] like a mountain receiving a rain-cloud.
In the intermediate space, all the gods together with Indra murmured:
"Arjuna has cut down all the Kurus by the power of his weapons;
these two heroes, Bhīṣma and Dhanañjaya, are the best among the Kurus in battle."
Skilled in all weapons in this world, both of these are great chariot-warriors (*atiratha*);
both are renowned among gods and men for their own prowess.
Both are exceedingly enraged, and both are wielders of flaming bows.
Those two tigers among men met like two swift tigers;
both were equal in their deeds to the Sun and Agni, O Bhārata,
and both were the equals of Vāsudeva and Kārtavīrya.
Both were renowned for their deeds; both were heroes of great strength.
They were the best among all those skilled in weapons and the foremost among all wielders of arms—[the equals] of Agni, Indra, Soma, Yama, and Kubera.

The prowess of these two is equal to that of Mitra and Varuṇa. Who else on earth, other than the son of Śāntanu, is there among the Kṣatriyas who would approach the son of Kuntī in single combat in battle?

Thus they honored Bhīṣma upon seeing Arjuna departed; and having seen him about to strike in battle, the gods together with Indra likewise paid homage. Then, with the sounds of many kinds of conchs and trumpets—
With various sounds mingled with lion-roars,
that army of the Kurus, possessing a splendor equal to the host of the gods, honored the bull among the Kurus.
Then the valiant Bhīṣma discharged eight arrows of great velocity at Pārtha’s banner, which hissed like serpents. Those winged shafts, having struck the banner of the son of Pāṇḍu, fell upon it.
Blazing with energy, they struck the monkey and those [demons] stationed upon the tips of the standards;
moreover, they pierced his charioteer and his horses with ten arrows,
and struck Pārtha in the chest with three iron shafts.
Then Arjuna, having pierced the grandfather of the Kurus with sharp arrows,
the Pāṇḍava next swiftly cut off Bhīṣma’s umbrella with a great, broad-edged *bhalla* arrow; it fell to the earth.
The son of Kuntī, acting with swiftness, struck his banner firmly with arrows,
as well as the horses of the chariot and both the flank-guarding charioteers;
yet Bhīṣma, though he knew him to be the Pāṇḍava, could not endure that.
With a great divine weapon, he covered Dhanañjaya; likewise, the son of Pāṇḍu, of undaunted soul, invoking a divine weapon in turn, received Bhīṣma as a mountain receives a massive cloud.
Between those two there occurred a tumultuous battle that made the hair stand on end,
like the encounter between Bhīṣma and Pārtha, or between Bali and Vāsava;
all the Kauravas and their warriors, along with their troops, watched it.
The sky became filled with continuous rows of arrows released from the bows of those two, like clouds with torrents of rain;
and in that battle, broad-headed shafts met broad-headed shafts as Bhīṣma and the Pāṇḍava struck one another.
The Gandīva bow, O King, appeared like a circle of fire whirling to the left and right as Pārtha discharged his arrows, shining in the sky like fireflies in the rainy season.
He covered Bhīṣma with hundreds of sharp arrows,
just as a rain-cloud covers a mountain with torrents of water.
That rising shower of arrows was like a surging tide.
Bhīṣma, warding Arjuna off with his arrows, scattered them;
then those nets of arrows, cut apart piece by piece,
fell shattered upon Phalguna’s chariot in the battle.
Then Bhīṣma, with hundreds of sharp arrows, once more dispersed that shower of gold-tufted shafts rising swiftly from the Pāṇḍava’s chariot like a flight of locusts.
The sky was covered with arrows as they fell like the wings of birds;
then the Pāṇḍava discharged fierce nets of arrows,
and Bhīṣma sent forth as many nets of arrows in return toward the son of Pṛthā.
O Bhārata, he covered Pārtha— along with his horses, charioteer, and chariot— with calf-toothed arrows,
and he shrouded all the directions.
And the sky was filled with arrows having golden shafts;
then all those Kurus cried out, "Excellent! Excellent!
saying, "Bhīṣma has performed a difficult feat in that he fought against Arjuna."
The son of Pāṇḍu is powerful, youthful, skillful,
and swift in action; who else besides Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu, or Kṛṣṇa, the son of Devakī, is capable of withstanding the force of Pārtha in battle?
Or even from the preeminent teacher Bhāradvāja of great strength— those two bulls among men, possessing great power, sported while warding off weapons with their own weapons,
bewildering the eyes of all living beings.
Employing the *prājāpatya*, the *aindra*, and the most terrible *āgneya* weapons,
as well as the *kaubera*, the *vāruṇa*, the *yāmya*, and the *vāyavya*,
those two high-souled ones moved about in battle.
Then, seeing those two in combat, all beings were struck with wonder and cried out, "Excellent, O Pārtha, mighty-armed one! Excellent, Bhīṣma!
"This great feat that is being witnessed here is not possible among ordinary men."
The employment of great weapons in battle between Bhīṣma and Pārtha proceeded in this manner;
thus did the combat of missiles take place between those two who were experts in all weapons. When the combat of missiles had concluded, the combat of arrows ensued.
Then Jishnu, having turned back, cut through Bhishma’s gold-adorned bow with a broad-headed shaft. In the mere twinkling of an eye, Bhishma took up another bow in the battle.
Taking it up, the mighty-armed and immensely powerful one strung the bow;
and filled with rage, he swiftly loosed a great many arrows at Dhanañjaya.
Arjuna, for his part, also discharged many sharp and variegated arrows at Bhīṣma.

The one of great splendor hurled [his weapons] at the Pāṇḍava, and Bhīṣma likewise at him. O King, as those two high-souled masters of divine weapons discharged their arrows incessantly, no distinction could then be perceived between them.
Then the great car-warrior, the heroic son of Kuntī adorned with a diadem, and likewise the son of Śantanu, covered the ten directions with their arrows.
The Pāṇḍava exceeded Bhīṣma, and Bhīṣma likewise exceeded the Pāṇḍava.
O King, that was a marvel in the world during that battle:
the heroic protectors of Bhīṣma’s chariot, slain by the Pāṇḍava,
lay there on all sides around the chariot of the son of Kuntī.
Then, released from the Gāṇḍīva bow and desiring to rid the world of enemies,
the feathered arrows of the one with white horses arrived, their nocks joined together;
as they sped forth from his chariot, they were polished and adorned with golden feathers.
In the sky, they appeared like rows of swans;
for all the gods, including Vāsava, standing in the firmament, gazed upon that divine, intense, and wonderful weapon as he discharged it.
Seeing that wonderful and marvelous sight, the powerful Gandharva Citrasena was filled with supreme joy and reported it to the king of the gods:
"Behold these destroyers of enemies, moving as if they were locked in close combat."
This wondrous form is manifested as the divine weapon of the victorious one as he brandishes it;
men would not believe this, for such a thing does not exist among them.
This is a marvelous convergence of ancient, great weapons.
As he took up his arrows, fixed them, and released them, and as he drew the Gāṇḍīva bow, no interval could be perceived between these actions,
like the sun blazing in the sky at midday.
The armies are unable even to look upon the son of Pāṇḍu;
likewise, the people do not venture to gaze upon Bhīṣma, the son of Gaṅgā.
Both are renowned for their deeds, and both are experts in warfare.
"Both are performers of similar deeds; both are difficult to overcome in battle.
Having been addressed thus, O Bhārata, the King of the Gods honored the encounter between Pārtha and Bhīṣma with a divine shower of flowers.
Then Aśvatthāman, having approached Karna quickly, spoke to him:
"I alone shall slay all the Pāṇḍavas assembled here."
"O Karna, this was spoken by you in our presence in the midst of the assembly: 'I shall slay all the sons of Pṛthā, taking refuge in you.
But that was not done; out of fear of a single man, O son of a Sūta, you are running away. All the sons of Vicitravīrya rely upon you against the sons of Pṛthā."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Hearing these words spoken by Aśvatthāman, Duryodhana then [spoke]. "They desire to conquer him in battle; you yourself must fight Phalguna."
Desiring to do what was pleasing to Karṇa, he replied to the son of Droṇa with anger: "O best of Brahmins, do not cause the loss of honor for one of such renowned deeds;
for by the loss of honor, the strength of kings will surely diminish."
Heroes speak in battle and perform deeds with their speech;
they exert themselves in combat according to their respective prowess. Therefore, you ought not to censure him who is esteemed as a hero.
Thus addressed by the king, the son of Droṇa then became free from anger.
Then Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, stationed himself on the left flank,
having aimed against Savyasācin as he was shooting with his body fully turned.
Then, laughing, Bībhatsu cut through the bow of Bhīṣma, who possessed immeasurable splendor, with a broad-edged, vulture-feathered shaft;
he then pierced him in the center of the chest with ten arrows.
As he exerted himself with great prowess, Dhananjaya, the son of Kuntī,
pressed upon him; then the mighty-armed Gāṅgeya, difficult to overcome in battle, seized the pole of his chariot and stood there like one long afflicted by illness.
Then Pārtha fixed an excellent arrow, resembling fire and like a blazing serpent, into the forehead of Bhīṣma; at that moment,
Bhīṣma became bewildered and stood as if for a long duration.
And with a long-drawn voice, Bībhatsu spoke toward the Kauravas:
"Let them behold the wondrous horn of this aged nobleman for the sake of his son—
his pride, as he, a man of wisdom, fights against his own offspring."
Then Pārtha, though himself unconscious and knowing the duty of a warrior,
struck back; the charioteer of the steeds, remembering his instructions and protecting the great car-warrior, carried him away while he was still unconscious.
Having won back those cows in battle while the Kurus looked on in the forest,
Pārtha, intent on further combat, then set out toward the five chariot-warriors.
Taking up iron shafts and feeling his two quivers,
Aśvatthāman,
while touching the Gāṇḍīva bow, once again advanced against Karṇa.
O Karṇa, that which you spoke so much nonsense in the midst of the assembly— saying,
"There is no one equal to me in battle"— that very thing has now arrived.
Here he is, enraged like the God of Death himself, the crusher of all beings.
Karna,
having approached from nearby, yawned like a lion;
"I do not fear Bibhatsu, nor Krishna, the son of Devaki."
Devoted to the duty of a Kṣatriya even more than all the Pāṇḍavas,
pride arises merely from the sight of men who possess superior strength and subsist by the science of archery, yet his own voice does not falter.
"Let the son of the preceptor behold me fighting with Arjuna in battle, well-prepared and exerting myself;
yet fate is indeed difficult to overcome. Vaiśampāyana said: [He spoke thus as he fought, fully prepared.]
Five chariots, surrounding Dhanañjaya on all sides,
discharged their arrows with precision, even though they were willing to sacrifice their lives;
regarding it as a great gain, they swiftly rushed toward Dhanañjaya.
Discharging volleys of arrows like clouds in the rainy season,
they rushed forward with many various sharp shafts that pierce to the very marrow, and having halted their advance, they struck Dhananjaya in return.
Then Bībhatsu, the best among all wielders of weapons,
smiling and manifesting a divine weapon, advanced against those foremost of chariot-warriors,
just as the sun covers the earth with its rays.
Thus, with arrows released from the Gāṇḍīva, he covered all directions;
there was not even a space of two finger-breadths among the chariots, elephants, banners, or horses that remained unpierced by his sharpened shafts.
All the warriors, intent on peace, were no longer conscious of their own minds;
the elephants and horses, terrified,
collapsed in every direction like a sixty-year-old elephant with rutting temples trampling a grove of reeds.
In this way, Arjuna crushed all [his enemies] with the fiery power of his weapons;
by the roar of the Gāṇḍīva, the earth trembled,
and Dhanañjaya cut through the hearts of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Then, having plunged into the midst of the armies, that best of weapon-bearers,
the valiant one, addressed his heroic charioteer in the battle:
"O charioteer, restrain these horses and drive them slowly."
"I shall fight the unconquered son of the preceptor in battle;
for he who was formerly released by me has now come behind me.
Thus spoke Arjuna in the fray, directing his chariot toward Aśvatthāman.
Karna urged on the swift horses of Virata’s son; "Behold,
Bībhatsu approaches, distressed and in intense pain."
"I shall go to that very place; he shall not escape with his life.
Drona said:
"This high-souled son of Indra has not departed out of fear."
Terrified in this way, they turn back; those in deep agony do not return.
If you should again attack him while he is thus enraged, he knows many weapons and you shall not escape.
"By good fortune Duryodhana has been released; by good fortune the cattle have fled.
Now that the battle has ended with fists unclenched, what will you achieve with further fighting?
Let us advance a distance of one *krośa* and bring back the army."
"Endowed with such powers, O Pārtha, you shall once again advance against him;
for in prowess, heroism, valor, and strength in great battle,
as well as in all weapons and missiles, in agility, and in long-range striking, [you are superior]."
He who has no equal in the world and who received boons from his father; he who has conquered fatigue, conquered his enemies, is free from sloth, and devoid of weariness;
he who was born with the power to die at his own will and remained devoted to the service of his parents.
Having fought with Pārtha in battle for the sake of Duryodhana’s welfare,
he became as if defeated for the sake of Pṛthā’s son,
Arjuna.
Drive the horses toward the southern direction, O charioteer; let them go northward.
Before this sound of theirs becomes a caravan, let them remain here.
O charioteer, drive forward toward the east to meet the counter-chariot of Aśvatthāman.
"I wish to see the illustrious son of my preceptor before long.
