Vaiśampāyana said:
"But the Pāṇḍava, having confounded them all with the roar of his bow..."
Having turned counter-clockwise in this manner, he then rushed forward for half a *krośa*,
just as a well-aimed arrow or a swift-moving *suparṇa* bird;
likewise, Pārtha’s chariot moved rapidly through the sky.
When the noise had ceased for a moment and Dhanañjaya had departed,
all the great car-warriors, led by Droṇa and Bhīṣma, placed the elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry at the front and proceeded to the rear of the army.
The soldiers,
exerting themselves and wounded by arrows, could not see Pārtha; they gathered together and said,
"By good fortune Duryodhana has escaped, and the majority of the army has arrived."
"Having traveled only a *krośa*, let us bring up our forces.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Let us go to where there is a forest thicket by the river Anvaśmakā."
Then Duryodhana, seeing his own army broken in battle,
could not endure it; filled with wrath, he sought out Dhanañjaya and turned back, surrounded by his own division, O best of the Kurus.
Though being vehemently restrained by the invincible Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and Kṛpa,
Arjuna, having observed the wonderful and noble-speeding Gāṇḍīva, spoke these words:
But now, this bow of the Kurus— which brings misfortune [to enemies], is auspicious, destroys foes,
is exceedingly swift, powerful, and acts with speed— [is ready].
Irresistible for a great battle, a shatterer of the enemy's ranks, a breaker of armies in combat, it is like a thunderbolt.
Go where this Suyodhana is,
for I shall strike him down with my very sharp arrows,
as well as the son of the preceptor and the grandfather.
Having warded off Suyodhana, the son of the Sūta, and Droṇa and Kṛpa in battle,
I shall take the head of Suyodhana.
Seeing that wonderful bow of great power and those sharpened arrows, Uttara,
filled with fear, spoke to Arjuna in the midst of the battle.
"I am not able to restrain your horses," he said.
Then the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, the slayer of enemies, laughed and spoke to that son of the Matsya king.
"With me as your companion, from where could you have any fear?
Go forth, urge on the northern horses!
Thus was he encouraged by Dhanañjaya.
The son of Virāṭa swiftly lashed the horses, while Jīṣṇu,
desiring once more to fight, drew that bow of fierce speed.
By the sound of the Gāṇḍīva bow, many warriors there fell violently to the ground; likewise,
by the sound of the conch of the monkey [Hanumān], they were struck down.
Arjuna said:
"By this sound, those best of warriors on all sides [know]:
'This is the excessively arrogant son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.'"
At the head of the army, possessing all-encompassing splendor and never tolerating defeat,
he turns back from the front with his mind fixed on battle.
"Go there with diligence, having carefully observed Suyodhana and his younger brothers," said Vaiśampāyana.
Beholding him rushing forward,
all the Kuru heroes suddenly advanced;
but that hero, laughing, passed right by them.
He drove two arrows into Duryodhana; afflicted by them like an elephant with its temples split open,
the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra was pierced by Pārtha.
Desiring to fight with that great car-warrior (Atiratha) in battle,
he himself restrained Arjuna and approached him.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When Bhīṣma had abandoned the front of the battle and was fleeing,
the high-souled son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra raised his standard and uttered a loud roar.
Having himself challenged Arjuna,
he approached Dhananjaya— that one of terrible bow and fierce valor— who was moving among the ranks of the enemy.
With a broad-headed arrow drawn back as far as his ear and released, he pierced him in the middle of the forehead;
by that arrow being struck home, he was deeply wounded.
O King, he of noble deeds shone with his well-sharpened [spear] that had the luster of Jāmbūnada gold,
like a beautiful single-peaked mountain with its solitary summit.
Then, as he was torn apart by the arrow,
warm blood flowed forth incessantly;
it was variegated like the blossoms of the Jāmbūnada tree.
Struck by that arrow, the impetuous one, his surge of fury aroused by Duryodhana, shone forth like a variegated garland.
Taking up arrows resembling poison and fire,
he of undaunted spirit pierced the king;
and Duryodhana, too, of fierce splendor, [pierced him].
And Pārtha, the peerless hero, and Duryodhana,
those two foremost of men among the descendants of Ajamidha, struck each other equally in battle.
Then Vikarṇa was again attacked by a great elephant in rut, resembling a mountain,
which was protected by four chariots serving as its foot-guards.
Then he rushed toward Jiṣṇu, the son of Kuntī;
as that lordly elephant charged swiftly,
Dhanañjaya struck it between the frontal lobes.
With a firm iron arrow of great velocity drawn back to his ear,
Pārtha released that shaft fletched with vulture feathers.
It entered the serpent up to the region of its feathers,
piercing through that which shone like the finest mountain,
just as a thunderbolt hurled by Indra splits a mountain.
Scorched by the arrows, that king of serpents,
his limbs trembling and his inner soul distressed,
fell to the earth, sinking down.
When that excellent elephant was struck down to the earth like the peak of a mountain struck by a thunderbolt,
Vikarṇa suddenly descended from it in terror.
Having quickly gone eight hundred paces,
he mounted the chariot of Vivimshati after having slain that elephant with that arrow.
With such an arrow, which was like a thunderbolt and resembled a mountain peak or a rain cloud, Pārtha pierced Duryodhana in the chest.
Then, when the elephant and the king himself were pierced,
and Vikarṇa along with his foot-guards was broken,
they were driven away by the arrows released from the Gāṇḍīva.
Upon seeing the elephant slain by Bāṇa and hearing all the warriors fleeing, those chief combatants suddenly retreated.
Turning his chariot away from the battle, that hero of the Kurus fled to where Pārtha was not; him,
of terrifying form, as he was fleeing in haste—
The diadem-wearing Arjuna, slayer of enemies and bearer of the quiver, eager for battle, let out a lion’s roar at Duryodhana,
who was pierced by an arrow and vomiting blood.
When that foremost of great archers had been thus deeply pierced in battle by the peerless Dhanañjaya,
all the troops were overcome with fear.
Beholding Pārtha, those [weapons] were struck with fear;
then they all became intent on peace upon seeing Arjuna like a rutting elephant.
Roaring loudly and powerfully in battle,
standing like a lion in the midst of bulls,
by the sound of the Gāṇḍīva bow of the Pāṇḍava—
The warriors, afflicted by fear and scorched by the arrows of Pārtha, suddenly fell from their chariots like lordly elephants attacked by lions.
With bloodshot eyes, Indrakarmā once again struck Vaikartana with twelve arrows; having seen them fleeing, he pursued those who were running away.
And with a single chariot, Pārtha [pursued] Duḥśāsana;
Karna, tormented by the arrows of Pārtha,
spoke to Duryodhana and Duḥprasaha upon seeing them.
"Arjuna has been seen; let us return quickly. By going from here, we shall provide for our welfare.
I believe, my dear son, that your task is accomplished."
Since Arjuna has been seen by us here today,
let Savyasācin go back to the forest once more;
I see that their appointed time has not yet reached its full measure.
Afflicted by the arrows of the Pāṇḍava in battle,
they fled while calling out to one another;
then Karṇa said, "Here comes Jiṣṇu!"
Let us go, surrounding Duryodhana—
he who is skilled in all weapons, who resembles the leader of a herd of elephants,
and who strikes his enemies at the proper time in battle.
And here is Pārtha returning again;
the root of the Bharata bulls must be protected.
Having observed Pārtha rushing forward with speed—
Duryodhana, his appearance stricken with fear, sought refuge with Droṇa, Karṇa, Kṛpa, and Bhīṣma, who stood like Time itself with weapon raised.
To Duryodhana, who was terrified in appearance and seeking refuge, the diadem-wearing Arjuna, the subduer of enemies and wielder of the quiver, spoke with a joyful heart: "Do not fear."
Seeing him pierced by the arrow and vomiting blood,
Arjuna said:
"Having abandoned both great fame and extensive renown..."
Why do you flee, turning away from battle? Today your musical instruments are not being struck as they used to rise up properly when you went forth to war.
Today you shall not enjoy the entire earth—
its vehicles, garments, foods,
and sandalwood of auspicious fragrance.
Having defeated him in battle, what will you enjoy—
golden garlands and earrings,
and necklaces with cushions made of lapis lazuli?
O sinful one, when you have fallen from battle today, there will be no sounds of conchs for you,
nor will there be excellent sandalwood for the sake of enjoyment.
And for the son of a king who has departed for battle, there may be prominent women with sweet speech in the next world,
but not in this one.
"I am the executor of Yudhiṣṭhira’s command;
I am Pārtha, the third, and steadfast in battle.
Therefore, turn your face toward me and give me battle."
Remember the conduct of kings, O son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra! This name "Duryodhana" which was given to you here in the past has become meaningless on this earth.
You are renowned by the name Duryodhana,
and you are Suyodhana, preeminent in deceit; for in this matter,
the quality of being "hard to conquer" (duryodhanatā) does not exist in you.
O Duryodhana, as you flee, abandoning the battle, I see no protector for you, neither in front nor behind.
Depart from battle, O hero of the Kurus;
protect your dear life today from the Pāṇḍava,
since I am here [to face] him when he is terrified, stripped of his garments, and deprived of his chariot.
I have come to you for refuge, speaking thus as I flee from battle— unconscious, mangled, naked, with disheveled hair.
To one who thus prattles, "I am yours," and who says, "Protect me," I do not strike him down, even though he speaks like an enemy with his back turned. Ah! I do not kill him.
Therefore, O Jīva Suyodhana,
if you still remember your own words spoken when you won at the gambling match in the assembly hall— ah!— then [act accordingly].
Displaying his own thigh in our very presence,
he insulted us and said to Kṛṣṇā:
"These sons of Pāṇḍu are indeed as good as dead."
Just as leather tigers and snakes whose fangs have been broken, as eunuchs with beards,
and as wild sesame seeds— so too are these.
"Just as people speak of 'crow-barley' (kākayava), know that the Pāṇḍus are merely bearers of a name; come,
take this lap of mine."
"Be the ornament of my kingdom, O sir,
for you have spoken at length in many ways while Droṇa, Bhīṣma, and Kṛpa were listening."
Come then, O sir; do not be afraid of my armies.
Even with all your own chariots and many of your own warriors, you cannot withstand me on a single chariot.
Fight me alone here, O hero;
do not flee for the sake of saving your life,
O dull-witted one, but remember what you yourself vowed in that assembly.
"Seek to win back the Kurus in battle before my very eyes,
with your lives surrendered through the strength of my arms.
Vaiśampāyana said:
But when challenged by him in battle,
that high-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra was turned back by the goad of his words.
Like an intoxicated elephant struck by a goad,
that powerful atiratha, unable to endure being thus addressed by the mahāratha, [replied].
Then Duryodhana, enraged and brandishing his excellent bow,
summoned great fortitude and replied to Dhanañjaya.
"O bull of the Bharata race, I do not fear even a wrathful Indra.
Having enjoyed a vast kingdom, wealth, and pleasures," said Vaiśampāyana.
"O best of men, for what reason would I flee at the time of battle?
Having spoken thus, O great king, the monarch fought back against Phalguna,
charging forward with swift horses like an elephant tormented by a goad.
Resplendent and possessing great coils, like a curved serpent,
he, having encountered the chariot with his own chariot, fought the Pāṇḍava;
then that hero turned back on his chariot.
Like a serpent trodden upon by the sole of a foot,
Karna, seeing him wheeling around,
turned back and steadied himself, his limbs pierced by arrows.
The heroic man among men, Bhīṣma the son of Śantanu, wearing a golden garland, turned back from the battle and approached Duryodhana on his right, while Pārtha was on his left.
Urging on the horses adorned with golden girths,
the mighty-armed one, his bow strung, protected Duryodhana from behind while facing the sons of Pṛthā.
Droṇa, Kṛpa, Vivimśati,
and Duḥśāsana quickly turned back; all of them stood in front with their bows drawn and arrows ready.
They hastened forward for the sake of Duryodhana;
and seeing those armies returning like a full flood, Pārtha [beheld them].
Just as a swan might fly toward an approaching cloud,
the impetuous Dhanañjaya rushed forward;
they all surrounded Pārtha from every side.
Taking up divine weapons,
they approached and rained arrows from all sides,
just as clouds shower a mountain with torrents of water.
Then, having neutralized their weapons with his own weapon,
the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, the subduer of enemies, discharged another weapon called Sammohana against those bulls among the Kurus.
Then the son of Indra manifested an irresistible power,
pervading the cardinal and intermediate directions with sharp-edged, whetted arrows furnished with beautiful feathers.
With the roar of the Gāṇḍīva, that one of great strength caused their minds to tremble; then,
once again taking up his terrible-sounding [bow], he—
With his two arms, Pārtha, the slayer of enemies, caused the great conch of lofty sound to resound through the intermediate directions, the cardinal directions, the sky, and the earth.
Stupefied by the blast of the conch shell sounded by Pārtha, those foremost heroes of the Kurus cast aside their formidable bows.
Then all became intent on peace, while the enemies lay unconscious; and Pārtha,
having recalled the words of Uttarā as well.
"Depart from the midst," he said to the son of Matsya,
"as long as the Kurus remain unconscious. Then [he spoke] to the two teachers, Śāradvata and Suśukla:
O hero among men, take for yourself the beautiful yellow garment of Karṇa, and likewise the two blue garments of the son of Droṇa and the king.
I believe Bhīṣma still possesses his senses;
he knows how to counter my weapons. Therefore, turn his horses to the left.
Thus indeed must one proceed with undeluded consciousness;
then the high-souled son of Virāṭa, letting go of the reins, leaped down from the chariot.
Various kinds of wonderful-colored garments, large Chinese silk robes (*cīnāṃśuka*) and fine linen cloths (*dukūla*),
and various beautiful silken fabrics (*paṭṭāṃśuka*).
O noble one, [he gave] necklaces belonging to kings, ornaments of gems, golden *niṣka* pendants, and armlets, bracelets, and rings made of rubies.
Having taken other jeweled ornaments and garments belonging to kings and great chariot-warriors,
he quickly mounted his own chariot again.
With his fingers placed at the tip of his nose, he rendered all the kings— who appeared like the dead— as if unconscious by means of the *saṃmohana* (stupefying) weapon.
Pārtha laughed, his heart filled with a sense of wonder;
then Arjuna, having fixed the fierce *svāpana* weapon upon his bow, turned toward the Kurus.
Having spared his preceptor Bhīṣma along with his son and Kṛpa, the indignant one released [his weapon] at the heads of others;
then, having reached those heads, it [the weapon] proceeded [to sever them].
The sleep-inducing weapon of the bulls among the Kurus [cuts] each one individually— half the head and half the beard—
separately from one another.
Having shaved off the portion of hair on his head that grew from the tuft,
he returned that weapon to the hand of Pārtha;
then that hero among men was filled with joy.
Having paid homage to his elders, he spoke aloud:
"O heroes, go quickly to the inner apartments and show yourselves to each of your beloveds."
"Having restrained my vital breaths, I have released them today;
ah, I shall release my own anger once more!
Then he urged on his four excellent horses.
The son of Virāṭa [drove] horses with golden girths; those white steeds bore Arjuna through that host of bannered warriors from the midst of the battle.
As that hero among men was thus proceeding,
the powerful Bhīṣma struck him with arrows;
and he, in turn, having slain Bhīṣma’s horses;
He pierced him in the side with ten arrows;
then Arjuna, whose bow was unerring, having bypassed Bhīṣma in battle, pierced his charioteer.
He stood released from the midst of the multitude of chariots,
like the thousand-rayed sun after piercing through Rāhu;
and having regained consciousness, that hero of the Kurus—
Then, beholding Pārtha— who was like Mahendra himself—
standing alone in the fray and withdrawn from the battle,
that son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra spoke in haste.
All of you have been conquered, with shaven heads and beards,
each one distinct in portion, deformed, and fierce;
how indeed has this man been liberated by you?
"Bind him firmly so that he may not escape.
Śāṃtanava, laughing, said to him:
"Where has your intelligence gone? Where is your prowess?"
Just as you have become peaceful again after sighing for peace,
having cast aside your arrows and your wonderful bow— so too, Bībhatsu is not at all capable of such cruelty.
His mind is not inclined toward evil, nor would he abandon his own duty for the sake of the three worlds;
therefore, not all have been slain in this battle.
"O King, even now there is no consciousness in you here; alas, your sense of shame has departed! Guard yourself, O subduer of enemies!"
"O you of undaunted spirit, where has your bark garment gone, now that you have beheld all these warriors stripped naked?
Therefore, O son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, you must not speak thus."
"O hero of the Kurus, go quickly to the Kurus;
having conquered them, let Pārtha return with the cattle,
lest he, being enraged, slay you all assembled together."
Therefore, let us conquer that city; may this be our gain,
lest your own purpose fall away through delusion.
Therefore, O Ariṣṭadhanvan,
you must take precautions; for you have been completely stupefied by the *saṃmohana* weapon and do not perceive the theft of your wealth.
"O King, behold your own garments and ornaments,
which have been taken away by the son of Virāṭa while all the kings were rendered unconscious."
"If he wishes to kill, he shall kill"— thinking thus, that hero among men, out of his righteous nature,
did not slay you, O son of Indra.
It was by good fortune that Pārtha did not slay you while he was seeking peace with the Kurus;
therefore, depart now along with your soldiers.
With those who remained after the slaughter, [he marched] toward the city named after the elephant (Hastināpura).
Then Duryodhana, having heard those words of his grandfather which were for his own benefit, [acted accordingly].
Having observed that his garments had been taken away by Phalguna,
the king felt ashamed in his heart;
though he was exceedingly intolerant in battle, his desire for combat had passed.
Sighing deeply, the king became silent,
having observed those beneficial words of Bhīṣma and the ever-increasing fire of Dhanañjaya.
"Let them set their minds solely on returning,
guarding Duryodhana. To those who had thus departed, Pārtha, with a joyful heart, [spoke].
Beholding the Kuru heroes, the high-souled Dhanañjaya followed them for a moment, addressing them and honoring his elders there.
Beholding their ranks with their trumpets, banners, and bows shattered, Pārtha,
the preeminent archer of the Kurus, wielded the Gāṇḍīva bow.
The powerful one blew his conch shell with all his might;
they, hearing that tumultuous sound of the conch and hearing the banner shouting in the sky, [were struck with fear].
Terrified by the sound of the Gāṇḍīva bow, they repeatedly fled, abandoning all their wealth;
Arjuna drove them even further away.
Having returned all his wealth in its entirety and having taken leave of them, let him depart to a distant place;
and having saluted all his elders with arrows, let him go.
With his mind uplifted, he slowly withdrew,
having honored with a bow of his head the aged grandfather Śāntanava and his preceptor Droṇa.
Having saluted with various wonderful arrows the son of Droṇa, Kṛpa, and all his teachers,
and [having honored] Duryodhana’s [chariot] variegated with the finest jewels;
Having proclaimed his name, Pārtha then turned back after cutting off that crown with an arrow,
like a lion with its mouth agape facing Dhanañjaya.
Those kings were unable even to look upon him as he advanced directly toward them after having conquered the Gā river,
just as one cannot look upon the sun when it has reached the meridian.
Taking those jewels and garments, Pārtha,
like a rutting elephant fierce in battle,
spoke after defeating the son of Virāṭa.
With a joyful countenance, that best of chariot-warriors addressed the heroes and those worthy of honor,
making the worlds resound with the roar of the Gāṇḍīva bow.
That hero, having suddenly roared at Devadatta and rent asunder the hearts of his enemies,
overcame all his foes with his banner.
Shining with a net of gold,
the Diademed One (Kiritin), seeing the Kurus departing,
spoke joyfully there to the son of Matsya:
"Turn back the horses; your cattle have been won. The enemies have fled; go to the city with joy.
But the gods, having seen that great marvel, [were amazed].
Having fought with Phālguna, the Kurus returned to their respective abodes,
satisfied and reflecting upon the deeds of Pārtha.
Shining with a golden garland on his blood-stained chariot, that hero proclaimed:
"Let your victory be quickly proclaimed today!"
May your body be graced with garlands and perfumes;
may your mother and your kinsmen rejoice upon seeing you today thus exultant with joy.
The gods, the hosts of gandharvas, and the royal sages were all filled with joy, O Pārtha,
as they all celebrated that very speed.
Placing Mahendra at their head, they then departed.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Uttara, with a joyful heart, replied to Pārtha.
Seeing the Kurus defeated and the Pāṇḍava shining forth, [he said]:
"By good fortune you are victorious, O invincible one, O mighty-armed Dhanañjaya!
Seeing both your manifestation and your victory, I am delighted, O Pāṇḍava."
Having heard those words of the high-souled Uttara, Arjuna, the slayer of enemy heroes, then replied to him:
"By good fortune you have returned unhurt, my dear; by good fortune your cattle are safe, O sinless one."
"The enemies have been restored to their rightful place and defeated in battle;
turn the chariot back quickly, urge on these excellent horses,
drive all the cattle away, and proceed toward the *śamī* tree."
Then, having conquered the Kurus in battle, he whose eyes are like those of a bull brought back the great wealth of Virāṭa.
And when the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra had fled, broken on all sides, [he took the spoil].
Emerging from the dense forest, many Kuru soldiers,
their minds terrified by fear, gathered here and there;
they were seen standing with disheveled hair and palms joined in reverence.
Exhausted by hunger and thirst, situated in a foreign land, and deprived of their senses, they bowed down in agitation and said: "O Pārtha, what may we do for you?
We shall offer our very lives, which have entered within our minds."
Arjuna said:
"We are indeed your servants, O Arjuna, and we are to be protected by you as those who are helpless. We are protectorless, suffering, wretched, emaciated, aged, and defeated."
I do not slay those who have laid down their weapons, those who are hopeless, or those who stand with palms joined in supplication. May you go forth with confidence, fearless and as if immortal;
protected by the dust of my feet, may you live for a very long time upon this earth.
Arjuna said:
"Go in safety; may it be well with you. You must not fear in any way.
I do not wish to kill those who are distressed; I reassure you most earnestly."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard those words of his granting them safety, the assembled warriors gladdened him with blessings for long life, fame, and glory.
Having performed that supreme and noble deed,
the slayer of enemies, having struck down his foes,
departed from all sides after paying homage to Dhanañjaya.
Then, seeing Arjuna— who was like a rutting elephant turning back from his enemies after letting them loose—
advancing toward the kingdom of Virāṭa, [he spoke].
The Kurus were unable to advance against him;
then Pārtha, having put to flight that army of the Kuru-clouds as it fell upon him like a cloud, [prevailed].
The slayer of enemies addressed those words once more to that son of Matsya, embracing him:
"O dear one, all of you [shall remain] in the presence of your father."
The Pārthas dwell there, as is well known to you alone;
do not praise them once you have entered the city,
lest that King of the Matsyas, becoming afraid, should perish.
That army of the Kurus was conquered by me,
and the cattle were won back from the enemies by me;
thus, having entered the city according to my desire—
Uttara said:
"Tell me yourself the deed you have performed— that deed which you committed and which cannot be undone."
"I do not have the power to perform that deed;
I will not speak of you in the presence of my father.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Until you tell me, O Savyasācin,
that Jishnu has conquered the enemy host and seized all the wealth from the Kurus.
Having returned to the cremation ground and approached that *śamī* tree once more, he stood there with his limbs wounded by arrows. Then that great monkey, who resembled fire itself—
Together with the spirits, he flew up to heaven;
likewise, the illusion was established,
and he again yoked the lion to the chariot.
Having set aside that weapon which increases one's life-span,
as well as the quivers and banners of the best of the Kurus,
that Matsya departed for his city, filled with joy.
With Kirīṭin as his charioteer, the high-souled Pārtha,
the slayer of enemies, performed a supreme noble deed and struck down his foes.
Having likewise tied his hair into a braid once more,
he took up the reins of the northern horse again;
the high-souled one entered the city joyfully.
Having assumed the form of Bṛhannalā as the charioteer,
the Kurus then retreated; broken and fallen under his power,
they all went toward Hastināpura in a state of dejection.
Having approached the path, Phalguna spoke these words:
"O Prince, look here; O mighty-armed hero, all the herds of cattle have been brought together from every direction along with their cowherds."
"O Arjuna,
let them go ahead to the city and proclaim our victory;
then, in the afternoon, we shall proceed toward the city of Virāṭa."
Having comforted, watered, and bathed the horses,
let the cowherds dispatched by you go with all haste to the city to announce the pleasant news and proclaim your victory.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Uttara, hurrying, gave orders to the messengers, saying,
"By the word of Arjuna himself, announce my victory."
Then Uttara, hurrying, gave orders to the messengers according to the word of Phalguna:
"Proclaim the victory of the king!"
The enemies were broken and the cattle were won;
then those cowherds, filled with joy, entered the city and proclaimed the victory of Virāṭa, saying, "By good fortune, the wealth of cattle has been recovered."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having thus consulted and met together, those two heroes of the Bhāratas and the Matsyas then went to that śamī tree.
Having returned again with victory, though they were not yet satiated,
they loaded their own goods that had been left behind;
he, having utterly overwhelmed the entire enemy army...
Having seized all that wealth from the Kurus,
the son of Virāṭa returned to the city in high spirits,
he who was a peerless hero with Bṛhannalā as his charioteer.
Vaiśampāyana said: Having conquered the wealth as well, Virāṭa, the commander of the army,
entered the city joyfully together with the four Pāṇḍavas.
Having defeated the Trigartas in battle and recovered all their cattle,
the great king, surrounded by splendor, shone resplendent together with the sons of Pṛthā.
As that hero sat upon his throne, increasing the joy of his friends—
All the Pāṇḍavas, together with their soldiers, paid him homage;
all the subjects, along with the Brāhmaṇas, waited upon him.
Then the King of Matsya, having been honored by them and his army, greeted them in return.
Then he dismissed the twice-born and likewise the subjects;
thereafter, Virāṭa, the king of the Matsyas and commander of the army,
entered his beautiful inner apartments, which were graced by hundreds of women.

He asked further, "Where have they gone? and spoke thus. The women and maidens in his residence, as well as those who moved within the inner apartments, joyfully informed him that the cattle-wealth had been carried off by the Kurus.

Resolute in his desire for victory, Pṛthivīñjaya, out of extreme rashness, set forth alone with Bṛhannaḍā as his companion; he encountered the approaching Atirathas— Droṇa, the son of Śantanu, and Kṛpa.
King Virāṭa was deeply distressed upon hearing that his son had set out with only a single chariot against Karna, Duryodhana, and the son of Droṇa— those six great car-warriors.
Then the king spoke to all his chief ministers regarding Bṛhannaḍā as the charioteer, who increases the strength in battle.
Overpowering my own son, all the Kurus, who are experts in warfare, are driving away hundreds of thousands of cattle;
for these Kurus and whatever other lords of the earth there may be, they act in every way [to seize them].
"Having heard that the Trigartas have been defeated, they will never remain [in their place]. Therefore, let my warriors, surrounded by a great force,
go forth to rescue Uttara, who has been wounded by the Trigartas."
For the sake of his son, he quickly dispatched horses, elephants, chariots, and hosts of heroic foot soldiers.
Thus King Virāṭa, the lord of the Matsyas and commander of an akṣauhiṇī, quickly commanded that fourfold army, which was equipped with various weapons and ornaments.
"Find out quickly whether the prince lives or not—he whose driver has gone [back] as a eunuch; I believe he does not live. Having gone swiftly to my army and reached the Kurus in the north..."
Seeing that the cattle had been won back, he rejoiced in his victory.
Dharmarāja, laughing, spoke to Virāṭa, who was distressed and tormented by the Kurus:
O lord of men, if Bṛhannaḍā is the charioteer,
the enemies shall not carry off those cows of yours today,
nor all the kings assembled together with the Kurus.
In that very same way, your son, when well-guided by that charioteer, is fully capable of conquering the gods, asuras, yakṣas, and nāgas in battle.
Then those swift-moving messengers sent by him reached the city of Virāṭa and announced the victory. Thereupon,
the minister reported that supreme victory to the king.
He also described the defeat of the Kurus and the subsequent events;
all the cattle had been won back and the Kurus were defeated.
O scorcher of foes, Uttara, along with his charioteer, was safe and well.
Kaṅka said:
"By good fortune, the cattle have been won back by you and the Kurus have been defeated.
By good fortune, O bull among kings, it is heard that your son is alive."
"I do not consider it at all surprising that your son conquered the Kurus;
victory was certain for him whose charioteer was Bṛhannaḍā,
and whose driver was Mātali, the renowned charioteer of the Lord of the Gods."
"Even the charioteer of Kṛṣṇa is not equal to Bṛhannalā.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then King Virāṭa, his hair standing on end with joy, [spoke].
Having heard of the victory of that prince of immeasurable prowess,
he covered those messengers with garments and dispatched his ministers;
for once that supporting force had departed, he listened to the words of the envoys.
Delighted by Uttara’s victory, Virāṭa replied:
"Let my royal roads be made ready and adorned with banners; let the deities everywhere be honored with offerings of flowers."
Let the princes, the chief warriors, and well-adorned courtesans,
along with all musical instruments, go out to meet my son; may they be present for my son when he has achieved victory.
May the citizens, the women, and all mortals in the city wear white garments upon the road;
and may the women be adorned with fragrant garlands and ornaments.
Let all the courtesans attend upon my son,
as well as all the women together with the soldiers— those well-adorned and fortunate prostitutes.
Let them follow the path of my son.
Let Ghaṇṭāpaṇavaka quickly mount an elephant in rut and proclaim my victory at all the crossroads.
"And let Uttarā, surrounded by many young maidens and adorned with elegant attire and ornaments, go out to meet Bṛhannaḍā.
Having heard those words of the king, [he acted accordingly].
Furthermore, all of them had their hands marked with the svastika;
there were kettledrums, cymbals, and lutes,
and beautiful women in the most exquisite attire.
Likewise, the bards along with the panegyrists, playing the *nandī*, *paṇava*, and various musical instruments,
[departed] from the city of the mighty Virāṭa.
Having heard the words of the king, the citizens, with auspicious objects in their hands, as well as all the charioteers and the bards, went out to meet the son of infinite prowess.
In the city of Virāṭa, the throngs of people were delighted;
the kettledrums, trumpets, and lutes resounded,
and the women appeared in their most excellent attire.
With the sounds of panavas and ānakas proclaiming praise, as well as other musical instruments, the blare of conchs,
and sweet singing accompanied by cymbals and rhythmic clapping.
Taking him from his city, the women went out to meet their son of infinite prowess;
they were the foremost Brahmins, devoted to peace.
Those who were experts in the sequence of Vedic recitation and study,
and who were primarily devoted to auspicious rites, songs, and hymns of victory— all returned with well-pleased minds, each according to what was appropriate.
Having dispatched his army, as well as beautifully adorned maidens and courtesans,
Kaṅka, the slayer of enemies and king of the Matsyas, addressed [his men]:
"All the Trigartas and Kurus have been utterly defeated by me in battle."
Having entered the inner apartments, the two of them, filled with joy, said, "We shall play at dice with the queen.
Then the highly wise King of Matsya, being delighted, spoke these words:
"Sairandhrī, bring the dice; Kaṅka, let the game of dice begin!"
"Prepare a seat,
and taking a fan yourself, stand close by at his side.
Seeing him speaking thus, the Pāṇḍava replied.
"We have heard it said that one should not gamble with a joyful gambler;
therefore, I do not venture to play with you today while you are filled with such joy.
However, I wish to do what is pleasing to you; let the game proceed, if you so desire."
"I do not wish to play at dice in your assembly, O lord of men.
Virāṭa said:
"Women, cattle, gold, and whatever other wealth there may be—"
Grain, draft animals, goats and sheep,
and various kinds of jewels—
there is nothing of mine that you need protect, even apart from gambling.
Kaṅka said:
"O Indra among kings, O giver of honor, what use have you for gambling, which is fraught with many evils?
There are numerous faults in playing at dice; therefore, one should avoid it."
"Have you heard of, or have you seen, the Pāṇḍava Yudhiṣṭhira?
He considered his vast and prosperous kingdom, as well as his brothers who resemble the gods,
as merely a single stake."
And having lost his beloved wife Kṛṣṇā,
that gambler, the son of Pāṇḍu, will undoubtedly suffer remorse later on,
as well as for the loss of various jewels and riches.
The destruction of what has not been consumed, followed immediately by harshness of speech;
being constantly untrustworthy in the eyes of the wise, and the loss of wealth in a single day—in gambling, one may lose everything; therefore, I do not approve of gambling.
"Or rather, O King, if it pleases you, let us play. Having spoken these words, those two best of men began to play.
Vaiśampāyana said:
While the gambling match was proceeding, the King of Matsya said to the Pāṇḍava:
"Behold, such Kurus as these have been defeated in battle by my son! All these Kurus are great chariot-warriors (*atiratha*), who would be exceedingly difficult to conquer even for the gods."
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, said to the King of Matsya:
"O Kaṅka,
by good fortune your cattle have been won back and the Kurus have been defeated."
"I consider it most extraordinary that Uttara would conquer the Kurus;
how could he not be victorious when Bṛhannaḍā is his charioteer?
Then Virāṭa, agitated and overwhelmed with indignation, [spoke].
Immediately thereafter, filled with rage, he spoke these words to the wandering mendicant:
"By such a warrior, a wise and great archer as [I am],
Kaṅka— "

The Kurus were defeated in battle; what wonder is there in that for a Brahmin? When such a heroic charioteer stands upon his chariot, what would not be considered a marvel if he were to perform this difficult feat?
Virāṭa said:
"I have seen many men and powerful charioteers;
yet, though I have exerted myself, I have never before seen anyone who could be both a driver and a warrior."
"One should not act against the wishes of kings, but should speak what is agreeable and favorable to them;
by acting against the wishes of kings, one never prospers in happiness. Having been addressed thus, the king of Matsya became angry and spoke to the Pāṇḍava.
"O wretched Brahmin, you praise my eunuch as being equal to my son!
You do not know what should and should not be said; surely you hold me in contempt.
Why would he not defeat all those heroes, with Bhīṣma and Droṇa at their head?"
"O Brahmin, because of our friendship, I forgive this offense of yours.
You must not speak such words to me again, if you wish to live.
Then, O enhancer of the Kurus, Kaṅka laughed and spoke once more.
"O Indra among kings, let the victory of Bṛhannalā be proclaimed throughout the city!
Surely Uttara will perform the work of a charioteer;
some omen has arisen, and my reasoning is firm."
"O Indra among kings, since I know this, it shall not be otherwise.
Even the Kurus, though possessed of great heroism and difficult even for the gods to conquer— along with Soma, Varuṇa, and Āditya, together with Kubera and Hutāśana."
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Where Droṇa, as well as Bhīṣma, the son of Droṇa, Vaikartana, Kṛpa,
Aśvatthāman, Vikarṇa, Somadatta, and Jayadratha [are stationed];
Bhūriśravas, Śala, Bhūri, and the heroic Jalasaṃdhi;
Duryodhana, Duṣprasaha, Duḥśāsana, and Vivimśati;
Vṛṣasena, Aśvasena, Vātavega, and Suvarcas.
Bāhlīka, Bhūriṣeṇa, and Yuyutsu, the scorcher of foes; Śakuni the son of Subala, Dyumatsena, and the king of the Śālvas; and many other heroes who were lords of various realms.
O King, accompanied by Kṛpa, the foremost of teachers, the Kurus— chariot-warriors and leaders of chariot-divisions, equipped with bows and swords—
along with Duryodhana, O Indra among kings, and other great car-warriors, [prepared for battle].
Even Śatakratu himself, surrounded by the hosts of Maruts,
could not conquer that army when it was filled with Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and others— even if he were enraged.
Who else but Bṛhannaḍā could fight against them when they were all assembled?
He whose equal in the strength of his arms has never existed nor will ever exist;
he in whom great joy arises upon seeing a fierce battle;
he who conquered all the gods, asuras, and great serpents together.
With such an ally as this, why would he not be victorious?
Is there any man like him in the world, whether in heaven or on earth?
How much more so here, where he has already been conquered by a mere human?
Vaiśampāyana said:
Agitated by that [news] and with a heart torn asunder, O dear one, the king spoke these words, not knowing Yudhiṣṭhira’s [true state].
"Kaṅka, O best of the twice-born, do not speak such disagreeable words.
Virāṭa said:
"Though you have been forbidden many times, you still do not restrain your speech."
"If there were no restrainer, no one at all would practice dharma.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thereupon, the king, becoming enraged, struck him violently with the die.
Raising his right arm, which resembled the expanded hood of a *takṣaka* serpent,
the enraged Virāṭa struck at Karṇa’s right side,
while rebuking Yudhiṣṭhira in the face out of anger, saying, "Not so! in the midst of the battle.
Strongly struck, blood flowed from his nose; King Virāṭa, the lord of the earth, was hit by the dice. The mighty-armed king remained silent, looking sorrowfully at Kṛṣṇā.
Then, from the head of that great-armed high-souled one, blood resembling a red lotus began to flow due to the blow.
Before it reached the ground, Pārtha caught it with both his hands.
And the righteous-souled one glanced at Draupadī, who was standing by his side. She, who followed the will of her husband’s mind, understood that intention;
and the daughter of Drupada became despondent, terrified, and enraged.
Restraining her tears and her grief, she who sought her husband’s ultimate welfare quickly caught the blood with her fine upper garment; dazed by sorrow, the Sairandhrī held the blood in the cloth.
Having filled a golden vessel and a flawless bronze one,
and having filled a golden water-vessel,
she received that blood which flowed from the Pāṇḍava.
Virāṭa said to her there, "What should be done about this?
Sairandhrī replied,
"O Sairandhrī, answer my question truthfully and in its entirety."
O King, as this blood of Kaṅka falls upon the earth,
your kingdom will undoubtedly perish swiftly;
furthermore, Purandara shall not send rain for twelve years.
Calamities arise and crops do not grow anywhere; O Indra among kings, misfortune shall befall both the monarch and his city. — Virāṭa.
"Sairandhrī, why is this blood being caught by your upper garment?
O large-eyed one, tell me the reason for it as I ask you. Sairandhrī:
O King of kings, for as many drops of Kaṅka’s blood as fall upon the earth,
for that many years shall there be no rain in your kingdom;
this is the omen, O Indra among kings, regarding Kaṅka’s blood that has been shown by me.
"Let it be held by your upper garment so that no harm may come to you.
Janamejaya said:
"Furthermore, the gods have come to witness this superhuman battle."
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O sinless one, tell me what they did after that—
those gods, headed by Vāsava and preceded by the ṛṣis."
The hosts of Yakṣas and Gandharvas, as well as the throngs of Apsarases,
beheld that superhuman battle between the Kurus and Phalguna—
the fierce and most terrifying encounter of one against many.
Then [he described] the employment and withdrawal of divine weapons,
performed with lightness, skill, and variety by those masters through their diligent efforts;
and [the combat between] Bhīṣma, Śaradvata, Droṇa, Karṇa, and the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow.
Seeing that other kings had been conquered, the denizens of heaven departed;
all of them were thoroughly delighted and praised him again and again as he traveled swiftly in that celestial chariot of unimpeded course.
The celestial dwellers returned to the third heaven without attachment,
while the Kurus, struck by Arjuna’s arrows and mangled by shafts,
marched toward the Kurus with their full forces and mounts.
And from the city of Virāṭa, an army crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots,
commanded by powerful Kṣatriya warriors,
set out swiftly from the city, dispatched by Virāṭa.
Accompanied by his charioteer, he returned to that subduer of enemies; while hundreds of musical instruments resounded and the area was crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots,
Arjuna [remained there].
A tumultuous roar of joy arose from the women and children;
a tumultuous sound filled the city, and dust ascended toward the sky.
"Have the Kurus indeed retreated and gone back to the city? they asked.
And those very great archers, who were so mindful, have been defeated by us. O hero, put on your armor and urge on your horses; proceed with speed toward the city of Virāṭa.
Uttara might perhaps not hear the thundering of the palm-strikes nor the twang of the Gāṇḍīva, nor would he see the banner, thinking, "This may be my own kinsman."
This is the vanguard of the Matsyas, with well-adorned courtesans;
maidens are seen upon chariots, and warriors in various garments. Here I see Uttarā, surrounded by her companions.
The divisions of the army shine forth— elephants and armored horses,
chariot-warriors and foot-soldiers; though many are not armed with weapons,
they all appear to me joyful, clad in garments of bright colors.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"And there was no obstruction to my mind here as there was regarding my own kinsmen;
therefore, Uttara quickly assembled many of his own people."
The slayer of enemies, that tiger among men, full of affection and joy, embraced him who had arrived once again, time and again, saying:
"By good fortune you are victorious; may prosperity be yours! By good fortune the charioteer Bṛhannalā [is here]."
"O Uttara, by good fortune you have come to the battle; there is no fear for you whatsoever. This victorious one has conquered those Kurus in combat with but a single chariot."
By the strength of his arms, those cows were won by me;
because the Kurus of immeasurable splendor were defeated by him in battle,
this youth, who resembles a son of the gods, performed that deed.
Having agitated the Kuru circle, that tiger among men forcibly won back the cattle in battle and protected me as well—
Vaiśampāyana said.
Having heard the words of Uttara as he praised Arjuna,
and being urged by the prince, those who proclaimed auspicious victory then [honored him] with well-prepared perfumes, garlands, and incenses.
The maidens honored Pārtha, the slayer of enemies, by scattering [garlands] over him. Then Uttara, being showered with auspicious perfumes and various garlands,
entered his city at his ease, filled with joy.
Kettledrums, trumpets, and flutes,
along with women in diverse attire,
[issued] from the city of the mighty Virāṭa.
Having emerged, he congratulated Bhūmijaya;
yet, though being praised there for his victory,
the son of Virāṭa did not rejoice.
Being thus addressed by those people, he,
with his mind inwardly fixed on the son of Pāṇḍu, looked at him;
then the son of Virāṭa [offered] excellent gifts.
The son of Pāṇḍu took garments from his friends,
honoring those assembled women, while the maidens exclaimed, "By good fortune, the army has been conquered!"
Having praised the charioteer Bṛhannalā,
and being honored by the citizens, as well as by the women and the people of the countryside,
he reached the palace gate and announced himself to his father.
Then the gatekeeper, having entered and prostrated with palms joined in reverence, addressed Virāṭa as follows,
after first honoring him with blessings of victory.
"O King, Pṛthuyaśas has returned after defeating his enemies;
accompanied by Bṛhannaḍā, your son stands waiting at the gate."
Surrounded by the chief warriors and courtesans,
and accompanied by the people of the city and the countryside, being honored with blessings of victory,
the King of Matsya, filled with joy, then spoke these words to his steward:
"Let both of them be ushered in quickly; I am eager to see them.
But Karna, the king of the Kurus, whispered softly to the *kṣattṛ*:
"Let Uttara enter alone; Bṛhannaḍā must not be admitted."
For this is the solemn vow undertaken by him, O mighty-armed one:
"Whoever should inflict a wound upon my body or cause blood to appear,
except when engaged in battle, shall undoubtedly not live."
Highly incensed upon seeing me covered in blood, he would not tolerate it and might slay Virāṭa here, along with his ministers, army,
and mounts. Therefore, Uttarā alone should be brought in from him, and not Bṛhannaḍā.

Whether it be Indra, or Kubera, or Yama, or likewise Varuṇa—the one who sheds my blood he would crush; how much more so a mere mortal? Let that valiant man stand right there at the gate for even a moment.
Thus spoke the righteous Yudhiṣṭhira of noble intellect.
Having spoken thus, the virtuous King Yudhiṣṭhira, endowed with forgiveness,
sat down silently in the assembly hall together with the King of Matsya.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then the king’s eldest son, Pṛthivīñjaya, entered;
having saluted his father’s feet, he beheld Dharmarāja.
Beholding Yudhiṣṭhira with a sidelong glance at his father’s feet, Uttara— seeing him drenched in blood, distracted, and yet innocent—
then burned within his heart like one seized by death.
Who, desiring to go toward death, has been touched by a serpent at his feet?
[He is] Vaiśampāyana, a learned Brāhmaṇa, the best of Brahmins, capable of occupying the throne of Indra.
"One such as this is worthy of worship and salutation; he must not be troubled.
Having heard his son's words, Virāṭa, the enhancer of the kingdom, his mind overwhelmed with trepidation, replied with these words to Uttara.
Virāṭa said:
"O mighty-armed son, having heard of your victory, I was filled with joy;
however, I allowed time to pass by means of playing at dice."
"Then Uttara, the increaser of the kingdom, conquered all the Kurus.
"I said this, my son, but Kaṅka replied, 'No, it was Bṛhannalā.
She indeed conquered all the Kurus," he said to me repeatedly.
"O son, while your celebrated victory was being praised by me,
Kaṅka spoke with anger regarding the victory of Bṛhannalā,
as you sat in a secluded spot attended by Sairandhrī."
Then Uttara, as if in great haste, questioned his father:
"O King, by whom has he been struck? By whom has this evil deed been committed?
Virāṭa said:
"This crooked man has been struck by me, for he does not deserve even this much:
that while you, a hero, were being praised, he praised a eunuch.
O son, this evil-souled one, who has joined the side of the enemy, has been struck by me."
At that time, I was filled with envy because of the praises bestowed upon Bṛhannalā.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard this from his father, he became exceedingly angry and spoke these words to his father.
Uttara said:
"O King, you have committed an improper act; let him be propitiated immediately, lest the terrible poison of a Brahmin consume you along with your very roots."

Until the entire lineage of the Matsyas has reached its end without exception— this [fire], having grown great and increased, shall consume it all. Having prostrated like a staff upon the surface of the earth at his feet, [they said:]
"Taking his feet in his hands, let him first be propitiated.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard these words of his son, Virāṭa, the enhancer of the kingdom, [acted accordingly].
He asked forgiveness from the son of Kuntī, who was like a fire covered by ashes.
But as the king was seeking his pardon, the Pāṇḍava replied:
"O King, this has been forgiven for a long time; no resentment remains within me."
"For if this blood from my nose were to fall upon the earth, O great king, you would perish along with your kingdom; of this there is no doubt.
I do not blame you, O King, for that which might strike one who is innocent."
"O Great King, one who is powerful will swiftly meet with a terrible fate.
Having said this, that lord of men wiped away the blood;
but when the bleeding had ceased, Bṛhannaḍā entered.
The son said to the king:
"It is not fitting for that great-souled one— whose arms are unsurpassed, who is praiseworthy, and whose deeds are marvelous— to stand here at the gate."
Having paid homage to Virāṭa and Kaṅka, he stood before them. Having asked forgiveness from the Kuru prince Uttara who had returned from the battle,
the king embraced him firmly and led him into his magnificent palace.
Then Matsya praised him while Savyasācin listened:
"O increaser of Kaikeyī’s joy, through you I have a true heir;
there has never been, nor will there ever be, a son equal to you."
He who would not miss his mark even when walking at a pace of a thousand steps— he who is a hero, light-handed, and swift in prowess,
that Karna— how, O dear one, did your encounter with that Karna come to pass?
In the entire world of men, there is no one equal to him;
he who is as unshakeable as the ocean and as difficult to withstand as the fire of time— O dear son, how was your encounter with that Bhīṣma?
He whose great and unsurpassed vow is renowned throughout the world— by whom,
for the sake of his father, a terrible and most difficult life of celibacy was undertaken,
and by whom war was formerly waged against the son of Jamadagni.
O tiger among men, he was never defeated in battle by Bhīṣma;
he is indeed valiant, invincible, learned, heroic, and has conquered his senses. He acts with speed, is firm, wise, and renowned for all his deeds.
"O dear one, tell me all of this: how did your battle take place in combat with Bhīṣma, the elder of the Kurus,
who had defeated in battle the exceedingly powerful Rāma of the Bhṛgu lineage?"
How did that encounter take place with the hero who was the end-maker of the Kṣatriyas, a mass of splendor difficult to approach,
the disciple of Akṣa, mighty-armed, invincible even by the gods,
and resembling Rudra at the fire of cosmic destruction?
O dear one, how was your encounter with that Drona— the twice-born preceptor of the Vrishni heroes and the Pandavas, the teacher of all the Kshatriyas, and the foremost among all wielders of weapons?

How did he meet with that hero known as Aśvatthāman, the son of the preceptor, who is the foremost among all wielders of weapons? For all the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra are indeed possessed of great heroism and mighty strength.
And how, O dear one, was your encounter with those heroes?
Seeing whom in battle they sink down like merchants whose wealth has been stolen.
And how, O dear one, was your encounter with that Kṛpa?
"How was your encounter, my son, with Duryodhana, that prince who could pierce even a mountain with his great arrows?
My enemies have been submerged; a pleasant breeze blows upon me."
Since you have won back that wealth seized by the Kurus in battle—
having surely driven away all those bulls among men, though they were all mighty-armed and overcome by fear— in that conflict, [you have achieved this].
All the cattle-wealth, snatched away like meat by tigers,
was seized and recovered by the powerful one who had escaped;
O Uttara, best of Kṣatriyas, by what means did he overcome his enemies?
You are utterly victorious in battle...
[and] all those sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who possess great heroism and mighty strength—
how, O dear one, did your encounter with those heroes take place?
Uttara said:
"The cattle were not conquered by me, nor were the enemies conquered by me;
rather, all that work was performed by some son of the gods."
For that son of a god restrained me as I was fleeing in fear; seeing the Kurus led by Bhīṣma and Droṇa, he prevented me from becoming despondent in battle.
And that youth, resembling the wielder of the thunderbolt, stood upon the seat of his chariot;
by him those cattle were won back, and by him those Kurus were conquered.
That deed belongs to that hero; it was not done by me, O dear one.
For that heroic one, with his arrows, turned away Śāradvata Droṇa, the son of Droṇa, the Sūta’s son, and Bhīṣma;
and in that battle, he [overwhelmed] Duryodhana like a leader of an elephant herd.
He spoke to the terrified prince of great strength as he was being routed:
"I see no protection for you whatsoever in Hastināpura;
nor can the pleasures of Hastināpura be enjoyed by one who is fleeing."
"O son of the Kauravas, strive with all your might to preserve your life;
you shall not escape by fleeing, O King—set your mind on battle! By conquering, you shall enjoy the earth, or being slain, you shall attain heaven."
That tiger among men turned back, discharging arrows resembling thunderbolts;
surrounded by his ministers, the king roared from his chariot like a hissing elephant.
At that moment, O noble one, my hair stood on end and my thighs grew stiff with fear.

That youthful hero of lion-like build, having scattered with his arrows that army which resembled a mass of thick clouds, drove back that host of chariots; O King, laughing at those Kurus, the powerful youth stripped them of their garments.
By that single hero, six chariot-divisions were surrounded,
like grass-eating deer in the forest by a maddened tiger;
[he overcame] the horses, the elephants, and the heroic archers.
Thousands were slain and the Kuru army was broken;
having pierced the Sūtaputra with arrows and killed his horses, that great car-warrior,
equal to the sons of gods in battle, took up a blood-red cloth.
Furthermore, in that battle, he struck Bhīṣma with four arrows;
having pierced him and his horses, he then seized his white garment.
And the powerful one pierced Duryodhana with seven arrows.
Having pierced him, he struck his horses and seized his yellow garment;
then that powerful one [attacked] Droṇa, Kṛpa, Somadatta, Jayadratha,
Bhūriśravas— who resembles Indra— and the great car-warrior Śakuni.
Having pierced even those led by Duḥśāsana with three arrows each,
he took away their various costly garments;
likewise, having pierced the preceptor’s son in battle with two arrows.
Having cut through the bow of Vikarṇa, he took his two blue garments.
Virāṭa said:
"Where is that hero, the mighty-armed and highly illustrious son of a god?"
"He who won back my wealth that was seized by the Kurus in battle—
I wish to see and honor that one of great strength,
by whom both you and the cattle were protected, O son of a god."
"I shall give that daughter to him, as well as villages and gold,
a shimmering waistband, and hundreds of thousands of women.
Uttara said:
"O dear one, that powerful son of a god has vanished;
however, I believe he will manifest himself again tomorrow or the day after.
Vaiśampāyana said:
While the Pāṇḍava was thus living there in disguise under the name Satra, Virāṭa did not recognize him as Pārtha Arjuna.
Then, having been granted permission by the high-souled Virāṭa, Pārtha—
Having consulted with the son of the King of Matsya, Dhanañjaya said:
"Speak thus to King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Virāṭa. Having spoken these words, Pārtha suddenly entered the auspicious inner apartments.
Having addressed the son of Kuntī, Uttara spoke these words:
"I shall thus report to King Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma.
He himself then gave those garments to the daughter of Virāṭa.
But the beautiful woman, having accepted those various, fine, and costly garments, was filled with joy. Vaiśampāyana said:
Having bestowed his garments upon his friends in the palace of Virāṭa, the wearer of the diadem and garland rejoiced,
having performed that great feat in the midst of the battle.
Desiring to see him, he approached Pārtha;
then, looking toward Dharmarāja,
Pārtha questioned Bhīmasena.
"Does the King of Dharma not speak to me at all, as he did before, with his face averted?
Having spoken thus to him who was filled with apprehension, [he continued:]
Seeing Arjuna and Bhīmasena there,
King Yudhiṣṭhira, having wiped away his blood, looked at those two heroes and spoke.
O Pārtha, while you were being honored by that evil-minded King Virāṭa, I was struck;
from that blow, drops of blood [fell].
Thinking, "If they see me, they might touch the earth," I then covered my face and sat down, restraining my anger.
But while you, the hero, are enraged and dissatisfied,
King Virāṭa shall find no peace;
for he did not recognize your very prowess.
O Pārtha, the strength of Channa was increased by his armor;
this [armor] was bestowed upon me by Virāṭa,
yet beholding you, I have not attained joy.
When he, immeasurable and possessed of great strength,
who had resorted to tranquility, had spoken thus,
the powerful and impatient Bhīmasena [attacked him].
Enraged, he spoke these words to Dhanañjaya:
"O Pārtha, even Bṛhaspati, the foremost among the wise, has never declared that forgiveness is always the right time."
For one who is patient is indeed despised by all,
just as a serpent deprived of its venom;
therefore, slay Virāṭa this very day with speed.
Together with our sons, grandsons, kinsmen, and armies,
we shall today swiftly install the son of Dharma upon the throne; for this Matsya is now our enemy.
Furthermore, because the daughter of Pañcāla, Kṛṣṇā, was neglected by him when she was being pursued by Kīcaka,
he therefore does not deserve the title of "King."
O Pārtha, by your prowess, you shall become king;
this Yudhiṣṭhira shall be the king of the Kurus,
and let the renowned one be king among the Mātsyas.
Today I shall split his body into a hundred pieces,
just as Arjuna splits a water-filled jar with a mace.
"O King, by your forbearance, all our faults have been forgiven.
Therefore, having indeed slain him along with his army and his kinsmen— " Vaiśampāyana said:
"And afterwards, we shall slay all the Kurus without a doubt.
Bhīmasena and the others likewise said to him, "So be it.
Then the high-souled son of Dharma spoke to him.
If he— who is patient and generous— does not present himself to meet his enraged and terrible father along with his wife,
then let him be fit for execution despite his efforts at conciliation.
"This evil-minded man must not be killed, nor indeed should you, O Kurus, O Arjuna.
Tomorrow at dawn, we shall enter the assembly hall here upon our thrones,
adorned in royal attire, provided that he does not disregard us there."
"Later, we shall all be slain along with our kinsmen by Virāṭa. Then, O son of Kuntī, having deliberated in secret with Uttara,
he [Arjuna] explained the entire course of action to be taken toward King Yudhiṣṭhira.
Then, O bull among men, that bull of the Bharata race, being delighted, carried out those arrangements exactly as they were, together with the son of Matsya;
and having deliberated upon all their duties, the Pāṇḍavas [acted accordingly].
The Pāṇḍavas, who are devoted to righteousness, dwelt that night there;
and the wise King of the Matsyas, together with his son, remained delighted throughout that night with a tranquil mind.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, on the third day, the five Pāṇḍava brothers,
perceiving that it was their own counsel [that had been followed], had their eyes wide open with joy.
Having fulfilled their supreme vow, they went to the assembly hall of Virāṭa;
and there they all accepted everything from the king, the son of Dharma. But when Arjuna saw that [the time] had come according to the agreement, he took up the umbrella.
Bhīmasena took the yak-tail whisk, the two sons of Mādrī took their excellent weapons,
and Draupadī took her choice betel-leaf box along with her own vessel;
his daughter went forth joyfully, intent on performing service for him.
Having bathed, wearing white garments, having observed their vows at the appointed time,
and adorned with all ornaments, those great chariot-warriors shone brilliantly like elephants with lotuses on their foreheads, placing Yudhiṣṭhira at their head.
Having entered the assembly hall of Virāṭa, they then sat upon the royal thrones;
all of them, radiant as fire, were like the sacrificial fires upon their altars. When they had thus taken their seats there, Virāṭa, the lord of the earth, [approached].
When that night had passed, having completed his morning rites and given cows, gold, and other gifts to the Brahmins according to the prescribed rules,
he came to the assembly hall to attend to all matters of state.
He wondered: "How have these beings, who resemble gods, come to this assembly and taken their seats so adorned? How did they enter here, seeing the illustrious Pāṇḍavas blazing like fires?"
Having assumed the royal attire, the king was struck with wonder:
"What is this? What kind of ritual is this? and the king became as if afflicted by fear.
Upon seeing those foremost of men, the monarch fell into despair.
Seeing him seated upon the royal throne, the king was struck with amazement; and after reflecting for a moment, the lord of the earth, filled with wrath,
then spoke to Kaṅka, who stood there in the form of a god.

He was seated by the hosts of Maruts, like the lord of the thirty gods. You, it is said, were appointed by me as the superintendent of the dice-game and a member of the assembly; why then are you now seated upon the royal throne, adorned with ornaments?
O King, having heard those words of Virāṭa with a desire for jest, Arjuna, smiling, spoke these words: "O King,
this man is worthy even to ascend the throne of Indra."
Devoted to Brahman, learned in the scriptures, renounced, dedicated to sacrifice, and firm in his vows— he is Dharma incarnate, the best among the valiant,
preeminent in wisdom in this world, and the ultimate refuge of asceticism.
He is skilled in weapons in battle within the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile;
no other man knows this, nor will anyone ever know it—
not any gods, nor any asuras, nor any humans, nor any rākṣasas.
The foremost of Gandharvas and Yakṣas, along with Kinnaras and great serpents;
far-sighted and of great splendor, beloved by the people of the city and the countryside;
the Atiratha of the Pāṇḍavas, devoted to sacrifice and righteousness, and self-controlled.
A royal sage equal to a great ṛṣi, renowned throughout the three worlds,
he was powerful, steadfast, gentle, truthful, and had conquered his senses;
in wealth and accumulated treasures, he was like Śakra and Vaiśravaṇa.

Just as Manu, possessed of great splendor, was the protector of the worlds, so too is this one of great splendor, who acts for the benefit of all creatures. This Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī, is the bull among the Kurus.
"O King, it is by his power that all of us brothers have come to possess great majesty, great strength,
and great prowess; indeed, it is through his asceticism alone that we possess these manifold powers."
"O sirs, let us all become equal to this man;
as long as we remain attentive to his command, we shall be most highly honored by the gods while protecting [him]."
His fame remains established in the world like the radiance of the rising sun; the rays of his glory traverse all directions,
just as the rays of light follow the splendor of the risen sun.
Ten thousand swift elephants followed behind him, O King, as long as he dwelt among the Kurus; and thirty thousand chariots adorned with golden garlands followed him.

Always accompanied by excellent horses, they followed behind him; and at that time, O King, ten thousand horses followed him. Eight hundred charioteers, adorned with polished gem-studded earrings, followed him.
In former times, they praised him along with the bards, just as the ṛṣis praised Śakra; the Kurus constantly waited upon him like servants,
and all the kings, O King, attended him as the immortals attend the Lord of Wealth.
At that time, O great king, he caused all the rulers of the earth to pay tribute—
whether they were independent or even powerless— just as one might tax commoners.
There were eighty-eight thousand high-souled *snātakas*.
They depend upon this king who is steadfast in his vows of good conduct.
He [provides for] the aged, the helpless, the deformed, and the lame; those who are mute, squint-eyed, diseased, and so forth, as well as the wretched, the blind, the deaf, and others.

O lord, he protected his subjects with righteousness as if they were his own sons. This king was restrained in his vows regarding dharma, self-control, and even anger; he was possessed of great serenity, devoted to the Brahmins, and a speaker of truth.
O lord of men, by his glorious majesty, that Suyodhana, along with his followers, Karṇa, and even the son of Subala, is scorched; indeed,
his virtues cannot be fully enumerated.
This son of Pāṇḍu is eternally devoted to dharma and compassionate; endowed with such qualities, this great king, this bull among monarchs and lord of the earth—
how could he not deserve a seat worthy of a king?
Until he was bound by his enemies with the snare of truth through deceit,
this [conduct] remained common among men; however,
this vow of secret wandering belongs to his thirteenth year.

That vow was indeed fulfilled in your very presence; today that son of Pāṇḍu has emerged from it, having properly observed his observance, like the sun emerging from the midst of clouds. Behold him now, O wonder, who has become as unbearable in his prowess!
"I consider this king worthy even of the throne of Śakra;
therefore, let there be no astonishment in you, for I do not speak falsely to you.
Virāṭa said:
"If this king is Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī and descendant of Kuru,
which of these is his brother Arjuna, and which is the mighty Bhīma?
Which is Nakula, or Sahadeva, or the illustrious Draupadī?"
When the Pārthas had been defeated at dice and were no longer known to be anywhere,
Arjuna said:
"O lord of men, this Ballava who speaks here is your cook."
This is the mighty-armed Bhīma, possessed of terrible speed and prowess;
having slain the Krodhavaśas on Mount Gandhamādana,
he brought back divine *saugandhika* flowers for the sake of Kṛṣṇā.
"This Gandharva is indeed the slayer of the evil-minded Kīcakas;
he has killed tigers, bears, and boars in your women’s quarters,
as well as Hiḍimba, Baka, Kirmīra, and Jaṭāsura."
Having slain [the enemies], he made the forest free of thorns and pleasant in every way.
He who was the horse-keeper is this Nakula, the scorcher of foes;
and Sahadeva, the counter of cattle—these two sons of Mādrī are great chariot-warriors.
Adorned with erotic attire and ornaments, handsome and illustrious,
those two bulls among men were capable of contending against many thousands of chariots.
This woman, with eyes like lotus petals, a slender waist, and a lovely smile—
O King, Sairandhrī Draupadī, on whose account the Kīcakas were slain—
she who is the beloved daughter of Drupada and the younger sister of Dhṛṣṭadyumna— [is here],
O Bhīma!
Let it be understood that Draupadī was born from the sacrificial fire-pit. There is no one else on earth so skilled in weapons;
likewise, this Dhanañjaya, the son of Kuntī, is the foremost among those who handle the bow.

By him, O lord of men, the Khāṇḍava forest and the Nāga grove were burnt along with the serpents, even though Śatakratu was unwilling; and the rain was indeed checked by that invincible one with a shower of arrows.
O Lord of the Earth, all the kings have been brought here by him; O King, he has assumed the dress of a woman in your palace—
he whom they call Bṛhannaḍā, Arjuna, the best among victors.
"I am Arjuna, O Great King; clearly my name has reached your ears. I am the son of Pṛthā, born after Bhīma and before the twins. We have dwelt happily in your residence, O Great King."
They lived their life in concealment like creatures dwelling in a womb.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When those five Pāṇḍava heroes had been described by Arjuna...
Then Uttara, the son of Virāṭa, his hair standing on end with joy, recounted the prowess of Arjuna, who was like Mahendra himself. Uttara said:
Then Uttara once again pointed out those sons of Pṛthā:
"This one, whose body is as fair as pure gold and who is like a full-grown great lion— "
With a fierce nose and broad, long eyes, with copper-colored, elongated eyes— this is the King of the Kurus;
moreover, he moves with the gait of a lordly elephant in rut.
Pure and fair like refined gold,
with broad and expansive shoulders and long, heavy arms, and a large belly— behold him, behold him!
But this great archer at his side,
dark-complexioned and youthful, resembling the leader of a herd of elephants,
with shoulders as high as a lion’s and the gait of a king of elephants—
This hero Arjuna has eyes as broad as lotuses;
those two best of men who are near the king are these twins, equal to Viṣṇu and Mahendra.
In the entire world of humans, there are none who are equal to these two in beauty, strength, or virtue; yet, by their side stands she whose limbs are like the finest gold.
This radiance, appearing as if embodied as a fair Gaurī,
with the luster of a blue lotus like a goddess of the gods,
stands there black-hued as if Lakṣmī herself were incarnate.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having thus introduced those five Pārtha-Pāṇḍavas to the king,
his eyes blossomed with joy at what had never before happened to anyone.

04,066.011d–04,066.012c Just as it was seen before King Virāṭa regarding the Kurus: "This is he who, like a lion among deer, moved through the multitudes of chariots in the midst of his enemies, slaying their best and most excellent warriors."
Pierced by this single arrow, the great elephant Mātaṅga was struck down;
wearing a golden girth, he fell to the earth on his tusks in the midst of battle. By him the cattle were won and the Kurus were conquered in combat.
"O father, that deed of that hero was not performed by me;
my ears were deafened by the blast of his conch shell,
and as I recall the sound of his bow, my hair stands on end."

I see this monkey on the banner being reviled by the spirits along with their followers; I do not see him taking up terrible arrows, nor discharging volleys of shafts, nor drawing his bow in the midst of battle.
And these arrows released from that bow, feathered one after another—
those blood-drinking iron shafts (*nārāca*)— did not fall upon unintended targets in battle. [The heads,
arms, thighs, and chests of those] severed by sharp iron shafts [fell].
The corpses of warriors, along with their horses and riders, are seen there; by this [battle] was set flowing that river of blood-water,
so terrible in form, remembering which my mind even now [is still shaken].
He trembles like a plantain tree shaken by a fierce wind.
By this hero of terrible deeds, O father, the car-warriors headed by Bhīṣma and Droṇa, together with Duryodhana, have been utterly defeated.
"This son of a god restrained me as I was fleeing in fear;
by the strength of his arms, I have returned alive once more.
Having heard those words of his, the powerful king of the Matsyas [spoke].
Overwhelmed by Yudhiṣṭhira, he replied to Uttara as follows:
"I believe the time has come to appease the Pāṇḍava;
and I shall give Uttara to the son of Pṛthā, if it is your wish."
Uttara said:
"They are worthy of honor, worship, and respect; it is my opinion that the time has come for them to be honored. Let the illustrious Pāṇḍavas, who are deserving of worship, be honored."
Virāṭa said:
"Indeed, I too had fallen under the power of my enemies in battle;
I was liberated by Bhīmasena, and likewise the cattle were won back."

"By the strength of their arms, our victory in battle has been secured. Therefore, may you be blessed; let us all, together with our ministers, propitiate Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī and bull among the Pāṇḍavas, along with his younger brothers."
"Whatever we, in our ignorance, may have said to the lord of men, he,
being a righteous son of Pāṇḍu, ought to forgive it all.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Virāṭa, being exceedingly gratified,
met with the king and made an agreement;
he surrendered his entire kingdom to him.

Then the high-souled and powerful King of Matsya, placing Dhananjaya at the forefront, spoke thus: "By good fortune! By good fortune!"—addressing all the Pāṇḍavas along with their army, treasury, and city.
Having smelled their heads and embraced them again and again—
Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīma, and the two Pāṇḍava sons of Mādrī—
the commander of the army, Virāṭa, could not have enough of gazing upon them.
Being well-pleased, he then spoke to King Yudhiṣṭhira:
"By good fortune, you have all arrived safely from the forest;
by good fortune, this period of hardship has been endured in secret from those of evil intent."
"I ask you about a certain matter; let it be told exactly as it is.
I believe that even for you gods, the power to transform your forms exists; yet I perceive that your appearance now is not as it was before."
When you were like ordinary men,
your form, radiance, strength, fortitude, and all your qualities were unlike those of others;
yet in an instant, you became like gods, born like Sūrya, Agni, and Rudra.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Delighted by our virtues of truthfulness, purity, and austerity, the gods—
Dharmadurgā and the others— bestowed upon us the qualities that cause the manifestation of [divine] forms."
"O Pārthas, let this kingdom of ours, and whatever other wealth we possess,
all of that be accepted by the sons of Kuntī without hesitation.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard those words of his, the powerful King of Matsya embraced Dhanañjaya and all the Pāṇḍavas;
and, O King, having paid homage to the king who had been consecrated in the kingdom, he [honored them].
Virāṭa, the commander of the army, could not have enough of beholding them;
being filled with joy, he then addressed King Yudhiṣṭhira:
"By good fortune, you have all arrived safely from the forest."
"By good fortune, those evil-minded ones have remained unaware of the hardships you endured.
This entire kingdom and whatever wealth you possess is undivided; you ought not to feel any anxiety."
Having heard the words of Virāṭa and of the high-souled Pārtha,
Uttara, overcome with emotion toward Yudhiṣṭhira, replied as follows.
I consider it the right time to bring about the reconciliation of the Pāṇḍava;
he is radiant, powerful, heroic, the sovereign lord of kings, and a master. And [bring] Uttarā, the one of excellent limbs, to the son of Pṛthā, O crusher of enemies.
Having prostrated ourselves, we shall then become submissive; and we,
along with all our ministers, having propitiated Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, shall wait upon him, O King— what shall we do?
"O King, you were captured in battle and released by him;
through the prowess of their arms, the cattle were won back by you,
and since the Kurus of immeasurable splendor were defeated by them in combat."
Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, has accomplished all of this.
The Pāṇḍavas are worthy of honor, worship, respect, and rising to greet;
they are worthy of the guest-offering (*arghya*) and salutation. In my opinion, the time for this has arrived.
Let the Pāṇḍavas—who are worthy of worship, venerable, and highly fortunate—be honored;
for if they were provoked to anger, these men, who are like venomous serpents, would leave nothing remaining.
Therefore, let us quickly approach Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī.
"May it be well with you; together with the high-souled Pārthas, we seek your favor.
Having placed Uttarā at our head—she who has bathed her head and is adorned—I know all this regarding their strength and prowess."
Having heard from Uttara about the birth of Phalguna in a great lineage and his prowess, Virāṭa was overwhelmed by grief and delusion;
and beholding Uttarā as well, he reflected upon what the occasion required.
Then Virāṭa, together with his ministers, his wife, and his kinsmen,
having placed Uttarā— who had bathed her head— at the forefront, joined his palms in reverence.
Virāṭa said:
He quickly fell to the ground in the presence of the Pāṇḍava, saying:
"May the great king Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, be gracious. Because his form and attire were concealed, the fire was not seen, being covered by grass."

Together with my sons and attendants, I have come before you with bowed head. Whatever we, in our ignorance, reviled the lord of the earth— all that was done out of disrespect, like common folk, and was improper.

"O King, he who knows the Dharma and is affectionate toward his kinsmen ought to forgive all of this. O Ruler of the Earth, I relinquish to you this kingdom of mine—my city and my realm, along with its army and treasury; I am your servant, O King."
Vaiśampāyana said:
