"We all, together with our ministers, have come to you for refuge.
Then Dharmarāja [beheld] him fallen upon the surface of the earth.
Having gazed upon the king together with his circle of kinsmen, he who perceives the world beyond— his anger extinguished and his grief and envy gone— spoke these words.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O King, you have no fear from me;
having reflected upon your mind, I appear to you in my true form."
This has been rightly accomplished by you here,
together with the twice-born ministers and like-minded scholars;
and this maiden is also most beautifully adorned.
"Having observed this, O best of kings, I am pleased. O mighty-armed monarch, I have forgiven what you have said to me; I perceive no fault whatsoever in you, O lord of men."
04,066.026d*1144_057 Vaiśampāyana said:
04,066.026d*1144_058 (21a) Then Virāṭa, being exceedingly pleased, 04,066.026d*1144_058 (21b) approached the king and made an agreement.
The high-souled Virāṭa bestowed his entire kingdom upon him—
the great-souled one— along with the scepter, the treasury,
and the city.

And whatever I shall say to you, do not doubt it, Yudhiṣṭhira. I shall bestow upon you this entire kingdom, together with its cities, its forests, and its women; I myself shall consume only the leftovers.
"O King, I am old and have long enjoyed pleasures and lived in happiness;
having given the kingdom to you all, I shall go forth into the forest.
Let Savyasācī Dhanañjaya accept the northern region."
"For this best of men is indeed a suitable husband for her.
Thus addressed, the King of Dharma (Yudhiṣṭhira) looked toward Pārtha Dhanañjaya;
and being looked at by his brother, Arjuna spoke these words to the King of Matsya.

"We have come from the depths of the forest; we do not take your kingdom, O King, but rather we take the kingdom of Duryodhana and the other kings. I myself, O King, accept your daughter-in-law as my daughter."
"For this alliance between us, O best of the Matsyas and Bhāratas, is indeed fitting.
Virāṭa said:
"O best of the Pāṇḍavas, for what purpose [do you seek] my daughter as a wife?"
"You do not wish to accept this girl, given by me here.
Arjuna said:
"I have always lived in the inner apartments, constantly seeing your daughter."
Whether in secret or in public, you trust me as if I were your father; I am dear to you and highly esteemed, for I am a skilled dancer and an expert in song,
and your daughter always regards me as her own teacher.
"O King, having lived for a year with her while she was still in the prime of youth,
it would be a matter of grave suspicion for you and for the world, O Lord.
Therefore, O Ruler of the Earth, I invite you [to accept my daughter]."

"Pure, with senses conquered and self-controlled—by him her purification has been performed. Whether it be a daughter-in-law, a daughter, a son, or even oneself, I see no cause for doubt in this matter; therefore, her purity shall be established."
"O scorcher of foes, fearing reproach and the practice of falsehood,
O King, I accept your daughter Uttarā as my daughter-in-law;
she is the sister’s son of Vāsudeva, like a divine child himself."
O lord of the people, my son Abhimanyu— the beloved of the wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu), mighty-armed, and skilled in weapons even while still a youth—
is indeed a worthy son-in-law for you and a fitting husband for your daughter.
Virāṭa said:
"It is fitting for Dhanañjaya, the son of Kuntī, the best of the Kurus—
that Pāṇḍava who is ever constant in dharma and possessed of born wisdom."
"O Pārtha, whatever you deem to be your duty, let that be performed immediately. All my desires are fulfilled, O Arjuna, since I have you as my kinsman.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When the lord of kings had spoken thus, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī,
gave his consent to the alliance between the Matsya king and the son of Pṛthā.
Then, O Bhārata, among all his friends and Vāsudeva as well—
The son of Kuntī and Virāṭa, the lord of the earth, sent word [to Arjuna],
who, having accepted [the proposal] for the sake of his daughter-in-law, demonstrated his own conduct; Phalguna then made known to the world his character, purity, and behavior.
Having proclaimed his greatness and fame throughout the world, that scorcher of foes,
Yudhiṣṭhira,
having accomplished his purpose, pure, undistracted, and contented, was then filled with satisfaction.
"O King, I am pleased; may prosperity be yours! You are my friend, O scorcher of foes.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O ruler of the earth, they have all dwelt happily with you, remaining unrecognized."
In the city of Virāṭa, the righteous king, firm in his vows,
was honored, consecrated, and provided with hundreds of jewels;
seeing him speaking thus, the king—
Greatly delighted by those kinsmen,
the king embraced him with both arms out of affection and bestowed that wealth upon the bulls among the Kurus.
For while the Kurus were traveling on the road after departing from the battle,
they all met together there and spoke only what was beneficial;
namely, the son of the preceptor, Śakuni, and the king.
O King, Duryodhana and Karṇa, the son of the Sūta, having consulted together, being capable and united,
all of them together dispatched a messenger.
And Yudhiṣṭhira, being greatly delighted,
saw a messenger arrive from Duryodhana;
and having approached, he spoke to the King of Dharma.
O Pārtha, you were exiled to the forest by Dhanañjaya against the will of Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Pāṇḍu of fierce valor; abide now by your agreement.
"For indeed, this son of the Pāṇḍavas, wearing his diadem and garlands, has been seen today after thirteen years. Then the son of Dharma laughed and said:
"Go quickly and speak to that Suyodhana:
'Let the Grandfather, the son of Śaṃtanu, speak; if today the thirteenth year of ours is indeed complete.'"
But at the end of the year, when Dhananjaya has stretched the Gandiva bow in the midst of battle,
let him say, "Is it full? Is it not full?"
"Whatever he said that was true, let that be my authority.
Having been addressed thus, the messenger returned and,
having reached Duryodhana, reported the truth of the matter.
Having met with the messenger,
Prince Duryodhana held counsel there with Bhīṣma, Karṇa, and Kṛpa.
Having deliberated at night with Droṇa, Bhūriśravas, and many friends,
the high-souled Bhīṣma spoke to the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
When those sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra heard that Dhananjaya had fulfilled his vow and had stretched the Gāṇḍīva bow in the midst of the battle, they [were struck with fear].
When Dhanañjaya had fulfilled his vow,
all the kings, having deliberated together with their friends, returned to their own homes.
Then, when the thirteenth year had passed, the five Pāṇḍavas settled themselves entirely at Upaplavya in the domain of Virāṭa,
dwelling there while being honored by Virāṭa and his sons.
The son of Kuntī and King Virāṭa dispatched messengers to all their allies, as well as to their kinsmen and relatives;
while residing there, Bībhatsu also brought Janārdana.
From the Ānartas [he went] to the Dāśārhas, and the Pāṇḍava [met] Abhimanyu;
then, taking Abhimanyu with him, accompanied by Rāma and surrounded by all the leaders of the Yādavas, that slayer of enemy heroes departed.

Amidst the sounding of conchs and kettledrums, he went to the city of Virāṭa. O lord of the earth, the King of Kāśī and Śaibya, both well-disposed toward Yudhiṣṭhira, arrived accompanied by two akṣauhiṇīs.
And the radiant Yajñasena, possessed of great strength,
accompanied by his sons of mighty prowess— Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Śikhaṇḍin—
those exceedingly powerful ones went swiftly to Upaplāvya for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas.
Then hundreds of thousands, millions,
and tens of millions of warriors advanced toward the army of Yudhiṣṭhira,
like the greatest rivers flowing separately toward the ocean at the end of the summer heat.
And the heroic sons of Draupadī, and the unconquered Śikhaṇḍin,
and the invincible Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the best among all wielders of weapons;
all these protectors of akṣauhiṇī divisions were performers of sacrifices who bestowed abundant sacrificial fees.
All were fully equipped with weapons and missiles; all were heroes ready to lay down their lives.
Seeing them arrived, Matsya, the best among the upholders of dharma, honored them according to the prescribed rites, along with their servants, troops, and mounts.
He was filled with joy after giving that daughter to Abhimanyu.
Then, as the kings returned from here and there,
Vāsudeva arrived there, wearing a forest garland and armed with a plow.
Those messengers, having arrived at Dvārakā and seen the Vṛṣṇi great-chariot warriors,
then spoke with joined palms there regarding the intention of the Pāṇḍavas.
At that time, Janārdana, having heard the words of the messengers, [acted accordingly].
Kṛtavarman, the son of Hṛdika, and Yuyudhāna Sātyaki; as well as Anādhṛṣṭi, Akrūra, Sāmba, and Niśaṭha— [all of whom were] highly honored, beloved sons of their own sisters and of Subhadrā.
Many other heroic kings, devoted to affection, also arrived;
some came out of fear, while others were well-wishers of the Pāṇḍavas.
Among them were the long-armed Pradyumna and the exceedingly powerful Ulmuka.
Taking Abhimanyu with them and accompanied by their mother, those subduers of enemies,
all the Pāṇḍavas together with Kṛṣṇa, arrived to see [the sons of] Pāṇḍu;
and Indrasena and the others likewise came on those well-prepared chariots.
Having stayed together for a full year, they all arrived at once:
ten thousand elephants, a hundred thousand horses,
a full hundred million chariots, and a billion foot soldiers.
Many Vṛṣṇis, Andhakas, and Bhojas of supreme prowess followed Vāsudeva, that tiger among the Vṛṣṇis and possessor of great splendor. Then,
seeing Vāsudeva approaching in that manner, the sons of Pāṇḍu—
Accompanied by Matsya, they all went out to meet Janārdana; with the sounds of conchs, drums, and auspicious instruments,
all the Pāṇḍavas joyfully paid homage at his feet.
All the Pāṇḍavas, together with the King of the Matsyas, were overwhelmed with tears of joy; indeed,
it was through your grace alone that all these years have passed for us in this manner.
O descendant of Daśārha, just as that agreement was made, so have we stayed for thirteen years, O Lord of the World; you are our protector, O Janārdana.
—Vaiśampāyana.
"Protect us, O Lord of the gods of gods; today we have come to you for refuge. Janārdana, surrounded by all the Yādavas, suddenly embraced those who were bowing down—those allies of Virāṭa.
Filled with supreme joy, he honored them according to their merit; and all those Vṛṣṇi heroes likewise received him with due respect. Then Kṛṣṇā likewise paid homage at the feet of the son of Devakī.
Lifting up that woman of beautiful hair and wiping her eyes, the Lord of Gods spoke these words in the presence of all the Yādavas:
"Do not grieve, O blessed lady; the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra have been brought under my control."

"Having soon caused him to be slain along with Pārtha, I shall give the earth to Yudhiṣṭhira; let the fever of your mind depart. I swear this to you by Abhimanyu, by Pārtha, and by the son of Rukmiṇī."

"O blameless one, understand these words of mine to be the truth. Having spoken thus and dismissed her, that tiger among the Vṛṣṇis, being well-pleased, then sat down beside Yudhiṣṭhira together with the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas.
When the time had passed, Kṛṣṇa gave to the high-souled Pāṇḍavas various gifts of dowry—
women, jewels, and garments— in great numbers and individually;
so too did the kings and princes at that time.
Honored as was fitting for the best of the Pāṇḍavas, they remained there with joyful minds and then presented him with wedding gifts. Vaiśampāyana said:
When they had assembled there, kings together with the Vṛṣṇis—
lords of men from various directions— arrived in great numbers at Virāṭa’s city, accompanied by elephants, horses, and chariot-warriors.
And indeed, many jewels produced in various lands,
as well as costly garments and heaps of gems,
and gold-worked cloth of diverse kinds, both fine and soft.
Divine ornaments variegated with jewels and gold,
as well as horses— some dappled like partridges, others white— in their entirety,
arrived for the sake of the marriage of the high-souled son of Subhadrā.
Resounding with auspicious sounds and the chanting of the Veda,
and filled with the Vedic *udgītha*, *sāman* chants, and the hymns of the celibate students (*brahmacārin*),
an altar adorned with every kind of jewel was constructed there.
The place was crowded on all sides with joyful and well-fed people, all dressed in white garments; singers from various lands had arrived there,
and Brāhmaṇas who had mastered the Vedas had gathered there from every direction.
Then the marriage between the Matsya king and the son of Pṛthā proceeded according to the prescribed rites.
Thereupon, conchs, kettledrums, trumpets,
and drums resounded in the palace of the Matsya king as he was being united with the sons of Pṛthā.
They slaughtered various kinds of wild animals and hundreds of sacrificial beasts;
they brought forth abundant drinks of *surā* and *maireya*. Furthermore, there were singers, storytellers, actors, and bards.
Praising them, the bards along with the *māgadhas* approached;
so too did the elderly women, the matrons, and those skilled in festive rites with auspicious offerings.
And in the inner apartments of Virāṭa’s palace, the women gathered around Draupadī.
Placing Sudeṣṇā at their head, the most excellent women of the Matsyas arrived— women whose every limb was beautiful, wearing polished jeweled earrings;
those ladies were endowed with fine complexion, possessed of beauty, and well-adorned.
And Kṛṣṇā surpassed them all in beauty, fame, and splendor;
surrounding the princess Uttarā, who was richly adorned,
they stood before her as if honoring the daughter of Mahendra.

There, Dhaumya, the learned priest of the Pāṇḍavas, having established the fire according to the rites with the great ṛṣis, offered oblations in accordance with the rules. Then, taking up a golden water-pitcher filled with water—
Virāṭa, the commander of the army, suddenly placed that lotus-eyed woman into the hands of Pārtha at the gate to be his daughter-in-law;
Dhanañjaya, the son of Kuntī, accepted her for the sake of his son.
Then,
assuming the form of Indra, the great king Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī, stood there and received that daughter of Virāṭa, the faultless-limbed daughter-in-law of the son of Subhadrā.
Drupada, Virāṭa, and the highly illustrious Śikhaṇḍin;
the King of Kāśī, Śaibya, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, and Sātyaki—
these seven were commanders of akṣauhiṇīs, performers of sacrifices, and givers of abundant sacrificial fees.
Having surrounded the Pāṇḍava, they all then established their camp.
And having received her, Pārtha, placing Janārdana at the forefront,
caused the marriage of the high-souled son of Subhadrā to be performed.
Dhaumya, surrounded by his disciples like the sun with its rays, was there;
then the wedding proceeded, prosperous, endowed with every excellence,
and wonderful for the son of Subhadrā and for your father’s father.
Dhaumya, surrounded by his disciples, offered oblations into the fire according to the prescribed rites.
As he circumambulated the fire, the son of Subhadrā took her hand.
Then the King of Matsya, greatly rejoiced, bestowed vast wealth upon the son of Pṛthā.
To him, the delighted Lord of Matsya then gave seven thousand horses with the speed of the wind, two hundred preeminent elephants, and much wealth as an unsurpassed dowry for his daughters.
The bull among the Matsyas bestowed a dowry upon the son of Pṛthā,
which the son of Kuntī accepted in abundance along with Kṛṣṇa.
Having properly offered oblations into the kindled fire and honored the twice-born, he [proceeded].

Then Virāṭa, filled with joy, offered his kingdom, his army, his treasury, and even his very self to the Pāṇḍavas. This occurred after the marriage had been performed, at which time Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, was present.
The infallible one gave to the Brahmins all the wealth he had brought:
thousands of cows, jewels, various garments,
excellent ornaments, vehicles, and beds.
The king gave many variegated silk garments and numerous male and female servants;
he gratified the citizens with divine delights and provided them with heart-pleasing foods and various kinds of drinks.
O bull of the Bharatas, that city of the King of the Matsyas, filled with joyful and well-fed people and resembling a great festival, shone brightly,
crowded with priests, ministers, citizens, and even those from the countryside.
The illustrious King Virāṭa,
having given his daughter Uttarā to Abhimanyu, the son of Subhadrā, then rejoiced exceedingly.
When the marriage of the son of Pṛthā’s son had thus taken place, O scorcher of foes.
Then the sons of Pāṇḍu dwelt outside the city at Upaplāvya.
Janamejaya,
[having heard] what Yudhiṣṭhira, with a joyful heart, said when the wedding was completed.
Tell us all here what they did as their subsequent response.
This is the description of the extensive fourth book, the Vairāṭa Parvan;
herein, the number of chapters has been counted by the Great-Souled One.
Furthermore, hear from me that the number of verses is exactly sixty-seven;
two thousand and three hundred verses have been declared in this Parvan by the supreme seer.
In the Virāṭa Parva, various garments were to be given;
having performed the wedding of Abhimanyu, the partisans of that joyful hero, the foremost of the Kurus, then rejoiced.
Having rested for four mornings,
they then proceeded to the assembly hall of Virāṭa.
